The quotation appearing on pages 408 and 409 should read as follows:

> He is an excellent man in all respects and will most certainly be very helpful. He is at present in Hamburg with Lenz, but he was until recently in Göttingen where he has calculated on various problems together with Born: among other things, they have solved the problem of the helium orbits, and they have in all details verified our results, which I had outlined to Born in Berlin. Pauli has now carried through the calculations of $\mathrm{H}_{2}^{+}$, and his results, which I do not know in detail, will very soon appear in Ann. d. Phys. He would now like to try his hand on the helium atom, and is, I believe, at the moment busy looking at it by a method different from that used by you. He emphasized strongly that he was doing it only for his pleasure and that he, of course, would not publish anything before you have published your results. I have thought that perhaps it wouldn’t be amiss if you would think of writing a little note about it this summer. Also, we cannot wait much longer with publishing our calculations of the helium orbits. I am looking forward to discussing all this with you when you get home. (Bohr to Kramers, 15 July 1922)

# Chapter IV
## The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

The year 1922 brought the greatest triumph of the theory of atomic structure, which had been initiated by Niels Bohr about ten years earlier. The triumph did not last long; within a few months it was confronted by the discovery of serious and fundamental defects of the theory. The first of these defects to be noticed explicitly was the complete failure of the calculation of the energy states of the two-electron atom. Towards the end of 1922 and in early 1923 several people reached the same conclusion: the observed terms of the helium atom could not be represented at all by the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, unless one introduced drastic changes in its very foundations. Similar conclusions were reached in the case of other few-body systems, such as the hydrogen molecule or the corresponding $\text{H}_2^+$-ion. Simultaneously with these negative experiences the quantum physicists investigated more closely certain puzzling experimental facts connected with the magnetic properties of atoms: the anomalous Zeeman effects, known since 1897, and the Stern–Gerlach effect, discovered in 1922. These effects, in one way or another, did not fit into the available scheme of atomic theory, which was based on the validity of classical dynamics supplemented by certain quantum conditions. Another unexplained feature had sneaked into the consciousness of physicists without assuming the aspect of a novelty: by 1920 it had been demonstrated that the gyromagnetic ratio (i.e., the ratio of magnetic moment and the angular momentum) of metal electrons was twice as large as derived from classical electrodynamics. This magnetic anomaly seemed to be connected with the anomalous Zeeman effect, which had been treated since 1920 by several physicists, notably by Arnold Sommerfeld and Alfred Landé. By the end of 1922 Landé had found a reasonable description of the observed separation of doublet and triplet spectra by external magnetic fields. Then the detailed analysis of the spectra of many-electron atoms led to the establishment of much larger multiplicities than two- or three-component lines. These splittings, together with the corresponding Zeeman effects, could be described by an extension of Landé’s previous formulae. The question now arose about deriving the successful description of complex multiplets from the principles of atomic theory. However, a serious attempt in this direction revealed another failure of the existing quantum theory of atomic structure. The last discouraging result was obtained by Wolfgang Pauli, one of the ablest and most devoted physicists of the younger generation. Hailing from Vienna, he received his education at Sommerfeld’s Institute in Munich, from where he went on to Göttingen, Hamburg and Copenhagen. Pauli, in whose doctoral thesis of 1921 on the hydrogen molecule-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0008 -->

376 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

ion was recognized the first sign of a breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic theory, became, through the brilliance and rigour of his methods and the sincere honesty of his physical thinking, one of the leading personalities in the dismantling of the old and the preparation for the new quantum theory. Pascual Jordan, one of the participants in the erection of the new theory, would later describe Pauli’s role as follows:

> The importance and range of his influence on the further development of the pioneering ideas and discoveries of Planck, Einstein and Bohr can hardly be understood and estimated by those, who will later investigate the intellectual history of this century, to the same extent as by Pauli’s contemporaries, who were in a position to observe and witness themselves his central role in the intellectual development of physical research in our century. For his contributions to this intellectual development did not only consist of the papers and books that became renowned later on. By having personal exchange of thoughts with numerous physicists of his time, he exerted in discussions and through the many letters written by himself an excitation and stimulation which can hardly be measured. For us living today, the far-off time of the previous centuries—in which the intellectual life of Europe was carried on to a large extent by the exchange of letters among scholars—seemed to be renewed somehow, when Pauli was among us physicists.
> (Jordan, 1971, p. 30)^631

We shall first present the background and early scientific work of Wolfgang Pauli before going on to deal, in the following sections of this chapter, with the more important mechanical and spectroscopic failures of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure.

## IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work

Wolfgang Pauli, or Wolfgang Pauli junior—as he called himself until 1928—was born on 25 April 1900 at Vienna. His father, Wolfgang Joseph Pauli, had come from Prague and had embarked upon his academic career in 1898 as *Privatdozent* in the department of medicine at the University of Vienna. Seven years later he became extraordinary professor and in 1922 he would be appointed full professor and director of the new institute of medical colloid chemistry.^632 Vienna, at the turn of the century, was not only the capital of the large Austro-Hungarian

^631 Pauli’s scientific correspondence of the years from 1919 to 1929 has meanwhile been published, edited by Armin Hermann, K. von Meyenn and Victor F. Weisskopf (Pauli, 1979). We shall make use of this rich source of original information whenever necessary in this work.
^632 In 1938, Wolfgang Pauli *senior* joined his son in Zurich, where he died on 4 November 1955. He belonged, together with Richard Adolf Zsigmondy (1865–1929) and Wolfgang Ostwald (1883–1943)—the son of Wilhelm Ostwald—among the founders of colloid chemistry. He concerned himself especially with devising appropriate mechanisms for life functions.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0009 -->

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli's Background and Early Scientific Work 377

Empire, but also a centre of an active and flourishing culture. This applied not just to the fine arts, in which the city had been distinguished since long, and which now were represented by such extraordinary personalities as the painter Gustav Klimt, the architects Otto Wagner, Adolf Loos, Joseph Maria Olbrich and Josef Hoffmann, and the composer Gustav Mahler, then director of the famous *Vienna Hofoper*. At the same time Arthur Schnitzler and Hugo von Hofmannsthal created their poetic works in Vienna. Science also prospered and scientists of worldwide reputation taught at the University of Vienna: Sigmund Freud (since 1902) in medicine, Ludwig Boltzmann in physics and Ernst Mach in philosophy. Mach, who was a friend of Pauli's father—he would thank the latter (in 1905) in the preface of this book *Erkenntnis und Irrtum* for reading the proofs—became Pauli's godfather. More than fifty years later Wolfgang Pauli gave the following account:

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;... Among my books there is a somewhat dusty case; it contains a silver cup made in the *art nouveau* style (*Jugendstil*) and in it there is a card ... This cup is a baptismal cup, and on the card is written in old-fashioned, adorned letters: "Dr. E. Mach, Professor at the University of Vienna." It so happened that my father was a close friend of his family, and at that time he was intellectually under his [Mach's] complete influence. And he (Mach) had kindly agreed to assume the role of my godfather ... He must have been a stronger personality than the Catholic priest, for the result seems to be that I was baptized in this way to [become more] anti-metaphysical than Catholic. In any case, the card remains in the cup and, in spite of my major intellectual transformations in later times, it remains a label which I carry with me, namely: "of anti-metaphysical origin." In fact Mach considered metaphysics, to put it simply, as the source of all evil on earth—psychologically speaking, as the very devil—and that cup with the card in it remained the symbol of "*aqua permanens*" [holy water], which drives away the evil metaphysical spirits. ... ^633

One may indeed say that Mach exerted some influence on the young Pauli, who possessed several of his godfather's books in his library (some presented to him by Mach with a proper dedication). Mach also advised Pauli's father in matters concerning his son's scientific education.^634 The results of Mach's influence could be seen—apart from Pauli's hostility towards metaphysical speculation—in his

---
^633 This is from a letter of Pauli, dated 31 March 1953, which was quoted by Charles P. Enz in his article on Pauli's scientific work (Enz, 1973, p. 766, and footnote 2 on p. 792).
Although Wolfgang Joseph Pauli was of Jewish origin, he had converted to the Catholic religion. So his son grew up without knowing anything about his family's Jewish background. When, after his arrival in Munich, Paul Ewald mentioned to him that there was no doubt about his being a Jew, he replied: 'I? No. Nobody has ever told me that and I don't believe I am' (Ewald, AHQP Interview, 8 May 1962, p. 15). Ewald then asked him to look in a mirror and recognize that he was a proper Jewish type, which he did. On returning home for the next vacation, Pauli inquired from his family about their background; they confirmed Ewald's opinion.

^634 There exists a letter from Mach to Wolfgang Joseph Pauli, dated 12 January 1914, which contained such advice. (See Pauli, 1979, p. 11.)

    Pauli grew up in a bourgeois family with a strong intellectual background.636 At a young age he showed a gift for learning and concerned himself especially with mathematics and physics. Since the usual things taught at school in these fields did not satisfy him, he took lessons in them from Hans Adolf Bauer, then at the physics institute of the *Technische Hochschule* in Vienna.637 In July 1918 Wolfgang Pauli graduated from the humanistic section of the *Döblinger Gymnasium* with a class of 25 boys, out of which came two later Nobel prize winners (besides Pauli, the chemist Richard Kuhn), two famous actors (one being Hans Thimig), three university professors, two directors of medical schools, a music historian, a politician and several industrialists. He decided to leave Vienna, which he found to be a ‘spiritual desert’ (‘*geistige Einöde*,’ Enz, 1973, p. 767), and to pursue his studies of theoretical physics at the University of Munich under the guidance of Arnold Sommerfeld.
    In 1918, towards the end of World War I, much of the previous splendour of Vienna had faded away. The Austro-Hungarian Empire was about to disintegrate. Political changes took place which led to the establishment of the Republic of Austria, consisting solely of German-speaking parts (except those in some regions of Bohemia and Moravia) and governed by a coalition of parties under the socialist Karl Renner. Though Pauli never became involved in politics, his sympathies were not on the side of political revolutions.638 But these events could

<div style="margin-top: 2em;"></div>

635 Pauli, however, never adhered to the philosophical positivism or the logical empiricism of the so-called Vienna school, founded in the early 1920s by Moritz Schlick, Rudolf Carnap, Hans Hahn and others. This group of philosophers and mathematicians (who based their thinking on the ideas of Ernst Mach, Pierre Duhem and Henri Poincaré, and also came under the influence of Bertrand Russell and his Viennese student Ludwig Wittgenstein) shared a strong hostility towards metaphysics, a radical empiricist approach and a great faith in modern symbolic logic.

636 The family life of the Pauli’s was harmonious. During the years of his study in Munich and afterwards Wolfgang Pauli went home regularly for extended Christmas vacations. After his retirement from Vienna, Wolfgang Joseph Pauli moved to Zurich to be close to his son.
    Wolfgang Pauli had a younger sister, Hertha. ‘She was born when Wolfgang already was a schoolboy and, since he was rather used to being the only child in the family, he did not regard her as an entirely blessed event. Hertha improved in his eyes, however, as she grew older and could be taught things. Eventually he became very fond of his redheaded sister, who loved to tease him’ (Cline, 1965, p. 136). Later on, Hertha became a writer, but before that she acted on the German stage for several years. ‘This pleased Pauli, for he loved the theater; and he bragged about his sister to his friends. He liked to visit her after a performance, welcoming this opportunity to meet other actresses’ (Cline, 1965, p. 137). Pauli’s first wife, Kate, *née* Deppner, whom he married in Zurich in the late 1920s, was an actress trained in the *Reinhardtschule* of film and theatre arts; she later married the chemist Paul Goldfinger.

637 H. A. Bauer was born in Vienna on 25 March 1891. He later became *Privatdozent* (in 1925) and extraordinary professor of theoretical physics (in 1937) at the *Technische Hochschule*, Vienna. Bauer published papers on relativity theory and wave mechanics. On both subjects he wrote books (Bauer, 1922, 1938). Bauer died on 28 August 1953 at Kartitsch, Austria. (We owe the reference to the private lessons from Bauer to Paul Urban’s obituary of Pauli: Urban, 1959.)

638 Once, when, on the occasion of Empress Zita’s birthday, the majority of his classmates planned to read *Die Arbeiter-Zeitung* (i.e., the socialist newspaper) demonstratively during mass, he asked the family’s girl cook to write a letter of vigorous protest to the school director. (See Enz, 1973, p. 767.)

**IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli's Background and Early Scientific Work** 379

not have been the real reason why he called Vienna a spiritual desert. Rather, he had in mind the peculiar situation in theoretical physics at the academic institutions of the city. Both the University of Vienna and the *Technische Hochschule* lacked personalities who could attract Pauli. Friedrich Hasenöehrl, Boltzmann’s former student and successor at the University, had died on 7 October 1917, and theoretical physics was represented by the junior people like Erwin Schrödinger, Ludwig Flamm, Friedrich Kottler and Hans Thirring. At the *Technische Hochschule*, on the other hand, Heinrich Mache, also a former student of Boltzmann’s, was professor of experimental and theoretical physics. Arnold Sommerfeld, who had made important contributions to many modern aspects of theoretical physics and who had already trained numerous excellent physicists, seemed to be a more attractive teacher. Furthermore, he was considered an expert on relativity theory, a subject in which Pauli had been deeply interested for several years.639 Sommerfeld had only recently declined the offer to become Hasenöehrl’s successor at the University of Vienna. Since Sommerfeld had not come to Vienna, Pauli had to go to Munich.640

In October 1918 Wolfgang Pauli enrolled in the philosophical faculty of the University of Munich in order to study physics. He immediately became a member of the Institute for Theoretical Physics and began to attend Sommerfeld’s advanced courses of lectures on thermodynamics and kinetic gas theory as well as the special course on atomic physics and spectral lines. The following semester he attended Sommerfeld’s lectures on partial differential equations of physics and the special course on relativity theory. While the theoretical lectures constituted the principal part of his education, Pauli also took courses on experimental physics, mathematics and chemistry, which were required of a regular physics student. Besides, he attended the lectures of Wilhelm Lenz and of Peter Paul Ewald (on crystal dynamics), both of whom were members of Sommerfeld’s Institute. When Pauli enrolled in a course, it did not imply that he regularly went to classes. He learned many things by reading and attended only those courses which he absolutely needed. Thus he took the laboratory course in

639 Since 1907 Sommerfeld had published a large number of papers on various aspects of relativity and electron theory. He was also interested in preparing a new (third) edition of original papers on ‘*Das Relativitätsprinzip*’ (first edition by Otto Blumenthal in 1913: Lorentz, Einstein and Minkowski, 1913), including the papers on general relativity as well. This edition, with Sommerfeld’s introductory comments, finally appeared in 1920.

640 The question arises whether Pauli knew Sommerfeld personally before he went to Munich. About such a possibility Pascual Jordan reported later:
Only after Pauli’s death did I hear a story about his youth. I do not know whether it is exactly correct, but I regard it as credible and possible. According to it the twelve-year-old Pauli had once asked to be permitted to attend a lecture of Professor Sommerfeld on theoretical physics. Sommerfeld asked afterwards whether he had understood the lecture. “Yes,” replied young Pauli, “except what you have written on the upper left side [of the blackboard].” Sommerfeld looked up again at the blackboard, and then said: “There I have indeed made a mistake.”
(Jordan, 1971, p. 33)
This story may well be apocryphal. However, it is very likely that Pauli had heard Sommerfeld’s name some years before he met him personally. For instance, in connection with his call to the chair of theoretical physics at the University of Vienna, Sommerfeld’s personality and merits were certainly discussed in academic circles, to which Pauli’s father belonged.

Wilhelm Wien's Experimental Institute with his 'fellow sufferer' (*Leidensgenosse*) Otto Laporte, another student of Sommerfeld's (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 29 September 1924). Otherwise he preferred to concentrate on the active life at the Institute for Theoretical Physics, participating in the daily discussions of the intimate circle of Sommerfeld's scientific collaborators. These discussions were centered around the problems of atomic theory, and Pauli—through his quick understanding of problems, his deep knowledge of the literature, and his independent work on several problems—became a prominent contributor. Within a short time it was his advice that was requested by the other students and members of the Institute.

Pauli had not come to Munich as a normal student. Sommerfeld immediately realized that he was 'already in the full possession of [the knowledge of] the methods of mathematics and mathematical physics.' Moreover, 'He brought with him a finished paper on general relativity theory, which immediately aroused Einstein's interest and admiration.' (See Pauli, 1979, p. 1.) In this paper, which Pauli submitted to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* from Vienna in September 1918 and which was published in the issue of 15 January 1919, he discussed the energy components of the gravitational field (Pauli, 1919a). This problem was frequently treated in those days. For example, Erwin Schrödinger, then lecturer at the University of Vienna, had discussed it in a paper which had appeared earlier in 1918 in the same journal; he had come to the somewhat bewildering conclusion that real gravitational fields (which could not be transformed away) led to vanishing components of the energy-momentum tensor in finite regions (Schrödinger, 1918). Hans Bauer, Pauli's private tutor in mathematics and physics, had also contributed a paper on the same problem, published in *Physikalische Zeitschrift*: he had not only confirmed Schrödinger's result but also had shown that the energy-momentum tensor might have finite components, even when there was no gravitational field around (Bauer, 1918). Pauli then took up the problem of calculating the components of the energy-momentum tensor in a space with a general metrical tensor; he found, for example, that his result did not agree—in the case of small deviations from the flat metric—with Einstein's earlier calculations and he therefore concluded: 'In the latter case the energy components do not turn out to be uniquely determined' (Pauli, 1919a, p. 27). Although this result was not particularly surprising in the light of previous work, it provided the most general proof for a familiar situation. Pauli presented his work in December 1918 in a seminar at Sommerfeld's Institute. Besides receiving Einstein's approval, Pauli's paper established his reputation as an expert on relativity theory.

In Munich, Pauli continued to work on problems of general relativity and obtained an extension of Einstein's theory. Hermann Weyl had proposed this extension in a paper, entitled *'Gravitation und Elektrizität'* ('Gravitation and Electricity') and communicated to the Prussian Academy by Einstein on 2 May 1918 (Weyl, 1918a). He had started from the idea of a genuine infinitesimal geometry, in which lengths could be compared only when associated with two infinitesimally neighbouring points; thus he had arrived at a description, which

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0015 -->

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work  
381

‘when applied to the universe, surprisingly does *not only explain the phenomena of gravitation, but also those of the electromagnetic field*’ (Weyl, 1918a, p. 467). Pauli studied Weyl’s paper and wrote him a letter, asking several questions. Weyl replied: ‘I am extremely pleased to welcome you as a collaborator. However, I find it almost impossible to understand how you, being so young, managed to acquire the means of knowing and the intellectual freedom [necessary to understand relativity theory fully]’ (Weyl to Pauli, 10 May 1919). He then tried to answer Pauli’s question on the definition of the electric current and the energy-momentum tensor in his theory by referring to the forthcoming third edition of his book *Raum-Zeit-Materie*; further, he drew attention to a paper, which was to appear soon in *Annalen der Physik*, where he had treated the physical consequences of his theory, in particular the ones related to the electron (Weyl, 1919). However, Weyl encouraged Pauli to publish his questions and results independently and closed his letter with the remarks: ‘I would be very happy if the course of your studies will once lead you to Zurich. In case you would already now wish to come to Switzerland, then I don’t think it would be very difficult to obtain an entry visa for you from here’ (Weyl to Pauli, 10 May 1919).

Pauli was not able to take up this invitation. However, he was happy about Weyl’s friendly response, and during 1919 he published two papers on the consequences of Weyl’s theory. In the first, submitted to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* in June 1919 and published in the issue of 15 October, he discussed the physical consequences of the theory, which lay as he argued ‘still very much in the dark’ (‘*noch sehr im Dunkeln*,’ Pauli, 1919b, p. 458). After a detailed exposition of mathematical methods (‘*mathematische Hilfsbetrachtungen*’), motivated by the fact that ‘in the case of such a recent theory as Weyl’s the tools have first to be forged with which the solution of its problems can be attacked’ (Pauli, 1919b, p. 460), Pauli turned to his main problem: the definition of the electric current and the investigation of its properties. From a fundamental action principle, involving a special action function, he derived the equation for a current. From it Pauli concluded that if the charge density at one space point in the universe is different from zero, the universe must be a closed one. Next Pauli drew attention to a crucial fact in Weyl’s theory: ‘*The differential equations for the static field are symmetric with respect to positive and negative electricity*’; hence, ‘as long as no totally new principle is introduced into the theory, one can never hope to find an explanation for the difference between the masses of atomic nuclei and electrons’ (Pauli, 1919b, p. 462). Evidently, Pauli had hoped that on the basis of a fundamental theory, such as Weyl’s, one should be able to explain the existing difference in the masses of positively and negatively charged particles.<sup>641</sup> Finally, he attempted to obtain from the theory static, spherically symmetric solutions for describing the electron.

<sup>641</sup>Pauli had mentioned the conclusion about the charge symmetry of the theory already in his letter to Weyl in spring 1919. In his reply, Weyl had suggested a way out: ‘The inequality [of the two kinds] of electricity had therefore to be reduced to the inequality of past and future, although the latter does not occur explicitly in the “world laws”’ (Weyl to Pauli, 10 May 1919). Pauli took note of Weyl’s argument (Pauli, 1919b, p. 462, footnote 2).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0016 -->

382    Chapter IV    The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

The reason, why Weyl's theory attracted Pauli, was evidently the following: it seemed to provide 'the possibility to explain and to understand the existence of the electron' (Pauli, 1919b, p. 461). Pauli believed that the problem of the electron was one of the most fundamental problems of physics, and he decided to make it the centre of his early work.$^{642}$ Thus he returned to it in a second paper on Weyl's theory, submitted to the *Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft* in November 1919 and published shortly afterwards (Pauli, 1919c).$^{643}$ He devoted the main part of this article to showing, by explicit calculation, that in Weyl's theory the same results followed for the motion of the perihelion of Mercury and the deflection of light as in Einstein's theory. '*Accordingly it is evident*,' he concluded, '*that from observations of the motion of Mercury and of the deflection of light rays, which agree with the field equations of Einstein, no argument can ever be inferred against Weyl's theory*' (Pauli, 1919c, p. 748). Then, in the last part of his paper, he listed several difficulties of the theory. In particular, he repeated his earlier argument, namely, 'that the theory cannot describe in a satisfactory manner the asymmetry of both types of electricity' (Pauli, 1919c, p. 749). And he added a further 'physical-conceptual reservation,' which he formulated in the following way:

> In Weyl's theory one operates constantly with the field strength in the interior of the electron. For the physicist, however, this quantity is defined only as a force acting on a test-body; and, since there exist no smaller test-bodies than the electron itself, the concept of an electric field strength in a mathematical point appears to be an empty, meaningless fiction. In physics, one would like to stick to introducing only those quantities which can, in principle, be observed. Might we not altogether be on the wrong track in considering *continuum theories* for the field in the interior of the electron? (Pauli, 1919c, p. 750)

Pauli's last remark concerning the difficulty of the continuum assumption when applied to the interior of the electron appears to have been in the spirit of Ernst Mach's thinking: the principle of the economy of thought indeed forbade the use of concepts in physics, which could not, at least in principle, be observed. It elicited an immediate response from Hermann Weyl. In a letter to Pauli, dated 9 December 1919, he argued that the fields in the interior of an electron might still have physical significance; they could perhaps provide the reason why an electron in a Bohr orbit (in an atom) does not radiate. On the other hand, he agreed with respect to the limitation of applying the continuum hypothesis in physics. He wrote:

> Field physics, I believe, really plays only the role of "world geometry." In matter there is hidden still something else, something real, which cannot be understood in a

$^{643}$ Already in 1919 Wolfgang Pauli became a member of the German Physical Society. (See *Verh. d. Deutsch. Phys. Ges.* **21**, 797 (1919).) He was erroneously referred to as 'Dr.' at that time; he took his doctorate in 1921.

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 383

causal manner, but may perhaps be thought of according to the picture of "independent decisions," which is described in physics by statistical methods. It may indeed be possible that we shall have to let this [other feature] decide about the difference between past and future, between positive and negative electricity; the latter difference therefore finds no place in field physics. These are only *hints*, the exact discussion of which would take too much space. (Weyl to Pauli, 9 December 1919)

While Weyl reacted open-mindedly, Einstein raised objections to giving up the continuum description in physics. ‘How should one describe without the continuum the problem of $n$ points,’ he asked in a letter to Born, and added: ‘Pauli’s objection is directed not only against Weyl’s, but also against everyone else’s continuum theory. Even against one which treats the electron as a singularity’ (Einstein to Born, 27 January 1920). Several months later Pauli had the occasion to ask Einstein personally about his opinion. In the discussion following Hermann Weyl’s talk on ‘*Elektrizität und Gravitation*’ (‘Electricity and Gravitation’) at the 86th *Naturforscherversammlung* at Bad Nauheim in September 1920, Pauli drew attention to the problem again. He remarked as follows:

None of the erstwhile theories of the electron has succeeded so far in solving the problem of the elementary electric quanta satisfactorily, and it is natural to search for a deeper reason for this failure. I now wish to seek this reason in the fact that it is not allowed at all anymore to describe the electric field in the interior of the electron as a continuous function in space. The electric field strength is defined as the force on a charged test-body and, if there exist no smaller test-bodies than the electron ... , the concept of the electric field strength in a certain space point in the interior of the electron—with which all continuum theories operate—appears to be an empty, meaningless fiction, to which there corresponds nothing real. (Pauli, in Weyl, 1920, p. 650)

Pauli then asked Einstein, who was present at the discussion, whether he agreed with or was opposed to this view. Einstein avoided a clear answer; he said that in general the concepts in physics had the tendency to become more and more complex and that indeed the question arose whether one should abolish the existing concepts of spatial and temporal distances. ‘The answer,’ he remarked, ‘can be given in my opinion only on the basis of what is functional; what it will be seems to me to be uncertain’ (Einstein, in Weyl, 1920, p. 651).

With his three papers Pauli became widely known as an original contributor to the most advanced problems of general relativity theory and its extensions. Hans Thirring, then *Privatdozent* at the University of Vienna, who had himself written on general relativity, recalled the following story about Pauli’s abilities. He and Pauli met in Vienna during semester vacations, and Pauli suggested an extension of an earlier calculation of Thirring’s on rotating bodies in general relativity. Thirring reported: ‘We sat down, each by himself at a table, and continued to calculate until our heads burned (*uns die Köpfe rauchten*). We both arrived at the same result, just with the difference that he attacked the problem

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0018 -->

384 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

much more elegantly and skillfully and, therefore, finished it much earlier than I. Seldom have I recognized the ingenious superiority of a colleague so clearly as in the meeting with the then twenty-year-old student Pauli’ (Thirring, quoted in Richter, 1979, p. 13).

Pauli’s familiarity with relativity theory, his command of the most difficult mathematical methods and his wide knowledge of scientific literature persuaded Sommerfeld to assign him an important task: namely, to write the review article on relativity theory for the *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften*. The project for such an article had already existed for some time, and Sommerfeld—who was responsible for editing the fifth volume of the *Encyklopädie* containing the articles on physics—had hoped to win Einstein for the writing. After Einstein declined, the task fell upon Sommerfeld himself; but being burdened with a lot of other work and having Pauli available, he proposed to Pauli that they write the article together. Pauli immediately started to work. ‘But when he showed me the first draft of his essay,’ recalled Sommerfeld, ‘it proved to be so masterly that I renounced all collaboration’ (Sommerfeld, 1949, p. 315).<sup>644</sup> The work on the review article on relativity theory brought Pauli in contact with Willem de Sitter—whom he asked for papers on the cosmological aspects of relativity theory (see de Sitter to Pauli, 25 May 1920)—and especially with Felix Klein, the general editor of the *Encyklopädie*. Klein checked Pauli’s manuscript carefully and suggested in several letters a series of improvements (Klein to Pauli, 8 March, 28 April, 7 May, 8 May 1921). Thus he advised Pauli to take note of certain details of the historical developments: for instance, that Henri Poincaré had obtained his results on electrodynamics in 1905 independently of Einstein, and that in 1915 Hilbert and Einstein had arrived simultaneously at the equations of the gravitational field. Second, he insisted on a clear presentation of things also for nonexperts in relativity; he urged Pauli to avoid or explain properly the use of such phrases as ‘relativistic mechanics.’ Finally, Klein suggested to Pauli to present Einstein’s theory not as the final answer to all problems, but only as the result that had been achieved up to that time. He wrote: ‘In any case, if one takes as a basis the totality of all canonical substitutions (as proposed in the Erlangen programme [Klein, 1872]), then one has a point of view which far surpasses Einstein’s relativity theory’ (Klein to Pauli, 8 May 1921).

At the end of his encyclopedia article on relativity, Pauli noted: ‘Completed in December 1920’ (Pauli, 1921b, p. 775). However, Felix Klein did not receive the manuscript until March 1921 (see Klein to Sommerfeld, 8 March 1921). It went immediately into printing, and Pauli added certain improvements in proof during

<sup>644</sup>The decision that Pauli should write the article alone was already made in spring 1920. In a letter to the mathematician Samuel Oppenheim of Vienna, who edited Volume VI of the *Encyklopädie* (containing the articles on astronomy), Pauli gave a detailed outline of the points he was going to discuss in the article on relativity theory (Pauli to Oppenheim, 7 May 1920); there he spoke only of his own plans of work. Oppenheim was interested in Pauli’s outline, for in the volume which he was editing Friedrich Kottler contributed an article on gravitation and relativity theory (Kottler, 1922); Oppenheim wanted to make sure that the authors would arrange their respective treatments appropriately.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0019 -->

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 385

the months of April and May. The article was finally published in September 1921, forming the major part of issue No. 4 of the second part of Volume V of the *Encyklopädie*. In it Pauli treated all aspects of the theory of relativity in five parts, containing 67 sections in 237 pages: in part I he formulated the foundations of special relativity; in part II he described the mathematical tools of special and general relativity; in part III he discussed the various Lorentz invariant theories (i.e., the so-called relativistic kinematics, electrodynamics, mechanics, thermodynamics and statistical mechanics); in part IV he introduced general relativity theory, including its cosmological consequences; and in part V he presented the generalized field theories of the electron (such as Gustav Mie’s, Hermann Weyl’s and Albert Einstein’s).$^{645}$ Pauli’s article satisfied Sommerfeld very much, and he summarized his impression in a letter to Einstein, dated 14 March 1921, with the words: ‘simply masterly, especially for a student in [his] fifth semester.’ He also arranged the publication of the article as a separate book, for which he wrote in the preface:

> In view of the apparently inexhaustible demand for presentations of the relativity theory, popular as well as highly technical, which exists especially in Germany, I decided to advise the publisher to make a special edition of the admirable article, which Mr. W. Pauli jr. had written for Volume V of the *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften*. Though he was then still a student, Mr. Pauli not only knew the most subtle lines of thought in relativity theory from his own investigations, but was also completely familiar with the literature of the subject. (Sommerfeld, in Pauli, 1921b, p. III)

Not only did Sommerfeld praise his student highly, the same was done by Max Born, one of the foremost experts on relativity, and by Erwin Schrödinger. Schrödinger, while thanking Pauli for a reprint of his article, confessed:

> About the scientific content of your article I don't dare to judge, because in that respect you put me ten times in the sack (‘stecken Sie mich ja zehnmal in den Sack’ [outdo me ten times]). (Besides: By the way, [it is] a nice idea to imagine how Pauli puts ten Schrödingers into the sack! Don't you know a well-known cartoonist who could draw that?) However, what I may say is that I find your arrangement of the material very good from the didactic point of view: namely, that you first prepare all the mathematical tools without reference to any physical theory in order that the difficulties of one kind do not mix with those of the other kind; further, that you treat the tensor spook, which is new to many readers, as much *before* the Riemannian extension of the concept of space as possible, so that one sees exactly what in it [the Riemannian extension] is only *apparently* and what is *really* complicated—with the latter I just mean [the complication] which occurs first in a continuum with a variable metric. (Schrödinger to Pauli, 7 November 1921)

$^{645}$ In contrast to the final version, the original outline (which Pauli had sent to Samuel Oppenheim in his letter of 7 May 1920) contained seven chapters, for Pauli had planned to have three chapters on the theory of general relativity (one on foundations, one on the equations of gravitation, and one on cosmology).

**Chapter IV**  
**The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models**

However, Pauli received the most valuable appraisal of his article from Albert Einstein, who opened his review of it in the *Naturwissenschaften* by saying:

> No one studying this mature, grandly conceived work would believe that the author is a man of twenty-one. One wonders what to admire most, the psychological understanding for the development of ideas, the sureness of mathematical deduction, the profound physical insight, the capacity for lucid, systematic presentation, the knowledge of the literature, the complete treatment of the subject matters and the sureness of the critical discussion [devoted to them]. (Einstein, 1922a, p. 184)

The encyclopedia article established Pauli’s reputation as an author of remarkably competent reviews of new, difficult theoretical fields. ‘The little chap is not only clever but industrious as well,’ wrote Born to Einstein already on 12 February 1921. And the combination of cleverness and hard, devoted work would enable Pauli later on to write other excellent review articles, such as the ones on ‘*Quantentheorie*’ (Pauli, 1926b) and on ‘*Die allgemeinen Prinzipien der Wellenmechanik*’ (‘The General Principles of Wave Mechanics,’ Pauli, 1933c), both for the *Handbuch der Physik*. These extensive essays, in which Pauli succeeded in treating the most fundamental principles of theoretical physics, actually became classics.<sup>646</sup> With the review article on relativity, Pauli ended his active involvement in the problems of general relativity theory for a dozen years, and he turned to atomic theory, which was then the other field at the frontiers of physics.<sup>647</sup> The motivation for this change of interest could be seen from the answer which he gave at that time to a junior colleague at Sommerfeld’s Institute. Werner Heisenberg had asked Pauli about the relative importance of relativity and atomic theory, and he replied:

> The so-called special theory of relativity is now a closed chapter; you simply have to learn it and use it like any other theory in physics. Nor is it of particular interest to anyone anxious to make new discoveries. However, the general theory of relativity, or what comes much to the same thing, Einstein’s theory of gravitation, is still wide-open. But it is unsatisfactory in that, for each experiment, it will give you a hundred pages of theory with the most complicated mathematical derivations. No one can really say whether the whole thing is correct ... In atomic physics we still have a wealth of uninterpreted experimental results: nature’s evidence in one place seems to contradict that in another, and so far it has not been possible to draw an even halfway coherent picture of the relationships involved. (Heisenberg, 1969; English translation, 1971, pp. 25–26)

---

<sup>646</sup> Thirty years later an English translation of the relativity article appeared, to which Pauli added only a series of supplementary notes indicating the development since 1920 (Pauli, 1958a). Similarly the *Handbuch* article on wave mechanics was taken over, with a few minor changes, into the new *Handbuch der Physik*, edited by Siegfried Flügge (Pauli, 1958b).

<sup>647</sup> Pauli’s last paper which dealt fully with relativity was a reply to a criticism of the (special) relativistic equations of electrodynamics, which Pauli submitted in June 1920 to *Mathematische Annalen* (Pauli, 1920b). After a long interval he would return to the problems of general relativity by developing a five-dimensional (projective) formulation of tensors and spinors (Pauli, 1933a, b).

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 387

Pauli expected to help in clarifying the contradictions and explaining the so-far uninterpreted results himself.

At Sommerfeld’s Institute, atomic theory had assumed the most prominent place during the previous several years. Sommerfeld himself and most of his collaborators and talented students worked on important problems of the theory: thus Wilhelm Lenz and Adolf Kratzer discussed the band spectra of molecules; Sommerfeld and Gregor Wentzel treated the X-ray spectra of atoms; Sommerfeld and Werner Heisenberg tried to explain the anomalous Zeeman effects. Pauli did not especially become involved in any one of these problems. Of course, he learned about the status of all problems of atomic theory from his colleagues and in seminars and colloquia. The Physics Colloquium was a joint enterprise of the University of Munich and the *Technische Hochschule*, and it was held every Wednesday during the semester. The speakers, both experimental and theoretical physicists, discussed the latest developments of certain questions, whether they reported the results of their own research or from the literature. Pauli had begun to attend the Colloquium already in his first semester; he went there regularly, though he did not enjoy the experimental talks particularly, claiming that ‘experimental physics is exceedingly tedious’ (Heisenberg, *Conversations*; also AHQP Interview, 7 February 1963, p. 17). He delivered his first talk in the Colloquium in December 1918—it was on the Stark effect—and he gave further talks later on relativity theory and Weyl’s theory. Because of Pauli’s active interest in the problems of atomic theory, Sommerfeld soon began to hand over to him papers in this field (which he received from various people) to read and criticize. For example, in July 1919 Alfred Landé had submitted a paper to the *Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft*, in which he had applied the adiabatic hypothesis to perform the quantization of perturbed electron systems (Landé, 1919d). Pauli studied the paper carefully and found a considerable simplification of Landé’s calculation by applying the Hamiltonian instead of the Lagrangian formulation of the equilibrium condition involved (Pauli to Landé, 18 December 1919). Pauli remained a participant in the exchange of ideas between Sommerfeld and Landé on the explanation of X-ray spectra. For example, Landé criticized Sommerfeld’s generalized relativistic theory of X-ray spectra and proposed his own interpretation, which Pauli in turn criticized as being incorrect in some respects. He commented: ‘In short, my intention is the following: The theory of [X-ray] doublets has to be improved by taking into account the effects of retardation . . . The calculation indeed shows that your simple *Ansatz* is incorrect and must be replaced by a much more complicated one’ (Pauli to Landé, 12 May 1920). But, as we mentioned above, Pauli did not work himself on X-ray spectra. He rather turned to a sequence of problems, which arose from discussions with colleagues at the Institute.${}^{648}$

The need for obtaining reliable information about the dimensions of electron orbits represented a fundamental issue in atomic physics in the early 1920s. Peter

Debye, in a paper published in April 1920 in *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, had proposed a theory of Van der Waals forces, which made it possible to determine a certain combination of quadrupole moments of atoms from the parameters of the equation for real gases (Debye, 1920). Pauli now observed that from $\chi_A$, the diamagnetic moment per gram-atom of a substance, another combination $\Theta$ of quadrupole moments (corresponding to the sum $\sum er^2$, taken over all electrons in the atom, where $\overline{r^2}$ is the average—over an entire orbit—of the distance of an individual electron to an axis through the nucleus parallel to the direction of the external field) could be determined according to the equation

$$\chi_A = \frac{e}{6m_e c^2} N_0 \cdot \Theta, \qquad (188)$$

where $N_0$ is the number of atoms (molecules) per gram-atom, $e$ and $m_e$ denote the charge and mass of the electron, respectively, and $c$ is the velocity of light *in vacuo*. He developed the theory in a note on ‘Theoretische Bemerkungen über den Diamagnetismus einatomiger Gase’ (‘Theoretical Observations on the Diamagnetism of Monatomic Gases’), which was received on 18 June 1920 by *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Pauli, 1920a). By substituting the empirical data for helium and argon, he derived for $\Theta$ the values $7.7 \times 10^{-25}$ and $40 \times 10^{-25}$ (in cgs units), respectively, which appeared to be an order of magnitude larger than one would expect from Bohr orbits having a diameter of $10^{-8}$ cm. Pauli wondered, therefore, whether the known experiments did not contain larger errors than admitted and proposed ‘further measurements, which can decide the important question’ (Pauli, 1920a, p. 205). Erwin Schrödinger, to whom he reported his results, argued that the observed strong diamagnetism of helium (i.e., the large $\Theta$-values) might be due to a property of the nucleus (Schrödinger to Pauli, 12 July 1920). Later experimental investigations, however, would confirm Pauli’s suspicion and reduce the susceptibility of helium by a factor of about 25 (Wills and Hector, 1924).<sup>649</sup>

In the same year, 1920, Pauli submitted a second paper on the subject of atomic magnetism, this time on the paramagnetism of molecules. He presented it on the occasion of the 86th *Naturforscherversammlung* in September 1920 at Bad Nauheim in a talk, entitled, ‘*Quantentheorie und Magneton*’ (‘Quantum Theory and the Magneton,’ Pauli, 1920c). In this talk he first introduced the fundamental unit of the magnetic moment of an electron in a Bohr orbit by the equation

$$\mu_B = \frac{|e|h}{4\pi} N_0, \qquad (189)$$

$N_0$ being the number of atoms or molecules per gram-atom. He stated: ‘The

<sup>649</sup> With the data available in 1925 Georg Joos showed that the orbital dimensions of argon determined from diamagnetism—according to Pauli’s Eq. (188)—agreed perfectly with those determined from other methods (Joos, 1925).

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 389

magnetic moments per mole or gram-atom must, therefore, for all substances be multiples of a certain unit, which we call the Bohr magneton [ $\mu_B$ ]. Its numerical value is 5584 cgs units' (Pauli, 1920c, p. 615). Now Pierre Weiss had concluded ten years earlier that all magnetic moments of paramagnetic substances were multiples of the unit 1123.5 (Weiss, 1911). Pauli called the latter the ‘Weiss magneton,’ $\mu_W$, and wondered why it was much smaller than $\mu_B$ and ‘why the observed values [of the magnetic moments per gram-atom] were not multiples of the Bohr magneton’ (Pauli, 1920c, p. 615). He found that the correct application of quantum theory solved the puzzle to some extent. The crucial point was that the axes of the magnetic moments of atoms or molecules could make definite, discrete angles only with the direction of an external magnetic field. Hence, one obtained from the usual formula, which was derived on the assumption that all angles were equally possible, an ‘apparent,’ nonintegral number $p$ of Bohr magnetons, which was related to the ‘true,’ integral number $n$ via the equation

$$p = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(n + 1)(2n + 1)} . \qquad (190)$$

As the simplest examples, Pauli treated the cases of diatomic molecules since in monatomic substances no paramagnetism had been observed so far. He showed, in particular, that the observations on molecular oxygen ($O_2$) and nitrogen monoxide (NO) could be interpreted by associating a one-quantum magnetic moment ($n = 1$) with $O_2$ and a two-quantum magnetic moment ($n = 2$) with NO. Further, he argued that the axis of the magnetic moment stood perpendicular to the line connecting the two nuclei, in contrast to the case of Bohr’s ring models.$^{650}$

The theory of the magnetic and electric properties of molecules had been discussed in Munich for many years with the goal of obtaining a complete confirmation of Bohr’s view of atomic constitution. Thus Sommerfeld had treated the dispersion of light by molecules (Sommerfeld, 1915d) and Wilhelm Lenz had attempted to establish a theory of band spectra (Lenz, 1919). In the latter work, Lenz had also drawn attention to the magnetic properties of atomic and molecular models, in which electrons were assumed to revolve in Bohr orbits. With his note on the quantum theory of the magneton Pauli had continued this earlier investigation of Lenz’. Nearly one year later, in summer 1921, he made another contribution to the theory of molecules, this time more in the tradition of Sommerfeld and Debye. In a paper, entitled ‘Zur Theorie der Dielektrizitätskonstanten zweiatomiger Dipolgase’ (‘On the Theory of the Dielectric Constant of Diatomic Dipole Gases’) and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he calculated the characteristic property of molecules determining the dispersion of light (Pauli, 1921a). Nearly a decade earlier Peter Debye had derived from

where $\mu_{\text{el}}$ is the permanent dielectric moment of the molecules, $N$ their number per unit volume, $k$ Boltzmann's constant, and $T$ the absolute temperature (Debye, 1912a). The factor $\frac{1}{3}$ multiplying the number of molecules on the right-hand side of Eq. (191) had arisen from averaging the cosine of the angle $\theta$ between the axis of the dipole moment and the direction of the electric field over all $N$ molecules. Pauli now derived the equation corresponding to Eq. (191) in Bohr's theory. Evidently, it was not allowed to average over all possible angles $\theta$ as in classical theory, but one had to take into account only discrete values of $\theta$. Denoting by $\overline{\cos \theta}$ the time average of $\cos \theta$ over an orbit in the molecule with moment of inertia $A$, Pauli found the following discrete values for $\overline{\cos \theta}$:

$$\overline{\cos \theta} = \frac{4 \pi^2 \mu_{\text{el}} |\mathbf{E}|}{K^2} A \left( \frac{3}{2} \frac{J^2}{K^2} - 1 \right), \tag{192}$$

where $J$ is the action integral of the azimuthal angle $\phi$ in the plane perpendicular to the direction of the electric field and $K$ is the sum of the phase integrals connected with the angles $\phi$ and $\theta$. Both $J$ and $K$ assumed only integral multiple values of the Planck's constant, i.e., $J = nh$ and $K = mh$, where $|n| \le m (= 1, 2, 3, \text{etc.})$. Then Pauli performed the averaging procedure over all molecules, assuming a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution over their energy $W$, which depended only on the quantum number $m$ of the total rotation ($W = h^2 m^2 / 8 \pi^2 A$, $A$ being the moment of inertia of the diatomic molecule). He summed over all values of the quantum numbers $m (= 1, 2, 3, \text{etc.})$ and $n (= \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \dots, \pm m)$ and obtained the result

$$P = N \sum_{m} \sum_{n} \overline{\cos \theta} \exp\left( -\frac{W}{kT} \right) / \sum_{m} \sum_{n} \exp\left( -\frac{W}{kT} \right)$$
$$= \frac{\mu_{\text{el}} N |\mathbf{E}|}{kT} \frac{1}{2\sigma} \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{3}{4m^2} + \frac{1}{4m^3} \right) \exp(-\sigma m^2) / \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} m \exp(-\sigma m^2), \tag{193}$$

where $\sigma = h^2 / 8 \pi^2 AkT$. For small values of $\sigma$, the right-hand side of Eq. (193) passed over into $1.5367 \mu_{\text{el}} N |\mathbf{E}| / kT$. Thus the quantum-theoretical expression for the electric moment $P$ assumed the same form as the classical one, except that the numerical factor $\frac{1}{3}$ had to be replaced by the larger factor 1.5367. As a consequence, the quantum-theoretical dipole moments of molecules, determined from Eq. (193) came out smaller (by a factor 2.147) than those determined according to the classical equation (191). Pauli pleaded that his new formula should be tested by experiments, suggesting as most appropriate examples the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0025 -->

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 391

hydrogen-halogenides, whose dipole moments $\mu_{\text{el}}$ could be determined independently from the infrared spectra. He concluded: ‘Unfortunately the temperature dependence of the dielectric constant of the hydrogen halogenides [which is related to $P$ via the equation, $P = (3/4\pi)[(\epsilon - 1)/(\epsilon + 2)]|\mathbf{E}|$, where $\epsilon$ is the dielectric constant] has not yet been measured. It would be very desirable if these measurements, which should not present any difficulties, will soon be carried out’ (Pauli, 1921a, p. 327).$^{651}$

The concern with molecules dominated Pauli’s work in quantum theory at Munich. Thus, for his doctoral thesis, Pauli also treated a problem from molecular physics: namely, to obtain the correct model of $\text{H}_2^+$, the hydrogen molecule-ion. This problem had arisen in the following way. In this third communication on atomic and molecular structure of 1913, Niels Bohr had discussed a model for this ion, in which the electron moved on a circle in the middle plane perpendicular to the axis joining the two hydrogen nuclei; he had found, however, that this system did not satisfy his condition ensuring the stability against a displacement of the electron perpendicular to the plane of its orbit (Bohr, 1913e, p. 862). In 1919 Arnold Sommerfeld had devoted a section in *Atombau und Spektrallinien* to the hydrogen molecule-ion (Sommerfeld, 1919, Appendix 11, pp. 508–511). He had reproduced there a calculation of the energy of $\text{H}_2^+$, according to which it possessed an energy larger than that of a hydrogen atom plus a hydrogen nucleus, thus confirming the instability consideration of Bohr. And he had added: ‘The above calculations (according to a private communication from Mr. W. Pauli) point to a contradiction with experience, which speaks against the model’ (Sommerfeld, 1919, p. 510). Sommerfeld had then suggested to Pauli that a closer study of the models for the hydrogen molecule-ion might be a suitable topic for his doctoral thesis. The solution of this problem appeared to be of great importance, for it would provide an opportunity to compare in detail the theory and the available observations, which included—besides the fact that $\text{H}_2^+$ existed as a stable object in canal rays (Dempster, 1916)—the measurement of an ionization energy of $11.5 \pm 0.7 \text{ eV}$ (Franck, Knipping and Krüger, 1919; Krüger, 1921). Between fall 1919 and spring 1921 Pauli worked on his thesis. He later extended the results slightly while staying at Göttingen and published them in a paper, entitled ‘Über das Modell des Wasserstoffmolekülions’ (‘On the Model of the Hydrogen Molecule-Ion’) in *Annalen der Physik* (Pauli, 1922).$^{652}$

The quantum physicists believed at that time that atomic systems made up of several charged particles did not belong in general to the class of conditionally periodic systems, the theory of which had been established with the help of the

***

quantum conditions. However, a system of two nuclei, if fixed at their equilibrium positions, plus an electron—which should represent the hydrogen molecule-ion in good approximation—could well be treated within the scope of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. Therefore, Pauli investigated it in some detail, in order to find the stable state of lowest energy. He approached his goal in the most general way, prescribing the following guideline: ‘We do not select *arbitrarily* certain types of orbits, which are distinguished by simple geometrical properties; rather we try to obtain as accurate an insight as possible into the *totality* of mechanical orbits and to select the stable quantum orbits according to *general theoretical principles*’ (Pauli, 1922, pp. 178–179). With this goal in mind he organized the orbits of the electron in the $\text{H}_2^+$-ion into three classes: the orbits which lie in the middle plane (i.e., the plane perpendicular to the line connecting the two hydrogen nuclei and going through the centre of this line), the orbits which are symmetrical with respect to the middle plane, and the asymmetric orbits which lie on one side of the middle plane.

In order to determine the stability of the orbits under consideration Pauli proposed a new stability criterion, which he believed to be in agreement with the foundation of quantum theory, especially the adiabatic hypothesis: ‘Those mechanical orbits, which emerge from the original orbit by an infinitely small change of the initial conditions, must remain infinitely close to it [the original orbit] in its entire geometrical course’ (Pauli, 1922, p. 182). The new condition replaced Bohr’s earlier stability condition of 1913. With

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0027 -->

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 393

In the case of two fixed nuclei and a rotating electron, Pauli obtained an expression for the energy of the system by the method of separation of variables.^{653} This expression could not be written explicitly as a function of the three phase integrals for the separation coordinates $\lambda$, $\mu$ and $\phi$ (with $\lambda$ and $\mu$ being, up to a constant factor, the sum and the difference, respectively, of the distances of the electron to the two nuclei, and $\phi$ the angular variable of the electron's revolutions). However, Pauli showed that the energy increased monotonically with growing values of the phase integrals; this result enabled him to proceed with an analysis of the possible orbits in the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-problem. For this purpose he separated the orbits into two different categories: the planar orbits, in which the electron remains in a given plane containing the two hydrogen nuclei as well (in these cases the angular momentum $p_{\phi}$ is zero), and the spatial orbits, in which the plane containing electrons and nuclei rotates constantly around the $z$-axis (i.e., the axis connecting the nuclei). According to the known results of (celestial) mechanics the planar orbits could be a pendulum orbit (between two symmetrical points on the middle line perpendicular to the $z$-axis), a satellite orbit (around one of the nuclei), a lemniscate orbit (densely filling the interior area of an ellipse with the two nuclei as focal points), and a planetary orbit (around the two centres). The spatial orbits lying in the middle plane might be divided among those which are symmetrical and those which are asymmetrical to the middle plane. Pauli reduced the types of possible orbits immediately by imposing a condition, namely, that the time average of the force exerted by the electron on both nuclei must vanish. This condition led to what he called ‘equilibrium orbits’ (‘*Gleichgewichtsbahnen*,’ Pauli, 1922, p. 209). Only spatial orbits then qualified as possible motions.^{654} In applying his quantum-theoretical stability condition, Pauli was forced to exclude all orbits in the middle plane—a result, which agreed in the special case of the circular orbit with Bohr’s result of 1913 quoted above. Finally, Pauli also had to drop the unsymmetrical spatial orbits because he found them to be perturbable by the oscillatory motions of the nuclei.^{655} However, he succeeded in showing that at least one symmetrical spatial orbit existed, which remained stable under all conditions. By substituting the quantum numbers 0, 1, 1, for the three phase integrals (in the variables $\lambda$, $\mu$ and $\phi$), he obtained the energy of the lowest state of that type as

$$
W = -0.5175Rh, \tag{194}
$$

$R$ and $h$ being Rydberg’s and Planck’s constants, respectively. Evidently, this

^{654} Planar orbits were forbidden because of the following reasons: the pendulum orbits were instable against perturbation from the middle plane; the satellite and lemniscate orbits approached one nucleus infinitely closely.
^{655} Actually Pauli only showed that the nuclear oscillations did not perturb the symmetrical orbits (Pauli, 1922, §9).

394 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

energy was larger than the energy of a free hydrogen atom plus a hydrogen nucleus (with zero kinetic energy), which added up to — $Rh$. Hence, in principle, the decay process, $\mathrm{H}_2^+ \rightarrow \mathrm{H} + \mathrm{H}^+$, would be (energetically) possible. Still, such a process should not happen spontaneously because: ‘A decay of a dynamically stable model, which occurs spontaneously already when arbitrarily weak external fields of force act, is mechanically impossible’ (Pauli, 1922, p. 235). Also the decay via the transition into an instable state should not occur: stable and instable orbits belong to different classes, and no transitions are admitted between them. Thus only one possibility remained for the decay of the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion, namely, if it was caused by electron impact. ‘Then, on account of the attraction which exists between the electrons and the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion, the electron would obtain—as soon as it encounters the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion—a finite kinetic energy and also represent a strong perturbing field of force,’ Pauli argued, pointing to the empirical confirmation of this conclusion in earlier canal-ray experiments of Dempster (Pauli, 1922, pp. 235–236). He summarized the results by saying: ‘Therefore, we have to designate the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion as a *metastable* object. It does not represent the state of smallest energy for the system consisting of two nuclei and one electron, because one H-atom and one isolated electron [Pauli meant, of course, one isolated hydrogen nucleus] possess a lower energy. In spite of this, however, one needs the action of a finite field of force to transform the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion into this state’ (Pauli, 1922, p. 236).<sup>656</sup>

At the end Pauli discussed the quantitative comparison of his calculated energy for the lowest state of the hydrogen molecule-ion with the data. He pleaded for the repetition of the electron impact experiment because the previously measured value of 11.5 V for the ionization potential was much higher than the theoretical value (about 7 V). But he also claimed that a more decisive test of the theory would be provided by the comparison of the theoretical and experimental spectra of the energy states of the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion. For this purpose one had, on one hand, to isolate the true spectrum of the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-ion; on the other hand, one had to extend the theory to find the energy values of the excited states as well as the possible corrections due to the oscillation and rotation of the nuclei. Thus Pauli considered his theory as merely the first step towards a complete description of the hydrogen molecule-ion. He firmly expected that the theory could be perfected without any major difficulties by applying suitable perturbation methods (such as the ones he had used already for discussing the stability of the nuclear oscillations: Pauli, 1922, Section 9). He was aware, however, that ‘the special computation of the $\mathrm{H}_2^+$-spectrum implies, at any rate, an enormous amount of work,’ and he concluded: ‘Still it would perhaps be possible to calculate at least the band [in the spectrum] corresponding to the simplest possible quantum jump of the quantum numbers of the electron’ (Pauli, 1922, pp. 238–239).

Pauli’s work on the hydrogen molecule-ion represented a considerable progress in the theory of atomic models. For the first time someone had treated

IV.1 Wolfgang Pauli’s Background and Early Scientific Work 395

systematically all possible models of a few-body system in quantum theory. All previous investigations had made use of specific assumptions to narrow the choice down to a specifically selected model; examples of this approach were the helium models of Niels Bohr and Alfred Landé. Pauli showed that, by applying the advanced methods of celestial mechanics and a few fundamental principles of quantum theory, it was possible to solve the problem of the $H_2^+$-ion. Still, he was not completely satisfied with his result; his Munich colleague Gregor Wentzel reported that Pauli, towards the end of the work on his thesis, was rather discouraged about the apparent disagreement between experimental and theoretical values of the ionization potential (Wentzel, AHQP Interview, 3 February 1964, pp. 6, 8–9). However, the situation improved in 1922, when James Franck doubted the interpretation of the inelastic electron collision at 11.5 V as being due to the ionization of the $H_2^+$-ion. Hence Pauli, in his published paper of 1922 (it was submitted to *Annalen der Physik* early in March 1922) expressed the optimism that future experiments might confirm his theory. In any case, Pauli’s hydrogen molecule-ion paper could not yet be interpreted as showing a failure of the Bohr-Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, nor did Pauli express such an opinion.$^{657}$

In spite of the existing discrepancy between theoretical and experimental values of the ground state of $H_2^+$—which seemed to be present at least in spring 1921—Sommerfeld gave the highest mark to Pauli’s thesis, and praised it as showing ‘like the many, already published smaller investigations and his large encyclopedia article, the full command of the modern tools of mathematical physics’ (Sommerfeld, in his *Votum* on Pauli’s thesis, quoted in Pauli, 1979, p. 32). Since Pauli also passed the oral examinations in all subjects (physics with Sommerfeld and Wien, mathematics with Ferdinand von Lindemann, and astronomy with Hugo von Seeliger) with the mark of ‘very good,’ he graduated *summa cum laude*. After this final success in his studies, the young man could go on his *Wanderjahre* as a research scholar. Sommerfeld recommended Pauli immediately to Max Born in Göttingen, and in October 1921 he took up his first postdoctoral position as an assistant to Born at the famous *Georgia Augusta*.

Pauli was certainly sorry to leave Munich. He liked and respected Sommerfeld deeply. Having been born and brought up in a big city, he loved the life in a city like Munich. ‘Wolfgang [Pauli] was a typical night bird. He preferred the town, liked to spend his evenings in some old bar or café, and would then work on his physics through much of the night with great concentration and success. Quite naturally, and to Sommerfeld’s dismay, he would rarely attend morning lectures; it was not until noon that he generally turned up’ (Heisenberg, 1969; English translation, 1971, p. 27). Pauli enjoyed going to the theatre and movies. At the same time he read widely, and not just in the literature of physics. Through his talents, his education and early scientific achievements, Pauli was an infant

prodigy. Having come in contact with great scientific personalities—such as Ernst Mach, Hermann Weyl and Albert Einstein—at an early age, he had developed certain ease and familiarity in dealing with the celebrities of physics. Of course, he also impressed colleagues of his own age by the maturity of his knowledge and judgment, his understanding of and critical observations on the most up-to-date and most difficult theoretical results, and, above all, his sharp wit. However, the sharp criticism by word of mouth and pen, the biting and sarcastic treatment of all—even much senior and most respected people—whenever he felt that their work lacked clarity or contained half-truths, for which Pauli became famous within a few years, had not yet become his trademark. On the contrary, Max Born described him in October 1921 in a letter as follows: ‘W. Pauli is now my assistant; he is amazingly intelligent, and very able. At the same time, he is very human and, for a 21 year old, normal, gay and childlike’ (Born to Einstein, 21 October 1921). Thus the young Pauli was welcomed most heartily in Göttingen.

### IV.2 The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems

The very establishment of the nuclear atom immediately brought about the task of making detailed models of the simplest atomic systems built of few electrons and nuclei. Besides the hydrogen atom, these systems included the helium atom, the hydrogen molecule and its ion. The earliest models were proposed for them by Niels Bohr already in 1913. For instance, he proposed to describe the helium atom by a system of two electrons, situated at opposite points of the same (circular) orbit, which move synchronously around the nucleus in the same direction: then the radius of this orbit turned out to be $0.571a_\text{H}$ (where $a_\text{H} =$ the smallest hydrogen orbit $= 0.55 \times 10^{-8} \text{ cm}$); and the energy assumed the value of $6.13W_\text{H}$, where $W_\text{H}$ (corresponding to an ionization potential of 13 V) is the energy of the hydrogen ground state (Bohr, 1913c, p. 489). Bohr took a similar, simple model for the hydrogen molecule: its two electrons should move on a single (circular) orbit—as in the helium model—which lies in the middle plane perpendicular to the line connecting the (equilibrium) positions of the nuclei, the orbit having a radius of $0.95a_\text{H}$ and the total system an energy of $2.20W_\text{H}$ (Bohr, 1913e, p. 864). Bohr showed further that if an electron were removed from the hydrogen molecule, the system would become unstable against decay into a hydrogen atom and a hydrogen nucleus.

Bohr’s models of 1913 were taken during the following years as reasonable descriptions of the atomic and molecular few-body systems, and one began to examine in detail their consequences by calculating from them the physical and chemical properties of the atomic systems under investigation. Thus, for instance, Irving Langmuir showed in late 1913 that the value, which he had just measured for the heat of formation of one gram-atom of molecular hydrogen (i.e., the energy liberated as heat during the reaction of two gram-atoms of H to yield $\text{H}_2$),

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0031 -->

IV.2  The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems                                                     397

namely, 76,000 cal, agreed reasonably well with the 60,000 cal calculated from Bohr’s model (Langmuir, 1914).$^{658}$ Then Peter Debye studied the dispersion of light by Bohr’s H$_2$-model, and found that the theoretical curve fitted the observed one satisfactorily (Debye, 1915a). However, in later years several authors pointed out the difficulties of Bohr and Debye’s standard model. Thus Paul Epstein drew attention to the fact that the temperature dependence of the rotational energy of the Bohr–Debye H$_2$-model did not account for the specific-heat data of Arnold Eucken (Epstein, 1916f). A later discussion of the same problem by Debye’s student Gerda Laski, which showed agreement between theory and experiment (Laski, 1919a), rested on an erroneous interpretation of the data (Laski, 1919b). At about the same time James Franck, Paul Knipping and Thea Krüger reported a measurement of the ionization potential of H$_2$ (from collision with electrons); their value, $17.1 \pm 0.25$ V, corresponded to a heat of formation of $81,300 \pm 5700$ cal which exceeded Bohr’s value considerably (Franck, Knipping and Krüger, 1919). Finally, Wilhelm Lenz noted the fact that the observed nonexistence of any Zeeman effect in the hydrogen band spectrum implied a zero magnetic moment of the hydrogen molecules, in contrast to what followed from the standard model of Bohr and Debye (Lenz, 1919). Lenz, therefore, called for the construction of a suitable planar model of H$_2$, having no magnetic moment around the axis. ‘How the model will look in detail,’ he added, ‘cannot, however, be specified yet because of the extraordinary mathematical difficulty of the problem’ (Lenz, 1919, pp. 642–643).

In order to solve the above-mentioned difficulties, Arnold Eucken suggested in May 1922 the following model for the hydrogen molecule: the two nuclei should rotate around their common centre—even at the lowest temperature this rotation persisted as the zero-point rotation—and the two electrons oscillate on more or less straight lines, which would go through the nuclei if the latter did not perform the rotation (Eucken, 1922a). Against Eucken’s assumption of planar, degenerate electron motions in the hydrogen molecule, Max Born immediately raised fundamental objections. Born argued that any discussion of the structure of the molecule had to take into account the hitherto successful principles of quantum theory. ‘The time is over when it was up to the fantasy of the researcher to devise atomic and molecular models arbitrarily,’ he wrote in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften* (where Eucken had also published his note), and continued: ‘One is now much more in a position to construct the models by applying the quantum rules with a certain, though not complete, assurance’ (Born, 1922, p. 677). As the chief principle, Born suggested, one should use the adiabatic principle. Thus he obtained a model for the hydrogen molecule by taking two distant hydrogen atoms in the ground state and letting their nuclei approach each other infinitely slowly. In evaluating the energy of the molecule arising in this process by a suitable perturbation calculation, one had to be careful about the fact that the unperturbed system of two (free) hydrogen atoms was degener-

398 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

ate, for the electrons in both atoms moved with identical angular velocities. As a consequence of the degeneracy, the electron motions in the hydrogen molecule had to satisfy phase relations approximately. With this in mind, Born devised four possible models for the $\text{H}_2$-system: in all of them the two electrons moved in phase on orbits around their respective nuclei (as in the hydrogen atom); in two cases the planes of the orbits were parallel, while in the two others they made opposite angles with the axis connecting the two nuclei; finally, the electrons could move either in the same or opposite directions. Born claimed that only one model satisfied all conditions: in it the electrons moved on planes, which made angles of plus and minus $60^\circ$ with the nuclear axis, the electrons always occupying analogous points on their respective orbits but moving in opposite directions. As Born noted, this model had another desirable property: 'If one lets the nuclei gradually approach each other, one finally arrives at exactly that model of parhelium in the ground state, which has recently been given by Bohr and which, for many reasons, must be considered as the most probable configuration of helium' (Born, 1922, p. 678). The correlation of the hydrogen molecule model to that of the helium atom provided in Born's eyes a most convincing argument in favour of his model, especially since at that time—i.e., in summer 1922—Bohr announced a successful treatment of the ground state of helium by Hendrik Kramers.$^{659}$

Any realistic model of the helium atom had to explain the existence of two types of spectra. They had been discovered by Carl Runge and Friedrich Paschen in their analysis of the lines of the gas discovered recently in the mineral cleveite and identified with the solar helium (Runge and Paschen, 1895).$^{660}$ Paschen and Runge had separated the six series of spectral lines into two systems, one having three series of doublet lines and the other having three series of singlet lines. They had claimed that only the system of doublet lines was emitted by the solar 'helium,' and the other by atoms possessing a lower atomic weight. Afterwards this element had been named 'parhelium' (Rydberg, 1896). With the advent of the nuclear atom it became evident that both types of spectra, the normal helium spectra and the parhelium spectra, were emitted by the same atom. However, the model, which Bohr had constructed of the helium atom in 1913 (consisting of a doubly-charged nucleus and two electrons moving on the same one-quantum orbit), was shown by Peter Debye to yield too high dispersion (Debye, 1915a). In order to cure this difficulty, Paul Epstein suggested in a letter to Arnold Sommerfeld (in spring 1916) a rather different model: of the two
