electrons in the helium atom one should be tightly bound and stay in the vicinity of the nucleus, while the other moved in an orbit with larger dimensions (Sommerfeld, 1918a, pp. 547–549). Sommerfeld used this model to obtain the formulae for the spectral series of helium (Sommerfeld, 1916e, p. 153) and to derive an improved description of the dispersion data (Sommerfeld, 1918a, p. 547). Still, when Sommerfeld wrote his book on *Atombau und Spektrallinien* (Sommerfeld, 1919), the situation concerning the correct model of the neutral helium atom could by no means be considered as being clear. There, after discussing the respective models of Bohr and Epstein, he commented: ‘Further details, however, are hidden from us at the moment; they can only be obtained from the numerical explanation of the spectra of neutral helium. We should not be surprised that we have thus far not arrived at this goal, since even the astronomers have not yet satisfactorily solved the three-body problem in spite of efforts over centuries’ (Sommerfeld, 1919, p. 70). In a footnote to these remarks he drew attention to some progress, which had just recently been made while the book was in press, and he discussed it in an addendum at the end of the book (Sommerfeld, 1919, *Zusatz* 12, pp. 511–515). The progress in the helium problem, to which Sommerfeld referred, had been obtained by his former student Alfred Landé, who was then working for his *Habilitation* at the University of Frankfurt.

Alfred Landé was born on 13 December 1888 at Elberfeld. He studied physics first at the Universities of Marburg and Munich (from 1908 to 1910), then for two years in Göttingen (1910–1912), and finally completed his doctoral thesis under the supervision of Sommerfeld in Munich. From 1913 to 1914 he acted as assistant (i.e., physics ‘tutor’) to David Hilbert (succeeding Paul Ewald in this position). Shortly after he received his doctorate in 1914, the war broke out and Landé served with the Red Cross until Max Born placed him with the *Artillerie-Prüfungskommission* (‘Artillery Testing Commission’) in Berlin. There he started the collaboration with Born on the theory of crystal properties, which resulted in a refutation of Bohr’s coplanar orbits in atoms and molecules (Born and Landé, 1918a, b, c). When Born went to the University of Frankfurt in early 1919 to take up the chair of theoretical physics, he gladly took Landé with him as an assistant. In Frankfurt Landé continued to explore the possibility of having spatial arrangements of electron orbits in atoms and molecules. Thus he turned, among other things, to the problem of the helium atom.$^{661}$ He presented his results in two papers, submitted to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* in March and August 1919 (Landé, 1919c, 1920a).

In his first article on the series spectra of helium Landé discussed in detail a model of the helium atom, in which an outer electron moves in an orbit around an inner system consisting of a doubly-charged nucleus and an (inner) electron—

Landé made important contributions to the quantum theory of the anomalous Zeeman effect, which we shall discuss in Section IV.4. He died on 30 October 1975 in Columbus, Ohio.

the ‘double star’ system of Epstein and Sommerfeld. However, in contrast to the Epstein–Sommerfeld model, the orbits of the inner and outer electrons in Landé’s picture of the neutral helium did not need to be coplanar, but could make an angle $\theta$ with each other. Then the energy of a helium state depended—provided the inner electron was always on the same (one-quantum orbit)—on the three quantum numbers, $n_r, n_1$ and $n_2$, describing the orbit of the outer electron: $n_r$ denoted its radial and $n_1$ its spatial quantum number (i.e., the component of its angular momentum in the direction of the axis of the inner electron’s orbit); the sum of $n_1$ and $n_2$ represented the azimuthal quantum number $n_\phi$, and the cosine of the angle $\theta$ was given by the expression $n_1/(n_1 + n_2)$. By taking into account the mutual influences of the two electrons on each other’s orbits in some approximation, Landé derived the following equation for the series terms, i.e., the absolute values of the energy states $W = W(n_r, n_1, n_2)$:

$$|W(n_r, n_1, n_2)| = \frac{Rh}{(n_r + n_1 + n_2)^2} \left( 1 - \frac{n_1 + n_2}{n_r + n_1 + n_2} \delta_{n_1, n_2} \right)^{-2}, \quad (195)$$

where the factor $\delta_{n_1, n_2}$ could be written as a rational function of the quantum numbers $n_1$ and $n_2$, and $R$ and $h$ denote Rydberg’s and Planck’s constant, respectively. According to Eq. (195) the term spectra of helium possessed the following structure: two series of $S$-terms, for which the set of quantum numbers, $(n_r, n_1, n_2)$, assumes the values $(n_r, 0, 1)$ and $(n_r, 1, 0)$, with $n_r = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, respectively; three series of $P$-terms denoted by $(n_r, 0, 2)$, $(n_r, 1, 1)$ and $(n_r, 2, 0)$, with $n_r = 1, 2, 3, \dots$; four series of $D$-terms denoted by $(n_r, 0, 3)$, $(n_r, 1, 2)$, $(n_r, 2, 1)$ and $(n_r, 3, 0)$ with $n_r = 0, 1, 2 \dots$. Landé related all these sequences of terms to the empirical ones obtained from the spectroscopic data: he identified, especially, the two $S$-series as $S_{\mathrm{I}}$—described by the set of quantum numbers $(n_r, 0, 1)$—of parhelium and $S_{\mathrm{II}}$—described by $(n_r, 1, 0)$—of normal ortho-helium; the $P$-series $(n_r, 0, 2)$ with $P_{\mathrm{I}}$ of parhelium, and the two $P$-series $(n_r, 1, 1)$ and $(n_r, 2, 0)$ with the two series of $P_{\mathrm{II}}$ of ortho-helium. A difficulty arose in the case of the four $D$-series: while $(n_r, 0, 3)$ had to be associated with the $D_{\mathrm{I}}$-series of parhelium, there existed three theoretical $D_{\mathrm{II}}$-series, described by the sets of quantum numbers, $(n_r, 1, 2)$, $(n_r, 2, 1)$ and $(n_r, 3, 0)$, in contrast to only two observed empirically. However, Landé was not bothered by that difficulty and argued: ‘Further it would be possible that of the three observed $D$-terms, the $D_{\mathrm{I}}$-term and the two $D_{\mathrm{II}}$-terms, one might be a doublet; that is, $D_{\mathrm{II}}$ might actually constitute a triplet’ (Landé, 1919c, p. 232).

Landé’s theory of the helium term spectra indeed accounted for the observed data, at least in a reasonable first approximation. At that time one had measured the main lines of the visible and infrared lines of the singlet spectra—associated with parhelium—and doublet spectra—associated with normal or ortho-helium. To the states derived from these lines, Landé compared his calculated $S$-, $P$-, and $D$-states. Because of the insufficient approximation involved—Landé had neglected, for example, the fact that in cases, when the axes of the inner and the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0035 -->

IV.2 The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems
401

outer electron orbits make finite angles $\theta$ with each other a secular precession would arise—he expected that ‘the theory given here, especially the numerical values, may be viewed as providing only an initial orientation about the possibility of interpreting dynamically the series spectrum of helium’ (Landé, 1919c, p. 232). Therefore, in the case of the $S$-terms with $n = 1$, where the external electron comes close to the orbit of the inner electron, the approximation should be especially bad. As a result, Landé refrained from presenting the $S$-states of parhelium altogether, and he derived the $S$-states of normal helium by inserting the empirical value for the factor $\delta_{n_1, n_2}$, i.e., $\delta_1$, in Eq. (195).$^{662}$ For the $P$- and $D$-terms, however, the theoretical and experimental energy values were in reasonable agreement. Thus Landé was quite satisfied. As a particular test of his scheme he carried out a calculation of the lowest $S$-state, in which the outer electron moves in an approximately circular orbit having the quantum numbers, $n_r = 0$, $n_1 = 1$ and $n_2 = 0$, i.e., in an orbit (of normal helium) which is coplanar with the orbit of the inner electron. He obtained the energy of $-6.16Rh$ to $-6.20Rh$ for it and commented: ‘This model of normal helium stands in contrast to the one propagated by N. Bohr, in which the two electrons move on one and the same one-quantum orbit on exactly opposite sides. Bohr’s model has the energy content of $-6.125Rh$. From our interpretation of the $S$-term of He$_{II}$ [i.e., of normal helium] it follows that the He-model used above, with its energy of $-6.16$ to $-6.20Rh$, is a little more stable than the one proposed by Bohr’ (Landé, 1919c, pp. 233–234).

In his second paper, a shortened version of his *Habilitation* thesis, Landé tried to improve on the approximations made in the calculation of the energy states of helium. ‘The progress in comparison to the earlier work,’ he remarked in the introduction, ‘consists in systematically taking into account the orbital perturbations and in a new quantization of the inclinations of the orbits, which admits only two series systems (He$_{I}$ and He$_{II}$), in contrast to the multiplicity obtained earlier’ (Landé, 1920a, p. 114). A systematic application of perturbation theory meant for Landé the treatment first of the special case of the three-body problem, in which two electrons moved in the same sense on two coplanar orbits around the helium nucleus, by taking into account all Coulomb attractions and repulsions in the system.$^{663}$ Then he tried to consider the changes brought about if the two orbits were not coplanar.

***

$^{662}$Landé proceeded in his paper according to a proposal of Sommerfeld’s (Landé, 1919c, p. 233). He took the measured value of the ionization potential of the Fowler series of the ionized helium (Rau, 1914) and subtracted from it the energy necessary to bring the electron of He$^+$ from a one-quantum to a four-quantum orbit (this energy being equal to $(15/4)Rh$). The remaining energy, i.e., $1.80Rh$ to $2.16Rh$, then constituted the work required to remove the external electron from the neutral helium atom. Landé took this value ($1.80Rh$ to $2.16Rh$) and put it equal to $Rh(1 - \delta_1)^{-2}$—i.e., equal to the theoretical expression for the ionization energy derived from Eq.

# 402 \quad Chapter IV \quad The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

To start with, Landé rearranged the Hamiltonian of the coplanar helium system into the form of a sum, consisting of three terms: the first term describing the energy of the inner electron in the field of the nucleus, the second the same part of the energy of the outer electron (i.e., its kinetic energy plus the potential energy due to a screened nucleus of charge $|e|$), and the third the remaining periodic perturbation energy. In order to obtain the energy terms, Landé used his new ‘adiabatic’ quantization method of perturbed systems, which he had discussed in an earlier paper (Landé, 1919d). This method allowed one to work with the known quantization rules of the unperturbed orbits, provided one could transform the latter via adiabatic changes into perturbed orbits. Applying it to the helium problem with two electron orbits, Landé first looked at a system in which the outer electron was removed completely (i.e., it moved on an orbit having an infinite radius), and then changed it infinitely slowly to the situation in which it (i.e., the outer electron) was bound in an orbit of finite radius. Then he calculated the corresponding changes in the energy terms, and obtained the following result: the change in the energy of the inner electron could be neglected as being very small; the energy of the outer electron could be expressed as the sum of the energy it had in the Coulomb field of a hydrogen nucleus plus terms of order $(2r_0/R_0)^{5/3}$ and higher powers, $r_0$ being the lowest radius of the ionized helium and $R_0$ the radius of the outer electron in the field of the hydrogen nucleus. Evidently, the calculated energy values were reliable, except the energy value for the state in which the outer electron assumed a one-quantum (i.e., $n = 1$) orbit.

Landé did not carry out the same ‘exact perturbation theory’ for the case of a spatial orientation of the two electron orbits in the helium atom. However, from an analogy to his earlier (less exact) calculations, he determined how $\cos \theta$ entered into the resulting expression for the perturbed energy of the system. Then he had only to insert the discrete values of the orientation angle and the two electron orbits. These he obtained by considering the composition of angular momenta of the two electrons to yield the total angular momentum (Landé, 1919c, e). That is, the orientation of the orbits could be found by taking **J**, the vector sum of the angular momenta of the orbits, say $\mathbf{J}_1 + \mathbf{J}_2$ in the case of two electron orbits denoted by the suffixes 1 and 2, and by imposing the condition that all three momenta be quantized. This procedure led to the following equations (involving the absolute values of the angular momenta, $J_1, J_2$ and $J$, and the angles $\theta_1$—between $\mathbf{J}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}$—and $\theta_2$—between $\mathbf{J}$ and $\mathbf{J}_2$; thus the sum of the angles, $\theta = \theta_1 + \theta_2$, denoted the angle between the two electron orbits)$^{664}$:

$$J = J_1 \cos \theta_1 + J_2 \cos \theta_2 = \text{const.} \qquad (196\text{a})$$

$^{664}$ Landé derived Eqs. (196a, b) in the following way (Landé, 1919c, p. 234). The interaction between the two electron orbits results in a perturbation term to the energy proportional to $J_1 \cos \theta_1 + J_2 \cos \theta_2$; this term must be connected with a periodic precessional motion, which in quantum theory possesses an integral quantum number. Hence Eq. (196a) follows immediately. On the other hand, the Hamiltonian of the problem does depend only on the sum of the two angles, $\theta_1 + \theta_2$. Then the equilibrium condition demands the validity of Eq. (196b). The derivation of these equations from the concept of the vector sum was proposed to Landé by the Munich people (see Landé, 1919e, p. 585, footnote 2).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0037 -->

IV.2  The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems 403

and

$$J_1 \sin \theta_1 + J_2 \sin \theta_2 = 0. \qquad (196b)$$

The quantization rules for the absolute values of the three angular momenta demanded that

$$J_1 = n_{\phi}^{(1)} \frac{h}{2\pi} , \quad J_2 = n_{\phi}^{(2)} \frac{h}{2\pi} , \quad \text{and} \quad J = k \frac{h}{2\pi} , \qquad (197)$$

$n_{\phi}^{(1)}$, $n_{\phi}^{(2)}$ and $k$ being the corresponding integral quantum numbers. Then, in the example of the helium atom, where the azimuthal quantum number of the inner electron was assumed to be $n_{\phi}^{(2)} = 1$, Eqs. (196) yielded three possibilities for composing the vector sum of $\mathbf{J}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}_2$: the total angular momentum $\mathbf{J}$ might possess the quantum numbers, $k = n_{\phi}^{(1)} + 1$, $n_{\phi}^{(1)}$, and $n_{\phi}^{(1)} - 1$. In the case of the helium $S$-terms the outer electron’s momentum should have the quantum number 1; hence the angle $\theta$ between the planes of the two electron orbits, which entered into the expression for the perturbed energy, assumed the values $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, respectively (Landé, 1920a, pp. 120–121). Similar results followed for the $P$-states, in which the three discrete angles were $0^\circ$, $104^\circ 28'$ and $180^\circ$, and for the $D$-states with angles $0^\circ$, $99^\circ 35'$ and $180^\circ$.

Although the quantum rules derived in this way applied strictly only when the periodic perturbation term in the Hamiltonian was small, Landé observed a reasonable agreement between the theoretical and the empirical values for the $P$- and $D$-terms, both for parhelium and ortho-helium, provided he took for the parhelium states the angles around $90^\circ$ (i.e., $104^\circ 28'$ for $P$- and $99^\circ 35'$ for $D$-terms) and for ortho-helium the angle $0^\circ$. $^{665}$ Again the approximation was very bad for $S$-terms, consistent with the fact that the perturbation in these cases could not be considered as being small at all. While, in the spectrum of normal (i.e., ortho-) helium, at least the higher $S$-terms corresponding to elliptical orbits of the outer electron ($n_r = 1, 2, 3, \dots$) were roughly accounted for by the theory, the calculation of the $S_{\text{I}}$-terms failed completely. Landé found, however, that the empirical $S$-terms of parhelium could be made to agree with the calculated terms by using an angle of $60^\circ$ between the two electron orbits. He concluded that ‘an inclination of $60^\circ$ is quantum-theoretically not admissible; perhaps one has to consider here another type of orbit’ (Landé, 1920a, p. 121).

In spite of the deficiencies mentioned above, Landé was pleased with his improved theory of helium because it accounted for the coarse structure of the observed term spectra of normal helium and, with some exceptions, for parhelium. ‘It appears to be especially satisfactory,’ he pointed out, ‘that the quantization of the precession restricts the multiplicity of the spatial positions for any $n_{\phi}$ [of the outer orbit] to just *two*, i.e., to coplanitarly for $\text{He}_{\text{II}}$ and an angle of inclination of nearly $90^\circ$ for $\text{He}_{\text{I}}$’ (Landé, 1920a, p. 121). At the same time,

$^{665}$Landé excluded the third spatial orientation of the orbits, described by an angle of $180^\circ$ (i.e., by two electrons moving on coplanar orbits in opposite directions) because it represented an unstable motion having a higher energy than the two others.

**404**  
Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

however, he noticed that ‘an explanation for the occurrence of the $S_{\text{I}}$-terms and the duplicity of the $\text{He}_{\text{II}}$-terms is missing’ (Landé, 1920a, pp. 121–122).  
Landé’s theory of the helium atom represented an important step in the treatment of the problem. It was followed by a lively activity of the physicists, who explored more deeply and in detail the experimental and theoretical properties of the two-electron atom. It began with the work of James Franck and Paul Knipping, who made a new determination of the ionization potential of helium, namely, $25.4 \pm 0.25$ V (Franck and Knipping, 1919, p. 486).$^{666}$ This value contradicted the theoretical values derived either from Bohr’s helium model (with the two electrons on the same one-quantum ring around the nucleus) or from Landé’s (and Epstein–Sommerfeld’s) model for the normal helium atom with the coplanar orbits: the former yielded an ionization potential of $28.77$ V and the latter roughly $30$ V. James Franck and Fritz Reiche concluded, therefore, ‘*that the measured value belongs to the less stable helium atom with the crossed electron orbits, and that it is this atom (i.e., the parhelium) which we have as normal helium in the non-excited state*’ (Franck and Reiche, 1920, p. 155). As a consequence, normal (i.e., ortho-) helium with coplanar orbits could occur only in a state where the outer electron moves on a two-quantum orbit, which represents the lowest state of this system. Franck and Knipping then showed that the electron collision experiments supported the existence of a ‘metastable’ helium state; it possessed larger energy than the lowest state of parhelium, but could not pass over into it by the emission of radiation (Franck and Knipping, 1920). Edwin C. Kemble objected strongly to this conclusion concerning the ground state of helium: first, he claimed that Franck and Reiche’s interpretation of the helium ground state was difficult to reconcile with Irving Langmuir’s assumptions on the structure of helium (Langmuir, 1919b), which accounted well for the chemical properties of the noble gas (see our discussion in Section III.3); in fact, an electron moving on an outer orbit—as assumed by Franck and Reiche—would not be consistent with the observed stability of helium; second, he proved that the observed lowest term did not correspond to the $S_{\text{I}}$-term of Landé; third, on the basis of the recently observed ultraviolet spectrum of helium, he concluded against the assumption that the ground state of helium should be a $1S$-state, i.e., an $S$-state with circular orbit (Kemble, 1921). In order to resolve these difficulties, Kemble proposed another model, in which the coordinates of the two electrons (denoted by subscripts 1 and 2) satisfied a symmetry condition with respect to an axis, say, the $z$-axis,

$$
x_2 = -x_1, \quad y_2 = -y_1, \quad \text{and} \quad z_2 = z_1. \tag{198}
$$

Kemble concluded his analysis of the helium model by saying that ‘the calculation of the energy [of the new model] promises to be a very tedious task, and has not yet been carried through. If the computed energy of the model proves not to

IV.2 The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems 405

be the same as the experimentally determined energy of the normal atom, a reconsideration of the hypotheses on which the energies of the various models have hitherto been calculated may be necessary' (Kemble, 1921, p. 133).$^{667}$

Further experimental work on the excitation potentials of helium in electron collisions by Frank Horton and Ann Davies (1921) seemed to support Langmuir's assumption that all electrons in the normal atoms of inert gases are arranged in peculiarly stable and symmetrical groups of orbits, and to contradict the views of Franck and collaborators concerning the states of helium and their combination properties. Especially, Davies concluded from her experiments that several edges appeared in the current versus voltage curves obtained from electron–helium collisions between 21.2 and 25.2 V (the latter corresponded to the ionization potential), which could not be interpreted as being due to the excitation of successive lines of an ultraviolet series, caused by the return of an electron after displacement to successive outer orbits of the helium atom (Davies, 1922, p. 620). James Franck replied in detail to these criticisms in a paper submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in the beginning of September 1922 (Franck, 1922). He referred to the recent X-ray results of Theodore Lyman, who had reported—in a letter to *Nature*, which had appeared in late August—about the observation of helium emission lines having wavelengths of 584.4 Å, 537.1 Å and 517.7 Å, which he had associated with the main series of parhelium (Lyman, 1922). In his letter, Lyman had also drawn attention to the fact that the limit of the new series agreed with an ionization potential of about 24.5 V, which was 0.8 V below the hitherto adopted value. Franck now investigated the experimental conditions carefully and discovered indeed that the old electron collision experiments had yielded too high excitation and ionization potentials. Correcting for this systematic error, he arrived at a complete agreement between the results of the collision experiments and the spectroscopic data: the series limit of 502 Å of the Lyman series corresponded to the ionization potential of 24.5 to 24.6 V, and the strong line at 584.4 Å to an excitation potential of 21.2 V; a further weak line at 600.5 Å, which was forbidden by the selection rules, corresponded to an excitation potential of 20.55 V; finally, no transition line was associated with the excitation potential of 19.75 V because it was related to the excluded transition from a one-quantum parhelium to a two-quantum, metastable orbit of normal (i.e., ortho-) helium. Franck commented happily: 'Not only do the numerical values agree perfectly, but also the intensity ratio and the structure of the observed lines; the non-appearance of a line, which corresponds to the transformation voltage [19.75 Volts], and the complete absence of an ultraviolet principal series of ortho-helium, confirm fully the conclusions of Franck and Knipping and, therefore, also the new helium model of Bohr' (Franck, 1922, p. 157).

$^{667}$In order to make his model work, Kemble had also demanded a violation of the usual (Rubinowicz–Bohr) selection rules for the emission of radiation from the atom.

It should be mentioned here that I. Langmuir considered further models of the helium atom: in one of them, for instance, the two electrons moved on parallel orbits symmetrically with respect to the nucleus; it gave the wrong (too low) ionization potential (Langmuir, 1921a). Langmuir, therefore, also suggested to modify the method of applying quantum theory to atomic systems (Langmuir, 1921b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0040 -->

406 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

Niels Bohr, to whose model Franck referred in the above remarks, had occupied himself with an attempt to determine the structure of the helium atom and to explain the presence of two separate spectra—the parhelium and the ‘ortho-helium’ spectra—since fall 1916.$^{668}$ He had studied, in collaboration with Hendrik Kramers, the problem of the mutual perturbation of the two electrons. The results they obtained agreed, as Bohr indicated in his letter of 27 July 1919 to Sommerfeld, to some extent with those of Landé, but rested on totally different foundations. ‘In contrast to Landé we have assumed,’ he wrote, ‘that though the orbit of the inner electron is eccentric, still the average value of the energy of the inner electron (kinetic energy plus potential energy relative to the nucleus) remains unchanged . . . That we have nevertheless obtained the same agreement with the data as Landé, comes about due to the fact that we have determined the stationary states in a somewhat different manner’ (Bohr to Sommerfeld, 27 July 1919). Thus Bohr and Sommerfeld did not put the average value of the angular momentum of the outer electron equal to the integral multiples of $h/2\pi$ (like Landé); they just assumed that the total angular momentum possessed values of integral multiples of $h/2\pi$, while the inner electron—because of its eccentricity—had an angular momentum slightly smaller than $h/2\pi$. This assumption about the stationary states satisfied, as Bohr claimed, the selection rules and the analogy argument (i.e., the correspondence principle) relating classical and quantum theory. ‘Thus Kramers and I obtain, in contrast to Landé, a relation between the energy differences in the stationary states and the frequencies of the harmonic oscillations, into which the motion of the external electron can be decomposed, and this relation is analogous to the one between the energy and the frequency of the stationary states of a simple central system,’ he concluded, and added: ‘Unfortunately Kramers is sick now in Rotterdam, and it will therefore probably be some time before we shall have the opportunity of publishing our detailed calculations’ (Bohr to Sommerfeld, 27 July 1919).

The opportunity for publishing the results of Bohr and Kramers did not come very soon. Early in 1920 Bohr received a copy of the proof-sheets of Landé’s helium paper in the *Physikalische Zeitschrift*. In a letter to Landé, Bohr discussed the relation of Landé’s results to his own and Kramers’, especially the deviations between them, and stated: ‘On reading through your paper I have arrived at the opinion that this deviation arises from the difference in the approximation methods, and that your treatment is not particularly suited for the purpose under consideration’ (Bohr to Landé, 24 February 1920). He then argued that Landé had not considered all the terms necessary for his approximation; however, had he done so, he would have arrived at exactly the same results as he—Bohr—and Kramers had already obtained. Later on, Bohr invited Landé—who was personally very interested in visiting Copenhagen—to present his ideas on the spatial structure of atoms. Landé spoke at the Physical Society of Copenhagen in

---

IV.2 The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems 407

October 1920, and his treatment of the structure of diamond influenced Bohr’s new views concerning atomic structure, formulated in the letter to *Nature* of February 1921 (Bohr, 1921a). Still no paper by Bohr and Kramers on the helium atom appeared in print because the new experimental results, especially the discovery of the metastable state by Franck and Knipping, had to be incorporated into the calculations. Bohr, who was in constant touch with Franck, learned that the helium model with coplanar electron orbits would not admit a state in which the outer electron moved in a one-quantum orbit. ‘Like Landé, this point had escaped us until I looked for it directly, guided by the points of view gained from the alkali spectra,’ Bohr wrote in a letter to Ehrenfest, dated 28 March 1921.

In spite of the fact that Bohr and Kramers published no paper on their helium calculations in the years between 1916 and 1922, interested physicists like Sommerfeld, Landé and Ehrenfest got to know the basic assumptions and results of the Copenhagen approach. Thus, for example, Bohr explained to Ehrenfest the main differences between his and Landé’s approaches:

> In my opinion the reason for the occurrence of the two separate helium spectra cannot be sought for in a simple spatial quantization of a continuously connected class of motions, as Landé has assumed in his paper. First, a similar situation would show up also in the case of other atoms; and second, combinations between the two spectra would not be excluded on the basis of such an interpretation [as Landé’s]. It is exactly this absence of such combinations—even when external fields of force, which cause some of the missing combination lines within each of the two spectra, are absent—, which indicates to me beyond any doubt that one has to conclude from the two spectra the existence of two entirely different types of motion, separated from one another by forms of motion that cannot be sharply quantized, such as the ones investigated by Kramers and myself. (Bohr to Ehrenfest, 28 March 1921)

Bohr gave a detailed account of his and Kramers’ helium models in an unpublished manuscript of spring 1921 (which was connected with the report which Bohr intended to give at the third Solvay Conference at Brussels in April 1921). In this manuscript he devoted a full section to the helium problem (Bohr, 1977. pp. 122–139). He noted that the investigations of many possible motions of the two-electron atom had led Kramers and himself to consider only two simple, periodic cases: ‘In the first of these cases the electrons move through all times in one and the same plane, and in the second the planes of the orbits form with a high degree of approximation constantly a right angle with each other, the major axis of the inner orbit remaining perpendicular to the plane of the outer orbit’ (Bohr, 1977, p. 125).

In the first case, with the electrons moving in the same direction in the same plane, the calculation led to the energy states

$$W_{n,n_\phi} = -Rh \left( n - \frac{9}{32} \frac{1}{n_\phi} \right)^{-2} \qquad (199)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0042 -->

where $n$ and $n_\phi$ denote the principal and the angular momentum quantum numbers, respectively, of the outer electron. The result, Eq. (199), agreed approximately with the observed ortho-helium spectrum. Bohr also explained the nonexistence of the lowest state with $n = n_\phi = 1$ as not being consistent with the formal conditions of quantum theory.$^{669}$ He further mentioned that Kramers, just recently, i.e., in spring 1921, had studied the mechanical problem of equivalent noncoplanar orbits, i.e., a model of the lowest state of the parhelium system, in which the two electrons move symmetrically in (approximately) circular orbits, and had calculated an energy of $-5.85 W_{\text{H}}$, where $W_{\text{H}}$ is the energy of the hydrogen ground state. This energy corresponded to an ionization potential of 25.2 V.$^{670}$ 'Since this does not differ more from the observed value of 25.3 [Volts] than was to be expected from the degree of approximation, with which the calculation has hitherto been carried through,' Bohr noted, 'this result may be said to offer a more interesting support of the general ideas as regards the constitution of the normal state of the helium atom, and the interpretation of the ortho-helium and parhelium spectrum, exposed in the preceding' (Bohr, 1977, pp. 136–137). Then, for closer information, Bohr referred to a paper of Kramers, which was supposed to appear in the near future, but no paper on that subject was published in 1921 or early 1922. Bohr treated the structure of helium again in his lecture at the Physical Society of Copenhagen on 18 October 1921 (Bohr, 1921e) and in his fourth Wolfskehl lecture at Göttingen on 19 June 1922. On the latter occasion, he reported the same formula, Eq. (199), for the normal helium spectrum, and he claimed that it represented the $S$-states very well, the $P$-states fairly well, but the $D$-states not so well; he attributed the discrepancies of the $D$-states to the large relativity corrections of the inner electron. With respect to the energy calculation, Bohr quoted Kramers' most recent result, that is, about $5.52 W_{\text{H}}$, and remarked: 'So far, this result is not very satisfactory; the energy comes out too small. This is perhaps not so strange, since such an expansion of the energy in powers of the nuclear charge [as made by Kramers] may converge well for large values of $Z$, but not for $Z = 2$' (Bohr, 1977, pp. 386–387). On his return home to Copenhagen, Bohr informed his collaborator Kramers about his experiences in Göttingen. Especially, he wrote that Wolfgang Pauli would come to Copenhagen in October for about half a year, and added:

He is an excellent man in all respects and will most certainly be very helpful. He is at present in Hamburg with Lenz, but he was until recently in Göttingen where he has calculated on various problems together with Born; among other things, they have solved the problem of the helium orbits, and they have in all details verified our results, which I had outlined to Born in Berlin. Pauli has now carried through the calculations of $\text{H}_2^+$, and his results, which I do not know in detail, will very

**IV.2 The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems**  

atom, and is, I believe, at the moment busy looking at it by a method different from that used by you. He emphasized strongly that he was doing it only for his pleasure and that he, of course, would not publish anything before you have published your results. I have thought that perhaps it wouldn’t be amiss if you would think of writing a little note about it this summer. Also, we cannot wait much longer with publishing our calculations of the helium orbits. I am looking forward to discussing all this with you when you get home. (Bohr to Kramers, 15 July 1922)  

Pauli’s personal association with the helium problem had begun in Göttingen, where he went for the winter semester, 1921–1922. Towards the end of his stay in Göttingen he had entered into a collaboration with Max Born, in which they continued the earlier work of Born and Brody on perturbation theory.⁶⁷¹ Born and Brody, in a paper submitted in July 1921 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, had discussed the finite amplitude oscillations of a mechanical system and their quantization (Born and Brody, 1921b). They had approximated the mechanical systems (describing atoms and molecules) under consideration by an assembly of anharmonic oscillators and had integrated the equations of motion with the help of canonical transformations suggested by Poincaré in his book on celestial mechanics (Poincaré, 1892). They had then quantized the periodic solution with the help of the phase integral and had obtained a consistent quantum solution to the problem.⁶⁷² In continuing this work, the task consisted in developing a method which would allow one to find successive approximations for arbitrary mechanical systems, i.e., to establish a systematic quantum-theoretical perturbation scheme for the description of any atom or molecule. This scheme should then enable the physicists to compute, for example, the energy of atomic systems to a given accuracy. Born and Pauli pursued this task systematically in their paper, entitled ‘Über die Quantelung gestörter mechanischer Systeme’ (‘On the  

⁶⁷¹ About his joint work with Pauli, Born wrote to Albert Einstein as follows:  
Pauli has unfortunately gone to [Wilhelm] Lenz in Hamburg. We recently started work on a joint paper, a continuation of the one published in collaboration with Brody about the quantization of non-harmonic oscillators. The approximation method developed there can be applied to all systems where the unperturbed system is quasi-periodic and the perturbation function can be developed in powers of a parameter. The case when the unperturbed system is degenerate can also be included and leads precisely to Bohr’s method of secular perturbations … Pauli took the paper to Hamburg with him and wants to finish it there. I cannot find the time because of the Encyclopaedia article [on crystal dynamics (Born, 1923b)]. (Born to Einstein, 30 April 1922)  
Pauli’s main duty at Göttingen during the winter semester, 1921–1922, had been to give lectures when Born—hindered by heavy asthmatic attacks—could not do so, something which happened often at that time (see Born to Einstein, 29 November 1921; Hedwig Born to Elsa Einstein, 7 January 1922). Pauli performed his duties to the satisfaction of people in Göttingen, for as Born reported: ‘Pauli is deputising for me, and seems to be doing quite well in spite of his mere twenty-one years’ (Born to Einstein, 29 November 1921). However, Pauli had some difficulty with the time of lectures, which was from 11 a.m. to 12 noon. As Born recalled: ‘He was inclined to forget it, and if our maid was sent to remind him at half past ten, she usually found him sound asleep. For he worked till late at night, and although a place like Göttingen is accustomed to all kinds of strange people, Pauli’s neighbours were worried to watch him sitting at his desk, rocking slowly like a praying Buddha, until the small hours of the morning’ (Born, 1978, p. 212). In Göttingen Pauli completed the paper based on his thesis on the hydrogen molecule-ion (Pauli, 1922).  
⁶⁷² An application of this method to calculate the high temperature behaviour of the specific heat of solids appeared to account successfully for the observations (Born and Brody, 1921a, 1922a).

where $W$ denotes the energy of the perturbed system, with $W = W(J_k)$. Born and Pauli assumed further that $S$ could be expanded in a power series in $\lambda$ as well, i.e.,

$$S = \sum_{k=1}^f J_k w_k^0 + \lambda S_1 + \lambda^2 S_2 + \dots, \tag{203}$$

where the $S_1, S_2, \dots$ were periodic functions of the angles $w_k^0$, and that an expansion in $\lambda$ also existed for the energy $W$. Then they substituted these expansions in Eq. (202) and derived a set of (partial differential) equations, one for each power of $\lambda$. The first few equations, i.e., those in the orders, $\lambda^0$, $\lambda$ and $\lambda^2$, took the form

$$H_0(J_k) = W_0, \tag{204a}$$

$$\sum_{k=1}^f \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_k^0} + H_1(J_k, w_k^0) = W_1, \tag{204b}$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=1}^f \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_2}{\partial w_k^0} &+ \sum_{k,j=1}^f \frac{1}{2!} \frac{\partial^2 H_0}{\partial J_k \partial J_j} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_k^0} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_j^0} \\
&+ \sum_{k=1}^f \frac{\partial H_1}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_k^0} + H_2(J_k, w_k^0) = W_2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{204c}
$$

In Eqs. (204a, b, c), expressing the perturbation scheme for nondegenerate (unperturbed) systems, the functions $H_i(J_k, w_k^0)$, $i = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, denoted the functions obtained by replacing the (unperturbed) action variable $J_k^0$ in $H_i(J_k^0, w_k^0)$ by the action variable $J_k$. Now Eq. (204a) just stated the fact that in the zeroth approximation the energy of the system, $W_0 = W_0(J_k)$, equalled the energy of the unperturbed system, $H_0(J_k) = H_0(J_k^0)$. Equation (204b), on the other hand, allowed one to calculate the unknown functions $S_1$ and $W_1$ in the following way. By averaging over a full period of the angles, $w_k^0$, Born and Pauli found the result

$$W_1(J_k) = \overline{H}_1, \tag{205a}$$

where $\overline{H}_1$ denoted the average of $H_1(w_k^0, J_k)$ over $w_k^0$. $S_1$, the periodic function in $w_k^0$, then had to satisfy the equation

$$\sum_{k=1}^f \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_k^0} = \overline{H}_1 - H_1(J_k, w_k^0). \tag{205b}$$

Similarly, the second-order equation (204c) yielded the second-order perturbation energy, $W_2$, according to the equation

$$W_2 = \overline{\Phi}_2, \tag{206a}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0046 -->

412 & Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models\

where $\overline{\Phi}_2$ denoted the average (over $w_k^0$) of the last three terms on the left-hand side of Eq. (204c); and the action function, $S_2$, followed from the partial differential equation

$$\sum \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_2}{\partial w_k^0} = \overline{\Phi}_2 - \Phi_2(w_k^0, J_k). \tag{206b}$$

With these results Born and Pauli confirmed Bohr and Kramers' previous findings: first, that the energy of the perturbed system, in the first approximation, was given by the energy of the unperturbed system plus the time average of the perturbation term over the unperturbed motion ($w_k^0$); second, that the changes of the energy (and of the other variables) were small and no *secular* perturbations arose. The reason for the absence of secular motions followed from Eq. (205b): since its right-hand side was a periodic function of the $w_k^0$, say a Fourier sum, $\sum A_{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_f} \exp \{ 2\pi i (\tau_1 w_1^0 + \cdots + \tau_f w_f^0) \}$, without a constant term, it could be integrated to yield

$$S_1 = \sum_{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_f} \frac{1}{2\pi i} \frac{A_{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_f}}{\tau_1 \nu_1^0 + \cdots + \tau_f \nu_f^0} \exp \{ 2\pi i (\tau_1 w_1^0 + \cdots + \tau_f w_f^0) \}. \tag{207}$$

As long as the denominator is not zero, the function $S_1$ turns out to be finite. In the case of a degenerate unperturbed system, however, this conclusion cannot be drawn.

In the case of systems satisfying Eq. (200) one is able to introduce such action and angle variables, $J_k^0$ and $w_k^0$, that the Hamiltonian depends only on fewer than $f$ action variables, say on $J_\alpha$, $\alpha = 1, \dots, \rho$ (with $\rho < f$). The variables, $J_\sigma^0$ and $w_\sigma^0$, with $\sigma = \rho + 1, \dots, f$, are then called 'degenerate' variables. However, since they do not determine the dynamics of the motion, they are not well-defined. Further, it can be seen immediately that the first-order perturbation equation (204b) does not lead to a function $W_1$, which is independent of all angles $w_k$, for in the first term on the right-hand side only the angles $w_\alpha^0$, $\alpha = 1, \dots, \rho$, enter. In order to remove these difficulties, Bohr had proposed to apply the method of secular perturbations, which was known from classical astronomy (Bohr, 1918b, p. 45 and the following discussion). This method implied as a first step to change the original variables, $J_k^0$ and $w_k^0$, to new variables, $\overline{J_k^0}$ and $\overline{w_k^0}$, by a canonical transformation generated by an action function $G$,

$$G = \sum_{k=1} \overline{J_k^0} w_k^0 + F_0(\overline{J_k^0}, w_\sigma^0). \tag{208}$$

The function $F_0(\overline{J_k^0}, w_\sigma^0)$ depends only on the degenerate variables of the system and will be determined by the partial differential equation

$$\hat{H} \left( \overline{J_\alpha^0} = J_\alpha^0, \overline{J_\sigma^0} = \frac{\partial F_0}{\partial w_\sigma^0}, w_\sigma^0 \right) = W_1 = W_1(\overline{J_k^0}), \tag{209}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0047 -->

IV.2  The Helium Atom and Other Few-Body Problems                              413

where \(\hat{H}\) represents the average of \(H_1(\overline{J_k^0}, w_k^0)\) over the nondegenerate angle variables \(w_{\alpha}\), \(\alpha = 1, \ldots, \rho\). Born and Pauli then proposed a classification of the degenerate systems into two types. They assumed that \(F_0\) could be obtained as a separable function in the variables \(w_{\sigma}^0\), i.e., \(F_0 = \sum F_{\sigma}^0\) (with each \(F_{\sigma}^0\) depending only on one angle, \(w_{\sigma}^0\)) and studied the individual differential quotients, \(\partial F_{\sigma}^0 / \partial w_{\sigma}^0\), as functions of \(w_{\sigma}^0\): this led either to closed curves, with \(w_{\sigma}^0\) oscillating in an interval smaller than the one between 0 and 1, or to periodic curves in \(w_{\sigma}^0\) with period 1. In the first case the system described what they called a ‘libration,’ in the latter a ‘rotation.’\( ^{673}\) For librating systems the new action variables were given by the path integrals over closed curves, i.e., \(\oint J_{\sigma}^0 \, dw_{\sigma}^0\), and for rotating systems by the path integrals, \(\int_0^1 J_{\sigma}^0 \, dw_{\sigma}^0\), in the old variables. The changes in the degenerate position variables, though caused by small perturbing forces, did not turn out to be small at all. However, the frequencies, \(\nu_{\sigma}^0\), which were previously zero, changed into small frequencies \(\overline{\nu_{\sigma}^0}\), where

\[
\overline{\nu_{\sigma}^0} = \frac{d \overline{w_{\sigma}^0}}{d t} = \lambda \frac{\partial W_1}{\partial \overline{J_{\sigma}^0}} \, . \tag{210}
\]

Born and Pauli then remarked: ‘Perturbations having the same character as the ones considered here are called *secular* in celestial mechanics. *Hence we recognize that they are connected with the degeneracy of the unperturbed system*’ (Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 149). The introduction of the secular perturbations then allowed them to quantize the degrees of freedom properly in agreement with the known principles of quantum theory, especially the adiabatic hypothesis. Born and Pauli noted that if Eq. (209) did not admit a solution by the method of the separation of variables, the above steps could not be taken and the system could not be properly quantized.

After the transformation with the action function \(G\), as in Eq. (208), the unperturbed system was not degenerate anymore; hence it was possible to take over the perturbation scheme given by Eqs. (204a, b, c), etc. However, in carrying through the approximation steps, there occurred a few changes. First, through Eq. (205b) the term with the action function \(S_1\) was determined only up to a function \(G_1(J_k, \overline{w_{\sigma}^0})\), which had to be determined from the equation of the next order, i.e.,

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{f} \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_2}{\partial \overline{w_k^0}} + \Phi_2\left(J_k, \overline{w_k^0}\right) + \sum_{\sigma=\rho+1}^{f} \frac{\partial H_1}{\partial J_{\sigma}} \frac{\partial G_1}{\partial \overline{w_{\sigma}^0}} = W_2. \tag{211}
\]

By averaging over all \(\overline{w_k^0}\) on the left-hand side of this equation, Born and Pauli obtained the second-order energy correction \(W_2\). \(G_1\), however, followed from the

\[
^{673}\text{For special values of the integration constants (i.e., the action variables) a third possibility might occur: the two libration limits do not coincide. This case, however, was not considered further by Born and Pauli.}
\]

414 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

equation

$$ \sum_{\sigma=\rho+1}^{f} \frac{\partial H_1}{\partial J_\sigma} \frac{\partial G_1}{\partial \overline{w_\sigma^0}} = \overline{\Phi}_2 - \hat{\Phi}_2; \qquad (212a) $$

and, finally, $S_2$ from the equation

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{f} \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J_k} \frac{\partial S_2}{\partial \overline{w_k^0}} = \overline{\Phi}_2 - \Phi_2, \qquad (212b) $$

again only up to a function $G_2(J_k, \overline{w_\sigma^0})$, which could be determined from the perturbation equation of the next higher order. The functions $\hat{\Phi}_2$ and $\overline{\Phi}_2$ were derived from the function $\Phi_2$: to obtain $\hat{\Phi}_2$ one had just to average in $\Phi_2$ over the variables $w_\alpha, \alpha = 1, \ldots, \rho$; to obtain $\overline{\Phi}_2$, however one had to average in $\Phi_2$ over *all* angle variables $w_k^0, k = 1, \ldots, f$.

Born and Pauli summarized the results of their perturbation scheme for atomic systems in three statements:

1. Upon the secular perturbation, which has been discussed above in detail, is superimposed still another one of short period, having the same character as the perturbations of the nondegenerate original system. 2. The already quantized $\rho$ variables $J_k^0$ of the nonperturbed system do not suffer any secular perturbation, but only one of a short period. 3. The terms $H'_1$ of $H_1$, which still depend on $w_k^0$, if expressed as a function of the quantum numbers, contribute only a term of the higher (second) order to the *energy*, though they occur already in the first order in the *motion* of the mechanical system. (Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 151)$^{674}$

They also argued that all systems, in which the frequencies $\nu_k^0$ nearly satisfied Eq. (200)—i.e., up to a term of order $\lambda$—had to be treated like degenerate ones. While in astronomy that situation seemed to occur in the case of the small planets, Born and Pauli tried to explain with its help certain ‘perturbations’ of the band lines, which could not be accounted for by the usual (Deslandres) formula. Such perturbations occurred only for certain special values of the rotational quantum number of the molecules, in agreement with the theoretical expectation that the system should be nearly degenerate only for specific values of the action variables $J_k^0$.

Born and Pauli completed their discussion of the perturbation theory for quantum systems by a discussion of convergence. It had been demonstrated earlier in celestial mechanics that the series for the action function, Eq. (203), never converged in the strict mathematical sense because for large values of the

$^{674}$These results agreed with the known results of celestial mechanics, as Born and Pauli did not fail to point out in their paper. For example, from their scheme they immediately proved a theorem of Laplace concerning the independence of the semi-major axis of planets from secular perturbations. (The reason for this was that the semi-major axis was determined already by the unperturbed Hamiltonian.)

on the invariant plane had a phase difference of $180^\circ$.<sup>675</sup> By the last assumption the mutual perturbation of the electrons on each other were minimized, and Kramers argued: ‘Considered from the point of view of energy, our assumption therefore implies a postulate of stability’ (Kramers, 1923a, p. 313). At the same time, however, he was aware of the fact that the stability assumption made sense only if the electron–electron interaction could be considered small in comparison to the electron–nucleus interaction. Although this condition did not appear to be satisfied at all in the case of helium, Kramers hoped to go along with it. He even put forward an argument in its favour: one might treat, he proposed, instead of the two-electron atom a system in which the electron–electron interaction was multiplied by a constant $\lambda$, much less than unity, and then the stability assumption made sense; then, by adiabatically increasing $\lambda$ to unity the helium system was obtained, and the adiabatic hypothesis ensured that the quantum states of the real helium system possessed the same structure as the quantum states of the system with weak electron–electron interactions. For the actual calculation, Kramers replaced his helium model by an *Ersatz* system: it consisted of an electron which moved under the influence of the nucleus (of charge $Z|e|$) at the distance $R$, subject to a repulsive force, which was inversely proportional to the distance $r$ from the $z$-axis. The potential energy of the electron was then given by the equation

$$
V = -\frac{Ze^2}{R} + \frac{e^2}{4r} . \tag{213}
$$

To obtain the energy of the helium atom, one had just to double the potential and kinetic energies of the *Ersatz* system.

Evidently, the *Ersatz* system possessed the angular momentum of the electron around the $z$-axis as a constant of motion. According to Kramers’ model for the ground state of the helium atom, this angular momentum (i.e., the projection of the electron’s angular momentum on the $z$-axis, the angle between the angular momentum axis and the $z$-axis being $60^\circ$) assumed the value $\frac{1}{2} h/2\pi$. Thus, in the zeroth approximation—where the second term of the potential in Eq. (213) was neglected, and only the electron–nucleus interaction retained—Kramers found that the energy of the *Ersatz* system became equal to $Z^2W_{\text{H}}$, $W_{\text{H}} (= -2\pi^2 m_e e^4/h^2)$ being the (negative) energy of the hydrogen ground state. In the first approximation, the perturbation term in the potential, Eq. (213), had to be averaged over the unperturbed motion, and Kramers calculated the following (positive) contribution to the energy:

$$
W_1 = \frac{e^2}{4R} \bar{g} = -\frac{\bar{g}}{2} ZW_{\text{H}}, \tag{214}
$$

<sup>675</sup>Kramers’ model agreed with the one proposed in the earlier paper of Edwin Kemble (1921). In his lecture at Copenhagen on 18 October 1921, Bohr remarked: ‘Previous to the appearance of this paper [Kemble’s] Kramers commenced a closer investigation of precisely this type of motion in order to find out to what extent it was possible from such a calculation to account for the firmness with which the electrons are bound in the helium atom, that is to account for the ionization potential’ (Bohr, 1921e; English translation in Bohr, 1977, p. 290).

$$g = \left[1 - \frac{3}{4} \sin^2(\omega t)\right]^{-1/2}, \tag{214a}$$
where $\omega = 2\pi/T$, $T$ being the period of motion in the *Ersatz* model. By averaging over $g/2$, a factor of 1.32788 was obtained. Thus there resulted an expression for the energy, whose terms were multiplied by powers of $Z^{-1}$. Kramers realized, of course, that for helium, where $Z = 2$, the convergence of the consecutive approximation steps was very poor. In order to improve upon it, he proposed to rewrite the potential, Eq. (213), as
$$V = \left[ - \frac{(Z - \alpha)e^2}{R} + \frac{C}{r^2} \right] - \frac{\alpha e^2}{R} - \frac{C}{r^2} + \frac{e^2}{4r} . \tag{215}$$
Now taking as the unperturbed system the one with the potential given by the two terms within the square brackets on the right-hand side of Eq. (215), he calculated its energy as
$$W_0 = (Z - \alpha - \beta)^2 W_{\text{H}}, \tag{216}$$
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ were constants, the latter being related to the constant $C$ in Eq. (215) as, $\beta = 32\pi^2 m_e ZC / h^2$. In the first approximation, Kramers had to average the perturbation terms again over the unperturbed motion (which corresponded to a Kepler motion around a nucleus with charge $(Z - \alpha)|e|$ with a reduced velocity), obtaining $W_1$ as the contribution to the energy, where
$$W_1 = - \frac{W_{\text{H}}}{Z} \left[ - \alpha \frac{\beta}{2} \overline{g^2} + \frac{1}{4} \bar{g} \right], \tag{217}$$
with $g$ being given by Eq. (214a). Finally, Kramers determined the constants $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in such a way that the interaction term in Eq. (215) was minimal.$^{676}$ This procedure yielded the values $\alpha = 0.078$ and $\beta = 0.133$ in the case of $Z = 2$, which resulted in a first-order energy value of
$$W_{\text{He}} = + 5.526266 W_{\text{H}}. \tag{218}$$
Unfortunately this method could not be extended to higher approximations. Hence Kramers developed still another procedure to calculate the energy of the helium ground state up to arbitrarily high order. Especially, he introduced a sequence of canonical transformations, by which he transformed the coordinates of the two-electron system to action-angle variables. Thus he finally found a second-order correction to the energy, Eq. (218), namely, $W_2 = - 0.002719 W_{\text{H}}$,

Kramers devoted the final, fourth section of his paper to an analysis of the stability of the model, used for the helium ground state, against perturbations of the initial positions and velocities of the electrons. This analysis, which he carried out just for the simplified case in which the electron–electron interactions were neglected, required a generalization of the computational method: the positions of the displaced electrons could not be considered as being symmetric to the $z$-axis. Kramers arrived at the unsatisfactory conclusion that the motion of the electrons in two equivalent orbits was unstable against phase shifts. Thus he summarized his results as follows:

> The calculations . . . have led to the conclusion that in the model for the normal state of the helium atom, where two electrons move in one-quantum orbits having inclined orbital planes around the nucleus, the energy of the atoms turns out to be too high by 3.9 Volts in comparison to experience [i.e., instead of an ionization potential of 24.6 Volts, Kramers calculated the value of 20.7 Volts], provided one assumes that the motion in the state under consideration and its energy can be computed according to the ordinary mechanical laws. The calculations in the fourth section show that the quantum motion investigated is unstable in the mechanical sense. (Kramers, 1923a, p. 339)

Another physicist arrived at almost the same result as did Kramers in Copenhagen: this was John Hasbrouck Van Vleck, who then worked at Harvard University under the supervision of Edwin C. Kemble.⁶⁷⁷ In the United States, as in Europe, the helium problem had been discussed intensively following the theoretical investigations of Langmuir and Kemble. For example, Robert Andrews Millikan, renowned for his precision measurements of the charge of the electron (Millikan, 1913) and of Planck’s constant from the photoelectric effect (1916a, b, c), had compared the models that had hitherto been suggested with his data on the single and double ionization of helium by $\alpha$-rays (Millikan,

He hailed from an academically distinguished family—both his father, Edward Burr Van Vleck, and his grandfather, John Monroe Van Vleck, had occupied professorships in mathematics at Wesleyan University. John H. Van Vleck studied at the University of Wisconsin, Madison (1916–1920), and at Harvard University (1920–1922), obtaining his doctorate in 1922 under Edwin C. Kemble with a thesis on the helium atom. After a year as instructor at Harvard, he was offered an assistant professorship at the University of Minnesota. In 1926 he became an associate professor at Minnesota, and in 1927 a full professor. From the University of Minnesota he went to the University of Wisconsin (1928–1934), and finally to Harvard University (associate professor of mathematical physics, 1934–1935; professor, 1935; chairman of the physics department, 1945–1949; from 1951, Hollis Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy; Dean of Engineering and Applied Physics, 1951–1957). Van Vleck, who shared with Neville Francis Mott and Philip Warren Anderson the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physics, pioneered the quantum-theoretical description of the magnetic properties of matter. He died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on 27 October 1980.

1921b).$^{678}$ He had found that Bohr's two-electron ring model could not be correct, for it offered no chance of ejecting both electrons; also the models used by Sommerfeld, Landé, and Franck and Reiche, in which an electron moved in a narrow orbit around the nucleus, did not predict as much double ionization of helium as was observed in experiments with electron impacts. Thus he had concluded:

> *In a word, the fact that every sixth shot [of α-particles] which detaches any electron at all from the atom, gets them both, demands that both electrons find themselves in the same part of the atomic volume a very appreciable fraction of the time [Millikan's emphasis]. This condition is well satisfied by the recent theories of Landé and Bohr, according to which the two electrons are in orbits of much the same diameter but inclined to each other at angles of $60^\circ$ or $90^\circ$. (Millikan, 1921b, p. 459)*

Millikan, therefore favoured the Landé–Kramers model of the helium ground state involving two equivalent orbits. But he had not discussed the problem of the energy calculation. This problem was attacked by Van Vleck at about the same time: he performed a most laborious calculation of the energy of the helium ground state, based on Kemble's model of two electrons moving symmetrically (with respect to a fixed axis) on orbits whose planes made an angle with each other. He presented the result of his calculation first at the annual meeting of the American Physical Society, which was held in Toronto from 28 to 30 December 1921 (Van Vleck, 1922a). A detailed description of the mathematical method, which included the use of the Hamilton–Jacobi partial differential equation (as in the three-body problem of celestial mechanics), followed in a paper which appeared in the November issue of *Philosophical Magazine* (Van Vleck, 1922b). Van Vleck obtained the energy as an expansion in the quantity $w$, where $w^{1/2}$ denoted the sine of half the angle between the planes of the two electron orbits. By trial and error he determined the lowest energy to occur for the value $w = 0.7216$, corresponding to an angle of about $92^\circ$ between the two planes. The energy of the helium ground state thus obtained was 5.53 times the energy of the hydrogen ground state.

Van Vleck's method of calculating the helium energy was criticized by Kramers. He pointed especially to the fact that Van Vleck had dropped terms of third order in the perturbing forces, and remarked: 'The method used by Van

Vleck, which gives rise to extremely tedious calculations, must therefore be considered as being unsuitable for providing the intended test of the model (Kramers, 1923a, p. 317). Still, Kramers’ more accurate evaluation provided nearly the same result. Therefore, after the papers of Van Vleck and Kramers it could be concluded that the calculation of the energy of the ground state from the model of parhelium—i.e., the model with two electrons on equivalent (i.e., one-quantum) orbits—had failed to provide agreement with the observed result, namely, 5.807 times the energy of the hydrogen ground state. The difficulties in the theory of the two-electron atom turned out to be even worse, as was revealed by the subsequent analysis of the models for excited helium states by Max Born and Werner Heisenberg.

Max Born, who had been preoccupied in the first half of 1922 with the writing of his article on crystal dynamics for the *Encyklopädie* (Born, 1923b), resumed in the fall with fresh vigour the investigation of atomic and molecular models by the methods of systematic perturbation theory. In the winter semester, 1922–1923, he arranged a seminar on these questions at the University of Göttingen. In it, besides his regular students, such as Pascual Jordan, his new assistant Werner Heisenberg also participated. Heisenberg had gone to Göttingen to be with Born during the winter semester because his professor in Munich—Arnold Sommerfeld—had gone to the University of Wisconsin as a visiting professor. Heisenberg immediately collaborated with Born on an extension of the Born–Pauli perturbation scheme to account also for systems with ‘accidentally’ degenerate degrees of freedom, that is, for cases in which the unperturbed system possessed a vanishing frequency just for a particular value of the action variables (Born and Heisenberg, 1923a).<sup>679</sup> The accidental degeneracy led to the existence of certain phase relations in the motions of the electrons; hence it seemed to play a role in Max Born’s model of the hydrogen molecule (Born, 1922). Moreover, it (the accidental degeneracy) should occur again in the model of the helium ground state, in which the two electrons were on equivalent orbits, such as the cases treated by Kramers and Van Vleck. Having recently become very interested in the theory of the helium atom, Heisenberg enthusiastically joined Born in the development and application of the appropriate perturbation schemes.

Heisenberg had started to think about the helium problem as a consequence of Bohr’s Wolfskehl lectures at Göttingen in summer 1922. He had then tried, in particular, to evaluate the energy for a model, in which the two electrons moved on coplanar, equivalent orbits, whose action integrals assumed the value $\frac{1}{2} h$.<sup>680</sup> His preliminary calculation of October 1922 had yielded a value for the ionization potential (about 25 V) which agreed with the data much better than the one of Van Vleck. After his arrival in Göttingen, Heisenberg continued these calculations optimistically, now making use of the improved mathematical methods which he learned in Born’s seminar. In spite of satisfactory progress, however, he did not publish anything about the helium model with half-integral quantum

Instead Born drew him into a collaboration with a much more ambitious goal: the two of them studied and analyzed the most general models for the excited helium atom with the help of perturbation theory.$^{681}$ Born and Heisenberg succeeded in determining—just as Pauli had done earlier for the hydrogen molecule-ion—all quantum-theoretically admissible types of electron orbits. After performing the energy calculations in all cases and comparing the values thus obtained with the empirical terms, they concluded:

> Thus we arrive at the conclusion that a systematic quantum mechanical calculation of the helium problem leads to wrong values for the energy terms. There are only two ways out of this difficulty: Either the quantum conditions are wrong [i.e., the assumption that the action variables take on values that are only integral multiples of Planck’s constant], or the motion of the electron does not satisfy the mechanical equations even in the stationary states. Both of the ways out lead to fundamental difficulties in the understanding of the hitherto secured quantum-theoretical results. (Born and Heisenberg, 1923b, p. 243)$^{682}$

This conclusion agreed to some extent with the one arrived at by Bohr and his collaborators in Copenhagen.
The failure of Kramers’ detailed and painstaking evaluation of the helium ground state changed Bohr’s earlier optimism—still expressed in his Wolfskehl lectures or even in his Nobel address of early December 1922—that the available principles of quantum theory would enable one to treat such systems as the helium atom. Kramers expressed this change of opinion in his helium paper as follows: ‘If we adopt for the time being the point of view that the model considered, i.e., two one-quantum orbits in crossed positions, is correct in its essential features, then we have to conclude from our calculations that already in this simple case mechanics has lost its validity’ (Kramers, 1923a, p. 340). Kramers and Bohr interpreted this result, however, not as due to the failure of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, but as due to the fact that in the procedure for calculating the energy states of the helium atom one had to abandon the range of validity of that theory. They argued that the energy of the helium atom depended on the process by which the second electron was bound in the helium atom. Kramers wrote:

> Even if we can describe the motion in the final state of the binding process exactly with the help of mechanics we could still not be certain that the energy function that occurs [in the equations] provides the physical energy, which is measured by observing the spectral terms and the ionizing potentials, because the identity of these two energies would be established strictly only when one considers a continuous connection between the state under consideration and the other stationary states of the atom. The impossibility of establishing such a connection is strongly

Thus the difference in the interpretation of the failure of the helium calculations between Copenhagen and Göttingen was this: while Bohr and Kramers still believed that the available principles of quantum theory could explain the failure, Born and Heisenberg called for new hypotheses to cure the situation.

In any case, the difficulties with the helium problem provided the first definite indication that atomic systems could not in general be treated by means of the theory of multiply periodic systems. In order to test this conclusion in the case of another few-body system, Lothar Wolfgang Nordheim discussed the hydrogen molecule models in his thesis at Göttingen.<sup>683</sup> For the calculations of the energy of the ground state, Nordheim made use especially of the perturbation method developed by Born and Heisenberg to treat accidentally degenerate systems (Nordheim, 1923a, 1924). Following an investigation of all possible types of motion, he arrived at completely negative conclusions: he found three models yielding stable equilibrium for the two nuclei, but they did not provide a satisfactory description of the observation on the distances of the nuclei and the binding energy; among these models the old Bohr–Debye model with the two-electron ring was still the best, while other models proved to be instable (Nordheim, 1923b). Thus the same situation as in the case of helium showed up again in the hydrogen molecule. In the course of the year 1923, further, even more serious, difficulties with the available quantum theory of atomic structure were revealed by two other theoretical investigations: Wolfgang Pauli's analysis of the anomalous Zeeman effects and the treatment by several authors of the hydrogen atom in crossed electric and magnetic fields. However, before presenting these difficulties, we shall turn to some important experimental results which also offered puzzles in their quantum-theoretical interpretation.

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect

The experimental and theoretical investigations of the spectra of atoms and molecules and their explanation formed the mainstream of progress in atomic physics in the early 1920s. Besides, several new, partly unexpected properties of atoms and their constituents, the electrons, were discovered: in particular, the so-called magnetic anomaly of the electron and the discrete spatial orientation of

Although these effects seemed to fit—at least qualitatively—into the picture of quantum phenomena, they gave rise to serious questions about the validity of the existing theory. We shall now discuss certain important observations and their attempted interpretation, which illuminate some vital aspects of the quantum theory around 1922 and are also related to the topic treated in the next section, the anomalous Zeeman effects and the complex structure of spectral lines.

Let us first turn to the magnetic effects created by the electrons moving on orbits in atoms. The fact that closed currents possess a magnetic moment had been observed and enunciated by André Marie Ampère in the early nineteenth century: he had noted that in ferromagnetic metals there exist permanent ‘molecular currents’—i.e., circular currents around atoms—whose axes possessed randomly oriented directions in space for a nonmagnetic sample, but in an external magnetic field they oriented themselves parallel to it (Ampère, 1822). With the advent of the electron theory, Ampère’s suggestion of molecular currents was attributed to rotating electrons, with the help of which Joseph Larmor explained the phenomenon of the (normal) Zeeman effect (Larmor, 1897a). Woldemar Voigt then discussed the magnetic properties of matter on the basis of electron theory and was able to account for the diamagnetism of substances (Voigt, 1901b). Paul Langevin extended the theory to describe para-magnetism as well: he assumed that the electrons in atoms and molecules moved in orbits; if the orbits were symmetrically distributed such that their magnetic moments cancelled, the substance exhibited diamagnetism; otherwise, if a residual magnetic moment of atoms or molecules remained, the substance showed paramagnetism (Langevin, 1905).<sup>684</sup> According to Langevin’s theory, purely diamagnetic substances assumed a temperature-independent susceptibility $\chi$ (i.e., the ratio of magnetization over the magnetic field strength) per unit volume, given by the equation

$$
\chi = - \frac{N e^2 r^2}{4 m_e c^2}, \tag{220}
$$

where $N$ is the number of molecules (or atoms) per cubic centimetre, $e$ and $m_e$

<sup>684</sup> Paul Langevin was born on 23 January 1872 at Paris. He was educated at the *École de Physique et de Chimie*, Paris (1888–1891) and at the *École Normale Supérieure* (1894–1897). He spent the year 1897–1898 as a research fellow with J. J. Thomson at Cambridge. From 1898 to 1902 he was at the University of Paris (1900–1902, *préparateur*; 1902, *Docteur-ès-science*, with a thesis on the recombination and mobility of gaseous ions). Then he joined the *Collège de France* (1902–1903: *professeur remplaçant*; 1903–1909: *professeur suppléant*; 1909–1946: *professeur titulaire*). At the same time he served as professor (1905–1926) and director (1926–1940) of the *École de Physique et de Chimie*. He died on 19 December 1946 in Paris.

Langevin worked both experimentally and theoretically, especially on problems of atomic and molecular physics, relativity and quantum theory. He was a brilliant teacher and trained many students. He received many honours, including the Fellowship of the Royal Society and its Hughes and Copley medals (1915 and 1940, respectively). After the death of Hendrik Lorentz, he served from 1928 to 1946 as President of the Scientific Committee of the International Solvay Institute for Physics, Brussels, Belgium.

In the case of not too large magnetic fields, Langevin obtained the approximate relation

$$\chi = \frac{N\mu^2}{3kT} , \tag{221}$$

$k$ being Boltzmann's constant. Thus, from Eq. (221), Pierre Curie's law, stating that the susceptibility of paramagnetic substances is inversely proportional to the absolute temperature $T$, followed immediately. For very high magnetic fields the susceptibility will decrease, because all elementary magnets are parallel-oriented and the magnetization per cubic centimetre cannot exceed the value $N\mu$, whatever the strength of the external field may be.$^{686}$ In 1907 Pierre Weiss generalized Langevin's theory to describe also the magnetic properties of ferromagnetic substances by associating an intrinsic, 'internal' or 'molecular,' field with them: i.e., in Langevin's function, representing the magnetization as a function of the external magnetic field **H**, he replaced the latter by the sum **H** + **H**$_i$, **H**$_i$ being a strong internal field of the substance, which creates a 'spontaneous' magnetization independent of **H** (Weiss, 1907).$^{687}$ Finally, in 1911, Weiss introduced quantum theory in the description of the magnetic properties of matter by demonstrating that the maximum magnetization (the so-called saturation value at an infinitely large external magnetic field) of a gram-atom of ferromagnetic substances could be expressed as integral multiples of what he called the gram-magneton ('Grammagneton,' Weiss, 1911, p. 941).

Ampère's assumption of 'molecular currents' or the modern version of it, namely, the electrons orbiting in atoms, thus described the magnetic properties of substances rather well. However, there now arose the problem of explaining the existence of permanent closed currents in atoms. Especially, classical electrodynamics could not account for electrons moving in circular orbits without losing energy by radiation. But in quantum theory a possibility did seem to show up: due to Planck's second hypothesis of 1911, any quantum system at the absolute
