he was looking for was the converse of the effect predicted and looked for by Richardson. ‘And it became apparent,’ he remarked later, ‘that both effects were immediate consequences of an idea advanced long ago according to which a magnet must behave like a gyrostat if the Ampèrian currents consist in the motion of actual matter’ (Barnett, 1915, p. 241).$^{690}$ While preliminary experiments seemed to confirm Barnett’s effect (Barnett, 1909), it disappeared in later observations (see the later report in Barnett, 1915, p. 240). But Barnett did not give up: from fall 1913 to spring 1915 he reported on the continuation of his experiments at meetings of the American Physical Society (November 1913, December 1914 and April 1915) and of the Ohio Academy of Sciences (November 1914), which indeed revealed a positive effect and allowed him to measure its magnitude. He published a long paper on it in the October issue of the *Physical Review* (Barnett, 1915).

On 19 February 1915, at a meeting of the German Physical Society in Berlin, Albert Einstein and Wander Johannes de Haas presented the results of a joint experiment dealing with the ‘direct proof of Ampèrian molecular currents’ (see their note in *Verhandlungen der Deutschen Physikalischen Gesellschaft* **17**, 1915, p. 63). De Haas had come over to Berlin from Holland to perform the experiments at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*.$^{691}$ The basic idea of the Einstein–de Haas experiment was extremely simple. An electron of charge $e$, moving with frequency $\nu$ on a circular orbit enclosing an area $F$, creates a magnetic moment $\mu$ normal to $F$, having the magnitude

$$|\mu| = |e|\nu F. \tag{222}$$

On the other hand, according to classical dynamics the electron possesses an angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$, whose direction is the same as that of the magnetic moment $\mu$ and whose magnitude is given by the equation

$$|\mathbf{M}| = 2m_e \nu F, \tag{223}$$

$^{690}$Barnett referred to James Clerk Maxwell, who, in the second volume of his *Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism* (Maxwell, 1873, §575), had discussed the plan for such an experiment and described the apparatus, which he had devised in 1861 for that purpose. Barnett’s idea of producing magnetism by rotation had also been mentioned earlier—in the same context of terrestrial magnetism —by Sir Arthur Schuster in 1901. (See Schuster, 1912.)

$^{691}$W. J. de Haas was born on 2 March 1878 at Lisse (north of Leyden). He was educated at the University of Leyden from 1895 to 1911, his professors being Hendrik Lorentz and Heike Kamerlingh-Onnes. The latter supervised de Haas’ thesis on the compressibility of hydrogen. After graduating with a doctorate in 1911 de Haas spent two years at the Bosscha Laboratory in Berlin as a private assistant to Henri du Bois (1863–1918). Then he served as a physics teacher at the Royal Academy (1913–1915) and the Deventer Secondary School (1915–1916). From 1916 to 1917 he was curator at Teyler’s Museum, Haarlem. In 1917 he accepted the call as professor of physics from the Technical University of Delft; in 1922 he moved as professor to the University of Groningen, and two years later he finally went to the University of Leyden as director of the cryogenic laboratory—later called the Kamerlingh-Onnes Laboratory—together with Willem Hendrik Keesom. De Haas retired in 1958 and died on 26 April 1960 at Bilthoven.

Besides his fundamental work with Einstein on the gyromagnetic effect, de Haas’ main contributions to physics were concerned with the behaviour of metals at low temperatures. He also pioneered the approach for obtaining the lowest temperatures; especially, he obtained by adiabatic demagnetization a temperature of 0.0002 degree absolute.

where $m_e$ is the mass of the electron. In a macroscopic ferromagnetic substance, the magnetic moments of all electron orbits add up to the magnetization $\mathbf{I}$, and in the case of a fully magnetized sample all orbits are parallel-oriented, thus yielding the ratio

$$\frac{\mathbf{M}}{\mathbf{I}} = \frac{2m_e}{e} = -1.13 \times 10^{-7} \text{ cgs units,} \tag{224}$$

which is the same as in the case of a single electron orbit (if $\mathbf{I}$ is measured in electromagnetic units). From Eq. (224) Einstein and de Haas derived the relation for $d\mathbf{M}/dt$, the change of the angular momentum with time, as

$$-\frac{d\mathbf{M}}{dt} = 1.13 \times 10^{-7} \frac{d\mathbf{I}}{dt}, \tag{225}$$

which seemed to imply a very small effect. However, when they took a cylinder of magnetized iron (radius = $0.1 \text{ cm}$) and demagnetized it in the axial direction, they calculated for the resulting rotation of the cylinder an angular velocity of $0.6 \times 10^{-2} \text{ s}^{-1}$, a quantity which could indeed be measured. They suggested the following method of observation:

> A cylinder of soft iron is suspended from a thin string concentrically in such a way that the period of [torsional] oscillation amounts to several seconds. The cylinder is then surrounded concentrically by a solenoid, with the help of which the iron cylinder is magnetized along the direction parallel to its axis. The oscillations performed by the cylinder should be observed when the direction of the [electric] current in the solenoid is commuted, i.e., when the magnetization in the cylinder is reversed. (Einstein and de Haas, 1915, pp. 156–157)

In order to enhance the observed effect they proposed to magnetize and demagnetize the cylinder periodically, choosing as the frequency of the electric current in the rod the frequency of the mechanical (torsional) oscillations of the suspended cylinder. Einstein and de Haas then measured the amplitude of the resonance oscillation of the system, whose magnitude was proportional to the ratio $\mathbf{M}/\mathbf{I}$. Thus they found the result

$$\frac{\mathbf{M}}{\mathbf{I}} = -1.11 \times 10^{-7}, \tag{224a}$$

which was very close to the theoretical value of $-1.13 \times 10^{-7}$. They concluded: ‘Even if the excellence of the agreement may be attributed to chance—since our determination must have an error of about 10 percent—, it has been shown in any case that the consequence of the theory of orbiting electrons, described in the beginning, is confirmed—at least in good approximation—even quantitatively by the experiment’ (Einstein and de Haas, 1915, p. 170).

The last remark about the accuracy of Einstein and de Haas’ experiment seemed to be surprising if it were compared to the result of another experiment which also yielded the ratio $\mathbf{M}/\mathbf{I}$. As we have mentioned earlier, Samuel Barnett

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0062 -->

428 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

had investigated over several years the magnetization $\mathbf{I}$ created in a cylindrical rod by rotation, having an angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$. In his paper of fall 1915 he gave the following result (Barnett, 1915, p. 270)$^{692}$:

$$ \frac{\mathbf{M}}{\mathbf{I}} = -0.5 \times 10^{-7}. \tag{224b} $$

The question, therefore, had to be asked whether the results of the two experiments of Einstein and de Haas and of Barnett were compatible. To answer this question, both Einstein and de Haas, on one hand, and Barnett, on the other, tried to improve their methods (Einstein, 1916b; de Haas, 1916; Barnett, 1917). Now de Haas completely confirmed his earlier finding and noted that 'the quantitative agreement between experiment and theory is satisfactory' (de Haas, 1916, p. 424). It was important, however, that Barnett also came to the same conclusion, and he commented on the difference between his old and new measurements: 'But the experimental errors, on account of the great difficulties involved, are such that importance cannot in my opinion be attached to the discrepancies' (Barnett, 1917, p. 21). Thus agreement was reached about the existence of the gyromagnetic effect and its magnitude. Especially, the ratio $\mathbf{M/I}$ was given by the classical value $2m_e/e$, as in Eq. (224).

A year later John Q. Stewart of Princeton University, who studied the same effect as Einstein and de Haas with a slightly different apparatus, arrived at another result, and he noted: 'The magnitude of the effect is only half that Richardson supposed would result from such rotation of negative electrons [on the basis of the classical theory]' (Stewart, 1918, p. 118). That is, he argued in favour of a value, which was about the same as the one obtained by Barnett in 1915. Thus the question concerning the real value of the gyromagnetic ratio appeared to be open again, but it was answered very soon by two independent investigations: those of Emil Beck from the *Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule*, Zurich, and of Gustav Arvidsson from the University of Uppsala. Beck improved upon the previous methods of Einstein and de Haas by observing the entire resonance curve of oscillating iron and nickel cylinders and found that his measurements gave too small an angular momentum, as compared to Eq. (224), with the known values of the charge and mass of the electron (Beck, 1919a, b). Beck noted:

> The quantity $m_e/e$ [as obtained from the experiment with the help of Eq. (224)] turned out to be too small for iron by 47% and too small for nickel by 43%. By that much would then the angular momentum of the molecules be smaller than one would expect if one assumes that electrons of known properties [i.e., given $m_e/e$] orbit within the molecules. (Beck, 1919b, p. 491)

This conclusion was confirmed completely by Arvidsson, who published his work a little later (Arvidsson, 1920). Finally, Samuel Barnett, together with his wife, repeated the investigation of his effect in the following years. They discovered

The implication and physical interpretation of the above result on the gyromagnetic ratio **M/I** did not seem to be immediately evident. Thus Emil Beck suggested in his paper the following possibilities:

> One must therefore assume either that in the case of Ampère’s molecular currents electrons of a special kind are involved, or else that the situation is not so simple as supposed in the theory. It should not be surprising if the latter were true, considering how complicated the magnetic phenomena are. If one prefers to stick to the known magnitude of $m_e/e$, then one could—as a simple calculation shows—give an explanation of the difference [between the results from electron theory and experiment] on the basis of the assumption that not only negatively-charged particles move in orbits, but also positive ones contribute to the molecular current. However, this assumption would contradict the prevailing view, unless one thinks of a rotation of the positive nucleus in the atom or molecule. (Beck, 1919a, pp. 147–148)

The latter possibility was advocated by Joseph Larmor during the discussion of Wander Johannes de Haas’ report at the third Solvay Conference in Brussels in April 1921. On the same occasion, however, Owen W. Richardson pointed out another possibility: the placing of an electron in a magnetic field yields an angular momentum and magnetic moment, whose ratio might depend crucially on the internal constitution of the electron. He repeated this argument in detail in a later paper, where he stated:

> If the electron is assumed to be a charged sphere, the charges being held in position by a non-electromagnetic tension of the amount suggested by Poincaré, the ratio of angular momentum to magnetic moment created is found to be $m_e/e$ instead of $2m_e/e$. This effect, however, is diamagnetic and very small, and, in fact, such ways of escape do not seem at all promising. The turning-orbit theory of the Langevin type goes so far in explaining magnetic phenomena that it is almost certain that it is true in its essentials. (Richardson, 1923, pp. 538–539)<sup>694</sup>

As a consequence of these conclusions, Richardson returned to the opinion that the motion of positive charges in atoms played a role in the case of gyromagnetic phenomena. He argued:

> For the ratio **M/I** to fall to the experimental value $m_e/e$ it is necessary and sufficient, on this view of the phenomena, that in the establishment by magnetization

tion of angular momentum the contribution arising from the positively charged parts of the atom should always be one half of that of the negative electrons and positively directed to it. This statement is exact to the degree of accuracy which disregards the effect on the magnetic moment of the positively charged parts in comparison with that from the negatively charged parts of the atom. (Richardson, 1923, p. 540)⁶⁹⁵

Atomic models with rotating nuclei seemed to account perfectly for the observed gyromagnetic ratio, **M/I**, for ferromagnetic substances.⁶⁹⁶ However, the question arose whether these models of ferromagnetic atoms were compatible with the accepted theory of atomic structure. It was noticed, especially, that the gyromagnetic ratio played an important role in the description of the magnetic splitting of spectral lines emitted by atoms. For example, the normal Zeeman effect, such as observed in the case of the hydrogen lines, could be described by the gyromagnetic ratio assuming the value given by Eq. (224); for the anomalous Zeeman effects, however, one found values ranging from $2m_e/e$ to $m_e/e$. The deviation from the normal ratio, $2m_e/e$, was considered by the experts in spectroscopic theory as a great difficulty. For instance, Alfred Landé noted:

> "Their solution [i.e., the solution of the difficulties presented by the observed gyromagnetic ratio in the anomalous Zeeman effects] would mean an enormous progress for the knowledge of atomic structure. The same difficulty seems to be responsible for the anomalous result obtained in the fundamental magnetomechanical effects of Barnett and Einstein–de Haas, which show, according to the experiments of E. Beck, an apparent *doubling of the value* $e/m_e$" (Landé, 1922b, p. 54). That is, if one looked at *both* kinds of phenomena—the gyromagnetic effects and the anomalous Zeeman effects—from the *same* point of view, one had to attribute the gyromagnetic ratio in ferromagnetic substances to a magnetic anomaly of the electrons orbiting in atoms. Still to be answered was the question of whether it was possible to explain both anomalies by means of a single assumption, that of essential contributions from positively charged objects—such as nuclei or positive ions—orbiting in atoms.

The investigations on the gyromagnetic ratio constituted just one topic in the general discussion of the magnetic properties of atoms and molecules at that

⁶⁹⁵ Richardson had earlier discussed the possibility that the positive charges in atoms also contribute to the gyromagnetic ratio (Richardson, 1908). The same idea was then mentioned by John Q. Stewart when trying to explain his experimental result for **M/I**, which was too low to be accounted for by electron motions alone (Stewart, 1918, p. 120). Then in 1923 Richardson went on to propose a special model of the iron atom based on it: in the iron atom two outer electrons should move on parallel or coplanar one-quantum orbits in the same direction, while the nucleus was supposed to move also on a parallel one-quantum orbit in the same direction. (This model accounted for the observed value of the saturation magnetization.) In this way Richardson derived the ratio **M/I**, which deviated, because of the large mass of the iron nucleus, only by about one part in 10,000 from $m_e/e$ (Richardson, 1923, p. 540).

With the help of his model, Braunbeck was able to explain another empirical fact: the lower saturation magnetization of nickel and cobalt (in comparison to iron).

time. Another concern, after Pierre Weiss’ pioneering work (Weiss, 1911), was the paramagnetic properties of atoms and ions, which seemed to be connected with quantum theory. The next investigators to contribute to this subject were two Dutch physicists, E. Oosterhuis and Willem Hendrick Keesom (Oosterhuis, 1913; Keesom, 1914a). They took over Langevin’s (classical) formula, Eq. (221), for the paramagnetic susceptibility and introduced the following quantum-theoretical change: instead of the quantity $kT$ in the denominator on the right-hand side, they put in the average quantum-theoretical rotational energy of the molecules. This replacement yielded, of course, noticeable deviations from the classical value of the paramagnetic susceptibility at low temperatures, which seemed to occur for certain substances. Later Jan von Weyssenhoff criticized the previous approaches in his Zurich thesis; he argued that the orientation of the magnetic moments $\mu$ of the molecules did not just depend on the average rotational energy, but rather on the distribution of the energy among the individual molecules (Weyssenhoff, 1916).$^{697}$ By carrying through the necessary steps, he found a new equation for the susceptibility, namely,

$$\chi = \frac{N\mu^2}{3kT} \left( 1 - \sqrt{\frac{\Theta}{\pi T}} - \frac{\Theta}{6T} + \dots \right), \tag{221a}$$

$\Theta$ ($= h^2/32\pi^2Ak$, where $A$ is the moment of inertia of the molecule, $k$ Boltzmann’s constant, and $h$ Planck’s constant) being a characteristic temperature, with $T \gg \Theta$. Equation (221a) deviated from the classical equation (221) by having additional terms, which played an important role at low temperatures. With it Weyssenhoff succeeded in reproducing the observed data on the susceptibility of liquid oxygen; he also explained other deviations from the law of Curie and Langevin. A shortcoming of Weyssenhoff’s approach was removed by Fritz Reiche: he treated the rotation of magnetic dipoles with two degrees of freedom (instead of one) with the methods of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems (Reiche, 1918a). Thus he found that, in the neighborhood of the absolute zero of temperature, the paramagnetic susceptibility approached a constant value, $N\mu^2(5\pi^2A/4h^2)$, and for high temperatures the value given by Eq. (221). However, Otto Stern declared that the apparently satisfactory description of the low-temperature data by the equations of Weyssenhoff and Reiche was not conclusive because one could easily fit the observed values by taking suitable values for the two parameters, the magnetic moment $\mu$ and the moment of inertia $A$ (Stern, 1920a). He remarked: ‘Indeed, it must even cause suspicion that the

He (Stern) criticized further that the previous authors had not paid proper attention to the fact that at low temperatures the substances were solid and therefore their molecules could not rotate freely, as had been assumed in Langevin's derivation of the law for the paramagnetic susceptibility, Eq. (221). Pierre Weiss had noticed this difficulty earlier and had argued that it was possible to derive the Curie-Langevin formula also without having freely rotating molecules: all that seemed to be necessary was that the axes of the elementary magnets should be able to perform small vibrations around their equilibrium positions (Weiss, 1913). Stern, however, discovered an error in Weiss' derivation: under the conditions assumed by Weiss Eq. (221) would not follow, but only a small temperature-dependent susceptibility (Stern, 1920a, p. 153). Wilhelm Lenz then succeeded in deriving Eq. (221)—which did represent the data for most of the solid paramagnetic substances except at extremely low temperatures—also for solid substances under a reasonable condition: namely, if the direction of elementary magnets could change discontinuously between several orientations that were symmetrically arranged in the solid crystal, then the classical law followed up to a constant factor of order unity (Lenz, 1920a).⁶⁹⁸

Thus far, quantum theory proved to be consistent with the earlier, successful description of the paramagnetic behaviour of matter, and it seemed to account also for the deviations observed for certain substances at very low temperatures. However, the crucial test for the new thoery had not yet been made. If the structure of an atom was given, it yielded immediately a well-defined magnetic moment $\mu$. For example, in the case of a Bohr orbit with quantum number $n$, the absolute value of the magnetic moment $\mu$ was given by the equation

$$\mu = n \frac{|e|}{2m_e} \frac{h}{2\pi} \qquad (226)$$

That is, a substance consisting of atoms, whose magnetism was caused by electrons in $n$ quantum orbits, should possess $n$ Bohr magnetons. As we have discussed earlier (in Section IV.1), an apparent difficulty showed up in explaining Weiss' observation that the measured magnetic moments or saturation magnetizations per gram-atom of ferromagnetic substances could be expressed in terms of the 'gram-magneton' or the Weiss magneton, $\mu_W$. Now $\mu_W$ was only one-fifth of a Bohr magneton $\mu_B$, where $\mu_B$ was given by Eq. (189); hence the magnetic moments determined by Weiss were not integral multiples of $\mu_B$. Pauli then removed the difficulty by showing that, when the magnetic moments of mole-

(221) by a different factor, namely, $\frac{1}{3}((n + 1)(2n + 1)/2n^2)$ (Pauli, 1920c). Evidently, for low quantum numbers $n$ this factor exceeded the classical one considerably; hence from an application of the classical law, Eq. (221), to the empirical data, as done by Weiss, too small magnetic moments $\mu$ had been determined. While Pauli rescued the quantum-theoretical interpretation by invoking the idea of space quantization, Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach proved the reality of space quantization by means of a crucial experiment in early 1922. Their finding not only confirmed quantum theory, it also presented new difficulties.

Before Stern concerned himself with the empirical test of spatial quantization of electron orbits in atoms, he had had a nearly ten-year-old association with quantum physics. As a student of Otto Sackur’s at Breslau, he had investigated the problem of the chemical constants for atoms and molecules—one of the most fruitful applications of quantum theory since the pioneering work of Walther Nernst—and had concluded from it important arguments in favour of the existence of zero-point energy (Stern, 1913; 1919); in Zurich he had, together with Albert Einstein, analyzed the specific-heat data of molecular hydrogen, again finding support for the existence of zero-point energy (Einstein and Stern, 1913).$^{699}$

Returning after World War I to the University of Frankfurt to resume his position as *Privatdozent* he eagerly plunged into the study of the properties of atoms and molecules with the help of a special experimental method: the method of molecular rays or beams. The idea behind this method, which had been applied previously by Louis Dunoyer, was to produce directed beams of neutral atoms or molecules—having thermal velocity distribution—in an evacuated region of space for the purpose of investigating their properties.$^{700}$ When Born

$^{699}$Otto Stern was born in Sohrau, Upper Silesia, on 17 February 1888. He studied physics and chemistry at the University of Breslau (1906–1912), but for the summer semesters of 1906 and 1908, which he spent at the University of Freiburg-im-Breisgau and the University of Munich, respectively. After obtaining his doctorate in 1912 he joined Einstein, first at the University of Prague (1912) and later at the E.T.H., Zurich (1912–1914). In 1914 he became *Privatdozent* at the University of Frankfurt-am-Main. During World War I he did military service; towards the end (in 1918) he worked with Nernst in Berlin, before returning to his position at Frankfurt. In 1921 he accepted a call as full professor at the University of Rostock, and the following year he took the chair of physical chemistry at the University of Hamburg. He left Germany in 1933 and became research professor in the physics department of the Carnegie Institute of Technology, Pittsburgh. He retired in 1945 to live in Berkeley, California, where he died on 17 August 1969.

Stern’s main contribution to experimental physics was the development of the molecular beam method, with the help of which he discovered the Stern–Gerlach effect (1922) and the anomalous magnetic moment of the proton (1933), for which he received the 1943 Nobel Prize in Physics.

$^{700}$Although beams of charged particles had been used since William Crookes employed them in his investigations of cathode rays in 1871, Louis Dunoyer obtained the first beam of neutral atoms forty years later. Thus he proved that sodium atoms moved along a straight line (Dunoyer, 1911). Later, Robert W. Wood used Dunoyer’s method for the spectroscopic observation of atoms unaffected by external fields.

went to the University of Frankfurt in early 1919 as professor of theoretical physics, he fully supported the experimental plans of Otto Stern—who became a member of his institute—and even participated in them. He recalled later:

> Stern’s first apparatus was designed to produce direct evidence for the velocity distribution law of Maxwell and to measure the mean velocity. I was so fascinated by the idea that I put all the means of my laboratory, workshop and mechanic at his disposal. And I started myself, with the assistance of Fräulein [Elisabeth] Bormann, on a similar experiment, the direct determination of molecular cross sections (measuring the intensity of a beam of silver atoms *in vacuo* and in a gas). Stern’s experiments were entirely successful, and mine went well enough to meet, many years later, with the approval of the greatest experimentalist of our time. I was then in Cambridge and lecturing in the Cavendish. One morning I met Rutherford, who said to me: “There must be an experimental physicist who has exactly the same name as you. When I was preparing a lecture on kinetic theory of gases, I found a paper in the *Physikalische Zeitschrift* signed by Max Born and Elisabeth Bormann [Born, 1920c] containing the description of experiments much too good for a mathematician like you.” I assured him that the idea at least was mine, while the actual work was mostly done by my assistant. (Born, 1978, p. 195)

Otto Stern applied the molecular beam method first in a problem similar to Born and Bormann’s, namely, to measure the thermal velocity of silver atoms (Stern, 1920b). For this purpose he performed the following experiment. He produced a ‘ray’ (or ‘beam,’ as it would be called later) of silver atoms by heating a platinum wire covered by a thin film of silver in an evacuated vessel. From the silver atoms thus emitted he fashioned a directed ray by putting two narrow slits, one after the other, in the vessel. The ray finally hit a cooled glass plate, on which it could be observed (under a microscope) as a dark spot. For determining the velocity of the silver atoms in the ray, Stern let the apparatus (the entire vessel) turn around an axis through the platinum wire with a given angular velocity: the shift of the silver spot on the glass plate—with respect to the position when the vessel was at rest—then provided a measure of the thermal velocity of silver atoms. Now the atoms in the ray possessed, of course, a thermal (Maxwellian) velocity distribution. Hence the spot on the plate, obtained when the system was rotating, was spread out into a band of finite extent, with maximum intensity in the centre. From the shift in position of the centre of the spot, Stern determined that most silver atoms in the beam possessed a velocity of $600 \text{ to } 675 \text{ m} \cdot \text{s}^{-1}$, and this value agreed with the theoretical value for the average thermal velocity of silver atoms at a temperature slightly above the melting point at $961^{\circ}\text{C}$ (Stern, 1920b, c). Stern also expected to be able to measure the velocity distribution of the silver atoms. He soon discovered, however, that this problem demanded many improvements of his apparatus and methods; instead he turned his attention to another problem of fundamental interest at that time: the experimental test of the so-called space-quantization of atoms.

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect  
435  

Spatial quantization had been introduced by Arnold Sommerfeld in 1916 in connection with the description of the hydrogen atom in external electric and magnetic fields (Sommerfeld, 1916b, § 7).<sup>701</sup> According to Sommerfeld’s idea, an electron orbit could assume only certain discrete directions in space: for example, in the case of an external magnetic field in the *z*-direction, the normal to the electron orbit made an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the magnetic field, and $\cos\theta$ was given by a rational fraction $n_1/n_\phi$, where $n_1$ was an integer whose absolute value was smaller than or equal to the azimuthal quantum number $n_\phi$. The introduction of spatial quantization, denoted by the spatial quantum number $n_1$, had led to a very satisfactory description of the Stark and Zeeman effects of hydrogen lines. In later years it had also played a role in the attempts to explain the X-ray spectra—especially by Alfred Landé and Adolf Smekal—and in the discussion of the helium problem. But no one had so far demonstrated experimentally the existence of spatial quantization. Certain quantum physicists even doubted its physical reality. Thus Peter Debye, who had himself used spatial quantization in calculating the Zeeman effect (Debye, 1916a, b), remarked to Walther Gerlach: ‘But surely you don’t believe that the [spatial] orientation of the atoms is something physically real; that is [only] a prescription for the calculation—a timetable of the electrons’ (Gerlach, 1969b, p. 472). As Born recalled later, he had looked at spatial quantization in a similar vein: ‘It took me quite a time before I took this idea seriously. I thought always that direction quantization was a kind of symbolic expression for something which you don’t understand. But to take this literally like Stern did, this was his own idea . . . I tried to persuade Stern that there was no sense, but then he told me that it was worth a try’ (Born, Conversations, p. 27). After obtaining some experience with atomic beams in experiments on the thermal velocity distribution of atoms, Stern went ahead determinedly to establish the existence of directional quantization, despite the skepticism of the theoretical experts. He encountered many experimental obstacles, but he also had the good luck of obtaining the assistance of Walther Gerlach, an excellent experimentalist, in carrying out his plans.<sup>702</sup>  

Gerlach had received a long and thorough experimental training under Friedrich Paschen in Tübingen: for instance, he had worked for his doctorate on a precision measurement of the constant which occurred in the Stefan–Boltzmann law (the constant *A* in our Eq. (3), in Chapter I: Gerlach, 1912), and later, together with Edgar Meyer, on a problem of the photoelectric effect (Gerlach

and Meyer, 1913).<sup>703</sup> When he came to Frankfurt and joined Richard Wachsmuth’s experimental institute in late 1920, he soon got in touch with Born and Stern, whom he already knew from Berlin. Although, meanwhile, the ‘theoreticians’ possessed much greater experience with the experimental techniques of molecular beams—Stern had already completed his measurements of the mean thermal velocity of silver atoms, and Born and Bormann had obtained their cross sections—Gerlach immediately participated in an analysis of the mean free path of silver atoms. ‘Then I worried a bit with Miss Bormann about how to proceed,’ Gerlach remembered. ‘And then naturally I had enormous pleasure [in working] with molecular beams, especially because I had already once prepared Dunoyer’s sodium molecular beams at Paschen’s Institute’ (Gerlach, *loc. cit.*, p. 3). While at Tübingen, Gerlach had applied the molecular beam method for spectroscopic purposes; he now wanted to use it for deciding a problem he had encountered recently: he had observed, in particular, that bismuth seemed to lose its magnetic property—it is highly diamagnetic—when bound in an alloy. To discover the reason for this behaviour, Gerlach asked the question of whether bismuth atoms were diamagnetic or not. He hoped to answer it by studying the deflection of atomic bismuth beams in an inhomogeneous magnetic field. During the preparations for this work—in which Born did not encourage Gerlach very much, because he claimed that the effect would be very small—Stern approached Gerlach with his project to test the space-quantization hypothesis. As Gerlach

<sup>703</sup> Walther Gerlach was born on 1 August 1899 at Biebrich (Rhein). He studied physics at the University of Tübingen from 1908. After taking his doctorate in 1912, he continued as an assistant to Paschen. From 1915 to 1918 he did military service: besides active duty at the front, he worked on wireless telegraphy at Jena (under the direction of Max Wien) and in the *Artillerie-Prüfungskommission* (under Rudolf Ladenburg). From 1919 to 1920 he worked in the physical laboratory of *Farbenfabriken Elberfeld*. In late 1920 he returned to an academic career—he had obtained his *Habilitation* in 1916 at the University of Tübingen—and became *Privatdozent* and, in 1921, extraordinary professor at the University of Frankfurt. In 1925 he was appointed to the chair held earlier by Paschen. Four years later, upon Wilhelm Wien’s death, he moved to the University of Munich. He held the professorship in Munich with brief interruptions (1945–1946, interned in England after the war; 1946–1948, professor at Bonn) until his retirement in 1957. He died in Munich on 10 August 1979.

Gerlach contributed to many experimental topics, especially the ones connected with radiation and quantum theory (e.g., together with Alice Golsen, he determined the pressure of light quantitatively); he made important contributions to the development of modern methods of chemical spectral analysis, the physics of the (technical) magnetization curve, and measurements on artificial and natural radioactivity.

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect

437

recalled: ‘And one day Stern came and said: “With the magnetic experiment one can do something else. Do you know what directional [space-] quantization is?” I said, “No, I don’t know anything about it.” Then he told me about it and asked: “Shall we do it? Well, then let’s go, we shall do it!”’ (Gerlach, AHQP Interview, 15 July 1963, p. 4). Still Stern and Gerlach did not start the experiment immediately. Stern first tried to estimate the magnitude of the effect and, after several wrong calculations, arrived at a definite result. Gerlach again recalled: ‘Then he said: “Do you think one can obtain an inhomogeneity of the field of about $10^4$ Oersted per cm?” And I told him “That much I shall *certainly* obtain, I shall even get more.” For in the meanwhile, in connection with my bismuth experiment—which I had not given up altogether—, I had tried to produce inhomogeneous fields, using still a small magnet . . . He [Stern] then said: “Now we should only have an atomic beam, which has a width of a tenth or a hundredth of a millimeter, and then the thing will work”’ (Gerlach, *loc. cit.*, p. 4).

In estimating the correct order of magnitude of the deflection of a beam of atoms with a magnetic moment, Otto Stern received some support from a calculation of Hartmut Kallmann and Fritz Reiche. These authors had discussed another problem of atomic physics: the measurement of the electric dipole moment of molecules with the help of the molecular beam method. Their idea was to obtain a quantitative determination of this property by observing the deflection of a beam of dipolar molecules in inhomogeneous electric and magnetic fields. Kallmann and Reiche made estimates, based on classical and quantum theory, respectively, and submitted a paper containing their results to *Zeitschrift für Physik* by the end of July 1921 (Kallmann and Reiche, 1921). Since Born and his associates were interested in dipolar molecules, too, Kallmann and Reiche sent a copy of their paper to Frankfurt. On seeing it, Stern became excited; he feared that the people in Berlin, where Kallmann and Reiche were, might also try to prove the existence of space-quantization, and he immediately sat down to write a note, entitled ‘*Ein Weg zur experimentellen Prüfung der Richtungsquantelung im Magnetfeld*’ (‘A Method of Testing Experimentally the Directional Quantization in a Magnetic Field’), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 26 August 1921. In it he explained the ideas of the experiment planned at Frankfurt, and in a footnote added the remark: ‘Herr W. Gerlach and I have been occupied for some time in carrying out this experiment’ (Stern, 1921, p. 250).<sup>704</sup> The method, which Stern proposed, rested on the fact

This quote from Stern’s paper also contradicts certain statements of Landé, who claimed that Gerlach entered into work on the experiment on space-quantization only at the last minute. ‘Stern had for his help a young assistant, Peter Lertes,’ said Landé. ‘He was a very energetic and fine young fellow, who worked with Stern and did the adjustment—all of it.’ (Landé, AHQP Interview, pp. 26–27). Now Peter Lertes indeed worked at that time as a student of Born’s: he investigated experimentally the properties of dipolar molecules in 1920 and 1921. He may have been interested in the problem of space-quantization also, but he certainly was not involved in the actual experiment, which was carried out by Gerlach and Stern.

438 **Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models**

that an electron with magnetic moment $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ experiences a force in an inhomogeneous magnetic field of gradient $\partial \mathbf{H}/\partial z$—the field being different from zero only in the $z$-direction—given by the equation

$$
K_z = \mu_z \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial z} \right), \tag{227}
$$

where $\mu_z$ is the component of $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ in the $z$-direction. The atoms—which possess a magnetization of one Bohr magneton per gram-atom, whose magnetic moment lies in the $z$-direction and which traverse along the $x$-direction through a region of length $l$ under a constant field gradient $\partial \mathbf{H}/\partial z$—will be deflected in the $z$-direction by the distance $s$, where

$$
s = 1.12 \times 10^{-5} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial z} \right) \frac{l^2}{T} \ \text{cm} \tag{228}
$$

if $(\partial \mathbf{H}/\partial z)$ is measured in gauss per centimetre and the temperature $T$ in degrees absolute. Hence, for a field gradient of $10^4$ G/cm and a temperature of $1000^\circ$C, Stern expected a deflection of the order of $10^{-2}$ mm, provided $(\partial \mathbf{H}/\partial z)$ was constant over a length of 3 cm.

Through the prospective experiment Stern hoped to obtain the empirical evidence for or against spatial quantization. The theoretical ideas underlying this test were the following. It could be considered as certain—for example, from the gyromagnetic effects or the Zeeman effect—that electrons moved in closed orbits in atoms. In classical theory the orientation of the electron orbits was not fixed. Even when an external (homogeneous) magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ acted on the atom, the axis of the orbit (an axis perpendicular to the plane of the orbit through its centre, which coincides with the axis of the angular momentum) was allowed to make an arbitrary angle $\theta$ with the direction of $\mathbf{H}$. All that happened in the Zeeman effect—according to Joseph Larmor’s theory—was that the axis of the electron orbit performed a precession around the direction of $\mathbf{H}$, the frequency of which was determined by the condition that the component of the angular momentum parallel to $\mathbf{H}$ should change only by the amounts $\pm h/2\pi$ or zero. (Note that in classical theory Planck’s constant appeared only as an arbitrary parameter.) The situation appeared to be completely different in the quantum theory. In the latter, due to space-quantization, only discrete positions of the electron orbits with respect to the direction of the magnetic field were admitted. Hence an electron orbit in an atom, having the azimuthal angular momentum $p_{\phi} = h/2\pi$, should be able to assume just three positions, described by the values of the angle $\theta$ obtained from the equations

$$
\cos\theta = \frac{n_1}{n_{\phi}} = 0, \pm 1. \tag{229}
$$

Moreover, Niels Bohr had excluded the possibility that the spatial quantum number $n_1$ be zero because then the plane of the electron orbit would contain the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0073 -->

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect  
439

direction of the magnetic field and the electron motion might become instable under certain conditions (Bohr, 1918b, p. 56). Therefore, in quantum theory, the magnetic moment $\mu$ of an atom should possess only two discrete positions, parallel or antiparallel to the direction of the magnetic field.

As a consequence of the different situations in the classical and the quantum theory, one could indeed use the observed deflection of an atomic beam in an inhomogeneous magnetic field to decide between the two theories. Thus Stern argued: ‘According to quantum theory, $\mu_z$ [i.e., the magnetic moment in the direction of the magnetic field] can only be $\pm (e/2m_e)(h/2\pi)$. In this case the spot on the receiving plate will therefore be split into two, each of them having the same size but half the intensity of the original spot’ (Stern, 1921, p. 252). Of course, the spots had to exhibit—due to the Maxwellian velocity distribution of the atoms—a structure having maximum intensity in the centre. Hence, in the quantum case, the separation by the inhomogeneous field should lead to two partially overlapping spots; however, at the position of the centre of the original spot (obtained without the magnetic field) there should exist a minimum of intensity.

Exactly the opposite happens according to the view of classical theory [Stern pointed out]. There $\mu_z$ can assume arbitrary values between zero and the quantum‑theoretical value $|\mu| = (|e|/2m_e)(h/2\pi)$. If we denote the angle between $\mu$ and $H$ by $\theta$, then $\mu_z = |\mu|\cos\theta$. Now the number of atoms, for which $\theta$ has a given value, is proportional to $\sin\theta$. The number of atoms has, therefore, a maximum value for $\theta = \pi/2$ . . . According to the classical theory, for any velocity [of the atoms in the beam] there thus occur all possible deflections between zero and the quantum‑theoretical one; and for each velocity the number of atoms, which are deflected by a certain angle, is the larger the smaller the deflection is. Hence the spot on the receiving plate will only become broader in the magnetic field, but retain the maximum intensity at the position of the original spot. (Stern, 1921, pp. 252–253)$^{705}$

In spite of their well‑defined programme and their deep involvement in the experiment, Stern and Gerlach proceeded very slowly. This had several reasons. Especially, the apparatus necessary was not easy to obtain at that time. They needed a magnet to create a strongly inhomogeneous magnetic field; sharp slits of tenths of a millimetre width for preparing the atomic beam of small cross section; a good vacuum in the region through which the beam passed so as to avoid collisions with other atoms; and large amounts of cooling substances for the glass, in order to obtain a good vacuum and enough condensated atoms.$^{706}$ Stern and Gerlach received support from various public and private sources for their experiment. Albert Einstein helped by providing some funds from the

**440** Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

*Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Physik*; he also arranged contacts with some wealthy people. Thus Gerlach informed Edgar Meyer: ‘Yesterday we met Einstein at the Oppenheims’ (Gerlach to Meyer, 4 November 1921). The company of *Hartmann und Braun* loaned them a suitable electromagnet (a half-ring magnet of the type developed by Henri duBois), and *Messer & Co., Luftverflüssigungsanlagen* in Frankfurt donated liquid air for cooling. However, the vacuum pumps represented the greatest source of difficulties. As Gerlach recalled: ‘At that time only the small vapour-jet pump (*Dampfstrahl-Pumpe*) and the first diffusion pumps of *Volmer* existed. Such pumps did not last very long, and if they became defective it was a catastrophe. We then started to make such pumps ourselves or to repair them when they broke. It was necessary to blow a lot of glass for that purpose’ (Gerlach, AHQP Interview, 15 July 1963, p. 7). Also the acquisition of solid carbon dioxide for cooling purposes was a problem in those days. But the *Notgemeinschaft der Deutschen Forschung* helped; and the industrial companies and private persons in Frankfurt helped through the association of friends and patrons of the University (*Vereinigung von Freunden und Förderern der Universität Frankfurt-am-Main*). In building and repairing the apparatus, Adolf Schmidt, the mechanic at Born’s Institute, worked devotedly during the entire time of the experiment from summer 1921 to March 1922. The physicists themselves worked very hard. Walther Gerlach, especially, occupied himself with the project day and night. About these efforts Wilhelm Schütz, then a doctoral student of Gerlach’s, reported later:

> Anyone who has not experienced it cannot imagine how great were the difficulties when one had to produce and maintain for several hours a vacuum of 10⁻⁵ Torr in an apparatus, which could not be fully heated . . . , and in a furnace for heating silver to a temperature of about 1300°K. We cooled with carbon-dioxide ice [dry ice] and acetone or with liquid air. The suction velocity of the Gaede mercury vacuum-pumps and of the Volmer mercury diffusion-pumps was ridiculously low in comparison with the capacity of modern pumps. Moreover, they were easily breakable; the pumps were made of glass, and frequently one broke from the thrust of boiling mercury—in spite of the addition of lead—or from the dripping of condensed water vapour. With that the effort of pumping of several days for the purpose of heating the furnace was lost. Also, it was by no means certain that the furnace would continue to burn through the four-to-eight-hour time of exposure. The pumping and the heating of the furnace had then to be started again. It was Sisyphus-like labour, and the main burden and responsibility rested on the broad shoulders of Professor Gerlach. In particular, W. Gerlach took over the night-watches. He would come in around 9 p.m. with a bag of reprints and books. During the night he corrected proofs, wrote reviews and articles, prepared lectures, drank many cups of hot chocolate or tea and smoked a lot. When I would return to the Institute in the morning and hear the familiar noise of the running pumps, and Gerlach would still be there, that was a good sign: nothing had broken during the night. (Schütz, 1969, pp. 343–345)

After many attempts Gerlach was able to report the first successful observation to Edgar Meyer (1879–1960) in early November 1921. He wrote: ‘It works.

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect 441

Instead of the round silver deposit [one obtains] an essentially broadened one; hence Sommerfeld [is right]’ (Gerlach to Meyer, 6 November 1921; quoted in Gerlach, 1969b, p. 472). Stern and Gerlach—like Stern, Born and Bormann before them—had made their investigation with beams of silver atoms. Sommerfeld had doubted—as did Peter Debye in Zurich, where Edgar Meyer was—that in the homogeneous magnetic field a clear separation of the spots on the glass plates would show up. On a visit to Frankfurt, at the time of Stern and Gerlach’s earliest observations, he had suggested that the following might happen: under the action of the external field the beam would split into three parts corresponding to the magnetic moments of the silver atoms in the $z$-direction, $\mu_z = \pm(e/2m_e)(h/2\pi)$ and zero, respectively. This possibility, which Sommerfeld believed to be in agreement with quantum theory, would mean that the observed figure on the plate should be symmetrical, with the maximum intensity in the middle (the position of the original spot) and on two sides of it. The initial result of the Stern–Gerlach experiment, though compatible with it, did not yet allow one to make a definite decision about the intensity distribution. Thus, in a preliminary note to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, which was received on 18 November 1921, Stern and Gerlach reported:

The three experiments with the magnetic field yielded a spot, broadened in the direction of $\partial\mathbf{H}/\partial z$, having a height of 0.1 mm and a width of 0.25 to 0.30 mm. One still cannot recognize with certainty an intensity structure within this band. The amount of the symmetric broadening corresponds to a magnetic moment of the silver atom of 1 to 2 Bohr magnetons. [And they added:] A more accurate result cannot be given at the moment: first, because we have not yet succeeded in measuring the gradient $\partial\mathbf{H}/\partial z$ very close to the edge [of the magnetic pole]; second, because we do not yet know what thickness of the silver [film] can still be detected by developing. On the basis of our experience thus far, we do not doubt that we shall be in a position to decide about the directional quantization through experiments with beams of smaller diameter and perhaps a better method of developing [the silver film]. (Gerlach and Stern, 1921, p. 111)

In any case, they concluded that they had provided the ‘evidence that the silver atom possesses a magnetic moment’ (Gerlach and Stern, *loc. cit.*, p. 111).

During the following weeks Stern and Gerlach worked hard to improve their technique. They produced narrower atomic beams by removing the first circular slit farther from the oven (the source of silver atoms) and reducing its dimensions. Until the end of the Christmas vacation, 1921, Stern and Gerlach occupied themselves jointly with such efforts. Then Stern had to go to the University of Rostock, where he had accepted a full professorship and Gerlach carried on the experiment alone. He then introduced another change in the setup, which he later recalled as follows: ‘I then carried on the work a bit on my own and made a change which turned out to be rather decisive: namely, instead of the round atomic beam, I used the one produced by a slit. In this I was guided by an observation I had made in my experiments on the Debye–Scherrer crystal investigations. There I had one day replaced the point-like slit by a rectangular

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0076 -->

442 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

slit, obtaining of course immediately a much larger intensity' (Gerlach, AHQP Interview, 15 July 1963). Thus he replaced the second, originally round, slit by a rectangular slit (of 0.8 mm length and 0.03 to 0.04 mm width). During the early weeks of 1922 Gerlach communicated with Stern by letters. On one occasion, in the beginning of February, the two of them met again. 'I met with Stern, Franck and Born in Göttingen,' Gerlach recalled, 'and then I returned to Frankfurt and performed an experiment. It started in the evening and went on during the whole night. And the next morning—I was still in the Institute—immediately developed [the plate] and this figure came out: absolutely nothing in the middle, only something on the right and left, though not yet symmetric' (Gerlach, AHQP Interview, 15 July 1963, p. 1).$^{707}$ Wilhelm Schütz recalled these exciting moments as follows: 'Full of expectation we followed the developing process and experienced the success of an endeavour which had lasted over months: the first splitting of a silver atomic beam in the inhomogeneous magnetic field. After the head of the workshop, Schmidt, and—if I remember correctly—also [Erwin] Madelung had seen the separation, we went to the Institute of Mineralogy, to Mr. Nacken, to record the result microphotographically. Then I was asked to send a telegramme to Professor Stern, which read: "Bohr is right after all!"' (Schütz, 1969, p. 345).

Besides Stern, Gerlach also informed friends and interested physicists. All of them agreed about the importance of the result. James Franck, who was still cautious, wrote: 'The important thing, however, is whether the directional quantization has really been proved now. Apart from your own conclusion [about it], please also write about what actually takes place [in this experiment]' (Franck to Gerlach, 15 February 1922). Wolfgang Pauli, who had taken a personal interest in the experiment and had even passed through Frankfurt earlier in January to see the apparatus, was less skeptical. He congratulated Gerlach heartily on the success and added: 'Hopefully now even the incredulous Stern will be convinced about directional quantization' (Pauli to Gerlach, 17 February 1922).$^{708}$ Bohr asked more specifically: 'I should be very grateful if you could interpret your experiments in the sense that the magnetic axis of the silver atom is always directed parallel to the field and never perpendicular—there are theoretical reasons for the latter [perpendicular] case' (Bohr to Gerlach, 18 February 1922). Gerlach and Stern gave a clear answer to this question in their paper, entitled 'Der experimentelle Nachweis der Richtungsquantelung im Magnetfeld' ('The Experimental Proof of Directional Quantization in a Magnetic Field'); they submitted it in late February after Gerlach had repeated the experiment several times successfully, and it was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 1 March 1922. In it they summarized their results in the following words: 'The atomic beam splits up into two discrete beams in a magnetic field. No undeflected atoms can be

IV.3 The Magnetic Anomaly and the Stern–Gerlach Effect 443

detected . . . *In these results we see the direct experimental proof of directional [space-] quantization in a magnetic field*' (Gerlach and Stern, 1922a, pp. 351–352). In a precision measurement, which they carried out jointly at Frankfurt during the Easter vacation, they showed further that the magnetic moment of the silver atom in the ground state was one Bohr magneton per gram-atom. They published this result in a further paper (received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 1 April 1922), ascribing to it an accuracy of about 10 percent (Gerlach and Stern, 1922b).<sup>709</sup>

The results of the Stern–Gerlach experiment confirmed the quantum-theoretical prediction completely.<sup>710</sup> They supported the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory in such a fundamental way that Friedrich Paschen claimed in a letter to Gerlach: 'Your experiment proves for the first time the reality of Bohr's stationary states' (Paschen to Gerlach [1922]; quoted in Gerlach, 1969b, p. 472). At the same time they created serious difficulties for the quantum physicists as well. One difficulty had been noticed by Stern already in his first publication: if an electron could take on only discrete positions in atoms, then the atoms should exhibit a strong double-refraction towards radiation falling in from a direction perpendicular to that of the magnetic field. 'Even in the case of complex one-quantum atoms, or indeed for many-quanta atoms, such an effect should occur, as one may easily see. Moreover, no significant change would occur if one takes into account the interaction between atoms in not-too-dense gases,' Stern argued and concluded: 'However, such an effect has never been observed so far, although it should have been detected earlier in the many experimental investigations that have been made in this field' (Stern, 1921, p. 249). A second difficulty connected with space-quantization was discussed in detail by Albert Einstein and Paul Ehrenfest in their joint paper on '*Quantentheoretische Überlegungen zum Experiment von Stern und Gerlach*' ('Quantum-Theoretical Considerations on the Experiment of Stern and Gerlach'), which they submitted in August 1922 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1922). They dealt in particular with the problem of how the orbits in the atom would obtain their discrete directions which they exhibit while passing through the inhomogeneous magnetic field. Under the assumption that the mechanism causing the orientation was provided by the interaction with the radiation field, Einstein and Ehrenfest estimated that for a field strength of 10,000 G a change in the direction of the orbit would take place in roughly 10<sup>11</sup> s; this long time interval would be reduced in the presence of heat radiation at room temperature (i.e., the temperature of the space between oven and magnet) to about 10<sup>9</sup> s. How could, they asked, the experimental situation be explained, which implied that the discrete orientations of the orbits in silver atoms were obtained in less than 10<sup>−4</sup> s. In order to deal with this evident puzzle, Einstein and Ehrenfest proposed two alternatives: first,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0078 -->

444
Chapter IV
The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

that the silver atoms were always in the states of spatial quantization; second, the orientations of the electron orbits arose from an interaction of the atoms with the radiation field, which involved much smaller reaction times than the usual interactions leading to transitions between stationary states in the atoms. However, they found that both alternatives created considerable difficulties in the understanding of the atomic processes. In the first case, a very weak magnetic field, such as the one existing in the neighbourhood of the source of the atomic beam (i.e., at the oven, which is removed from the magnet), must be able to impress upon the electron in the silver atoms the orientation—parallel or antiparallel—with respect to the direction of the field; further, this orientation should be adapted infinitely fast to the local direction of the magnetic field since the atoms move with high velocities from the oven to the collecting plate. Clearly, such an assumption had to contradict the accepted mechanical foundation of atomic physics; especially, it implied that quantum systems behaved under nonadiabatic and adiabatic changes in the same way. In the second case, the change of the electron orbits from nonquantum states to oriented quantum states had to occur extremely fast through the absorption and emission of infrared radiation. Such an assumption also led to several unpleasant consequences: it implied the emission and absorption of radiation having frequencies of the order of magnitude of the Larmor frequency; it required that only quantum systems consisting of electric charges could be spatially quantized; and, if one further assumed that all transitions between stationary states in atomic systems occurred through the same procedure, one would not be able to understand the observed quantum-theoretical behaviour of the specific heats of molecular hydrogen and diamond (which Einstein and Ehrenfest regarded as systems not possessing suitable electric charges). Thus Einstein and Ehrenfest concluded: ‘The difficulties mentioned above show how unsatisfactory are both interpretations of the results found by Stern and Gerlach, which we have discussed here’ (Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1922, p. 34).

The difficulties arising in the interpretation of the Stern–Gerlach effect in the light of the accepted rules of quantum theory could not easily be removed. One way out, which was mentioned by Einstein and Ehrenfest at the end of their paper, was to employ an argument which Bohr had already used in another context: atoms in complicated electromagnetic fields might not behave according to the rules of quantum theory at all (see Bohr, 1918b, p. 93). However, this argument, if taken seriously, would destroy the basis of any theoretical and physical understanding of the Stern–Gerlach effect. Therefore, in a paper, entitled ‘*Über die Anwendung der Quantentheorie auf den Atombau*’ (‘On the Application of the Quantum Theory to Atomic Structure’), and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in November 1922, Bohr suggested another possibility. He claimed, in particular, that Einstein and Ehrenfest’s calculation of the time to achieve the discrete orientation of electron orbits rested on wrong assumptions, and argued:

In connection with the fundamental difficulties standing in the way of a detailed description of such an adjustment, which are discussed in the above note [of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0079 -->

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect
445

Einstein and Ehrenfest], it may be pointed out that the effect of the [magnetic] field on the harmonic components, into which the motion of the atom may be resolved, consists not only in the addition of new vibrations, the frequencies of which are proportional to the external forces, but also in the introduction of a change in the harmonic components of the motion, already present in the undisturbed atom. The velocity of adjustment of the atom in the field can scarcely, therefore, be estimated from the life of the stationary states of an imaginary atom, in the motion of which only the first mentioned vibrations were present, as is attempted in the note under discussion [Einstein and Ehrenfest’s]. On the contrary, the life of the stationary states of the excited, unperturbed atom might be regarded as determining this velocity of readjustment. That, in the experiments mentioned, we have to deal with the undisturbed motion, not of the excited atoms, but only of atoms in the normal state, does not in principle stand in the way of such a conception. On the contrary, it is only the formal nature of the quantum theory in its present form that stands out here with particular clearness. (Bohr, 1923a, p. 149, footnote 1; English translation: Bohr, *Collected Works*, Vol. 3, 1976, footnote on pp. 484–485)

Bohr’s attempt at a solution met, in turn, the severe criticism of Adolf Smekal in Vienna, who pointed out a few months later:

> It appears that formal doubts can be raised against the considerations of Einstein and Ehrenfest, as also against the idea proposed by Bohr, namely, that the adjustment [of the atomic moments] can possibly be understood if one assumes the lifetime of the random orientations in the magnetic field to have the same order of magnitude as the stationary states of excited atoms: these random orientations *do not* correspond to *stationary states* in the magnetic field. (Smekal, 1923b, p. 17)

Smekal agreed with the general conclusion reached by Einstein and Ehrenfest—and adopted in 1923 also by Bohr—that in atomic systems the mechanical and dynamical laws were not valid anymore. He concluded: ‘One must only demand that the mechanical theory of *macroscopic* bodies remains valid within the macroscopic limits of accuracy’ (Smekal, 1923b, p. 18). These statements and conclusions illuminated a new situation in atomic theory: they implied that the fundamental assumptions hitherto employed in the description of atomic phenomena had to be abandoned. The same situation appeared in even sharper light in dealing with another type of magnetic phenomena: the anomalous Zeeman effects.

## IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect

Pieter Zeeman’s discovery of the effect of a magnetic field on the spectral lines (Zeeman, 1896; 1897a, b) and Hendrik Lorentz’ subsequent explanation of it (Lorentz, 1897) was considered as a triumph of the electron theory of matter. However, just a few years later it became evident that the magnetic changes of the line frequency, or the Zeeman effect, did not follow a simple pattern: that is, the lines could split into more than three components, with separations or

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0080 -->

446          Chapter IV          The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

distances $\Delta\nu$ that were different from the ones given by Lorentz' formula,

$$
\frac{\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}}{|\mathbf{H}|} = \frac{|e|}{4\pi m_e c}, \tag{230}
$$

where $|\mathbf{H}|$ denotes the strength of the magnetic field, $e$ and $m_e$ the charge and mass of the electron, respectively, and $c$ the velocity of light *in vacuo*. In other words, instead of always finding the Zeeman triplet, one observed in general what Lorentz called the ‘more complex types of the Zeeman effect’ (‘*kompliziertere Formen des Zeemanefektes*’) or Friedrich Paschen and Ernst Back ultimately named the ‘anomalous Zeeman effect’ (Paschen and Back, 1912). Although the anomalous Zeeman effect did not become associated with the quantum theory right away, it would be useful to give an account of the experimental and theoretical developments connected with it in order to understand the enormously important role it played in atomic theory during the early 1920s.
The discovery of the anomalous Zeeman effect goes back to the year 1897. Zeeman’s observation of 1896 had immediately attracted the interest of many experimentalists in Europe and the United States; for example, Walter König in Germany, Aimé Cotton, Alfred Cornu and Henri Becquerel in France, and Albert A. Michelson in the United States. These people were mainly concerned with improving the available spectroscopic methods to obtain a better resolution of the magnetic components. For instance, Michelson, who first applied the interferometer technique to the Zeeman effect (Michelson, 1897), designed and constructed an echelon spectroscope which allowed him to surpass the resolution of the best gratings used at that time by a factor of 5; as soon as the instrument was ready, he found with it the separation of the spectral lines into more than three components (Michelson, 1898a, b).<sup>711</sup> By that time, however, Thomas Preston of Dublin had already announced and published the same results (Preston, 1898).<sup>712</sup> Preston had learned about Zeeman’s discovery of the broadening of the spectral lines in the presence of a magnetic field through the English translation of Zeeman’s first article in the March 1897 issue of the *Philosophical Magazine*; there he also learned about Lorentz’ theory of this effect, and he wanted to test Lorentz’ prediction that the spectral line should become a triplet. After obtaining suitable equipment—a concave Rowland grating and a powerful electromagnet—Preston discovered that the blue cadmium line exhibited a very complex structure in a strong magnetic field. He reported his finding to the Royal Dublin Society of 22 December 1897. He exhibited photographs of the

---
<sup>711</sup> Michelson’s echelon spectroscope consisted of twenty plates of glass, each 18 mm thick. Michelson obtained a resolution of 300,000 by observing the 15,000-order spectrum.

He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1898. Preston died on 7 March 1900 in Dublin. He made contributions to the fields of heat, magnetism and spectroscopy.

Zeeman effects of the cadmium lines at 4680 Å and 4800 Å, and commented:

Thus if we refer to the photographs illustrating this paper, we see that while the normal triplet 4680, say, consists of three distinctly separated lines, of which the middle one is the most intense, yet the neighbouring lines, such as 4800 (the blue cadmium line observed by Zeeman and others) do not appear as triplets of this type. On the contrary, nearly all the light is sometimes concentrated in the two outside lines, leaving a weak middle, which exhibits the appearance, not of a single middle line, but of two weak middle lines, so that the resultant appearance of the modified line is a quartet, of which the two outside lines generally are much stronger than the two inside lines. Further, in some cases, the two inside lines are absent altogether, so that we are presented with what appears to be a doublet instead of a triplet (the light being still viewed across the lines of force). (Preston, 1898, pp. 388–389)

Preston further analyzed the two sodium $D$-lines, detecting that the $D_1$-line split into a quartet, of which the two middle lines were nearly completely absorbed, while the $D_2$-line separated into a sextet of bright fine lines.

A little later than Preston, Alfred Marie Cornu became interested in the Zeeman effect.<sup>713</sup> He possessed a Rowland grating, presented to him by Henry A. Rowland himself, which he had used already for solar spectroscopy. Cornu published his results on the magnetic influence on spectral lines in several notes, submitted to the Academy of Sciences, Paris: in the first, which was presented on 18 October 1897, he reported only about triplets and their polarization, which he found to agree with Lorentz’ theory (Cornu, 1897); however, in the second, presented on 17 January 1898, he corrected his earlier results, claiming in particular that the sodium $D_2$-line was split into a quadruplet and that the same situation occurred for the same lines of the magnesium spectrum and the green lines of the thallium and cadmium spectra (Cornu, 1898). In fall 1897, simultaneously with Cornu, Henri Becquerel also concerned himself with the Zeeman effect; in collaboration with Henri Alexandre Deslandres, he studied several visible and ultraviolet lines of iron and, like Cornu and Michelson, observed quadruplets and other complex structures (Becquerel and Deslandres, 1898a, b). At the same time, while investigating the effect of the magnetic field on the molecular band lines of carbon, cyanide and nitrogen, Becquerel and Deslandres found in no case any sign of the Zeeman effect.

In the following years people active in the field, like Preston and Michelson, refined their observational techniques further in the direction of higher resolution and stronger magnetic fields. Thus, for instance, Michelson succeeded already in 1898 in splitting the green mercury line of wavelength 5460 Å into eleven components (Michelson, 1898a). Preston, on the other hand, began a systematic study of various spectral lines in order to discover more about the regularities of the Zeeman effects. Already in his first paper he had concluded: ‘It is clear, that

448    Chapter IV    The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

the magnetic effect depends not so much on the wavelength of the spectral line as on some hidden quality which we may refer to as the character of the line; for lines of nearly the same wavelength, even of the same substance, show effects which differ remarkably in magnitude and character’ (Preston, 1898, p. 387). A year later he formulated what he called a ‘General Law of the Phenomena of Magnetic Perturbation of Spectral Lines,’ stating that all lines of a given series of a substance exhibit the same pattern of components in a magnetic field; moreover, analogous spectral lines of the same series, even if belonging to different elements, have the same Zeeman effect (Preston, 1899). Carl Runge and Friedrich Paschen assembled extensive data to test Preston’s law (Runge and Paschen, 1900). With respect to the assertion in its first part, they investigated the behaviour of mercury lines: they observed that the pairs of lines having wavelengths of 5461 Å and 3341.7 Å, 4359 Å and 2893.7 Å, and 4047 Å and 2752.9 Å, showed the same number of magnetic components, in the last pair a triplet, in the other pairs a more complex multiplet. Runge and Paschen argued further that a consideration of the frequency differences supported the result very well: the frequency differences for lines of the same type (multiplicity) turned out to be the same; e.g., in the case of the mercury spectrum the frequency differences were the same for the wavelengths around 3341.7 Å and 5461 Å, and the same for the lines having wavelengths around 2893.7 Å and 4359 Å (Runge and Paschen, 1900, p. 481). As a consequence the observation of the anomalous Zeeman effects allowed one to determine the multiplicity of a spectral line (emitted by the unperturbed atom), even when (in the absence of the magnetic field) only the strongest multiplets were known. Two years later Runge reported to the *Physikalische Gesellschaft der Universität Göttingen* certain results on the Zeeman effects of some triplet series—the so-called second series—of several elements, including magnesium, cadmium and mercury, and on the doublet spectra of copper, silver, aluminum, thallium and the sodium $D$-lines, which he had studied again in collaboration with Paschen: these results showed that in all cases of corresponding lines there occurred the same number of magnetic components with the same frequency differences (Runge, 1902). Runge also gave an interesting numerical relation between the component separations in doublet and triplet spectra. When he expressed the differences of the Zeeman components for triplet lines by integral multiples of $u$ and the differences of the Zeeman components for doublet lines by integral multiples of $v$, then he found that the relation $3v = 2u$ was observed (Runge, 1902, p. 442).

Further progress in the analysis of the complex Zeeman effects came in 1907. W. Lohmann of the University of Halle analyzed experimentally several visible lines of the helium spectrum in detail in his doctoral thesis (Lohmann, 1907). Carl Runge took these data, together with the ones he and Paschen had obtained previously, and tried to fit numerically the observed frequency differences. He arrived at the following conclusion: ‘The hitherto observed complex splittings of spectral lines in a magnetic field exhibit the following peculiarity: the distances of the components from the centre are integral multiples of just a fraction of the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0083 -->

normal separation, $a = \Delta\lambda / \lambda^2 = (|\mathbf{H}|/4\pi)(|e|/m_e)$. So far the fractions $a/2, a/3, a/4, a/6, a/7, a/11,$ and $a/12$ have been definitely observed' (Runge, 1907, p. 237). That is, in the complex Zeeman effects the quantity $c\Delta\nu$, with $c$ the velocity of light *in vacuo* and $\Delta\nu$ the frequency difference, assumed values that were integral multiples of the quantity $a/r$, where $a$ ($= |e||\mathbf{H}|/4\pi m_e$) is the corresponding value for normal triplets (see Eq. (230)) and the denominator $r$ is an integer between 1 (for the normal triplet) and 12.$^{714}$

Runge had derived this result, which would be called Runge's rule later, by a careful mathematical analysis of all available data. He was aware of the objection that 'for any arbitrary decomposition the distances can always be represented as multiples of a quantity, with any given degree of accuracy, if one only admits sufficiently large multiples of a correspondingly small quantity' (Runge, 1907, pp. 233–234). By evaluating the mean square errors he tried, however, to obtain the smallest integers possible as denominators. Though one could object to some of the assumptions underlying Runge's analysis—such as the assumption that the observed data exhibited no known regularities—his rule proved to be very valuable for future research. Friedrich Paschen praised it twenty years later in the following words:

> Runge's name is inseparably connected with the fundamental law of the magnetic splitting of spectral lines. He was the first to recognize that all separations were rational multiples of the normal separation. Since then, the common denominator occurring there has been called the Runge denominator. One should remind oneself, how inaccurate the data then were. At that time, not even the normal separation was known to within the accuracy of a few percent, because an accurate measurement of magnetic field strengths did not exist. Runge showed how one nevertheless arrived at the conviction that his rule was valid. This constituted a masterpiece of scientific perception, of a type quite similar to the discovery of the basic form of the laws of [spectral] series by Rydberg. (Paschen, 1927, pp. 232–233)$^{715}$

However, at that time, soon after its enunciation, Runge's rule (as well as Preston's 'general law') appeared to be at stake when W. Lohmann, who had meanwhile extended the work of his thesis, showed that *all* helium lines—independently of what series they belonged to—were decomposed in a magnetic field into normal triplets; only for certain satellites accompanying the main lines did he observe sextets (Lohmann, 1908). For several years Lohmann's helium lines remained the sole exceptions to the accepted rules of the anomalous Zeeman effects, until in early 1912 Woldemar Voigt and Hans Marius Hansen, his guest from Copenhagen, reported about the results of their observation of the

Michelson during his visit to Göttingen in summer 1911, they had originally studied the phenomenon of double refraction of absorption lines created by the application of a magnetic field. However, the resolution of the new apparatus was so good that Voigt and Hansen also looked for the inverse anomalous Zeeman effect of the red lithium line of wavelength 6708 Å, which had not been separated so far. They found a triplet, which surprised them very much, because if the lithium spectrum was analogous to the spectra of sodium and potassium, one had to expect—according to Preston’s rule—a complex Zeeman effect. Still Voigt and Hansen were not sure whether they had really found a violation of the known rule. After all, so far one had not observed the doublet structure in the lithium spectrum; hence the identity of the Zeeman effect of lithium with the ones of potassium and sodium lines could not be demanded (Voigt and Hansen, 1912, p. 223).

With the results of Lohmann and of Voigt and Hansen the Zeeman effects had become rather difficult phenomena to describe. There seemed to exist exceptions to the ordering rules that had been obtained so far and to the conceptions underlying them. This situation especially bothered Friedrich Paschen, who had been involved for a number of years in the systematic measurements of the emission lines of elements and in establishing their organization into series.717 Paschen got his student Ernst Back to investigate the case of lithium lines more carefully.718 Back reported later about this work as follows:

Paschen and Back especially studied the narrow, but still noticeable doublets and triplets, such as the oxygen triplet at 3947.438 Å, 3947.626 Å and 3947.731 Å. In a magnetic field of strength below 6000 G, each of these three lines separated in the pattern known for broad triplets, say the mercury triplet consisting of the components of wavelengths 5461 Å, 4358 Å and 4047 Å. With magnetic fields of 6000 G, however, the Zeeman components of different natural line components overlapped, and then began what Paschen and Back called the magnetic ‘transformation’ (‘*Verwandlung*’), which resulted in a pattern very different from the usual anomalous Zeeman effect pattern (determined by Runge’s rule). With further increasing field strength many magnetic components became weaker and Paschen and Back observed the following situation:  

> A strong magnetic middle component emerges at 3947.564 Å, i.e., at about the centre of the original triplet.
