However, in a field of 32,000 gauss there remain only parallel components . . . At 32,000 gauss, the diffuse side components already become narrower and separate from the middle component. They vibrate mostly in the perpendicular direction. (Paschen and Back, 1912, p. 912)  

By increasing the strength of the magnetic field to 40,000 G in a later series of experiments, Paschen and Back confirmed the complete change of the magnetic pattern of the oxygen triplet into a normal triplet (Paschen and Back, 1913). The above-mentioned phenomenon of ‘magnetic transformation’ with increasing strength of the magnetic field was observed in many examples.⁷²¹ This effect, which soon came to be called the ‘Paschen–Back effect’ (‘*Paschen–Backscher Effekt*,’ Sommerfeld, 1914a, p. 207), explained all the exceptions from Preston’s rules that had been found hitherto, including the ones of Lohmann and Voigt and Hansen. Paschen and Back also proposed a definite physical picture of the entire situation. They argued that the magnetic anomalies, as shown in the Zeeman effects of doublet and triplet lines, were caused by ‘a kind of stress condition of the light-vibrations,’ and added:  

> For then [i.e., on increasing the magnetic field strength] the complex of a multiple line is transformed into a single line, i.e., the anomalous type is transformed into a normal one, and it is likely that the condition of stress renders an originally single line into a multiple line. exhibiting no stress] and at the end [i.e., in a strong magnetic field] the single line, whose normal magnetic behaviour can be interpreted by the assumption, with the help of which Lorentz explained the simple Zeeman effect. Magnetic complications are caused by the same stress conditions, which are responsible for the formation of a line-multiplet. (Paschen and Back, 1912, pp. 904–905)

Lorentz' original theory of the Zeeman effect had stated that any spectral line of frequency $\nu$ is separated in a magnetic field into three (polarized) lines of frequencies $\nu$ and $\nu \pm \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, where $\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ is given by Eq. (230). Lorentz had assumed, in agreement with his electron theory of matter, that the spectral lines of atoms were created by electrons (of charge $e$ and mass $m_e$), elastically bound within their atoms and vibrating with the frequency $\nu$ (Lorentz, 1897). At about the same time, Joseph Larmor had discussed a different theory of the origin of spectral lines and their Zeeman effect: in his theory, charged particles moved on circular orbits in atoms and molecules, thus giving rise to spectral lines; the action of an external magnetic field led to an additional precession (later called the Larmor precession) of the electron around the axis of the field of strength $\mathbf{H}$ with an angular velocity $\omega_L$ ($= |e||\mathbf{H}|/(2m_e c)$, $c$ being the velocity of light *in vacuo*) (Larmor, 1897a). Evidently, Larmor's result agreed fully with that of Lorentz' theory in the case that the radiation came from an electron, for $\omega_L = 2\pi \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, with $\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ given by Eq. (230). However, it also described a more general situation, as Larmor noted three years later in connection with the anomalous Zeeman effect that had meanwhile been discovered: 'If we now drop the restriction of $\kappa$ [Larmor denoted the angular precession frequency $\omega_L$ by $2\kappa$] to the same value for all the effective ions of the molecule this feature will give a clue towards a more general representation of the facts' (Larmor, 1900b, p. 345).

The possibility of explaining the anomalous Zeeman effects by associating the origin of spectral lines not only with rotating electrons but also with other charged objects in atoms—though it was perfectly consistent with the knowledge around 1900—was not acceptable to men like Lorentz. Lorentz had the firm conviction that only electrons should be responsible for the processes involving radiation and matter. Therefore, he tried to account for the complex magnetic separation of spectral lines in another way, which he had indicated already in his first paper on the subject—i.e., before the discovery of the anomalous Zeeman effect. He had mentioned, in particular, that the magnetic triplet would not arise if the radiation was emitted by *'highly degenerate systems'* of several electrons (Lorentz, 1897). Still, the result he had obtained did not describe the observations of Preston and others. Nevertheless Lorentz remained hopeful that one would eventually be successful along the lines he had in mind. In his rectorial address at the University of Leyden on 8 February 1900 he remarked: 'There is no doubt about the possibility that one may understand the influence of the magnetic field most easily if one assumes the existence of oscillating charges, and if by means of suitable assumptions one can arrive at something other than simple triplets.' However, he admitted at the same time that 'we do not yet possess a satisfactory

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0088 -->

454 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

mechanism that gives rise to a quadruplet’ (Lorentz, 1900a, p. 517).[^722] Nine years later, he concluded rather pessimistically in his article for the *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften*: ‘To sum up, we are forced to conclude that the electron theory of light emission can explain the observed phenomena only to a very modest extent, and that perhaps much has to be altered in its foundations’ (Lorentz, 1909a, p. 225).

As an alternative to his theory Lorentz referred to a proposal of Walther Ritz, who had tried to describe the origin of spectral lines by the interaction of molecular magnets within the atoms (he was stimulated by Pierre Weiss’ theory of ferromagnetic substances) and electrons. According to Ritz the molecular magnets performed periodic rotations under the influence of an external magnetic field, and as a consequence any spectral line emitted by the atom ‘*will be separated into several lines, whose distances from the original position of the line are related to each other as rational numbers*’ (Ritz, 1908a, p. 682). Thus Ritz succeeded, for instance, in deriving Runge’s rule. The new theory, in spite of its attractive features, also contained serious difficulties, especially the assumption—so far unjustified—of molecular magnets which act on electrons moving in a plane. Other difficulties were pointed out by Woldemar Voigt: for example, from Ritz’ theory it followed that the probability for a given orientation of a molecular magnet leading to a certain Zeeman component depended on the temperature in a way that was not verified by experiment; moreover, according to the theory in all cases (infinitely) many components (with decreasing intensity) should be found, in contrast to observation (Voigt, 1911).

While Ritz had worked outside the electron theory of matter, Voigt had pursued for years an approach consistent with it. However, unlike Lorentz, he had assumed from the very beginning that the Zeeman effect phenomena had something to do with the motion of many coupled electrons; thus he had treated the inverse Zeeman effect and the Faraday effect (i.e., the rotation of the plane of polarization of incident radiation) by studying the absorption properties of a large system of vibrating electrons (Voigt, 1898, 1899a). In his theory he had also given up Lorentz’ assumption of isotropy; instead Voigt claimed that the forces acting on bound electrons in matter were *not* symmetrical in all directions, but possessed extremum values (maxima or minima) in the direction of the external magnetic field. In a later paper, submitted in September 1907, he combined the idea of anisotropic forces with Lorentz’ general formalism of 1897 for the Zeeman effect of emission lines; by coupling together all components of the electronic vibrations parallel to the direction of the magnetic field, and all perpendicular components separately, he arrived at a consistent description of the frequencies of the magnetic components (of the anomalous Zeeman lines) and their intensities, provided suitable assumptions were made concerning the number of coupled electrons and the specific nature of the anisotropy (Voigt,

[^722]: Lorentz had himself attempted to explain the quadruplets (Lorentz, 1899), which had been observed especially by Alfred Cornu (1898).

# IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect

1907).⁷²³ A special outcome of Voigt’s theory was that the number of coupled electrons determined the number of coupling parameters and thus the number of magnetic components.⁷²⁴ As a consequence of his calculations, Voigt proposed to attribute the occurrence of complex (anomalous) patterns to the coupling of not more than two electrons. That is, Voigt always considered pairs in the magnetic components of lines (showing the anomalous Zeeman effect), each pair being due to a particular type of coupling of two electrons (Voigt, 1907, p. 224).⁷²⁵

With the discovery of the Paschen–Back effect, Voigt attempted to use his formalism also to account for the behaviour of the Zeeman components in an increasingly stronger magnetic field. Since he had several parameters at his disposal, he had realistic hopes that he might succeed. Even more, Voigt now saw an excellent opportunity for determining from experimental data all the parameters entering into the theory. Thus, in the introduction of the first of three papers on the new situation, he remarked:

> The phenomena of the Zeeman effect indicate, for each spectral line, the existence of a certain number of corresponding *degrees of freedom* [of the system of electrons in atoms]; and with each degree of freedom is associated at least *one* parameter, or even *several* parameters under certain conditions … It is therefore rather unreasonable to reproach this method [of description] as “having to introduce for each type [of the Zeeman effect] a special, suitable hypothesis.” If, with the help of a single determination of a set of parameters entering into the differential equations [describing the motion of the coupled electrons], the method represents quantitatively correctly an entire sequence of phenomena—say, as in our case, the development of [the behaviour of] the Zeeman effect for increasing field strength—then this must still be regarded as a success. (Voigt, 1913a, p. 369)

In his papers, submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in January (Voigt, 1913a), April (Voigt, 1913c) and July (Voigt, 1913d), Voigt showed how the empirical behaviour of the Zeeman components in the case of hydrogen lines, and of many doublet and triplet lines, could be derived. Especially, he developed a complete and reasonably satisfactory theory of the components and their intensities for

---
⁷²³ Voigt, in the introduction of his paper, referred to an earlier theory of his doctoral student Alfred Arthur Robb, who had investigated systems of two and four coupled electrons vibrating under the influence of isotropic forces (Robb, 1904). When the coupling was described by a homogeneous function of second order in the coordinates of the electrons, Robb had found quintet and nonet patterns. Robb’s treatment, however, implied an essential difficulty, for as Voigt noted: a coupling condition of second order seemed to contradict the principle of superposition in the propagation of radiation.
⁷²⁴ In the case of isotropic forces any number of electrons led to normal triplets (provided one did not impose a condition of the type of Robb’s—see the previous footnote). For anisotropic forces the coupling of two electrons implied up to four parameters, which could be used to fit the frequency differences of the components and their intensities; three coupled electrons provided nine parameters, and four coupled electrons up to eighteen parameters.
⁷²⁵ By assuming independent couplings of several pairs of electrons Voigt hoped to avoid the problem of determining a simple Zeeman pattern (as given by Runge’s rules) from a complicated relation (involving square roots, etc.) of the coupling parameters of more than two electrons.

456 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

lines of the sodium $D$-type and their transformation in an increasingly stronger magnetic field (Voigt, 1913c, d).

Woldemar Voigt's equations for the doublets and their Zeeman effects were simplified considerably by Arnold Sommerfeld in a paper submitted to the Göttingen Academy in March 1914 (Sommerfeld, 1914a).$^{726}$ The reformulation also allowed Sommerfeld to draw certain consequences about the constitution of atoms emitting doublet lines. Since the equations of motion of Sommerfeld's system could be solved by a set of three complex position coordinates, which contained as factors the three cube roots of unity (i.e., 1, $\exp(2\pi i/3)$ and $\exp(4\pi i/3)$, respectively), Sommerfeld suspected that the solution described a situation in which three electrons moved, separated by the same distance, on a circular orbit in the atom under investigation. The role of the number 3 in the case of atoms emitting doublet lines, he argued further, would be played by a different integer in the case of atoms emitting triplet lines. Sommerfeld concluded: 'Perhaps the phenomenological investigation of the Zeeman effect, as Mr. Voigt has pursued it, provides the most reliable material for establishing atomic structure; the example of the $D$-lines allows us, in this respect, to expect remarkably simple number-theoretical relations' (Sommerfeld, 1914a, p. 226).

The connection between the description of the Zeeman effects and the ideas about atomic structure, to which Voigt had already referred earlier in March 1913 (Voigt, 1913c), seemed to be timely indeed, for it was also then that Niels Bohr developed his theory of the structure of atoms, consisting of nuclei and electrons, whose dynamics was governed by quantum conditions. Immediately after seeing Bohr's first paper on the constitution of atoms and molecules (Bohr, 1913b), Sommerfeld thought of investigating its consequences concerning the magnetic influence on the emitted discrete radiation. He wrote to Bohr: 'Will you employ your model to treat the Zeeman effect? I would have [actually] liked to do so' (Sommerfeld to Bohr, 4 September 1913). Bohr himself took the first steps towards this problem (Bohr, 1914b); Sommerfeld, in his communication to the Göttingen Academy cited above, did not refer to Bohr's new theory of atomic structure and stayed away from the problem of the Zeeman effect (within the context of Bohr's theory) until the middle of 1916. However, after developing the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, including its application to the relativistic hydrogen atom, Sommerfeld was ready to treat this problem systematically. In a paper, entitled 'Zur Theorie des Zeeman-Effekts der Wasserstofflinien, mit einer Anwendung über den Stark-Effekt' ('On the Theory of the Zeeman Effect of the Hydrogen Lines, with an Application to the Stark Effect'), which was received by *Physikalische Zeitschrift* on 7 September 1916, he calculated the Zeeman effect of the one-electron atom according to the extended Bohr theory (Sommerfeld, 1916d). The basic point in Sommerfeld's approach consisted in

$^{726}$Sommerfeld had become interested in the anomalous Zeeman effects the previous year. Thus he had attempted to develop his own theory of these phenomena, including the Paschen–Back effect, by assuming anisotropically bound electrons (as Voigt had done); however, he had succeeded only in accounting for the situation in strong magnetic fields (Sommerfeld, 1913).

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 457

introducing—besides the azimuthal and radial quantum numbers, $n_{\phi}$ and $n_r$, respectively, describing a Kepler orbit in a plane—a third quantum number, the ‘spatial’ quantum number $n_1$, whose values determined the discrete positions of the electron’s orbit with respect to the external magnetic field **H**, such that the cosine of $\theta$, the angle between the direction of **H** and normal to the plane of the orbit, was given by the equation

$$\cos \theta = \frac{n_1}{n_{\phi}} . \tag{231}$$

By solving the equation of motion of the electron in the magnetic field, Sommerfeld found—like Peter Debye a little earlier (Debye, 1916a)—the result that the frequencies of the hydrogen lines were shifted by an amount $\Delta \nu$,

$$\Delta \nu = \frac{f}{4\pi} \Delta n_1, \tag{232}$$

where $f$ denoted the quantity, $(e/m_e c)|\mathbf{H}|$, and $\Delta n_1$ the difference of the spatial quantum numbers in the initial and the final state, respectively. Due to Eq. (232) there always arose a Zeeman triplet, whose separation was determined by integral multiples ($\Delta n_1 = 0$ and $\pm 1, 0$ and $\pm 2, 0$ and $\pm 3, 0$, etc.) of the classical separation, $(|e|/m_e)(\mathbf{H}/4\pi c)$.
In the same paper, Sommerfeld also calculated the Zeeman effect of the relativistic hydrogen atom, obtaining the same separation of the magnetic (triplet) components as in the nonrelativistic case. This result bothered him considerably, and he remarked:

> It is true that, because of its diffuseness, one does not know the Zeeman effect of the hydrogen lines well enough. However, it is very unlikely that there arises a normal triplet for each component [i.e., for each fine-structure component] of the hydrogen lines. [Of course, there was the possibility that the theory described the Paschen–Back effect, but Sommerfeld noted:] There is no indication of the Paschen–Back effect in our calculations ... The Paschen–Back effect shows up, as is known, if $f$ ceases to be small compared to $\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, i.e., small against the original separation of two components in the multiplet spectral line. In our formula, however, the ratio $f : \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ does not enter at all. (Sommerfeld, 1916d, p. 502)

With the selection rules established by Adalbert Rubinowicz (1918a, b) and Niels Bohr (1918a, b), it became clear that $\Delta n_1$ always assumed the values $0$ or $\pm 1$; hence the theory of Debye and Sommerfeld accounted only for the normal Zeeman effect (like the classical theories of Lorentz or Larmor). But how should one then describe the anomalous effects, which usually occurred in the spectral lines of non-hydrogen-like atoms? The experts did not know, and Sommerfeld summarized the situation in 1919 in the following statements: (i) the singlet lines of hydrogen-like atoms exhibit the normal Zeeman effect, while their triplet lines

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0092 -->

# 458 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

approach the normal Zeeman effect for magnetic fields of large field strength; (ii) in weak magnetic fields the doublet and triplet spectra of non-hydrogen-like atoms exhibit complex Zeeman effects, the Zeeman effects being the same for the same type and origin. Since the type of the lines in non-hydrogen-like atoms depended on the number of electrons in the atom, atoms of elements organized in a column ('Vertikalreihe') of the periodic system of elements emitted lines having the same anomalous Zeeman effects. Hence Sommerfeld concluded that

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;it is the outer electrons of atoms that determine the character of the Zeeman effect; especially, it is their magnetic fields, provided they cannot be neglected against the external magnetic fields (in which case Paschen–Back effect arises). These are, however, only general and vague conjectures. A genuine theory of the Zeeman effect in the case of non-hydrogen-like atoms cannot be given until the reason for the multiplicity of spectral lines has been clarified. (Sommerfeld, 1919, pp. 438–439)

Altogether Sommerfeld noted that the existing quantum theory of the Zeeman effect 'is as yet not in a position to explain the complex [i.e., anomalous] Zeeman effect and its transformation into the Paschen–Back effect' (Sommerfeld, 1919, p. 439).
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like the experimentalists earlier—especially, Paschen and Back in discussing the interpretation of their effect—Sommerfeld connected the understanding of the anomalous Zeeman effects with an explanation of the doublet and triplet structure of the spectra of non-hydrogen-like atoms: that is, the difficulty of the quantum theory of atomic structure to explain the anomalous Zeeman effect was connected with the difficulty of that theory to account for the doublet and triplet structure of the spectral lines emitted by free (undisturbed) atoms.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On the other hand, there was the old theory of Voigt dealing with the anomalous Zeeman effects, which accounted reasonably well for the observed phenomena. Hence Sommerfeld argued that Voigt’s formulae described the situation correctly and one had just to translate it in terms of the quantum theory of atomic constitution. The question then arose of how to approach this goal. Evidently, the most straightforward way was to treat many-electron atoms according to the principles of the existing atomic theory, but no such system had been dealt with successfully so far. Nevertheless, in order to make a start Sommerfeld proposed a new method, which he described in a long paper on 'Allgemeine spektroskopische Gesetze, insbesondere ein magneto-optischer Zerlegungssatz' ('General Spectroscopic Laws, Especially a Magneto-Optical Decomposition Rule'), submitted in March 1920 to *Annalen der Physik* and published in October (Sommerfeld, 1920f). In this paper he drew attention to the possibility of obtaining information about atomic structure by exploiting empirical relations concerning the multiplicities of spectral lines and their Zeeman effects. He remarked: 'The practical importance of the multiple lines for the organization of the spectroscopic observation in series is known (laws of constant frequency differences, etc.). The theoretical importance of the line structures for the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0093 -->

# IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 459

investigation of atoms by means of [mechanical] models will doubtless be no less’ (Sommerfeld, 1920f, p. 222). Sommerfeld assigned a special role to a new empirical law, which he called the ‘magneto-optical decomposition rule’ (‘*magneto-optischer Zerlegungssatz*’) and which he praised as revealing ‘a harmony of integral-number relationships of such purity, which would even surprise those who have been spoilt by the modern quantum theory’ (‘*eine Harmonie ganz-zahliger Verhältnisse von einer Reinheit, die auch durch die moderne Quantentheorie Verwöhnten überraschen wird*,’ Sommerfeld, 1920f, p. 222).

Sommerfeld had introduced his ‘decomposition rule’ (‘*Zerlegungssatz*’) in a lecture given in the middle of September 1919 at Lund and published it in a note to *Naturwissenschaften* with the title ‘*Ein Zahlenmysterium in der Theorie des Zeemaneflektes*’ (‘A Number Mystery in the Theory of the Zeeman Effect,’ Sommerfeld, 1920a).<sup>727</sup> To arrive at it, he analyzed the empirical values of Runge’s denominator, i.e., the integral values of the number $r$ appearing in $\Delta v_{\text{anomalous}}$, the frequency difference of the anomalous Zeeman components, due to the formula

$$\Delta v_{\text{anomalous}} = \frac{q}{r} \frac{|e|}{m_e} \frac{|H|}{4\pi c} \text{,} \quad (233)$$

where $q$, the integral numerator, assumes the values $0, \pm 1, \pm 2$, etc. The characteristic values of $r$ were 1, 2 and 3 for singlet, doublet and triplet lines, respectively. According to the quantum theory of atomic structure the lines arose from transitions between two stationary states, having energies $W_1$ and $W_2$, their frequencies being given by the quantity $(W_1 - W_2)/h$, where $h$ is Planck’s constant. In agreement with this and Ritz’ combination principle of energy terms, the frequency shift, $\Delta v_{\text{anomalous}}$, associated with the anomalous Zeeman effects, came about by taking the difference of two terms, $\Delta W_1$ and $\Delta W_2$, denoting the changes of the energies of the initial and final states under the influence of a magnetic field, i.e.,<sup>728</sup>

$$\Delta v_{\text{anomalous}} = \Delta v_1 - \Delta v_2 = \frac{\Delta W_1 - \Delta W_2}{h} \text{.} \quad (234)$$

<sup>727</sup>Sommerfeld wrote to Bohr on 11 November 1920: ‘I already lectured about my “decomposition rule” (“*Zerlegungssatz*”) in Lund in your presence.’

Sommerfeld had taken the phrase ‘number mystery’ (‘*Zahlenmysterium*’) from a letter of Rubinowicz (see Sommerfeld to Rubinowicz, 26 December 1919). We owe the reference to this letter to Paul Forman’s article on Alfred Landé and the anomalous Zeeman effect (Forman, 1970b), from which we have obtained other information as well about Landé’s involvement in this problem.

<sup>728</sup>Sommerfeld was not the first to apply the combination principle to the anomalous Zeeman effects. This had been done earlier by Tennis von Lohuizen, a former doctoral student of Zeeman’s, in an article presented to the Amsterdam Academy in May 1919 (Lohuizen, 1919). Sommerfeld probably learned about Lohuizen’s work from Niels Bohr in Lund (see footnote 727). (Bohr, in turn, had become acquainted with the result when he visited Leyden in April 1919.) And this fact (the knowledge of Lohuizen’s publication) motivated him to publish the ‘decomposition rule’ in his note in *Naturwissenschaften* (see Sommerfeld, 1920a, p. 64).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0094 -->

460
Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

Evidently the frequency shifts $\Delta \nu_i$ also satisfied Runge's rule; hence there followed the equations

$$\Delta \nu_i = \frac{q_i}{r_i} \frac{|e|}{m_e} \frac{|\mathbf{H}|}{4\pi c} \quad (i = 1, 2), \tag{235}$$

where $q_i$ and $r_i$ are the Runge numerators and denominators, respectively, of the individual terms. Hence $q/r$, the rational number describing the observed magnetic displacement of the spectral lines (caused by the transition from the state 1 to the state 2) had to be decomposed as

$$\frac{q}{r} = \frac{q_1}{r_1} - \frac{q_2}{r_2} = \frac{q_1 r_2 - q_2 r_1}{r_1 r_2} . \tag{236}$$

From this relation Sommerfeld concluded: 'We denote the equation, $r = r_1 r_2$, as the magneto-optical decomposition rule and: *The Runge number [r], observed in the anomalous Zeeman effect can be decomposed into the Runge numbers [$r_1$ and $r_2$] of the first and the second terms involved in the spectral lines*' (Sommerfeld, 1920a, p. 63).

The decomposition rule thus associated a Runge denominator with both the initial and the final state of an atom. Sommerfeld further proposed that in the case of singlet spectra the value of *all* $r_i$ was 1, while for doublet and triplet spectra only the denominator of the $s$-term was 1, and the denominator of higher terms assumed the values 2, 3, 4 for $p$-, $d$- and $b$- (or $f$-) terms involved in the triplet spectra, and 3, 5, 7 for the $p$-, $d$- and $b$-terms involved in the doublet spectra. Since the spectral series corresponded to term differences (i.e., the principal series to $s - p$, the sharp subordinate series to $p - s$, the diffuse subordinate series to $p - d$, and the Bergmann series to $d - b$) one could derive immediately from Eq. (236) the observed Zeeman effects for these series. For example, in the case of lines belonging to the principal and the sharp subordinate series, the combination of $s$- and $p$-terms provided the denominator $r = 1 \cdot 2 = 2$ for triplet lines and $r = 1 \cdot 3 = 3$ for doublet lines. In the diffuse subordinate series, $r$ assumed the value 6 for triplet and 15 for doublet lines, corresponding to the splittings $2 \cdot 3 = 6$ and $3 \cdot 5 = 15$, respectively. Sommerfeld obtained the values of $r$ in the Bergmann series by extrapolation, and expressed the hope that the Zeeman effects of the Bergmann series of doublets and triplets will soon be observed, adding cautiously: 'Nevertheless such a large denominator like 35 [$= 5 \cdot 7$ in the case of doublets; $r = 3 \cdot 4 = 12$ in the case of triplets] can hardly be determined with certainty . . . In these cases, our decomposition rule is of help, for it demands the testing of the number 7 rather than 35, and the number 4 instead of 12, as characterizing the Bergmann term' (Sommerfeld, 1920a, p. 64).

To test his new scheme of Runge denominators, Sommerfeld therefore asked the experimentalists to observe the Zeeman effects in the Bergmann series. Moreover, he drew attention to an advantageous use of the Paschen–Back effect: if

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0095 -->

**461**

the magnetic transformation occurred only with one of the triplet or doublet states involved in the transition, the Zeeman effects would allow one to determine the Runge denominator of the other term.

In deriving the decomposition rule Sommerfeld had made use of the precision data which Ernst Back had obtained before the war. He therefore hesitated in publishing his new results earlier than Back his data.$^{729}$ In any case he delayed the publication of a detailed paper, although he had had most of the results since 1919, in order to give Back the deserved priority. But the latter, never content with the accuracy and reliability of the data, was not ready any time soon. In fact, the first detailed account of Back's measurements on the anomalous Zeeman effects appeared only in 1923 (Back, 1923a). While this was still far away, Back allowed Sommerfeld to base his representation of spectroscopic laws in his paper for *Annalen der Physik* (Sommerfeld, 1920f) on his, i.e., Back's results. In a letter to Alfred Landé, Sommerfeld explained the reasons for his considerate attitude towards Back: 'Back is the experimental father of the entire field [of observations of anomalous Zeeman effects]; he must have priority in picking the fruits of his experimental labours himself. I had also asked his permission before publishing my decomposition rule, which he gave without hesitation, for he himself had no theoretical ideas at that time; these ideas have come to him as a result of the [decomposition] rule' (Sommerfeld to Landé, 3 March 1921). With the last remark Sommerfeld referred to an extended note, dated 10 February 1921, which Back sent to *Naturwissenschaften* and which appeared in the issue of 25 March 1921 (Back, 1921a). In this note, entitled '*Ein weiteres Zahlenmysterium in der Theorie des Zeemaneffekts*' ('A Further Number Mystery in the Theory of the Zeeman Effect'), Back presented an empirical rule —also derived from his old data—describing the number of Zeeman components in all cases observed. He simplified his 'number mystery,' stimulated by a hint from D. S. Roschdestwensky (Roschdestvenski), in a second note, which he submitted on 8 June 1921 again to *Naturwissenschaften* (Back, 1921b). It contained the following statement: If one takes the number of polarized components (either the parallel or the perpendicular ones) and adds to it what Back called the 'index sum' ('*Indexsumme*')—i.e., the sum of certain numbers characterizing the terms involved in the transition (see Back, 1921a, p. 200, and 1921b, p. 569)—then one finds the 'sum values of the series' ('*Summenzahlen der Serien*'). The latter assume regularly ordered values for the term series: for example, the value 1 for all singlet lines, the values 2, 4, 6 for the doublet lines in the principal (and sharp subordinate) series, the diffuse subordinate series and the Bergmann series, respectively, and the values 3, 5, 7 for the triplet lines of the same series (see Back, 1921b, p. 571, Table 6).$^{730}$ With this rule Back succeeded in organizing the

existing data on the number of Zeeman components and describing their position with respect to that of the original lines.731

The empirical rules described above for the line multiplets and their Zeeman effects did not offer immediate interpretation in terms of specific atomic models. They rather served to organize the vast spectroscopic data on line spectra in a systematic way, helping to adapt it to the fundamental principles of atomic theory, especially the combination principle. Sommerfeld tried to summarize the state of affairs in his paper in *Annalen der Physik*, where he listed five general spectroscopic laws. The first, the 'law of permanence of the multiplicities,' stated that for a given atom the $p$- and $d$-terms possess the same multiplicity (Sommerfeld, 1920f, pp. 224–225).732 The second law, the 'selection rule' ('*Auswahlprinzip*'), then determined the number of components arising from a given transition. For example, in the case of the diffuse lines, whose frequencies were given symbolically by the equation

$$ \nu = 2p_i - md_j, \quad i, j = \begin{cases} 1, 2 & \text{for doublets} \\ 1, 2, 3 & \text{for triplets,} \end{cases} \tag{237} $$

where 2 denotes the value of the principal quantum number (i.e., the sum of the radial and azimuthal quantum numbers) of the constant term and $m$ the principal quantum number of the variable term (also called its '*Laufzahl*,' i.e., 'running' or 'variable number'), the usual selection rule (requiring a change of the azimuthal quantum number by 0 or $\pm 1$) was automatically satisfied. However, there had to exist still another selection rule due to the structure of the series lines. For example, in the case of doublet series each line consisted of two components and one satellite, and the question arose of how to explain this fact in atomic theory. Sommerfeld answered it by introducing a new quantum number. He argued: 'The distinguishing characteristic of the different $d$- and $p$-terms must rather be an inner quantum number, something which might correspond to a hidden rotation. We know its geometrical significance as little as we know about the differences in orbits that give rise to the multiplicities of the series terms' (Sommerfeld, 1920f, p. 231). By assigning to this 'hidden' or 'inner' quantum number the values 1, 2 for the $d$-term and 2, 3 for the $p$-term in Eq.

731 Back summarized the value of his rule as follows:
We do not at all see the fundamental significance of the rules reported in this and the previous paper in the fact that they enable us, say, to predict experimentally the not yet investigated Zeeman types, or those, which perhaps cannot be approached by the present experimental techniques. Such predictions have no practical value and are always problematic . . . The real significance of the new index rules seems to us to lie rather in the fact that by the clarification which these rules provide of the index number, the old notation of the series and multiplicities is raised to a general point of view and, at the same time, new and readily prepared material is provided for the theory of quantum numbers. (Back, 1921b, p. 575)

732 Let us again emphasize at this point that the notation of optical terms arose essentially from the appearance of the lines. In the principal series the variable term is the $p$-term; in the sharp subordinate series (sometimes called the second subordinate series) the variable term is the $s$-term; in the diffuse series the $d$-term varies, and in the Bergmann (or fundamental) series the $b$-term (later also called $f$-term). Sommerfeld had shown earlier that in quantum theory the $s$-term always possessed the azimuthal quantum number $n_\phi = 1$, the $p$-term $n_\phi = 2$, the $d$-term $n_\phi = 3$, and the $b$- or $f$-term $n_\phi = 4$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0097 -->

463

(237) and also imposing on it the selection rule (that only the changes $0$ and $\pm 1$ were allowed for this inner quantum number), Sommerfeld indeed accounted for the observed doublet lines.$^{733}$ As the third general spectroscopic law, Sommerfeld included the spectroscopic displacement law connecting the arc and spark spectra of neighbouring elements in the periodic system of elements$^{734}$; as the fourth, Rydberg's rule that elements with even valency show doublet spectra and those with odd valency triplet spectra. Finally, as the fifth general law, he presented the magneto-optical decomposition rule (which he had discussed in his note in *Naturwissenschaften*) together with detailed spectroscopic evidence in its favour. He now observed that for triplets, the Runge denominator assumed the same values as the azimuthal quantum number (i.e., 1 for $s$-, 2 for $p$-, 3 for $d$-, 4 for $b$-terms, etc.) and progressed in the same direction for doublets (i.e., 1 for $s$-, 3 for $p$-, 5 for $d$-, 7 for $b$-terms, etc.), that is,

$$r = \begin{cases} n_{\phi} & \text{for triplets} \\ 2n_{\phi} - 1 & \text{for doublets.} \end{cases}$$ (238)

Sommerfeld considered the result contained in Eq. (238) as confirming the relation between the energy terms and the azimuthal quantum numbers $n_{\phi}$, as well as the relation between the Runge denominators $r$ and the azimuthal quantum numbers. He argued that, as in the case of the hydrogen atom and the normal Zeeman effect, also in the cases of non-hydrogen-like atoms and their anomalous Zeeman effects the magnetic moment of the atom should determine its behaviour in an external magnetic field. Thus he concluded:

> Therefore it is understandable that the Runge denominator $r$ must be a function (having, of course, integral values) of the azimuthal quantum number $n_{\phi}$, i.e., $r = g(n_{\phi})$. With it we do not imply that $r$ coincides completely with $n_{\phi}$. Actually, the case of doublet systems and of singlet systems [where $r = 1$ independent of $n_{\phi}$] shows that the relation, in general, is not $r = n_{\phi}$; that this relation is valid for triplet systems is a peculiarity, which cannot at present be explained theoretically. (Sommerfeld, 1920f, p. 248)

In the following year Sommerfeld devoted himself to other aspects of atomic theory, especially the explanation of X-ray spectra. During this time Niels Bohr introduced considerable changes in the prevailing views on atomic structure through his two letters to *Nature*, in which he developed the outline of a theory

$= \omega / 2\pi - \bar{\nu}$, where $\bar{\nu}$ is the average frequency of the sodium doublet), i.e.,  

$$
\frac{\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}}}{\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = 1 + \frac{v}{2}, \tag{240a}
$$  

$$
\frac{\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}}}{\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 \pm \sqrt{1 - \frac{2}{3}v + v^2} \right). \tag{240b}
$$  

In these equations, $v$ expressed the ratio $\Delta \nu_0 / \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, where $\Delta \nu_0$ denoted the frequency separation of the doublet.$^{736}$ Similarly, from Eq. (239b), Sommerfeld found three values for the shifts of the perpendicular components, namely,  

$$
\frac{\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}}}{\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = 1 + \frac{v}{2}, \tag{241a}
$$  

$$
\frac{\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}}}{\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( 3 \pm \sqrt{1 + \frac{2}{3}v + v^2} \right). \tag{241b}
$$  

These solutions described all the Zeeman components with positive frequency shifts with respect to the doublet lines. Those with negative frequency shifts were derived by solving the sets of Eqs. (239a) and (239b) with the *Ansatz* $\zeta_k = C_k \cdot \exp(+ i\omega t)$.$^{737}$  

$^{736}$ For very strong fields, where $v = 0$, Eqs. (240a, b) yielded the solutions: $\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} / \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}} = 1$ (twice) and $0$. Intensity considerations showed that the solutions $\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}} = 1$ disappeared. For weak fields, Eq. (240a) yielded a component which was shifted by an amount $\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ (with respect to the $D_2$-line), but had zero intensity. The two equations (240b), however, gave rise to two components with  

$$
\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0 + \frac{1}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}
$$  

and  

$$
\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = -\frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0 + \frac{2}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}.
$$  

That is, the first component was shifted by an amount $\frac{1}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ with respect to the $D_2$-line (at a position $\frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0$ from the centre of the doublet); the second component was shifted by $\frac{2}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ with respect to the $D_1$-line. These solutions, together with the negative frequency-shift solutions, accounted for the four parallel components of the anomalous Zeeman effect of the sodium $D$-doublet.  

$^{737}$ For strong fields, Eq. (241a) yielded a component with $\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, while Eqs. (241b) led to one solution with $\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ and another with $\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = 2 \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$. The latter could be shown to have zero intensity. For weak fields one found the results  

$$
\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0 + \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}},
$$  

$$
\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0 + \frac{5}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}},
$$  

and  

$$
\Delta \nu_{\text{anomalous}} = -\frac{1}{2} \Delta \nu_0 + \frac{4}{3} \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}.
$$  

These solutions, together with the negative frequency-shift solutions, described the six observed perpendicular components of the anomalous Zeeman effect of the sodium doublet.

and

$$I_{\sigma} = \frac{3}{4} \left| 1 \mp \frac{m(1 + \frac{1}{3}mv)}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{2}{3}mv + v^2}} \right|, \quad (243b)$$

for the intensities of the parallel and perpendicular components, respectively, with the upper sign valid in the case of transitions involving the $p_1$-term and the lower sign in the case of the transitions involving the $p_2$-term. Equations (243a) and (243b) implied that for a given $m$ of the $p$-states the sum $I_{\pi} + I_{\sigma}$ takes on a constant value. Several months later Sommerfeld treated the intensities of the magnetic components in the anomalous Zeeman effects of doublet and triplet lines in a paper written jointly with Werner Heisenberg and submitted in August 1922 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Sommerfeld and Heisenberg, 1922b). In this paper —which we shall discuss in Volume 2, Section I.6—the authors made use of the correspondence principle, but again did not refer to any specific model of atoms emitting multiplet lines. Heisenberg, however, did concern himself with atomic models: in a paper published in the same volume of *Zeitschrift für Physik*, which contained Sommerfeld's quantum-theoretical reformulation of Voigt's theory, he derived the Zeeman effects of doublet and triplet spectra by assuming that the atoms consisted of a core and one or two outer electrons emitting the radiation (Heisenberg, 1922a). Heisenberg was not the first to discuss models of such a kind in the literature; Alfred Landé had treated the anomalous Zeeman effects along similar lines.

Alfred Landé had been involved in atomic theory since 1917, when he worked with Max Born in Berlin on the properties of crystals. During the course of their joint work, Born and Landé had come up with the concept of a spatial atom having cubic symmetry, the 'cubic atom' (Born, 1918c; Landé, 1919a). Landé had then developed this concept further (Landé, 1919b, e, f, g; 1920c, f; 1921b) and had applied it to explain certain features of the periodic system of elements (Landé, 1920e) and of the structure of diamond (Landé, 1921a). At the same time he had investigated a model of the helium atom (Landé, 1919c), and this model had also been the subject of his *Habilitation* thesis (Landé, 1920a). Thus Alfred Landé, *Privatdozent* at the University of Frankfurt-am-Main since summer 1919, had made a good reputation for himself within a few years. His ideas on the cubic atom had attracted the interest of Niels Bohr, Arnold Sommerfeld and Peter Debye.$^{741}$ His treatment of the helium atom had also been received favourably. As a consequence, Niels Bohr had invited him to spend a few weeks in Copenhagen to discuss the problems of atomic structure (see Bohr to Landé, 29 July 1920). On his return from Copenhagen, Landé thanked Bohr 'for the stimulation on many physical problems which I have received from you,' and

---
$^{741}$ For example, at the Bad Nauheim *Naturforscherversammlung* in September 1920 Sommerfeld declared that Landé's cubic model of the atom—if slightly modified—provided a genuine opportunity to solve the difficult problem of explaining the spectra of non-hydrogen-like atoms (Sommerfeld, 1920g, p. 620).

remarked: ‘I also told Professor Born and Stern about your idea that the different electron spheres should penetrate through each other, and I am looking forward with the greatest expectation to the paper you promised’ (Landé to Bohr, 26 October 1920). While Bohr was stimulated by Landé’s ideas on the cubic atom, Landé himself felt encouraged to proceed with his investigation of the problem of diamond. However, after completing his calculations on it by the end of the year 1920, he started work on another problem: the anomalous Zeeman effects.⁷⁴²

Landé had the first results from his new involvement available already in the beginning of February 1921. He wrote to Bohr on 4 February: ‘I have found several empirical rules for the complex Zeeman types, which go considerably beyond Sommerfeld’s classification (Ann. d. Phys. [Sommerfeld, 1920f]) and which allow predictions for the neon spectrum; what these rules mean, however, is to me quite incomprehensible.’⁷⁴³ Two weeks later Landé reported his results in detail. He wrote:

> In reading Sommerfeld’s summary of “general spectroscopic laws and a magneto-optical decomposition rule” (Ann. d. Phys. **63**, 221 (1920)), I have further noticed the following empirical rules: 1. If the position of all π [i.e., parallel; Landé denoted them by *p*] -components and the position of the outermost σ [i.e., perpendicular; Landé denoted it by *s*] -component are given, then one can determine the positions of the other σ-components. Every π-component is surrounded on the right and on the left by two σ-components at distances of ±Δ, where Δ is the distance of the outermost π-component from the outermost σ-component. 2. For all *triplet* lines the following rule is valid: the number of π-components is equal to the sum of the “inner” quantum numbers of the terms giving rise to the line ... The rule is not valid for doublet lines. 3. In the centre of the Zeeman pattern, there is never a π-component in the case of doublets; in the case of triplets, a π-component exists in

⁷⁴² Landé’s interest in the problem of anomalous Zeeman effects had been stimulated by Heinrich Konen’s book on spectroscopy of gases and vapours (Konen, 1913). As Landé recalled: ‘There were chapters about Preston’s rule and Runge’s rule and this immediately fascinated me very much, because when you see such simple empirical rules there must be something very simple behind it’ (Landé, AHQP Interview, 5 March 1962, p. 28).
It should be mentioned that by the end of 1920 when he started to work on his analysis of the anomalous Zeeman effects, Landé had finally become settled in Frankfurt. Before that (since the beginning of 1919), he had lived and taught at the *Odenwaldschule*, a private progressive country school located between Frankfurt and Heidelberg. Landé had remained there even after his *Habilitation* because as *Privatdozent* in Frankfurt he did not occupy a paid position and—since he gave only advanced courses of lectures attended by few students—he could not live on student fees alone. He went to Frankfurt just once a week to give his lectures.
⁷⁴³ Before writing to Bohr, Landé had already informed Paschen about the fact that he was working on the analysis of anomalous Zeeman effects, and he asked him (Paschen) specific questions about the Zeeman effects of neon.
Landé had come into contact with Paschen in summer 1919 when he had become interested in the neon atom as an excellent example of his cubic atom. Paschen, who had just recently organized the neon spectrum into term series (Paschen, 1919, 1920), had sent Landé—on learning about the latter’s interest in the neon problem—a reprint of his first paper on the subject (Paschen, 1919). In an accompanying letter Paschen wished Landé full success in explaining the empirical data on the basis of the ideas of the cubic atom (Paschen to Landé, 27 July 1920). Landé, however, became engaged on the neon spectrum only later (Landé, 1923d).

the centre if and only if the two terms involved possess different “inner” quantum numbers. 4. The quantity $\Delta$ can be obtained *approximately* from the two “inner” quantum numbers of the terms involved, by dividing each of them by its associated Runge denominator and adding up the quotients. (Landé to Bohr, 16 February 1921)

Landé illustrated his rules by two figures representing the situation in doublet and triplet spectra, respectively, and a table giving the inner quantum numbers, the number of perpendicular components, and the quantity $\Delta$ according to rule 4. He emphasized:

> I believe that especially rule 1, stating that the complex Zeeman pattern can be resolved into separate groups $\sigma$-$\pi$-$\sigma$, will be of importance for the theory of the Zeeman effect.

And finally he suggested a possibility of interpreting the rules in quantum theory by saying:

> The different “inner” quantum numbers of a term will probably just signify the total quantum numbers of the atom around its invariant axis [i.e., the quantum numbers of the net angular momentum of the atom around the axis perpendicular to its invariant plane; see the example of the helium atom in Section IV.2], the valence electrons having different orientations with respect to the inner atom; and the multiplicity of the groups $\sigma$-$\pi$-$\sigma$ in the Zeeman pattern probably indicates several possibilities of the orientation of this invariable atomic axis with respect to [the direction of] the [external] magnetic field. (Landé to Bohr, 16 February 1921)

Landé feverishly continued his analysis of the Zeeman effects, and already on 23 February 1921 he gave, again in a letter to Bohr, the ‘complete representation of doublet splittings,’ which he formulated in six rules: first, in a magnetic field no unshifted parallel component appears, hence the number of $\pi$-components is always even; second, the number of $\pi$-components is equal to the sum of the two inner quantum numbers of the terms involved in the transition, provided the sum is an even number; third, every $\pi$-component is accompanied, on the right- and the left-hand sides, by one $\sigma$-component each, the frequency distances ($\pm\Delta$) being the same for each field-free line—if, however, two $\sigma$-components coincide, they cancel each other; fourth, all $\pi$-components of a given doublet component (of the field-free atom) have the same distance from each other; fifth, the position of the inner $\pi$-component follows by adding the ratios of the inner quantum number to the Runge denominator of the two states involved in the transition; sixth, the position of the $\sigma$-components accompanying the inner $\pi$-component is obtained by subtracting the two ratios mentioned.$^{744}$ Landé demonstrated the correctness of his rules in several examples: thus he concluded

$^{744}$The rules for triplets, which Landé gave in the letter to Bohr (dated 23 February 1921), were less complete than the doublet rules.

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 471

should wait until Back’s manuscript of a detailed paper was ready, and then write—if still necessary—a paper of his own and submit it also to *Annalen der Physik*.<sup>745</sup> This procedure, Sommerfeld argued, would help in continuing the fruitful collaboration between the quantum theorists and Paschen’s experimental institute.

Sommerfeld’s new letter made Landé rather unhappy. He was not only very ambitious and eager to publish quickly, but also thought that he had arrived at important results quite independently. Thus, for example, he had found recently—on Sommerfeld’s own suggestion—the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects occurring in the Bergmann series of atoms emitting doublet spectra.<sup>746</sup> Sommerfeld’s request appeared to him unfair, and he wrote to Back personally and told him that he (Landé) had reported about his results on the anomalous Zeeman effects at the Marburg meeting of 28 February 1921 and intended to publish the content of his talk in *Zeitschrift für Physik*; he asked whether Back wanted him to delay the publication (Landé to Back, 5 March 1921). Back replied politely that, in view of the fact that his own note to *Naturwissenschaften* was already in print, he considered it ‘only right and appropriate that you have your Marburg lecture printed exactly as if you did not know about my existence, since you did not indeed know anything about my activity at the time you gave the talk’ (Back to Landé, 7 March 1921). He added further that he did not wish to enter into any quarrel about priority; also, that he would return to Landé’s proposal (expressed by Landé in his letter to Back on 5 March) of publishing a joint paper at a suitable time.<sup>747</sup> Landé took Back’s letter as indicating complete agreement with his plans, and he felt even more justified by a letter from Paschen, who wrote: ‘Dr. Back has informed me about your letter. As far as I can judge, especially from the rules you wrote to Mr. Sommerfeld, the elements used [by you and Back] for the construction [of the rules] are of very different nature. Accordingly it would be advisable that each of you should carry on his investigation by himself. The common things can be sifted later on’ (Paschen to Landé, 8 March 1921). Sommerfeld, however, continued to raise objections against a quick publication of Landé’s results, claiming that, in addition to harming Back’s interests, they were not yet ready for publication.<sup>748</sup> When, on 17

March 1921, Landé sent him a simplified version of his scheme, Sommerfeld warned him again that he should not publish ‘unripe’ considerations (Sommerfeld to Landé, late March 1921). Landé had argued that it was urgent to publish his work because ‘Bohr apparently is [also] thinking about these matters, and why should a foreigner steal a march over us in it?’ (Landé to Sommerfeld, 17 March 1921). To this Sommerfeld replied: ‘That you wish to forestall Bohr is no reason to hurry. Bohr has got other things to publish now, and he is a theoretician anyway. I do not regard him as a foreigner’ (Sommerfeld to Landé, late March 1921).

In spite of Sommerfeld’s dissatisfaction, Landé did not give in. During March and April 1921 he completed the formulation of his rules and tried to relate them better to the principles of atomic theory. Indeed, he had reported the initial outcome of these attempts in his letter to Sommerfeld on 17 March, where he stated in particular an expression for the term energies of doublet atoms together with the selection rules. From Sommerfeld’s reply—i.e., the letter, which we have quoted above—‘a first-semester student’ of Sommerfeld’s in Munich had discovered the same results but not yet published them.$^{749}$ This made Landé hurry up even more, and on 16 April 1921 his paper—entitled ‘*Über den anomalen Zeemaneffekt (Teil I)*’ (‘On the Anomalous Zeeman Effect. Part I’)—was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* and published about a month later (Landé, 1921c).$^{750}$

Landé’s first paper on the anomalous Zeeman effects contained a cleaned-up version of all his rules. He started out from Sommerfeld’s invention of an inner quantum number, associated with each energy term of atoms emitting doublet and triplet spectra. This quantum number $j$—which Landé denoted by $k$, but we adopt the notation used later—obeyed the selection rule

$$\Delta j = 0, \pm 1. \tag{244}$$

The inner quantum number was not identical to the azimuthal quantum number, $n_{\phi}$, which obeyed the selection rule $\Delta n_{\phi} = \pm 1$. Landé then recalled the normal Zeeman effect, in which the external magnetic field led to a perturbation energy, $n_1 h \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$, $n_1$ being the spatial quantum number, $h$ Planck’s constant, and $\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}$ the normal magnetic frequency shift according to Eq. (230). In the case of the complex or anomalous Zeeman effect, Landé used—instead of the magnetic perturbation energy $\Delta W$—the quantity $\epsilon$, defined as

$$\epsilon = \frac{\Delta W}{h \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = gn_1, \tag{245}$$

$^{749}$ We shall discuss this, i.e., Werner Heisenberg’s work on the anomalous Zeeman effect of doublets (and triplets) in detail in Volume 2, Sections I.6 and II.5.

$^{750}$ Friedrich Paschen tried to calm Sommerfeld’s anger on Landé’s procedure in a later letter. After pointing to the fact that Back’s and Landé’s interests were rather different—Back was primarily devoted to the accurate experimental verification of his assumptions—Paschen argued in this letter: ‘For this reason I would regret if Landé’s speculations were not published. Ultimately an important fact, securely founded, has more value than all speculations, which might stimulate us to new conceptions but will soon be worn out’ (Paschen to Sommerfeld, 21 May 1921).

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect  
473

where \( g \) is a proportionality factor, having the value 1 in the case of the normal Zeeman effect. He then introduced three hypotheses. First, he claimed that one had to interpret the inner quantum numbers as 'the azimuthal quantum numbers of the atom as a whole in its invariable plane (in contrast to the "external" azimuthal quantum numbers of a jumping electron)' (Landé, 1921c, p. 234). Second, he associated the spatial quantum number \( n_1 \) with the projection of the total angular momentum of the atom on the direction of the magnetic field **H** and called it the 'equatorial quantum number,' denoting it by the letter \( m \).<sup>751</sup> Third, he concluded from the selection rule, \( \Delta m = 0, \pm 1 \), and the symmetry of the Zeeman components with respect to the field-free lines that \( m \) had to assume either of the two sequences of values:

\[ m = \pm \frac{1}{2}, \pm \frac{3}{2}, \pm \frac{5}{2}, \ldots, \pm \frac{2j - 1}{2} \tag{246a} \]

and

\[ m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots, \pm j. \tag{246b} \]

He substituted the values for \( m \) (\( = n_1 \)) in Eq. (245). The factor \( g \), which he called the 'splitting factor' ('*Aufspaltungsfaktor*,' Landé, 1921c, p. 235), could then be determined for singlet and doublet terms from the relation

\[ \overline{m}g = j, \tag{247a} \]

with \( \overline{m} \) denoting the maximum value of the equatorial quantum number, namely, \( \overline{m} = n_\phi = j \) for singlet and \( \overline{m} = (2n_\phi - 1)/2 \) for doublet terms. Hence the splitting factor \( g \) always assumed for singlet terms the value unity, and for doublet terms the value

\[ g = \frac{2j}{2n_\phi - 1} \, . \tag{248} \]

Landé found that Eq. (247a) did not hold in general for triplet terms; instead there arose several equations, depending upon the relation of \( j \) to \( n_\phi \), that is,

\[ \overline{m}g = \begin{cases}
j + 1 & \text{for } j = n_\phi \\
j + 1 + \dfrac{1}{n_\phi - 1} & \text{for } j = n_\phi - 1 \\
j + \dfrac{j}{n_\phi - 1} & \text{for } j = n_\phi - 2.
\end{cases} \tag{247b} \]

<sup>751</sup>Landé used for his equatorial quantum number the same letter \( m \) as Sommerfeld in his quantum-theoretical reformulation of Voigt's theory for the magnetic quantum number (Sommerfeld, 1922a). However, both quantities were not the same; Sommerfeld's \( m \) in Eqs. (242a, b) and (243a, b) assumed twice the value of Landé's.

474  
Chapter IV  The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

With these results, Landé prepared a table giving the magnetic perturbation energies (in units of $h\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$) of all $s$-, $p$-, and $d$-terms of atoms emitting doublet and triplet spectra. For example, in the case of doublet $p$-terms the term splittings were $\pm\frac{2}{3}, \pm\frac{6}{3}$ for the $p_1$-term, and $\pm\frac{1}{3}$ for the $p_2$-term; for triplet $d$-terms the splittings of $0, \pm\frac{4}{3}, \pm\frac{8}{3}$ for the $d_1$-term, $0, \pm\frac{7}{6}, \pm\frac{14}{6}$ for the $d_2$-term, and $0, \pm\frac{1}{2}$ for the $d_3$-term were found. Landé noticed that his results satisfied what Sommerfeld had demanded from an interpretation of the magnetic perturbation energies; but he also discovered that his results deviated from the ‘number mystery’ (‘Zahlenmysterium’), since for triplet $d$-terms, he obtained—besides Sommerfeld’s denominator 3—the denominators 2 and 6 (Landé, 1921c, pp. 236, 239).

The separations of the line components in the anomalous Zeeman effects followed by considering the difference of the magnetic perturbation energies, $mg - m'g'$, of the terms involved in the transition, due to the equation

$$
\frac{\Delta\nu_{\text{anomalous}}}{\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}} = mg - m'g'. \tag{249}
$$

In obtaining the observed components Landé had only to add a further selection rule, forbidding the transitions between states with quantum numbers $j = j'$ and $m = m' = 0$ (the primes referring to final states). This selection rule was a consequence of Bohr’s correspondence principle. He thus found that all lines originating from transitions between states with given quantum numbers $n_\phi$ and $j$ (initial state) and $n_{\phi'}$ and $j'$ (final state), but variable $m$ and $m'$, exhibited the same anomalous Zeeman effects. And he concluded: ‘The explanation of the anomalous Zeeman types is thus reduced to the problem of [determining] the anomalous fundamental factors $g$, which one may [due to Eq. (245)] interpret as apparently anomalous values of $e/m_e$’ (Landé, 1921c, p. 239).

Landé concluded his paper with some remarks concerning the intensity of the Zeeman components. Observation showed that among the field-free lines the most intensive ones corresponded to transitions with $\Delta n_\phi = \Delta j = -1$, while the transitions with $\Delta j = 0, +1$, gave rise to the weaker satellites. Landé interpreted this fact in agreement with Bohr’s correspondence principle by means of the following ‘*Ersatz*’ model, in which he represented the electron motion in the atom by two special electron orbits: one electron moved in a circular orbit of radius $c$ in the invariable plane of the atom, and the second electron oscillated with an amplitude $a < c$ along the axis of the same plane. If the direction of the magnetic field made an angle $\theta$ with the axis of the circularly orbiting electron (i.e., $m = j \cos\theta$), the intensities were $(c \sin \bar\theta + a \cos \bar\theta)^2$ for the component parallel to the magnetic field and $(c\sqrt{(1 + \cos^2 \bar\theta)/2} + a \sin \bar\theta)^2$ for the perpendicular components, $\bar\theta$ being the average of the angle $\theta$ in the initial and final states of the atom. As a consequence the $\pi$-components, originating from atoms having axes (of the total angular momentum) perpendicular to the field ($\theta = 90^{\circ}$),

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0109 -->

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 475

possessed the largest intensity, while the $\sigma$-components were strongest when the atomic axes were parallel to the field. That is, the parallel components for transitions between states with small quantum numbers $m$ and $m'$, and the perpendicular components for transitions between states with large $m$ and $m'$, were most intensive. In the case of transitions with $\Delta j = 0$, Landé's 'Ersatz' model implied $c = 0$; then the situation concerning the intensity was just the opposite to the one for transitions with $\Delta j \neq 0$ (due to the dominance of the $a$-term in the expressions for the intensity).

Since Landé rushed with the publication of his first paper, he postponed the most interesting application of the new rules to the next paper, which he submitted to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* on 27 June 1921; it appeared on 1 August and dealt with the anomalous Zeeman effects of neon and mercury (Landé, 1921d). By combining the initial term $-jg$ with the final term $-j'g'$, the initial term $-(j - 1)g$ with the final terms $-j'g'$ and $-(j' - 1)g'$, and the initial term $jg$ with the final term $j'g'$, where $j - j' = 1$, he managed to describe the observed triplet Zeeman components and—with additional help from the *Ersatzmodell*—their intensities.$^{752}$ Landé's success was augmented by an experimental check of his theory by Paschen and Back: they showed that certain lines, which were forbidden in weak magnetic fields but showed up in stronger fields, followed from the rules he had given. Paschen's student Raimund Götze finally analyzed particular combinations of the different sets of $d$-terms, i.e., $d_i - d_j$ transitions ($d'$ denoting a new type of $d$-terms besides the usual ones), which gave rise to a new series in the triplet spectra of alkaline-earth elements (Götze, 1921). Paschen reported Götze's result to Sommerfeld: 'The Runge denominator in the skew-symmetric group, corresponding to a combination [of terms] $d_i - d_j$, is 6, in agreement with Landé, and not $3 \times 3 = 9$' (Paschen to Sommerfeld, 15 September 1921). Thus Sommerfeld's splitting rule was violated and Landé's description (with the $g$-factor, Eq. (248)) proved to be correct. This fact persuaded the still grudging Sommerfeld to regard Landé with greater respect and, in his joint article with Back on 'Fünfundzwanzig Jahre Zeemaneffekt' ('Twenty-Five Years of Zeeman Effect'), which was published in the issue of 11 November 1921 of *Naturwissenschaften*, he admitted:

> Most recently Mr. Landé has succeeded in deducing these elementary Zeeman effects of the series terms just from observation, with the help of a decomposition of the Runge denominators into factors. Their [i.e., the factors'] combination represents, according to simple well-known rules, the totality of the magnetic types of spectral lines without any exception in an accurate quantitative manner; further, it allows one to predict a vast number of yet unknown, or not yet interpreted, Zeeman types with complete certainty. (Sommerfeld and Back, 1921, p. 912)

$^{752}$Landé had most of his results on neon ready in May, for Paschen mentioned in a letter to Sommerfeld: 'Landé must be very far ahead. He has sent me something on neon, which was right' (Paschen to Sommerfeld, 21 May 1921).

476 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

With this statement of approval Alfred Landé's reputation as the most successful theoretical organizer of the anomalous Zeeman effects was firmly established.
In October 1921 Landé still submitted his third paper of the year on the subject of the magnetic influence on atoms.$^{753}$ It was published again in *Zeitschrift für Physik*, and in it Landé sought to 'reduce the $g$-anomaly to a modification of Larmor's theorem concerning the precessional motions of electron-systems in a magnetic field' (Landé, 1921f, p. 398). For this purpose he proposed two possible modifications of Larmor's theorem. One possibility was to replace $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$, the frequency of precession given by Eq. (230), by an anomalous frequency, $\Delta\nu_{\text{anomalous}} = \Delta\nu_{\text{normal}} + \Delta\nu$, which should satisfy the relation, $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}} + \Delta\nu = \pm 2j\Delta\nu$, for doublet terms. The other possibility was that the atom obtained—besides a precession with the normal frequency $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$—another precession around its axis (i.e., the axis of the total angular momentum) with the frequency $\Delta\nu = (\text{const.})\cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the directions of the total angular momentum and the magnetic field (Landé, 1921f, p. 401). This assumption not only accounted for the observed Zeeman effects, but also for the so-called gyromagnetic effects, i.e., the Barnett effect and the Einstein–de Haas effect. In those effects the precession of the electron orbits occurring in an external magnetic field seemed to yield anomalous values for the ratio $e/m_e$, which were twice as large as the one measured for the free electron. Now the ratio of the anomalous value of $e/m_e$ (derived from the gyromagnetic effect) and its normal value (from the free electron) was just Landé's 'splitting factor' $g$. By assuming that the gyromagnetic effects were caused by the orbiting electrons in $s$-states, the observed result, i.e., $g = 2$, found its natural explanation from Landé's rules.$^{754}$
Thus far Landé had succeeded in establishing the rules describing the available anomalous Zeeman effects and a relation between the anomalous Zeeman effect and the (anomalous) gyromagnetic effect. Both phenomena seemed to require a modification of Larmor's theorem, but Landé also admitted that 'we are not able to provide the theoretical basis for this modification' (Landé, 1921f, p. 398). In other words, Landé had not been able to provide a reasonable model

$^{753}$ Earlier, on 27 June, Landé talked again at a meeting of the *Gauverein Hessen* (at Gießen) on certain aspects of the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects. Of this talk only an abstract exists indicating that he dealt with an *Ersatzmodell* (consisting of a system of electrons, which perform periodic motions) for the anomalous Zeeman effects (Landé, 1921e).
$^{754}$ Landé, in the same paper, also obtained new formulae for the $g$-factor (Landé, 1921f). In particular, he expressed $g$ by the ratio $\bar{\epsilon}/\bar{m}$, with $\bar{\epsilon}$ the maximal value of the perturbation energy term of a line component (of the field-free atom) and $\bar{m}$ the maximal value of the equatorial quantum number. In the case of doublet terms $\bar{\epsilon}$ and $\bar{m}$ assumed the values: $\bar{\epsilon} = n_{\phi} \pm \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}$ and $\bar{m} = n_{\phi} - \frac{1}{2}$; and in the case of triplet terms, alternatively, $\bar{\epsilon} = (n_{\phi} \pm \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}) \pm (1 + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2})$ and $\bar{m} = (n_{\phi} - \frac{1}{2}) \pm (1 - \frac{1}{2})$, and $\bar{\epsilon} = (f \pm 1/2n_{\phi} - \frac{1}{2}) \pm (1 + 1/2n_{\phi} - \frac{1}{2})$ and $\bar{m} = (f - \frac{1}{2}) \pm (1 - \frac{1}{2})$, with $f = n_{\phi} - 1, n_{\phi} - 2, \dots, 1, 0$. By this complicated writing of the expressions for $\bar{\epsilon}$ and $\bar{m}$, Landé wanted to bring out the similarities in them. He also pointed to a possible (physical) relation between doublet and triplet formulae: the first type of triplet formulae could be obtained from the doublet formulae by adding and subtracting from the latter the expressions $(1 + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2})$ and $(1 - \frac{1}{2})$, respectively; these were the expressions for the doublet ground state with $n_{\phi} = 1$.

# IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect

for atoms emitting doublet and triplet spectra and having the observed Zeeman effects. Werner Heisenberg—the same student of Sommerfeld's, who had earlier obtained the correct formulae for the Zeeman effects of doublets independently of Landé (Sommerfeld to Landé, end of March 1921)—approached exactly this part of the problem in fall 1921. He started out from a specific result of Landé's, according to which the maximum magnetic perturbation energy of triplet states was proportional to $n_\phi + 1$—see the first Eq. (247b)—and gave it a physical interpretation: he explained it as arising from taking the sum of $n_\phi h / 2\pi$, the angular momentum of the valence electron, and $h / 2\pi$, the angular momentum of the atomic core, which he considered to be built up of the atomic nucleus plus the other electrons. This assumption yielded a suitable description of the triplet states of the free atoms (i.e., without the external magnetic field), provided one considered quantized positions of the angular momentum of the outer electron with respect to the direction of the angular momentum of the atomic core (which was also the direction of the magnetic field created by the core). According to Heisenberg the momentum of the outer electron should be either parallel (giving the momentum sum $(n_\phi + 1)h / 2\pi$), or perpendicular (giving the momentum sum $n_\phi h / 2\pi$), or antiparallel (giving the momentum sum $(n_\phi - 1)h / 2\pi$) to the core's momentum.$^{755}$ When he further applied an external magnetic field on the system consisting of the atomic core and the outer electron, Heisenberg could also derive Landé's triplet rules and, in addition, the change of the anomalous Zeeman effects in a magnetic field of increasing strength.$^{756}$ At the same time, Heisenberg constructed a similarly successful model for doublet terms. For that purpose he simply assumed that the atomic core possessed the angular momentum $\frac{1}{2} h / 2\pi$, while the outer electron's angular momentum took on the values $(n_\phi - \frac{1}{2}) h / 2\pi$, with $n_\phi = 1, 2, \dots$. The doublet terms then arose from parallel and antiparallel alignments of the angular momenta of the atomic core and the outer electron, yielding the momentum sums $n_\phi h / 2\pi$ and $(n_\phi - 1)h / 2\pi$, respectively. Again Heisenberg derived from his model Landé's rules for the anomalous Zeeman effects of the doublet lines in the presence of a weak external magnetic field and

During the course of this work, which was completed in December 1921 and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, where it appeared soon afterwards (Heisenberg, 1922a), Werner Heisenberg kept contact with Alfred Landé through many letters. Landé, who had become a recognized expert on the Zeeman effects of spectral lines, gave Heisenberg encouragement in and criticism of his ideas. He especially supported Heisenberg's use of half-integral quantum numbers in the doublet case, which Sommerfeld disliked deeply, but which had also appeared in his—Landé's—own analysis.⁷⁵⁷ On the other hand, Landé was quite reluctant to accept Heisenberg's rather wild mechanical hypotheses. In the years since his first involvement in atomic theory Landé had become increasingly careful in applying atomic models. Moreover, he had a high respect for Bohr's new ideas on atomic structure, whose emergence he had witnessed during his visit to Copenhagen in October 1920, and Heisenberg's treatment seemed to be hardly in accord with them. Therefore, it took Landé nearly a year before he responded publicly to Heisenberg's model. Meanwhile he had become *Extraordinarius* of theoretical physics at the University of Tübingen, the mecca of experimental research on the anomalous Zeeman effects.⁷⁵⁸ In this first paper submitted from Tübingen, entitled '*Zur Theorie der anomalen Zeeman- und magneto-mechanischen Effekte*' ('On the Theory of the Anomalous Zeeman and Magneto-Mechanical Effects'), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 17 September 1922 and appeared in the last issue of its volume 11 in November, he presented a thorough analysis of Heisenberg's work (Landé, 1922a). Landé explicitly discussed Heisenberg's assumptions, namely, (a) the half-integral quantum numbers for series electrons and the atomic core, (b) the passive role of the core's angular momentum for the spatial quantization in the magnetic field, and (c) the fact that the direction of the core's angular momentum had to coincide with the direction of the vector sum of the external and the internal magnetic field. Especially, assumptions (b) and (c) appeared to Landé to be unjustifiable on the basis of the existing theory of atomic structure: they contradicted, for example, not only Larmor's theorem but also the hypothesis concerning the coupling of the angular momenta of radiation and of the atom underlying the successful selection rules. Nevertheless Landé admitted that the Zeeman effects, notably the symmetrical

(This can be noticed immediately from his selection rule, $\Delta m = 0, \pm 2$.)

IV.4 The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 479

separation of components ‘can hardly be interpreted, from the point of view of models, in a manner different from Heisenberg’s’ (Landé, 1922a, pp. 353–354).⁷⁵⁹ It was Landé’s goal to justify Heisenberg’s assumptions ‘as necessary consequences of a single basic assumption about the kinematics of the [atomic] core,’ which followed from both the analysis of the data and the application of Bohr’s correspondence principle.

In order to realize his goal of providing Heisenberg’s theory a ‘kinematic and quantum-theoretical foundation’ (Landé, 1922a, p. 354), Landé carefully analyzed a model of a periodic system which exhibited the observed Zeeman and Paschen–Back effects. Since in a weak external magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ every doublet or triplet line appeared to be decomposed into a sequence of several triplets, whose separation was not the normal one (i.e., $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$ of Eq. (230)), but $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}} + \Delta\nu$, and whose middle $\pi$-lines were shifted, he demanded the following from his model: the orbits of the electron emitting a given magnetic triplet precess with the anomalous frequency $\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}} + \Delta\nu$ about the axis of a magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ (the angle between the axis of the orbit and of the magnetic field being $\theta$); moreover, the frequency of the orbiting electron changes by an amount $\Delta\omega$, which is proportional to the frequency shift of the middle $\pi$-line. In the case of doublet atoms, Landé calculated for $\Delta\nu / \Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$ the values $\pm(2n_\phi - 1)^{-1}$ and for $\Delta\omega / \Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$ the values $\pm(2n_\phi - 1)^{-1} \cos\theta$. For the parallel or antiparallel position of the axis of the electron’s orbit with respect to the magnetic field (i.e., for $\theta = 0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$) the excess rotational frequency $\Delta\omega$ cancelled the excess precession $\Delta\nu$; thus a normal Zeeman effect showed up. With this model, Landé succeeded in deriving Heisenberg’s assumption (b)—that only the angular momentum of the series electron (i.e., the electron emitting the spectral lines) should be quantized with respect to the magnetic field—from Bohr’s assumption that the magnetic perturbation energy should be given by integral multiples of $h(\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}} + \Delta\nu)$ (Bohr, 1918b, §5). He further showed how the excess frequencies, $\Delta\nu$ and $\Delta\omega$, might be explained if one assumed that the atomic core’s angular momentum had the same direction as the vector sum of the external magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ and the ‘internal’ magnetic field $\mathbf{H}_i$ created by the orbiting series electron. Finally he obtained from his model a formula for the $g$-factor in weak magnetic fields (it being the ratio of the total angular momentum and the angular momentum of the core), the empirically observed change of Zeeman effects in an increasing magnetic field and the correct gyromagnetic effects. What remained to explain was ‘the non-mechanical orientation of the atomic core in the direction of the resultant of the external ($\mathbf{H}$) and the inner magnetic
