field ($\mathbf{H}_i$) due to the series electron, as assumed by Heisenberg in contradiction to the mechanically well-founded Larmor's theorem' (Landé, 1922a, pp. 362–363). Apart from that nonmechanical feature, however, the Heisenberg–Landé model allowed one to describe the Zeeman effects in doublet and triplet spectra perfectly.
    In the beginning of the 1920s a new situation arose in spectroscopy and it became clear that the doublet spectra of alkali atoms and the triplet spectra of alkaline-earth atoms were just the simplest examples of a more general class of many-component spectra. In a short note on line groups in the iron spectrum, submitted in April 1921, Ernst Gehrcke claimed that the ultraviolet arc spectrum of iron—observed by Ludwig Carl Glaser (Glaser, 1921)—consisted of line groups having up to sixteen components and suggested the following interpretation: 'Here one is possibly dealing with magnetic or electric line-splittings, respectively, which are *caused* by magnetic or electric fields *in the atom itself*' (Gehrcke, 1921, p. 641). Less than a year later, Miguel Catalán, a Spanish research student at Alfred Fowler's institute at the Imperial College, London, investigated the situation in some detail from the point of view of the quantum theory of atomic structure.$^{760}$ He published his results in a long memoir on 'Series and Other Regularities in the Spectra of Manganese,' which was received by the Royal Society of London on 22 February 1922, read on 23 March and published in the *Transactions* (Catalán, 1922). The main point was that the manganese spectrum contained, besides the ordinary triplet lines, what Catalán called 'multiplets.' He described his discovery as follows:

> Whilst the maganese series of ordinary type were under investigation, it was noted that there was a strong tendency for lines of similar character to appear in groups and that such groups included some of the most intense lines in the spectrum. In the blue region the lines are very numerous, but the nine strongest are apparently grouped together . . . At first glance these nine lines present the appearance of a diffuse triplet, but with the satellites in the wrong order. (Catalán, 1922, p. 146)

Catalán found other such multiplets, consisting of up to fifteen lines, which had similar properties; for instance, they showed the same variations with respect to temperature changes, and were related by exact numerical separations. He further pointed out that multiplets should exist for many other atoms and ions, including chromium, 'and that they may represent a form of regularity present in the spectra of many elements' (Catalán, 1922, p. 168). Independently of Catalán,

$^{760}$ M. A. Catalán was born on 9 October 1894 in Zaragoza, Spain. He studied physics at the Universities of Zaragoza and Madrid, receiving his doctorate at the latter in 1917. From 1917 to 1934 he worked at the National Institute of Physics and Chemistry, Madrid; from 1917 to 1930 as a physicist (he spent the academic year 1920–1921 at the University of London and 1923–1924 at the University of Munich), and from 1930 as a professor. In 1934 he was appointed to a professorship at the University of Madrid, and from 1950 until his death (on 11 November 1957 at Madrid) he directed the department of spectroscopy at the newly created Institute of Optics. Catalán, an authority on spectroscopy, was a member of the committee on spectroscopy of the International Council of Scientific Unions.

IV.4  The Anomalous Zeeman Effect 481

Paschen’s student Hilde Gieseler worked on the analysis of chromium lines at Tübingen. She reported her results in a paper on ‘*Serienzusammenhänge im Bogenspektrum des Chroms*’ (‘Series Organizations in the Arc Spectrum of Chromium’), which was received by *Annalen der Physik* on 19 June 1922 and published in the issue of 2 November (Gieseler, 1922). Gieseler noticed that great difficulties occurred when she sought to organize the chromium lines in the usual series and that many lines showed different Zeeman effects from those known in the cases of doublets and triplets. However, with the help of Landé’s theory (Landé, 1921c), she succeeded in determining the line groups according to their Zeeman effects and proved that they could be organized into definite series.

Gieseler and Catalán made use of the known rules of organizing spectral lines, especially Sommerfeld’s inner quantum number. Catalán also sent Sommerfeld a copy of his manuscript from London, which excited him (Sommerfeld) very much and immediately put him to work. Already in August 1922 Sommerfeld submitted an article, entitled ‘*Über die Deutung verwickelter Spektren (Mangan, Chrom, usw.) nach der Methode der inneren Quantenzahlen*’ (‘On the Interpretation of Complicated Spectra—Manganese, Chromium, etc.—According to the Method of Inner Quantum Numbers’), to *Annalen der Physik*, which appeared in January 1923 (Sommerfeld, 1923a). He started from the following assumption:

> As W. Heisenberg has informed me, the spectra of manganese and chromium—together with the known spectra of alkaline earths—suggest the following general behaviour with respect to multiplet structure: *The number of levels, in which an S, P, D ... [these being the terms that give rise to the singlet lines of an atom, corresponding to the triplet s, p, d-terms] or an s, p, d, ... term splits, first increases according to the sequence of odd integers, 1, 3, 5, ... . From a certain term onward, which is determined by the occurrence of [the inner quantum number] j = 0, the “law of the permanence of multiplicities” applies; that is, from this term onward the number of levels remains constant.* (Sommerfeld, 1923a, p. 52)

Sommerfeld now tried to substantiate this hypothesis by ‘a simple, though possibly rather formal interpretation.’ He argued: ‘We assume that the inner quantum number $j$ represents the total angular momentum of the atom in the initial state under consideration, and that this total angular momentum is composed vectorially of the angular momentum $j_0$ of the unexcited atom and the angular momentum $j_1$ of the excitation’ (Sommerfeld, 1923a, pp. 52–53). Then the total angular momentum $j$ (in units of $h/2\pi$) assumed integral values from $j_0 + j$ to $|j_0 - j_1|$, and each value of $j$ denoted a possible term of the excited atom. As long as $j_0 > j_1$, the number of terms, $2j_1 + 1$, increased with growing $j_1$, i.e., it was 1, 3, 5, ... for $s-, p-, d-, \dots$ terms; however, when $j_1 > j_0$, the number of terms remained a constant, or a ‘permanent number,’ namely, $2j_0 + 1$. Sommerfeld illustrated the situation with two terms of chromium: in the $D$-term he found $j_0 = j_1 = 2$, and with it he constructed from his vector rule (i.e., $\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{j}_0 + \mathbf{j}_1$, and all values, $j, j_0, j_1$, being integral) five terms having the inner quantum numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; in the $B$- (Bergmann or $F$-) term he found $j_1 = 3$ and $j_2 = 2$,

The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

hence five terms again resulted, denoted by the inner quantum numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. On the other hand, in the alkaline-earth atoms $j_0$ had to be 1; hence the highest multiplicity was 3 (already achieved for the $p$-term); for the manganese atom the triplet terms possessed $j_0 = 3$, leading to 9 as the highest multiplicity. In the case of atoms emitting doublet lines, the situation seemed to be different; for example, the assumption of $j_0 = 1$ would give 3 as the highest multiplicity of the terms, in contrast to the observed 2. Sommerfeld solved this difficulty by referring to Heisenberg's magneto-optical model of the atom, according to which the angular momentum of the ground state was distributed among the atomic core and the outer electron (Heisenberg, 1922a). That is, Sommerfeld replaced the vector addition rule, $\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{j}_0 + \mathbf{j}_1$, in the case of doublet atoms by the different rule, $\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{j}_0^* + \mathbf{j}_1^*$, where the values of $j_0^*$ and $j_1^*$ were $j_0 - \frac{1}{2}$ and $j_0 + \frac{1}{2}$, respectively. Then, for alkali atoms, one indeed obtained the maximal multiplicity of $2j_0^* + 1 = 2$. At the end of his paper Sommerfeld hinted at a possible application of the vector rule to determine the paramagnetic moments of atoms, which he treated in more detail in two later papers (Sommerfeld, 1923d, e).<sup>761</sup>

Sommerfeld's vector model was soon taken up by Alfred Landé, though he criticized certain details of it.<sup>762</sup> Thus he pointed out a theoretical difficulty: "The assertion that the angular momentum of the unexcited atom ($s$-term momentum), at different angles of inclination, combines vectorially with the angular momentum of excitation, cannot be understood from the model." At the same time he claimed: "The formal considerations of multiplet structure do not stand a comparison with the empirical results obtained thus far" (Landé, 1923a, p. 190, footnote 4). Landé had a decisive advantage over Sommerfeld, for he was now in Tübingen, where Paschen and his co-workers produced new experimental results every day, which were immediately available for analysis. Ernst Back, in particu-

In most cases, Landé tried to play down the importance of the work done in Munich and to point out its mistakes, without mentioning its good aspects. One may ask, however, whether Landé—who had not done anything for three years on problems which had occupied him in 1919 and 1920—would have reminded himself of his old vector addition without Sommerfeld's new model-dependent description of complex multiplets. And if so, why did he not mention it in his paper of September 1922 dealing with Heisenberg's model of doublet and triplet atoms? In support of the conclusion that Landé was decisively stimulated by Sommerfeld's paper in *Annalen der Physik*, published in early January 1923, we may mention the fact that he took over completely Sommerfeld's geometrical construction of vector sums. IV.4  The Anomalous Zeeman Effect                                                              483

lar, had started a series of measurements on the anomalous Zeeman effects of the manganese multiplet lines, in order to determine their pattern, their number and separations, and to derive from these data the Runge denominators and the $g$-values of the energy terms shifted by external magnetic fields. He submitted his results in a long paper on ‘Der anomale Zeemaneffekt des Bogen- und Funkenspektrums von Mangan’ (‘The Anomalous Zeeman Effect of the Arc- and Spark-Spectrum of Manganese’), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 5 March 1923 (Back, 1923b). This paper appeared in the same issue of the journal as Landé’s theoretical analysis, entitled ‘Termstruktur und Zeemaneffekt der Multiplettlinien’ (‘Term Structure and Zeeman Effect of Multiplet Lines’); in it Landé set up new empirical rules for the Zeeman effects of complex line multiplets, such as the ones observed in the spectra of manganese and chromium, and tried to generalize the earlier model-based considerations of Heisenberg and himself to account for the new multiplets (Landé, 1923a).

Landé described the energy terms of multiplet spectra by four quantum numbers, for which he adopted the notation of Niels Bohr (e.g., the one given by Bohr in his Wolfskehl lectures at Göttingen): the principal quantum number $n$, the azimuthal quantum number $k$ (formerly denoted by $n_{\phi}$), the inner quantum number $j$, and $r$, the quantum number denoting the angular momentum of the atomic core. Further, he introduced three quantities, $K$, $J$ and $R$, through the equations

$$K = k - \frac{1}{2}, \quad J = \begin{cases} j & \text{for even multiplets} \\ j - \frac{1}{2} & \text{for odd multiplets}, \end{cases} \quad R = \frac{1}{2}r. \quad (250)$$

Evidently, these quantities satisfied the relation

$$|R - K| + \frac{1}{2} \le J \le |R + K| - \frac{1}{2}, \quad (251)$$

which also yielded the multiplicity of the energy term denoted by $n, k, j$ and $r$. ($J$, like $j$, always increased by integral steps.) The associated $g$-factor was given by the equation$^{763}$

$$g = 1 + \frac{J^2 - \frac{1}{4} + R^2 - K^2}{2(J^2 - \frac{1}{4})} . \quad (252)$$

The magnetic perturbation energy was then obtained as the product $mg$, $m$ being the magnetic quantum number, whose values were defined by the relation

$$-\left(J - \frac{1}{2}\right) \le m \le +\left(J - \frac{1}{2}\right). \quad (253)$$

Finally, Landé wrote down a rule describing, to a good approximation, the frequency difference between two components of a term multiplet (in the

# IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory
485

Having the vector interpretation in hand, Landé went on to establish a mechanical or dynamical theory. To begin with, he pointed out a difficulty with Heisenberg’s assumption (c)—that the atomic core’s angular momentum should always have the direction of the vector sum of the internal ($\mathbf{H}_i$) and the external ($\mathbf{H}$) magnetic fields. If that was true, Landé concluded, the angular momentum of the core of a given atom had to depend on the type of multiplet considered. Because of this unwanted consequence, he now rejected ‘Heisenberg’s theory, even in its basic concepts, in spite of its beautiful success in explaining the Paschen–Back effect of doublet terms’ (Landé, 1923a, p. 202).$^{764}$ In order to develop an alternative theory, Landé suggested new models for doublet and triplet atoms: for example, in the ground state of a doublet atom the angular momenta of the atomic core and the outer electron should be perpendicular to each other and add up to give $J = 1$; however, in the ground state of the triplet, the core’s momentum should be $R = \frac{3}{2}$.$^{765}$ In spite of these and other assumptions (which involved subtle arguments about the real angular momenta and the ‘apparent’ ones, denoted by the vectors $\mathbf{R}$, $\mathbf{K}$ and $\mathbf{J}$), Landé had to admit finally: ‘An explanation of the [empirically] observed regularities—orderly and free of contradictions—has not been achieved’ (Landé, 1923a, p. 205). This remained a most serious problem for the quantum physicists in the period that followed; it was taken up especially by Wolfgang Pauli in Copenhagen.

## IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory: Anomalous Zeeman Effects and the Crossed-Field Problem

Although the investigations on the anomalous Zeeman effects during the early 1920s were followed with great interest in Copenhagen, they did not stimulate any activity there. The main reason was that Niels Bohr and his co-workers were concerned with different problems of atomic theory at that time.$^{766}$ These problems, especially the theory of the periodic system of elements, occupied Bohr from 1920 to the end of 1922; during that time he only rarely touched on the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects. One such occasion was provided by the seventh Guthrie Lecture, entitled ‘The Effect of Electric and Magnetic Fields on Spectral Lines,’ which Bohr delivered in London on 24 March 1922 (Bohr, 1923d); but Bohr restricted himself in it to elaborating on those questions which

---

This enabled him to dismiss his young competitor in Munich and to claim that the only reasonable approach to the anomalous Zeeman effects was his own. (See footnote 762 for Landé’s attitude towards Sommerfeld.)
$^{765}$ Landé explained this result—which seemed to contradict the building-up principle (*Aufbauprinzip*), according to which the core of the neighbouring atom has the same momentum as the preceding atom in the periodic table—by an ‘inner’ or ‘atomic’ Paschen–Back effect.

he had already treated earlier (Bohr, 1918b); he avoided entering into the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects. Again, in his Wolfskehl lectures at Göttingen in June 1922, he made just a few remarks on the latter problem. In particular, in his fifth lecture on 20 June 1922 he remarked: ‘I should like to say a few more words about the anomalous Zeeman effect which is very closely related to the complexity of the terms. The anomalous Zeeman effect points to very complicated circumstances which have been discussed from various sides’ (Bohr, 1977, p. 391). He went on to mention that Landé had succeeded in deriving the values for the energy terms of atoms in the presence of a magnetic field from an analysis of the spectroscopic data. But he also emphasized the difficulty of explaining the fractional multiples of the normal energy splittings. In this context he referred to Heisenberg’s attempt at a theory of the Zeeman effects of doublet and triplet spectra and claimed that it could not be justified on the basis of the usual assumptions of atomic theory. However, after the completion of the theory of the periodic system of elements by the end of the year 1922, Bohr’s inactivity in the question of the anomalous Zeeman effects also came to an end. On 14 February 1923 he wrote to Landé: ‘Thank you very much for your kind letters. All that you say has interested me greatly, and we are following with the deepest interest the progress of your work on the anomalous Zeeman effect. Pauli and I have just sent a little note on this subject to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, and I am enclosing a copy of it for you. You will notice that in the interpretation of the rules for the term values, which you have found, we subscribe to a different interpretation.’ Bohr emphasized that this note outlined only the general ideas and pointed out that Pauli had meanwhile obtained more specific and promising results on the complex structure of spectral lines and their Zeeman effects, which would be published soon in an extended paper. ‘As you will see from our note,’ he concluded, ‘we are always so conservative here in Copenhagen that we stick sincerely to the integral quantum numbers’ (Bohr to Landé, 14 February 1923). Bohr’s letter to Landé marked the beginning of a new phase in the theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects, a phase which was dominated by the endeavours of Wolfgang Pauli in Copenhagen during most of the year 1923.⁷⁶⁷

Pauli already had shown some interest in the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects in his Munich days. There he had followed quite critically the work of Sommerfeld and Heisenberg. Thus he had been skeptical, for example, about Heisenberg’s use of half-integral quantum numbers (see Heisenberg, 1971, Chapter 3), and had also called attention to the necessity of explaining the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio obtained in the Einstein–de Haas and Barnett effects (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 17 December 1921). He had also discussed these matters with Alfred Landé at the meeting of the German Physical Society in Jena in September 1921.⁷⁶⁸ In spite of his interest, however, Pauli did not become

Bohr had obtained a very good impression of Pauli and made him an important offer.771 As Pauli recalled:

> During these meetings in Göttingen, Bohr came to me one day, accompanied by his assistant, Oskar Klein, and asked me whether I could come to him in Copenhagen for a year. He needed a collaborator in the editing of his works, which he wanted to publish in German. I was much surprised, and after considering a little while I answered with that certainty of which only a young man is capable: “I hardly think that the scientific demands which you will make on me will cause me any difficulty, but the learning of a foreign tongue like Danish far exceeds my abilities.” The result was a hearty burst of laughter from Bohr and Klein, and I went to Copenhagen in the fall of 1922, where both of my contentions were shown to be wrong. (Pauli, 1946, pp. 213–214)772

When Pauli joined Bohr in Copenhagen, he was already a very self-confident junior scientist. He had not only given considerable proof of his ability to understand and contribute to the most difficult theories of the day, especially relativity and quantum theories, he had also developed an attitude of dealing with senior physicists as an equal. During his stay in Göttingen in winter 1921–1922 his self-confidence had grown because of several reasons. One was the fact that, in Göttingen, Max Born behaved like a very kind human being in all respects; he cared for his students and co-workers like a friendly father rather than as a patron or *Geheimrat*—in contrast to Sommerfeld in Munich. Born never pretended to be an infallible theoretician: he made mistakes and admitted them; he said so frankly when he knew of no good way of proceeding in a theoretical problem, and he treated his collaborators generously when they helped him in the solution. Pauli had soon found out that he could compete quite well with Born and the other physicists and mathematicians at Göttingen, who

He is an excellent man in all respects and will most certainly be very helpful’ (Bohr to Kramers, 15 July 1922).
772 Oskar Klein, who confirmed Pauli’s story, recalled that Pauli learned Danish well in Copenhagen. In summer 1923 Pauli told him: ‘I believe that I now speak better Danish, for I have meanwhile thought about it’ (O. Klein, AHQP Interview, 15 July 1963).

As a consequence, he believed by summer 1922 that he could successfully compete against theoretical physicists anywhere in the world; this was the feeling behind his remark to Bohr that Copenhagen physics should not present him any difficulty. And the same feeling contributed to Pauli’s uninhibited and at times irreverent behaviour towards well-known physicists. As an extreme, though still rather charming, example one thinks of Oskar Klein’s report on Pauli’s first meeting with Paul Ehrenfest—the successor of Lorentz at the University of Leyden and famous contributor to statistical and quantum physics—during the *Bohr Festival* at Göttingen. Klein recalled: ‘On this occasion Ehrenfest stood at a distance from Pauli, stared at him in his sarcastic fashion, and then remarked: “Herr Pauli, I like your Encyclopedia article [on relativity theory] better than I like you.” To which Pauli replied most calmly: “That’s strange. With me, regarding you, it is just the opposite”’ (O. Klein, 1959; also in conversations with Mehra).<sup>773</sup> However, Pauli’s behaviour did not repel Niels Bohr or Oskar Klein, and the latter summarized his first impressions of Pauli as follows: ‘He immediately made a sympathetic impression on me. Behind his strong intellectuality and his slightly comic, boorish and somewhat arrogant exterior, one could recognize a childlike attitude—in the good sense—, which indicated a rich personality’ (O. Klein, 1959; quoted from the German translation in Richter, 1979, p. 31). Nevertheless James Franck gave Pauli the advice: ‘When you go to Bohr, do please behave yourself’ (Franck, AHQP Interview, 13 July 1962).

Pauli arrived in Copenhagen towards the end of September 1922.<sup>774</sup> Since he had concerned himself with the helium problem earlier, his arrival had been eagerly awaited by Niels Bohr and Hendrik Kramers. Pauli’s official task consisted in helping Bohr in preparing several of his papers for publication in German. Bohr had promised these papers, for he had mentioned quite a few results in his Wolfskehl lectures without providing detailed proofs, and he had been requested then to publish all he had to say as soon as possible. In 1931, when Pauli lectured in the summer school at the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, Sommerfeld passed through for a visit. ‘As Sommerfeld came in, Pauli always stood up,’ Uhlenbeck recalled (Uhlenbeck, AHQP Interview, 30 March 1962, p. 10). As time went on, Pauli directed his sarcastic criticism preferably against older and established scientists. ‘He was much sharper to older than to younger people,’ said Uhlenbeck. ‘Born was really afraid of him; Ehrenfest too, although he got along with Pauli very well’ (Uhlenbeck, *loc. cit.*, p. 3).

German journals: first, one on the helium atom in *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Kramers, 1923a; it was received on 31 December 1922 and appeared in print in February 1923); second, a general review paper on the correspondence principle and its application to the theory of atomic structure in *Naturwissenschaften* (Kramers, 1923c; it appeared in the issue of 6 June 1923); third, a paper on the absorption of X-rays by atoms and the continuous X-ray spectra in *Philosophical Magazine* (Kramers, 1923d; it appeared in the November issue); fourth, an article with the Copenhagen chemist Jens Anton Christiansen on the kinetics of the chemical reactions in *Zeitschrift für Physikalische Chemie* (Christiansen and Kramers, 1923); and fifth, two papers on the quantum theory of band spectra in *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Kramers, 1923b; Kramers and Pauli, 1923, both received on 3 January 1923 and published in February 1923).$^{777}$ In the second article on the theory of band spectra Kramers collaborated with Pauli. In it, they treated very general models of diatomic molecules, which were characterized by the fact that the total angular momentum of the molecules (i.e., the sum of the angular momenta of all electrons in their orbits) could make an arbitrary angle with the axis joining the two nuclei. This assumption enabled Kramers and Pauli to describe the infrared spectra of hydrogen halogenides without invoking—as Adolf Kratzer in Munich had done—half-integral rotational quantum numbers (Kramers and Pauli, 1923, pp. 359–360).

Pauli became good friends with Kramers and the experimentalist Hans Marius Hansen. In summer 1923 he began a theoretical investigation based on Hansen’s experimental results on the influence of an external electric field on the complex structure of mercury lines (Hansen, Takamine and Werner, 1923).$^{778}$ Although Pauli profited from the people around Bohr in Copenhagen, he received most from Niels Bohr himself. Bohr had not only founded the quantum theory of atomic structure in 1913; through his fundamental contributions to the theory since then, such as the formulation of the correspondence principle and the theory of the periodic system of elements, he had become by far the most important and original thinker in the field. In fact, the physicists in Munich and Göttingen agreed that in the first place one had to learn from Bohr the direction in which atomic theory would go; and Pauli, with his sharp, analytical mind and quick understanding, soon convinced himself how completely justified this opinion was. He discovered further that in the special situation existing in atomic theory at the end of 1922 Bohr’s methods offered definite advantages over those followed in Munich or Göttingen. That is, at a time when both Sommerfeld’s phase-integral approach and Born’s detailed quantum-theoretical perturbation scheme did not yield the correct solution of the most pressing problems—such as

IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory 491

the calculation of the energy terms of helium—the only approach promising any progress appeared to be Bohr’s method of greater physical than mathematical reasoning, based on the correspondence principle and the other fundamental principles of atomic theory. In other words, Pauli fully recognized the virtues of the programme followed at Copenhagen: namely, to concentrate first on answering the question of whether or not the available foundation of quantum theory provided a consistent description of atomic structure. This programme implied not so much an indulgence in learned mathematical formalism—which seemed to Pauli to be the essence of the programme followed in Göttingen and which he would later describe as ‘Göttingen’s deluge of formal learning’ (‘*Göttinger formale Gelehrsamkeitsschwall*,’ Pauli to Kronig, 9 October 1925)—but a thorough analysis of the empirical facts in the light of basic principles. Pauli, who had demonstrated, through his work on relativity theory and on the quantum-theoretical perturbation theory (with Born), his mastery of the most complicated formal methods, now felt happy and relieved to try Bohr’s approach in Copenhagen; he became, as Heisenberg remarked with some annoyance, ‘very Bohrian’ (‘*sehr “verbohrt”*,’ Heisenberg to Sommerfeld, 14 January 1923). Bohr, of course, accepted the new collaborator and partisan of his ideas and views with great pleasure, and got along perfectly with him. Many years later he remarked: ‘When Pauli, after working with Born in Göttingen, came to Copenhagen in 1922, he at once became, with his acutely critical and untiringly searching mind, a great source of stimulation in our group. Especially he endeared himself to us by his intellectual honesty, expressed with candour and humour in scientific discussions as well as in all other human relations’ (Bohr in his foreword to Fierz and Weisskopf, 1960, pp. 1–2).

The main problem to which Pauli turned his ‘acutely critical mind’ in Copenhagen was the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects. On Bohr’s advice he started to work on it immediately after his arrival and completed a manuscript containing the initial results by the end of the year 1922. ‘Upon Bohr’s suggestion Pauli has written a paper on the anomalous Zeeman effects, the manuscript of which I have with me,’ reported Heisenberg to Sommerfeld in January 1923. He added: ‘The essential content is the following: First there is a general discussion of the hypotheses on which the theory is founded. Of these, certain hypotheses are arbitrarily retained as being correct, while others are declared to be wrong; the fundamental assumption is that the magnetic moment is always smaller than the impulse moment by $h/2\pi$’ (Heisenberg to Sommerfeld, 4 January 1923).$^{779}$ By ‘magnetic moment’ Heisenberg meant the (angular) momentum associated with the inner quantum number $j$, and by ‘impulse moment’ the angular momentum of the series electron. Pauli assumed, in

I shall be in Munich up to about 9 January; if you go to Vienna, please be so kind as to write to me to Munich from somewhere. I am so very curious to learn about your views.’)

Zeeman effect. It was, as you must have seen, a despairing attempt to remain true to integer numbers; and we hoped to recognize just in the paradoxes a hint of the direction in which one should look for a solution of the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effect' (Bohr to Landé, 3 March 1923). He continued: 'In the meantime doubts about the necessity of these paradoxes have constantly grown, and I now believe to have found a way out to explain the complex structures in close connection with your paper on the analysis of the Zeeman splittings.' Bohr then stated that he now agreed to take half-integral values for the quantum number of the angular momentum around the direction of the magnetic field (i.e., for $j$ and $m$), but he still desired to keep integral values for the quantum numbers $n$ and $k$, i.e., the principal quantum number of the atom and the azimuthal quantum number of the series electron. For details he referred to a forthcoming article of his own. In this article, a long memoir, which was entitled 'Linienspektren und Atombau' ('Line Spectra and Atomic Structure') and submitted in the middle of March 1923 to *Annalen der Physik* for the special issue in honour of Heinrich Kayser’s seventieth birthday, Bohr discussed in greater detail than ever before the problem of the complex structure of spectral lines and the anomalous Zeeman effects (Bohr, 1923c, especially pp. 274–285). He argued there in connection with the case of doublet spectra that ‘we must be prepared for the possibility that the coupling between the series electron and the atomic core cannot be described directly after the model of the quantization rule for periodicity systems’ and that the analysis of the empirical data forced one to assume that ‘the orientation of the orbit of the series electron relative to the atomic core cannot be described either by integer values of $j$’ (Bohr, 1923c, pp. 276–277; English translation in Bohr, 1977, p. 647).<sup>782</sup> At the same time, however, Bohr again excluded the use of half-integral values for the azimuthal quantum number $k$ of the series electron because it seemed ‘to contradict our experiences about spectra’ (Bohr, 1923c, p. 277, footnote 1; English translation, *loc. cit.*, p. 647).<sup>783</sup> Although Bohr, in his article, did not hide ‘the incompleteness of the theoretical foundations’ of the available atomic theory, he remained hopeful that ‘desperate’ steps could be avoided.

Pauli, who assisted Bohr in formulating the content of the paper, was less optimistic. For some time he had been familiar with the weak points of the models proposed by Landé and Heisenberg for the anomalous Zeeman effects. For instance, he had doubted the stability of the atomic core–series electron model (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 25 November 1921), and he had reminded Landé and Heisenberg to explain both the anomalous Zeeman effects and the

***

This explanation bore similarities with the explanation of half-integral values of the rotational quantum numbers of molecules, as assumed by Kramers and Pauli (1923).
<sup>783</sup> Especially, he argued that in the case of elements with high atomic numbers the electron orbits with $k = \frac{1}{2}$ approached the nucleus too closely.

494 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

gyromagnetic effects with the same model (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 17 December 1921). Having these difficulties in mind, he was quite prepared to accept Bohr’s new opinion that something was wrong with the application of the usual classical mechanics, modified by quantum conditions to many-electron atoms or molecules.$^{784}$ Then it would follow immediately that in the case of the models of the anomalous Zeeman effects neither the usual stability considerations were applicable nor any relation existed with the gyromagnetic effects. However, with this conclusion accepted, one had to ask whether it made any sense at all to construct a model of many-electron atoms. Therefore, Pauli preferred to assume that the situation was not really that bad and searched seriously for a consistent mechanical model describing the complex structure and the anomalous Zeeman effects of many-electron atoms. This search occupied him during his entire stay at Copenhagen. He recalled many years later:

> The anomalous type of [magnetic] splitting . . . was hardly understandable, since very general assumptions concerning the electron, using classical theory as well as quantum theory, always led to the same triplet. A closer investigation of this problem left me with the feeling that it was even more unapproachable. A colleague who met me strolling rather aimlessly in the beautiful streets of Copenhagen said to me in a friendly manner, “You look very unhappy,” whereupon I answered fiercely, “How can one look happy when he is thinking of the anomalous Zeeman effect?” (Pauli, 1946, p. 214)

In spite of the overall unsatisfactory situation with the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects in terms of models, Pauli made some progress in obtaining certain formal relations from the data. In a paper entitled “Über die Gesetzmäßigkeiten des anomalen Zeeman effektes” (“On the Laws of the Anomalous Zeeman Effect”) and submitted in April to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he published his most important results (Pauli, 1923a).$^{785}$ In the introduction, Pauli referred to the recent successful classification of the data by Alfred Landé (Landé, 1923a) and remarked: ‘On the other hand, the model-dependent interpretation of the empirical relations is at the moment still plagued by very great

***

IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory 495

difficulties, and the solution of this problem might not be given completely within the framework of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems but require new concepts’ (Pauli, 1923a, p. 155). Heisenberg’s model, he went on to say, could also not be considered as a satisfactory solution because of its conceptual and mechanical deficiencies. ‘In this situation,’ he concluded, ‘it is perhaps fitting to try, quite apart from model-dependent considerations, to ascertain the simple, formal properties of the values of combination terms in the anomalous Zeeman effect’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, pp. 155–156). That is, Pauli proposed to obtain a new formal description of the empirical data by sticking as closely as possible to the principles of Bohr’s atomic theory, especially to integral values for the principal and the azimuthal quantum numbers of the atoms considered.

In order to arrive at this goal, Pauli described the terms of many-electron atoms by four quantum numbers; besides $n$ and $k$ he took the inner quantum number $j$ (characterizing the number of terms of a complex multiplet) and a quantum number, which corresponded to Landé’s quantity $R$, characterizing the angular momentum of the core. The quantum number $j$ then assumed half-integral values for even multiplets and integral values for odd multiplets, i.e., for multiplets having even and odd number of components, respectively. Pauli further assumed that the angular momenta of the core and of the series electron combined to give the total angular momentum of the atoms, or $jh/2\pi$, with $j$ denoting Sommerfeld’s inner quantum number; hence both $j$ and the quantum number of the core had to assume half-integral values. Finally, he claimed that the magnetic quantum number $m$ satisfied the relation, $|m| < j$; that is, $m = \pm \frac{1}{2}, \pm \frac{3}{2}, \dots, \pm (j - 1)$ for even, and $m = 0, \pm 1, \dots, + (j - 1)$ for odd multiplets. With these assumptions Pauli formulated the spectroscopic displacement law as follows: ‘The spectrum, emitted by the neutral atom of a given element, exhibits in the case of the Zeeman effect either always half-integral or always integral values of the quantum number $m$, and for elements that follow each other in the periodic system the values of $m$ are alternately half-integral and integral’ (Pauli, 1923a, p. 159). He regarded this statement ‘as the most beautiful formulation of Rydberg’s alternation law, since it can always be directly controlled by experience’ (Pauli, *loc. cit.*, p. 159).

Having these assumptions and definitions at hand, Pauli approached the description of the magnetic perturbation energy $\Delta W$ of the Zeeman terms as a function of the quantum numbers. He turned first to the case of strong magnetic fields and proposed the following relation:

$$\frac{\Delta W}{h \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}}} = m + \mu = m_1 + 2\mu, \qquad (255)$$

where $m_1$ and $\mu$ are two numbers, such that

$$m = m_1 + \mu \qquad (255\text{a})$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0130 -->

496 Chapter IV The Mechanical and Spectroscopic Failures of Atomic Models

and

$$m_1 = 0, \pm 1, \dots, \pm (k - 1); \quad \mu = \begin{cases} \pm \frac{1}{2} & \text{for doublet atoms} \\ 0, \pm 1 & \text{for triplet atoms.} \end{cases}$$

(255b)

For extremely strong magnetic fields the selection rule, $\Delta \mu = 0$, should be valid, which indeed yielded normal Zeeman triplets with $\Delta W / h \Delta \nu_{\text{normal}} = 0, \pm 1$ for doublet and triplet atoms ($\Delta \nu_{\text{normal}} = |e||\mathbf{H}| / 4 \pi m_e c$, where $\mathbf{H}$ denotes the magnetic field). Pauli claimed that Eqs. (255) and (255a) also described the cases of the Zeeman effects of higher multiplets in strong magnetic fields, provided he let $\mu$ assume appropriate values. Though he had so far no empirical data available to test the latter prediction, he believed it to be true because it followed from the following rule: ‘*The sum of the energy values in all the states, which belong to a given set of values of $m$ and $k$, remains a linear function of the field strength during the entire transition from weak to strong [magnetic] fields*’ (Pauli, 1923a, p. 162). That is,

$$\sum_{m_1 + \mu = m} \Delta W(m, k; m_1, \mu) = \text{const.} |\mathbf{H}|$$

(256)

where the sum extended over all values of $m_1$ and $\mu$, such that $m_1 + \mu = m$. This rule had been recognized to hold for the special cases of doublet and triplet atoms by Heisenberg, who had even tried to provide a theoretical derivation of it based on a kind of correspondence argument.${}^{786}$ Pauli, however, did not attempt to justify his extended sum-rule—he criticized Heisenberg's previous derivation—but just used it to derive several results which could be compared with experiment. Thus he concluded, for example, that Eq. (256) implied the following result: the arithmetical average of all $g$-values associated with a fully developed multiplet (having the maximum number of components) of an atom in magnetic fields becomes equal to unity. Or, in case the sum on the left-hand side of Eq. (256) contains only one term, this term itself increases linearly with the strength of the magnetic field. But, as Pauli emphasized, Eq. (256) proved to be an even more powerful relation: ‘Going beyond Heisenberg's results, we emphasize the fact that the rule allows one to calculate the $g$-values uniquely from the energy values in strong fields, if one applies it [the rule] successively to the stationary states having—for a given $k$—different values of $m$. This can be done not only for the doublets of the alkali atoms and the triplets of the alkaline-earth atoms, but also for the higher multiplets’ (Pauli, 1923a, p. 163). For example, in the case of the quintet $b$-term with $k = 4$, he found five linear equations for five $g$-terms which yielded $g$-values in agreement with Landé's previous analysis of the

<sup>786</sup>For details of Heisenberg's theory of doublet and triplet atoms and their Zeeman effects, see Volume 2, Sections I.6 and II.5.

IV.5  The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory 497

data.$^{787}$ Thus he proudly noted: *‘In this way all the g-values given by Landé can be calculated numerically’* (Pauli, 1923a, p. 164).$^{788}$

In his paper Pauli noted that he had not succeeded in constructing a mechanical model to derive his ‘formal rules’ (Pauli, 1923a, p. 164). He emphasized this deficiency again in a letter to Landé, written four weeks after submitting his paper. He wrote: *‘I am very sad about the fact that I have not succeeded in finding a model-dependent interpretation for the amazingly simple rules. Perhaps you, or someone else, will be more fortunate than I, and perhaps I shall later on make progress in this matter myself’* (Pauli to Landé, 23 May 1923). He remarked further: *‘Now, however, I want to report to you briefly some considerations about the problem of models of the Zeeman effect, which, to be careful, I have not included in the paper.’* According to these considerations Pauli proposed to interpret $m_1h/2\pi$ as the component of the angular momentum of the series electron, and $\mu h/2\pi$ as the component of the angular momentum of the inner system (core) parallel to the direction of the magnetic field. *‘The energy values for strong fields [Eq. (255)] can be interpreted on this view by the assumption that the magnetic moment of the inner [atomic] system assumes twice the value that it would have corresponding to its angular momentum in the classical electron theory of magnetism, while the outer electron creates a magnetic moment in agreement with Biot and Savart’s law’* (Pauli to Landé, 23 May 1923). Pauli explained to Landé that the situation in his model was different from the one in Heisenberg’s model; in the latter, the Biot–Savart law was always satisfied, but the dynamical equations expressing the time derivative of the angular momentum had to be altered by introducing a new, dynamical definition of angular momentum besides the usual kinematic one. Both models, however, Pauli concluded, led to difficulties: his own (which he called the ‘magnetic formulation’) did not yield Landé’s g-formula, Eq. (252), but one in which the term $J^2 - \frac{1}{4}$ was replaced by $J^2$ (equal to Pauli’s $j^2$); in Heisenberg’s model one had to exclude without justification the occurrence of some combinations of the angular momenta of atomic core and series electron. Pauli further remarked to Landé that at the moment, however, he had become weary of the anomalous Zeeman effects and was dealing with another problem: namely, to calculate the effect of electric fields on complex multiplets.

Landé received these remarks with great interest. He immediately used Pauli’s model to generalize his previous vector model of the anomalous Zeeman effects (Landé, 1923a) and to analyze with its help the transitions of the anomalous

$^{787}$The sum of energy perturbation terms $\Delta W$ for magnetic quantum numbers $m = 5, 4, 3, 2$ and $1$ was $7, 11, 12, 10$ and $5$ (in units of $h\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$). Since, in agreement with Eq. (245), the left-hand side of Eq. (256) had to be equal to $m$ times the g-sum of the corresponding terms, Pauli obtained the equations: $5g_1 = 7$; $4(g_1 + g_2) = 11$; $3(g_1 + g_2 + g_3) = 12$; $2(g_1 + g_2 + g_3 + g_4) = 10$; and $g_1 + g_2 + g_3 + g_4 + g_5 = 5$. From these he derived: $g_1 = 7/5$; $g_2 = 27/20$; $g_3 = 5/4$; $g_4 = 1$; $g_5 = 0$.

He remarked further: *‘I knew already that the theorem is correct also for Landé’s multiplets ... But I had overlooked the possibility of obtaining the entire empirical material from it alone’* (Heisenberg to Pauli, 26 March 1923).

Zeeman components of complex multiplets in the Paschen–Back terms with increasing strength of the applied magnetic field. He informed Pauli about his new results and proposed that they should write a joint paper. Pauli refused, however, to join Landé in writing a paper, ‘before one has a complete theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects,’ and suggested to Landé: ‘You may, without bad conscience, publish a note alluding to my (earlier) communications by letter, especially to the fact that I drew your attention to the possibility of interpreting $m_1h/2\pi$ and $\mu h/2\pi$ as components of the angular momentum of the outer and inner system parallel to the magnetic field’ (Pauli to Landé, 26 July 1923).$^{789}$ Landé followed this proposal eagerly and submitted in the middle of August a paper to *Zeitschrift für Physik* on ‘Termstruktur und Zeemaneeffekt der Multipletts’ (‘Term Structure and Zeeman Effect of the Multiplets’); it was received on 16 August 1923 and published in the issue of 9 November of the same year (Landé, 1923f).

Landé’s new paper, which he called a continuation of his previous one (Landé, 1923a), contained a new rule. It described the displacement of the ‘centre’ (‘*Schwerpunkt*’), $\nu_0$, of a complex line multiplet in a magnetic field, i.e.,

$$\nu_0 \to \nu_0 + \gamma\omega, \tag{257}$$

where $\omega$ was a frequency common to the multiplet under consideration and $\gamma$ denoted an ‘interval factor’ dependent on the inner quantum number $J$ (equal to Pauli’s $j$). In a weak magnetic field, $\gamma$ should satisfy the relation

$$\gamma = \frac{J^2 + \frac{1}{4} - R^2 + K^2}{2RK} . \tag{257a}$$

As a consequence, the net change of the Zeeman components of a complex line multiplet was composed of the change, described by the $g$-factor ($\Delta\nu = mg\Delta\nu_{\text{normal}}$), plus the change $\gamma\omega$.

The main issue in Landé’s paper was to find out how the anomalous Zeeman components changed when the strength of the external field was increased. For this purpose he now made use of Pauli’s models. Pauli had stated that in a strong magnetic field the product $mg$, characterizing the magnetic perturbation energy, could be written as a sum of two terms, $m_1 + 2\mu$, where $m_1$ denoted the magnetic quantum number of the series electron and $\mu$ the magnetic quantum number of the core. Landé now concluded that, in the spirit of Pauli’s model, the strong field limit of the factor $\gamma$ had to be

$$\gamma = \frac{m_R}{R} \cdot \frac{m_K}{K} , \tag{258}$$

$^{789}$ Pauli had meanwhile concerned himself not only with the problem of complex structure in external electric fields mentioned above; during several weeks of absence from Copenhagen (which he spent partly in Hamburg), he had also worked on a paper dealing with the thermal equilibrium between radiation and free electrons (Pauli, 1923b).

IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory

where $m_K = m_1$ and $m_R = \mu$. Similar to Pauli’s sum-rule, Eq. (256), which he reformulated as the principle of the ‘permanence of $g$-sums’ (‘*Permanenz der g-Summen*,’ Landé, 1923f, p. 116), or as the equation (with the summation over all values of $J$),

$$\sum_J mg_{\text{strong}} = \sum_J mg_{\text{weak}} = \text{const.} \tag{259}$$

Landé now proposed a sum-rule for the $\gamma$’s, expressing the ‘permanence of $\gamma$-sums’ (Landé, 1923f, p. 119), that is,

$$\sum_J \gamma_{\text{strong}} = \sum_J \gamma_{\text{weak}} = \text{const.} \tag{260}$$

He claimed that Eq. (260) enabled one—similar to the sum-rule in the case of $g$-factors, Eq. (259)—to derive the $\gamma$-values in weak magnetic fields from those in strong magnetic fields. Still the question remained of how to relate the individual Zeeman components in weak and strong magnetic fields, as had been done previously, e.g., by Sommerfeld and Heisenberg in their approach to the problem.

In a letter to Landé, dated 5 June 1923, Pauli had proposed to associate $m_R$ and $m_K$ (the quantum numbers describing, in particular, the strong field situation) to the quantum numbers $J, K$ and $R$ (describing the weak field situation) as follows:

$$m_R = J - K, \quad m_K = m - (J - K) \quad \text{for } m \geq R - K,$$
$$m_R = m - (R - J), \quad m_K = R - J \quad \text{for } m \leq R - K, \tag{261}$$

without giving any proof.$^{790}$ Landé, after comparing this suggestion with the data, had found it to be correct. In his paper he noted further:

> Now one can see that this particular relation can be obtained—instead of using the hypothesis [(261)]—also by means of the following postulate: The values of $g$ and $\gamma$, belonging to a given set $m, R, K$, for different values of $J$ in a weak magnetic field, pass over into such singular values of $g$ and $\gamma$ in a strong field that the summation relation, $\sum_J |(mg_{\text{strong}} - mg_{\text{weak}}) + (\gamma_{\text{strong}} - \gamma_{\text{weak}})|^2 = \text{minimum}$, holds among all possible relations [between the strong- and weak-field values of $g$ and $\gamma$]. (Landé, 1923f, p. 120)

Assuming the validity of this postulate, Landé was able to describe the transition of the $g$- and $\gamma$-values in magnetic fields of increasing strength as

$$mg = \cos(\mathbf{J}, \mathbf{H}) \left[ J + R \cos(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{J}) \right] \rightarrow K \cos(\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{H}) + 2R \cos(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{H}) \tag{262a}$$

***

$^{790}$Pauli had used his own notation, i.e., $\mu$ and $m_1$ for Landé’s $R$ and $K$, respectively, etc. He had also only given the relations for $m_R$ (or $\mu$); however, the relations for $m_K$ (or $m_1$) then followed by taking into account Eq. (255a).

IV.5  The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory
501

Pauli claimed that one did not have to use the minimum principle, and the relation (261) could be derived directly from the mechanical model.

> I suspect further [he added] that the equations [(262a, b)] will follow—due to mechanical reasons—also for other coupling forces, independent of the specific model chosen, so long as one does not pass [in a mechanical transformation] through motions that are mechanically instable. Up to now I have not succeeded in proving this generalization. If I do, I shall eventually publish a note in the *Zeitschrift für Physik*. (Pauli to Landé, 23 September 1923)

Pauli indeed succeeded in obtaining the desired proof and he presented it in a paper, entitled ‘Zur Frage der Zuordnung der Komplexstrukturterme in starken und in schwachen Feldern’ (‘On the Problem of Relating Complex Structure Terms in Strong and Weak Fields’), which he submitted from Hamburg in October 1923, a few weeks after he had returned from Copenhagen (Pauli, 1924a).$^{791}$

The basic idea behind the proof was that Pauli applied three quantum conditions: one for the total angular momentum of the atom in the magnetic field, another for the angular momentum of the series electron, and a further quantum condition which provided an invariant quantity under adiabatic changes of the magnetic field strength. With these conditions he derived two sets of relations between the quantum numbers determining the anomalous Zeeman and Paschen–Back effects: besides the relations (261), he found a set of relations, valid in the situation that the energy terms of the free atoms did not become larger but smaller with increasing values of the inner quantum number $j$. These relations were

$$m_k = j - r, \quad m_r = m - (j - r) \quad \text{for } m \geq k - r,$$ (261')
$$m_k = m - (k - j), \quad m_r = k - j \quad \text{for } m \leq k - r.$$

In his new paper, Pauli proposed to take—instead of Landé’s quantum numbers $J$, $K$ and $R$—the quantum numbers $j$, $k$ and $r$; the latter were larger by a constant, i.e., $j = J + \frac{1}{2}$, $k = K + \frac{1}{2}$, and $r = R + \frac{1}{2}$. The change in the notation allowed him to write Landé’s equations for the $g$- and $\gamma$-factors in a slightly more convenient form as$^{792}$

$$g = 1 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{j(j - 1) + r(r - 1) - k(k - 1)}{j(j - 1)}$$ (252'')

$^{791}$ The date on which Pauli left Copenhagen can be ascertained from a letter of Hansen to Bohr. Hansen wrote on 1 October 1923: ‘Tonight Pauli will talk at the Physical Society; on Thursday [4 October] he will leave, and I have the impression that he is again quite happy, so that his stay [at Copenhagen] ends in harmony in all respects.’

In the middle of September Pauli had been rather unhappy about the status of his endeavours (see Pauli to Bohr, 12 September 1923). It would seem, therefore, that Pauli had made important progress by the end of September 1923.

$^{792}$ The energy terms derived from experiments in weak and strong fields did fix the values of the quantum numbers $m$, $m_r$, and $m_k$. Hence the ‘weak field’ quantum numbers could be determined only up to a common constant; this was also reflected in the relations (261), in which one could insert either Pauli’s or Landé’s or even Sommerfeld’s quantum numbers (Sommerfeld’s $j$, for example, was smaller than Landé’s by one unit).

and

$$\gamma = \frac{j(j-1) - r(r-1) - k(k-1)}{2(r - \frac{1}{2})(k - \frac{1}{2})} . \tag{257a'}$$

In spite of the success of his efforts in obtaining Landé’s results from general quantum-theoretical considerations, Pauli was not satisfied. He simply remarked in the conclusion of his paper: ‘It seems essential to us that the assumptions employed here be of such a general nature as they are, because the mechanical models *per se* are so inadequate for deriving the relations [between terms in weak and strong magnetic fields]—obtained with the help of [classical] mechanics and the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems—for the anomalous Zeeman effect’ (Pauli, 1924a, p. 387). That is, with respect to the status of the model-dependent considerations and the real theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects he still subscribed to the statement which he had made to Sommerfeld in summer 1923: ‘It’s a great misery with the theory of the anomalous Zeeman effect and altogether with the atoms containing more than one electron’ (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 19 July 1923). However, the situation in atomic theory was even worse than these words conveyed. As the physicists, especially Pauli, would recognize clearly in late 1923 and early 1924, the available quantum theory failed even in treating a one-electron atom on which external electric and magnetic fields were applied simultaneously. The development of this problem had begun in 1918, and in the course of years several theoreticians—including Paul Epstein, Oskar Klein and Wilhelm Lenz—had become involved in it.

In part two of his memoir on the quantum theory of line spectra, Niels Bohr had remarked:

> In case that we consider the general problem of the effect on the hydrogen atom of a small electric or magnetic field which does not possess axial symmetry round an axis through the nucleus, or of the simultaneous effect of two such fields, which do not possess such symmetry round a common axis, we must expect that the secular perturbation of the orbit of the electron will in general not be of the conditionally periodic type. In such a case we cannot obtain a complete fixation of the stationary states, and we may conclude that the presence of external forces will not give rise to the splitting up of the hydrogen lines into a number of sharp components but to a diffusion of these lines. (Bohr, 1918b, p. 93)

While Born and Pauli, in their joint paper on the quantum-theoretical perturbation theory three years later, agreed with Bohr’s opinion, and again claimed that the problem of the hydrogen atom in simultaneous electric and magnetic fields in different directions would not admit a multiply periodic solution (Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 150), Paul Sophus Epstein arrived at exactly the opposite conclusion. With the help of a quantum-theoretical perturbation method, which he published in papers submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Epstein, 1922a, b, c) and *Physical Review* (Epstein, 1922d), respectively, he obtained the desired solution

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0137 -->

# IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory  
503  

(Epstein, 1923).<sup>793</sup> For the energy terms of the hydrogen atom in an electric field $\mathbf{E}$ and a magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$, whose directions made an angle $\alpha$ with each other, Epstein found the expression  

$$
W = -\frac{2\pi m_e e^4}{h^2 n_3^2} + \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2} \left[ \left( f^2 + 2f g n_3 \cos \alpha + g^2 n_3^2 \right)^{1/2} n_1 - \left( f^2 - 2f g n_3 \cos \alpha + g^2 n_3^2 \right)^{1/2} n_2 + (f \delta \sin \alpha) n_3 \right], \tag{263}
$$

where $n_1$, $n_2$ and $n_3$ are three quantum numbers ($n_3$ corresponds to the principal quantum number of the atom; the difference, $n_1 - n_2$, corresponds to the quantum number $m$ of the Zeeman effect in the case of zero electric field strength, and to the quantum number $s$ of the Stark effect for zero magnetic field strength); $f$ and $g$ denote the quantities $\pi |e| |\mathbf{H}| / m_e c h$ and $3 |\mathbf{E}| / 2 m_e c$, respectively; $\delta$ is a constant which can assume the values $+1$, $0$, or $-1$.  

Epstein had worked out a perturbation-theoretic method as early as 1917 in connection with the treatment of the helium problem.<sup>794</sup> The same idea had been used in principle by the French astronomer Charles-Eugène Delaunay in lunar theory about sixty years earlier (Delaunay, 1860, 1867). Without referring to action and angle variables, Delaunay had treated the astronomical problem by writing down the Hamiltonian as a sum of an unperturbed term plus a perturbation, which he assumed to be expandable in an $f$-fold Fourier series. Knowing the solution of the unperturbed problem (i.e., of the two-body system consisting of the earth and the moon), he had proposed to solve the perturbation problem (including the attraction of other celestial bodies) in successive approximations: first, considering only the periodic term having the largest Fourier coefficient, then the term with the second largest Fourier coefficient, etc. Epstein, in his papers of 1922, introduced action and angle variables explicitly into Delaunay’s perturbation theory and gave a quantum-theoretical formulation of the scheme (Epstein, 1922b, pp. 315–320). His results agreed in most respects with the results obtained from the perturbation methods of Bohr and Kramers or of Born and Pauli. However, Born and Pauli criticized certain points of Epstein’s treatment.<sup>795</sup> Epstein reacted quite angrily to such criticism; he wrote a rather impolite letter to Max Born, accusing him of attempting to ruin his (Epstein’s) scientific reputation.  

---

<sup>793</sup> Epstein had indicated the existence of the multiply periodic solution of the hydrogen atom in fields of different directions already in his second paper on the quantum-theoretical perturbation theory (Epstein, 1922b, p. 319, footnote 2).

<sup>795</sup> For example, Born and Pauli claimed that libration motion of the perturbed system could occur only if the unperturbed system was a degenerate one, in contrast to what Epstein had assumed (Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 147, footnote 2).

tion. Pauli replied to this letter and emphasized that, ‘we have certainly not written our paper with the *a priori* intention of attacking you; however, it was necessary for us *for factual clarification* to state our opinion more precisely at those points where it deviates from yours’ (Pauli to Epstein, September 1922). Pauli further remarked in his letter that Epstein’s method did not provide, in a finite number of steps, a solution of a system of weakly anharmonic resonators and added: ‘As for the combined Stark and Zeeman effects in the case of the hydrogen atom in fields having different directions, we stick at the moment to our opinion and await the publication of your paper’ (Pauli to Epstein, September 1922). The main difficulty in the perturbation schemes at that time consisted in reliable estimates of their convergence; hence Pauli was not sure whether Epstein was right when he claimed that a hydrogen atom in crossed electric and magnetic fields could still be considered as a multiply periodic system. Epstein, on the other hand, did not publish any details of his calculation of the energy states of hydrogen atom in simultaneous electric and magnetic fields, but he reported about it in talks. When Epstein visited Hamburg in summer 1923, Pauli learned about his result and wrote to Copenhagen:

> In Hamburg I met Epstein, who is on a visit to Germany. He gave a long talk on the subject of Balmer lines in crossed electric and magnetic fields. The result is that, contrary to our opinion up to now, mechanics leads to harmonic [multiply periodic] solutions in this case; the mechanical equations for the secular perturbations can be integrated. Hence one must expect sharp [line-] components. I have checked the calculation and found that Epstein is right. I am writing this with the purpose that Bohr should not state anything wrong in writing his Guthrie Lecture. (Pauli to Hansen, 6 July 1923)<sup>796</sup>

Since Epstein had not published the details of his investigation of the ‘crossed field’ problem, Otto Halpern of Vienna carried out the calculation and submitted a paper on it in August 1923 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Halpern, 1923a).<sup>797</sup> Halpern essentially used the perturbation scheme of Born and Pauli. He obtained an approximation solution by expanding the perturbed system in powers of the

In his manuscript of September 1923, ‘On the Application of the Quantum Theory to Atomic Structure II. Theory of Series Spectra,’ he mentioned only Epstein’s result at the end of Section 1 (see Bohr, 1976, p. 536).

<sup>797</sup> Otto Halpern was born in Vienna on 25 April 1899. He studied at the University of Vienna (1922–1927), receiving his doctorate in 1927. He spent two years as an International Research Fellow at the University of Leipzig (1928–1930), after which he went to America, becoming an associate professor at New York University (1930–1941). Later he occupied various positions at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (1941–1945), Columbia University (1947), University of Southern California at Los Angeles (1947–1952), Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory (1946–1952), Naval Research Laboratory (from 1949), Brookhaven National Laboratory (1949–1953), and Livermore Radiation Laboratory (1959–1961). In 1960 Halpern received the Distinguished Service Medal of the U.S. Department of Defense. Halpern’s main contributions were to quantum theory and neutron optics.

IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory 505

In this way he arrived at the conclusion that the solution of the problem was perfectly periodic and could be expressed in terms of three phase integrals.<sup>798</sup> At the Cincinnati meeting of the American Physical Society, 27 to 29 December 1923, Oskar Klein, then at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, gave a talk on 'The Simultaneous Action on a Hydrogen Atom of Crossed Homogeneous Electric and Magnetic Fields.' In the abstract of this talk, published in the February 1924 issue of *Physical Review*, Klein stated: 'The motion is shown to be of a strictly doubly periodic character when powers of the fields higher than the first are neglected. This agrees with the statements of Epstein and Halpern who did not, however, obtain a closed solution' (O. Klein, 1924a, p. 308). Klein submitted a full account of his talk in a paper to *Zeitschrift für Physik*; it was received on 23 January 1924 and published in the beginning of March 1924 (O. Klein, 1924b).

Klein had thought about the crossed-field problem already for some time. The reason was that before going to the United States he had met Erik Hulthén in Lund, who got him interested in the theory of molecules. This led him to search for a simple analogy of the rotating molecule. As he recalled later: 'I thought that if you take the hydrogen atom, and then if you have an electric field, that would be a little like the action of the other atom on the electron of the first atom; and the magnetic field would be a little like the rotation [of the molecule]' (Klein, Conversations, p. 75). Klein was aware of Bohr's claim that the crossed-field problem had no multiply periodic solution, hence he was rather surprised that he obtained one by simply applying the method with the help of which Bohr had treated the Stark effect.<sup>799</sup> Klein replaced the equation of motion of the electron (in the hydrogen atom under the influence of electric and magnetic fields **E** and **H**) by the equation describing the motion of **R**<sub>el</sub>, the coordinate vector of the electric centre of the atom averaged over the unperturbed orbit, i.e.,

$$\frac{d\mathbf{R}_{\text{el}}}{dt} = |e| K^2 (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{M}_{\text{el}}) + \frac{|e|}{2m_e c} (\mathbf{H} \times \mathbf{R}_{\text{el}}), \qquad (264)$$

where $K = 3nh / 8\pi^2 m_e |e|$, $n$ being the principal quantum number, and **M**<sub>el</sub> denotes the angular momentum of the electrical centre, again averaged over the unperturbed orbit. Equation (264) then described the 'secular' motion of the centre of electric charge of the atom. As Klein showed, this motion consisted of

He further proved that the quantities

If integral multiples of Planck's constant were substituted for $I_1$ and $I_2$, one would arrive at the quantum-theoretical energy terms; consequently the atom would emit discrete lines, in contrast to Bohr's earlier assertion.

A couple of weeks after Klein's paper was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 9 February 1924, Wilhelm Lenz of Hamburg presented another complete solution of the crossed field problem at a meeting of the Lower Saxony Section (*Gauverein Niedersachsen*) of the German Physical Society at Braunschweig. He submitted a paper on his calculation, which avoided the use of perturbation theory by a clever trick, to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Lenz, 1924). Lenz' trick consisted of introducing a special

IV.5 The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory

507

and the aphelion of the electron’s orbit, and its magnitude was equal to the eccentricity of the orbit. To solve the crossed-field problem one had just to find the expressions for the vectors **M** and **A**. Both of them were constants of the unperturbed motion. When the electric and magnetic fields were switched on, however, they changed slowly with time, obeying the equations

$$\frac{d\mathbf{M}}{dt} = \frac{3}{2} |e| a (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{A}) + \frac{|e|}{2m_e c} (\mathbf{H} \times \mathbf{M})$$

and

$$\frac{d\mathbf{A}}{dt} = \frac{3}{2 |e| m_e} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{M}) + \frac{|e|}{2m_e c} (\mathbf{H} \times \mathbf{A}), \quad (269)$$

where $a$ is the semi-major axis of the unperturbed orbit. The integration of these equations immediately yielded the results obtained by Oskar Klein, given by Eqs. (265)–(267).

Although all authors—Epstein, Halpern, Klein and Lenz—gave the formulae for the perturbation energy of the states of hydrogen atom in the crossed fields, they discussed the consequences only in special cases.$^{801}$ Thus Klein treated those cases in which the motion was simply periodic. However, he denoted his paper as [Part] I, indicating that he might publish a second part, in which he would deal with the other conclusions following from his calculation.$^{802}$ He indeed started to write the second part, but because of other things he did not complete and submit it. ‘By the time I had made a treatment such that I believed in the results, I think it was about Easter 1925,’ he recalled later. ‘I was rather definite at that time, but I [got] strong doubts that there could be something wrong because the whole [thing] was a perturbation calculation’ (Klein, Conversations, p. 77). Meanwhile the crossed-field problem had gained another, important aspect: the question had arisen whether its solution provided a further example of the failure of atomic theory. Besides Bohr, Pauli was especially interested in that aspect in connection with his article on quantum theory for the *Handbuch der Physik*. Since he could not wait until Klein was ready to publish his second paper on the crossed-field problem, he analyzed it carefully himself. In particular, he studied the expression for the perturbation energy. In the special case of parallel electric and magnetic fields $\Delta W$ assumed the form

$$\Delta W = mh \Delta \nu_H + sh \Delta \nu_E, \quad (270)$$

where $\Delta \nu_H$ ($= |e| |\mathbf{H}| / 2m_e c$) and $\Delta \nu_E$ ($= 3nh |\mathbf{E}| / 8\pi^2 m_e |e|$) are the frequency shifts in the external magnetic (**H**) and electric (**E**) fields, and $m$ and $s$ are the

***

quantum numbers of the Zeeman and Stark effects, respectively. (The quantum numbers $m$ and $s$ satisfied the condition that the value of $m$ differed from the value of $n + s$ by an even number, $n$ being the principal quantum number.) Pauli rewrote Eq. (270) as

$$\Delta W = \left(n_1 - \frac{n}{2}\right)h\nu_1 + \left(n_2 - \frac{n}{2}\right)h\nu_2, \qquad (270')$$

with $\nu_1 = \Delta\nu_H + \Delta\nu_E$ and $\nu_2 = |\Delta\nu_H - \Delta\nu_E|$. The new quantum numbers, $n_1$ and $n_2$, satisfying the relations, $0 \leq n_1 \leq n$ and $0 \leq n_2 \leq n$, were related to $m$ and $s$ by the equations

$$s = n_1 - n_2 \quad \text{and} \quad m = \begin{cases} n - n_1 - n_2 & \text{for } m > 0 \\ -(n - n_1 - n_2) & \text{for } m < 0. \end{cases} \qquad (270\text{a})$$

The right-hand side of Eq. (270') represented, of course, a special case of Klein's expression for the perturbation energy, Eq. (267).

Pauli's next step was to consider an adiabatic transformation of the system, involving changes of the directions and strengths of the external fields. Since the quantities $I_1$ and $I_2$, Eqs. (266a) and (266b), had been recognized as adiabatic invariants, it became possible to calculate the perturbation energy of all states, which could be obtained from a state of known energy by an adiabatic transformation. One particular transformation of this kind, however, led to serious trouble. Pauli began by considering a state in which the electric and magnetic fields possessed the same direction and strengths such that $\Delta\nu_H > \Delta\nu_E$. Its perturbation energy was then given by Eq. (270) or Eq. (270'). He then transformed the system by adiabatically turning around the directions of the fields with respect to each other and by increasing (again adiabatically) the strength of the electric field, such that at no instant a degeneracy of the motion (described by only one secular perturbation frequency, $\nu_1$ or $\nu_2$) occurred. Finally, he arrived at a state in which $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ had the same direction, but $\Delta\nu_E > \Delta\nu_H$. In the initial and final states the perturbation energy became

$$\Delta W = h(n_1 + n_2 - n)\Delta\nu_H + (n_1 - n_2)\Delta\nu_E \qquad (271\text{a})$$

and

$$\Delta W = h(n_1 + n_2 - n)\Delta\nu_E + (n_1 - n_2)\Delta\nu_H, \qquad (271\text{b})$$

respectively. Pauli commented on this result by saying: 'Since the factors multiplying $\Delta\nu_H$ and $\Delta\nu_E$ indicate the magnetic quantum number ($m$) and the electric quantum number ($s$), respectively, we have thus shown that in the process considered these quantum numbers exchange their values. Hence the "allowed" orbits, $s = 0, m \neq 0$, pass over into the "forbidden" orbits, $m = 0,$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0143 -->

IV.5  The Breakdown of the Bohr–Sommerfeld Theory 509

$s \neq 0$, and *vice versa*’ (Pauli, 1926b, pp. 163–164). Now, according to the fundamental principles of atomic theory, one should always be able to obtain from a given quantum state another state by an adiabatic transformation, which implied that both states should exist theoretically. However, one had reasons to exclude from consideration certain orbits as being inadmissible: e.g., the pendulum orbits of the electron, which could approach the atomic nucleus closely. This restriction also excluded the orbits with $m = 0$, i.e., the pendulum orbits parallel to the direction of the magnetic field. And if these had to be excluded, then the adiabatic hypothesis also broke down in the simple case of the hydrogen atom under the simultaneous influence of electric and magnetic fields.

Pauli concluded his treatment of the crossed-field problem with the remark: ‘An escape from this difficulty can be achieved only by a radical change in the foundation of the theory’ (Pauli, 1926b, p. 164). However, at that time—i.e., in summer 1925—not only had the failure of the mechanical principles of atomic theory been demonstrated in great detail, but also the special assumptions made about radiation had been proved to be questionable. This situation was brought about by the new experimental and theoretical results bearing on the nature of radiation and its interaction with matter, which we shall discuss next.

# Chapter V
## The Problems of Radiation Theory

At the very origin of quantum theory had stood a special problem of radiation theory, that of blackbody radiation. While Max Planck had based the derivation of his blackbody radiation formula in 1900 on the assumption that radiation could be treated as electromagnetic waves described by classical electrodynamics (Planck, 1900f), Albert Einstein showed in 1905 that at least some radiation exhibited properties similar to those of material particles, which he tried to account for by what he called the light-quantum hypothesis (Einstein, 1905b). With this hypothesis Einstein immediately obtained a reasonable interpretation of several radiation phenomena, especially the so-called photoelectric effect. In 1913 Niels Bohr used an equation, modelled after Einstein’s equation relating the kinetic energy of the photoelectron to the frequency of the incident ultraviolet light, Eq. (60), as one of the fundamental hypotheses of the theory of atomic structure: namely, the frequency condition, Eq. (118). In spite of these and other successful applications of the light-quantum concept, the large majority of the physicists working on quantum theory did not believe in it. They subscribed to what Planck, Nernst, Rubens and Warburg wrote in 1913 about Einstein: ‘that he may have sometimes missed the target in his speculations as, for example, in his theory of light-quanta.’⁸⁰³ And during the following decade hardly anyone took light-quanta seriously until there appeared a paper to settle this question completely: this was the paper presented by Arthur Holly Compton in December 1922 (Compton, 1923b). The main result of this paper—the so-called Compton effect—demanded almost inevitably an interpretation of the radiation as consisting of light-quanta of definite energy and directed momentum, which created great difficulties in Bohr’s theory of atomic structure, for it could not be made to agree with the correspondence principle. Therefore, Bohr and his collaborators, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater, proposed in early 1924 a new radiation theory: especially, they stuck to the classical description of radiation as electromagnetic waves and explained the Compton effect as being due to the peculiar interaction of radiation with atoms in which the laws of energy and momentum conservation were satisfied only on the statistical average (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924). Before one could prove or disprove the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory experimentally, the light-quantum hypothesis received some theoretical
