Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

support from a paper of Satyendra Nath Bose of Dacca: he obtained the first systematic derivation of Planck’s blackbody radiation formula on the basis of the light-quantum hypothesis by associating with light-quanta new statistical properties (Bose, 1924a). Einstein made use of Bose’s statistics at once to develop a quantum theory of monatomic ideal gases (Einstein, 1924c; 1925a, b). At about the same time Louis de Broglie in Paris completed his doctoral thesis dealing with the general quantum-theoretical properties of radiation and matter: he came to the conclusion that a correct description of quantum phenomena required matter to possess certain properties of waves (L. de Broglie, 1924e). In spring 1925 the experiment of Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger (1925a)—and a few months later the experiment of Arthur H. Compton and Alfred W. Simon (1925c)—disproved the radiation theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater, thus leaving only the light-quantum theory of Einstein and Bose as a consistent quantum theory of radiation. In spite of this success, however, the quantum theory of radiation raised serious conceptual problems in relation to the classical description of radiation and with respect to the thermodynamic properties of radiation and matter. These problems would continue to plague the physicists beyond the period which is treated in this book. The quantum theory of radiation would again become a subject of serious discussions in the years following the discovery of quantum mechanics and wave mechanics. In the beginning of that period Gilbert N. Lewis (1926) would give a new name—‘photon’—to the light-quantum, in order to emphasize its fundamental role—besides that of electrons and protons—in the structure of atoms.

## V.1 The Proof of the Light-Quantum Hypothesis

When Albert Einstein introduced in 1905 what he called a ‘heuristic point of view’ or the ‘light-quantum’ into radiation theory, he had in mind to explain three different radiation phenomena: the high frequency, low density part of blackbody radiation described by Wilhelm Wien’s law of 1896; the so-called rule of George Gabriel Stokes stating that the frequency of fluorescent light was always smaller than the frequency of radiation exciting it; and the principal aspects of the photoelectric effect, i.e., the facts that the velocity of the ejected electrons depended only on the frequency of the incident (ultraviolet) radiation, and their number on its intensity. Certainly, the light-quantum hypothesis accounted for all these phenomena; however, since this hypothesis contradicted completely the conventional concepts of radiation theory, the question had to be asked whether it was really necessary. In the case of blackbody radiation, for example, Planck argued that the classical undulatory description sufficed and that the quantum effects just arose from the peculiar interaction between radiation and the elementary resonators (or material particles) in a cavity (Planck, 1913). Although the attempts of Planck and others to use such an idea for obtaining a consistent derivation of the blackbody radiation law were not

514                          Chapter V  The Problems of Radiation Theory

as the selective photoelectric effect, Millikan expected to ‘account for all the relations thus far known between corpuscular and ethereal radiations’ by ‘a modification of Planck’s formulation’ (Millikan, 1916b, p. 387).

We have referred to Millikan’s theoretical interpretation of his photoelectric measurements, for it represented the opinion of most quantum physicists at that time. Millikan even claimed that: ‘Despite the apparently complete success of the Einstein equation, the physical theory of which it was designed to be a symbolic expression is found so untenable that Einstein himself, I believe, no longer holds to it’ (Millikan, 1916b, p. 384). Indeed Einstein, who had advocated the light-quantum hypothesis eagerly until 1912, had kept rather quiet about it during the following years, until he returned to it in 1916. We shall briefly outline the steps towards Einstein’s renewal of interest in light-quanta.

As we have discussed in Chapter I, Einstein had tried hard to develop since 1905 a consistent radiation theory on the basis of the light-quantum hypothesis. Especially, he had analyzed the energy fluctuations in blackbody radiation (obeying Planck’s law) in order to determine the properties of light-quanta (Einstein, 1909a, b). He had thus found that the fluctuations had a twofold origin: one part arose from the wave theory, while the other part—describing the situation for large frequencies and small intensities (i.e., the region in which Wien’s law was valid)—could be explained as the ‘crudest illustration of the light-quantum hypothesis’ (‘*roheste Veranschaulichung der Lichtquantenhypothese*’), namely, the assumption that radiation consisted of ‘objects of very small extension having the energy *hν*, which propagate in space independently of each other, and are reflected [say, from a wall] independently of each other’ (Einstein, 1909b, p. 824). Einstein had thus arrived at the following conclusion:
‘*Besides the spatial non-uniformity in the distribution of the momentum of radiation due to the undulatory theory, there exists yet another non-uniformity in the spatial distribution of the momentum, which—for low energy density of the radiation—dominates the former non-uniformity by far*’ (Einstein, 1909b, p. 824).

While Einstein had been rather careful in using the idea of free, independent light-quanta, Johannes Stark, the other leading advocate of the light-quantum hypothesis, had gone ahead and considered in some detail the process of interaction between light-quanta (of energy *hν* and directed momentum of magnitude *hν/c*) and matter. Thus Stark, in a paper submitted in November 1909—i.e., shortly after Einstein’s talk at Salzburg, in which he had presented the above-mentioned conclusion about the momentum of radiation—had treated the production of X-rays by the impact of electrons on the anticathode by taking into account energy and momentum conservation between the electron and a single light-quantum (Stark, 1909d). Stark’s explanation of X-ray production had been criticized, as we have discussed in Section I.5, by Arnold Sommerfeld. Sommerfeld showed that the observed asymmetry in the intensity distribution of X-rays could be accounted for perfectly by the classical wave theory (Sommerfeld, 1909b). Then, after the discovery of the X-ray interference phenomena in 1912, the extreme light-quantum hypothesis of Einstein and Stark had been

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0148 -->

reservation on Einstein’s part which Millikan interpreted as his abandoning the

Millikan’s detailed account of the verification of Einstein’s photoelectric
equation appeared in the March 1916 issue of *Physical Review*. On 21 July of the
same year Einstein gave a talk at the German Physical Society in Berlin on the
quantum theory.$^{804}$ In it he discussed a new derivation of Planck’s law based on
a discussion of the processes of emission and absorption of radiation by atoms
(Einstein, 1916d). In a letter to Michele Besso he characterized his approach as
follows:

> The fundamental thing is that the *statistical* consideration, which leads to Planck’s
> formula, has become *unified* and thereby as general as one can imagine, since one
> has not assumed anything about the nature of the mediating molecules other than
> the most general quantum idea. From it follows the result (which was not contained
> in the paper I sent you [Einstein, 1916d]) that in each energy transfer from radiation
> to matter the momentum $h\nu/c$ is also transferred to the molecule. Hence we
> conclude that every such elementary process is a *completely directed* event. With
> that the light-quanta must be considered as good as being substantiated. (Einstein
> to Besso, 6 September 1916)

Einstein presented these conclusions at a meeting of the German Physical Society
in Berlin on 27 October 1916 (see the note in the *Verhandlungen* on p. 367, giving
the title: ‘*Zur Quantentheorie der Strahlung*’ (‘On the Quantum Theory of
Radiation’)) and in the paper submitted to the *Mitteilungen der Physikalischen
Gesellschaft Zürich* (Einstein, 1916e), which was reprinted later in the issue of 15
March 1917 of *Physikalische Zeitschrift* (Einstein, 1917a).
The considerations, in which Einstein returned to the light-quantum hypothesis,
were contained in the last section (§6) of his paper. There he calculated the
fluctuation of the momentum transfer from blackbody radiation to atoms or
molecules by an elementary mechanical method; especially, he assumed that the
momentum transfer was always associated with the process of absorption and
emission of radiation of frequency $\nu$.

If a pencil of rays hits a molecule in such a way that it gains or loses an amount of
energy $h\nu$ in the form of radiation by an elementary process (irradiation), then the
momentum $h\nu/c$ is transferred to the molecule. In the case of energy absorption the
momentum transfer has the direction of the propagation of the rays, while in case of
energy loss it has the opposite direction . . . . If a molecule suffers an energy loss of
the amount $h\nu$ without [the effect of] external action, giving this energy away in the

516 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

form of radiation (emission), then this process is also a *directed* one. During the elementary process of emission the molecule experiences a recoil of the amount $h\nu/c$ in a direction, which is determined on the basis of present theoretical understanding only by "chance". (Einstein, 1917a, p. 127)

The fact that the processes of absorption and emission of radiation thus yielded the correct expression for the fluctuation of momentum transfer, in agreement with the expression derived from Planck's law, rendered 'the formulation of a real quantum theory of radiation almost inevitable' (Einstein, 1917a, p. 127). Einstein emphasized that in such a theory one had to take into account the transfer of both energy *and* momentum between matter and radiation. One was not allowed to neglect the momentum transfer, even if it gave only a small contribution. Einstein argued:

> In the *theoretical* consideration those small effects [i.e., the momentum transfer] must be regarded as important as the *energy* transfer through radiation, since energy and momentum are most closely connected; hence a theory can be considered to be the right one only after one has shown that the momenta, transferred according to it from the radiation to matter, lead to such motions as demanded by the [kinetic] heat theory. (Einstein, 1917a, p. 128)

Since both relativity theory and kinetic theory demanded the existence of the light-quantum, Einstein noted in a letter to Besso: 'The quantum-theoretical paper, which I sent you [i.e., Einstein, 1916e], has led me back to the view that radiant energy possesses a quantum structure in space' (Einstein to Besso, 9 March 1917).
Although Einstein was convinced about the reality of light-quanta, he felt that direct evidence was lacking and he thought about experiments which might provide it. Thus, at a meeting of the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 8 December 1921, he proposed a crucial experiment devised to decide between the wave theory and the light-quantum theory of radiation (Einstein, 1921b). Einstein argued, in particular, that according to the wave theory the frequency $\nu$ of radiation, emitted by an atom moving with velocity $v$, should be shifted with the respect to $\nu_0$, the frequency of the atom at rest, by an amount $\Delta \nu$,

$$\Delta \nu = \frac{v}{c} \cos \theta, \quad (272)$$

where $\theta$ denoted the angle between the direction of motion and the direction of emission ($c$ being the velocity of light *in vacuo*). In quantum theory, however, he argued that Bohr's frequency condition, Eq. (118), must hold; hence only one frequency, $\nu_0$, would be observed, whatever the angle $\theta$ might be. In order to make use of this difference between the theoretical predictions for an experimental test, Einstein considered an experiment, in which the light emitted by canal rays moving in a direction perpendicular to the direction of observation was observed through a telescope, consisting of two lenses (an objective and an

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0150 -->

V.1  The Proof of the Light-Quantum Hypothesis  517

eyepiece) with a slit in between. Because of the finite size of the objective, the radiation emitted by a particular atom (formed by the recombination of an ion in the canal rays) would fall at different angles on its upper and lower rims. According to wave theory and Eq. (272), the radiation of different frequencies would hit the rim of the objective, and one could make this frequency difference visible by placing a dispersive material in the telescope: the position of the image of the light source would then become dependent on the frequency of the radiation; that is, the light emitted by the canal rays would appear as being deflected compared to the case in which there was no dispersive material in the telescope.$^{805}$ Einstein persuaded Hans Geiger and his associate, Walther Bothe, to perform the experiment. Its result was available just a few weeks later, and Einstein reported it to Paul Ehrenfest: ‘The radiation experiment has given a reliably negative answer. One may conclude, therefore, that the emission field [of radiation] does not have a component having simultaneously the two properties of being (a) undulatory and (b) uniform (*allseitig*)’ (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 11 January 1922). Ehrenfest, who understood the fundamental importance of the radiation problem, immediately analyzed Einstein’s theoretical arguments. He found that Einstein, in calculating the classical effect, had not taken into account the fact that radiation was always emitted as wave packets of finite size, and if one did so, then also the undulatory theory would not lead to any observable shift (see Ehrenfest to Einstein, 19 January 1922). Upon Ehrenfest’s criticism, Einstein tried to improve his derivation, but ultimately admitted that the previous conclusions had been wrong.$^{806}$ He submitted a further note at the meeting of the Prussian Academy on 2 February 1922, in which he presented the correct result based on the wave theory (Einstein, 1922b). He noted:

> Thus we have shown that, contrary to the above consideration [of Einstein, 1921b], the light produced by moving canal rays does not experience any deflection in dispersive media. This has also resulted from the experiment which was performed by Messrs Geiger and Bothe under E. Warburg’s friendly auspices at the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*. In the light of this theoretical result, deeper conclusions cannot be derived from the experiment concerning the nature of the emission process. (Einstein, 1922b, p. 22)

A little later it became evident that Einstein’s proposed crucial experiment would not be able to decide between the wave theory and the light-quantum theory due to another reason. Erwin Schrödinger, in a note entitled ‘*Dopplerprinzip und Bohrsche Frequenzbedingung*’ (‘Doppler’s Principle and Bohr’s Frequency

# Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

Condition'), obtained the result that in the light-quantum theory exactly the same Doppler effect followed for the frequency of spectral lines emitted by moving atoms as in the wave theory (Schrödinger, 1922a).<sup>807</sup> To arrive at this conclusion he considered an atomic system (i.e., an atom or a molecule) having stationary states of energy, $W_1$ and $W_2$, when at rest, and consequently the transition frequency $\nu_0 (= (W_1 - W_2)/h)$. If the system was moving with respect to the observer with the velocity $v_1$ in the initial state and $v_2$ in the final state, and if the angles between the directions of the velocities and the direction of the line joining the system and the observer were $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$, respectively, Schrödinger found that the observed frequency, corresponding to the same transition, was given by the equation

$$
\nu = \nu_0 \sqrt{ \frac{1 - (v_1/c)\cos\theta_1}{\sqrt{1 - v_1^2/c^2}} } \cdot \sqrt{ \frac{1 - (v_2/c)\cos\theta_2}{\sqrt{1 - v_2^2/c^2}} } . \tag{273}
$$

This result, which agreed with the classical formula for the Doppler effect and also with Eq. (272), was achieved only by including—besides the energy of the light-quantum—also its directed momentum.<sup>808</sup>

Schrödinger's Doppler effect calculation provided another theoretical argument in favour of the light-quantum hypothesis, for one preferred to expect—in contrast to Einstein's argumentation of December 1921—that a quantum-theoretical treatment of the radiation had also to yield the same frequency shift of the emitted spectral lines as the classical theory. Schrödinger even thought of testing Eq. (273) by measuring the observed broadening of the spectral lines. However, such a test seemed to be far off in 1922, when one did not know what the width of the lines was without the Doppler effect. Hence a more direct experimental evidence for light-quanta was needed, and this evidence came in very soon from the investigations of Arthur Holly Compton on the scattering of X-rays. In order to understand his decisive discovery, the so-called Compton effect, let us summarize the development of the work on X-ray scattering.<sup>809</sup>

X-rays, as we have mentioned before, somehow initiated the reconsideration of the corpuscular properties of radiation. Between the years 1907 and 1912 a serious debate went on among several experimentalists, including Charles Glover Barkla and William Henry Bragg, on the question of whether the phenomena of X-ray production and scattering could be accounted for by the classical electromagnetic theory or not. In the course of this debate Barkla had discovered the

homogeneous X-radiation arising from the scattering of primary radiation by matter (Barkla and Sadler, 1908a). This discovery had supported the electromagnetic wave interpretation of X-rays, even before the advent of the X-ray diffraction experiment in 1912, because the homogeneous X-radiation appeared to be a special kind of characteristic radiation emitted by atoms. In the years after 1912 the experimental and theoretical investigations of X-rays and their properties had been continued. For example, the X-ray series of atoms were studied with the help of spectrometers, such as those developed by William Henry Bragg and his son William Lawrence Bragg (Moseley, 1913; 1914a, b). Besides, homogeneous X-rays, i.e., those having a definite wavelength, were used for scattering experiments. The characteristic quantity determined from the scattering was the so-called ‘mass-absorption coefficient,’ $\mu/\rho$, i.e., the ratio of the absorption factor $\mu$ (occurring in the exponent of the expression for intensity) and the density $\rho$ of the absorbing material.$^{810}$ The result obtained with different materials could be described by a formula given by Albert Wallace Hull and Marion Rice, namely,

$$ \frac{\mu}{\rho} = \frac{\tau}{\rho} + \frac{\sigma}{\rho} = a\lambda^3 + b, $$

$\lambda$ being the wavelength of the scattered X-rays (Hull and Rice, 1916). The factor $a$ denoted a quantity depending on the material; for example $a = 14.9$ in the case of aluminum (if $\lambda$ was measured in Ångström units) and 150 in the case of copper. The factor $b$ turned out to be a constant having the value $0.12 \text{ cm}^2 \text{ g}^{-1}$. The two terms on the right-hand side of Eq. (274) represented two different absorption coefficients, the so-called ‘transformation coefficient’ or ‘mass-fluorescence coefficient’ $\tau/\rho \ (= a\lambda^3)$ and the ‘mass-scattering coefficient’ $\sigma/\rho$. According to Eq. (274) the mass-scattering coefficient was independent of the wavelength of the scattered X-rays and the material of the scatterer, in agreement with the prediction of the electromagnetic theory. Barkla and Margaret P. White studied the question in detail with several scattering substances, using very intense homogeneous X-rays having wavelengths between 0.145 Å and 0.509 Å; they confirmed that the mass-absorption coefficient did indeed decrease systematically when the wavelength became shorter (Barkla and White, 1917). Barkla and White pointed out further that in the case of aluminum their data connected smoothly with those for the still shorter-wavelength $\gamma$-rays. If this observation was confirmed, a difficulty arose with its interpretation based on classical electrodynamics because the mass-scattering coefficients, $\mu/\rho$, that had been obtained for $\gamma$-rays (e.g., Soddy and Russell, 1909; Ishino, 1917) were much smaller than the ones predicted by classical theory.

Barkla and White noted further that the mass-absorption coefficient as a function of the wavelength $\lambda$ showed for each substance a sudden discontinuity; for carbon this discontinuity occurred at $\lambda = 0.42$ Å, for oxygen at $\lambda = 0.39$ Å,

and for aluminum at $\lambda = 0.37$ Å. Barkla and White claimed that the discontinuities reflected the existence of the so-called *J*-series of the atoms, i.e., characteristic lines having wavelengths below those of the *K*-series, which Barkla had introduced in his Bakerian lecture of 1916 (Barkla, 1917). Barkla's *J*-series created great excitement and skepticism among the physicists, especially those who believed in Bohr's atomic theory. The observation of William Duane and Takeo Shimizu that *J*-radiation did not appear in the emission (Duane and Shimizu, 1919a) added to the skepticism. Further investigations of absorption yielded contradictory results. In 1922 Arthur Compton was asked to write a status report on the 'Secondary Radiations Produced by X-rays, and Some of their Applications to Physical Problems'; in this report he re-examined the evidence for and against *J*-radiation and concluded that it was 'strongly against the existence of a characteristic radiation' (Compton, 1922d, p. 36).

Compton had been associated with research on X-rays since 1913, when he became a graduate student at Princeton University. In early 1914 he had obtained Owen Willans Richardson's X-ray equipment, which he had improved, and used it to investigate the X-ray spectra of tungsten (Compton, 1916c, d) and the intensity of X-rays reflected from crystals for his doctoral thesis (Compton, 1917a, b).<sup>811</sup> Then, at the University of Minnesota, he had started a research programme with the goal of explaining the observation that the mass-scattering coefficient, $\sigma/\rho$, of X-rays dropped *below* the value of $0.188$ cm$^2$ g$^{-1}$ determined from classical electrodynamics. He investigated, in particular, various models of an extended electron, i.e., an electron having a radius of the order of $10^{-10}$ cm (Compton, 1918; 1919a, b, c).<sup>812</sup> He had continued his programme at the

<sup>811</sup> A. H. Compton was born on 10 September 1892 in Wooster, Ohio, where his father Elias Compton was professor of philosophy at the College of Wooster. He studied from 1906 to 1913 at the College of Wooster and then continued as a graduate student—like his older brother Karl Taylor Compton (1887–1954)—at Princeton University. Upon taking his doctorate from Princeton he went to the University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, as instructor (1916–1917); then he accepted the position of a research engineer in the Lamp Division of Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company in East Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (1917–1919). In fall 1919 Compton returned to an academic career: with a National Research Council Fellowship he went to Cambridge, England, and did experimental work at the Cavendish Laboratory. The following year he was appointed as professor of physics and head of the physics department at Washington University, St. Louis. In 1923 he moved to the University of Chicago, where he remained until 1945. Returning to St. Louis he served as Chancellor of Washington University (1945–1954) and as Distinguished Service Professor of Natural Philosophy (1954–1961). He died on 15 March 1962 at Berkeley.

Compton's work was primarily devoted to X-ray and cosmic ray physics. In 1941 he was appointed Chairman of the National Academy of Sciences Committee to Evaluate the Use of Atomic Energy in War. He contributed importantly to the construction of the uranium fission reactor at Chicago and the plutonium-producing reactor at Hanford, Washington. Besides many other national and international honours, Compton received the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of the Compton effect.

<sup>812</sup> According to J. J. Thomson's scattering formula, $\sigma/\rho$ assumed the value $(8\pi/3)(Ze^4/m_e^2c^2\rho) = 0.188$ cm$^2$ g$^{-1}$ in case the atomic number of the absorber, $Z$, was roughly equal to half the atomic weight. To account for the deviations from this classical formula Compton assumed first the electron to be represented by an extended charged ball, later as a charged ring. He used the ring model especially to account for the ferromagnetic properties of matter (Compton and Rognley, 1918, 1920). Both models, the extended shell and the ring model, yielded $\sigma/\rho = 0$ in the limit of X-ray wavelength $\lambda = 0$.

521

Cavendish Laboratory, Cambridge, by proceeding to still shorter wavelengths, i.e., to the scattering of $\gamma$-rays by matter (Compton, 1921a, b). In the investigations on $\gamma$-rays he had noticed that most of the secondary radiation, especially at large scattering angles, was far softer than the primary radiation; he had, therefore, assumed that this radiation was a new kind of 'fluorescent radiation,' for he did not see then any possibility by which the frequency of the primary radiation itself could be changed very much by the process of scattering. After coming to Washington University in St. Louis in fall 1920 he had turned again to the problem of X-ray scattering and had studied in detail the intensity of the secondary radiation as a function of the scattering angle and the wavelength, finding a similar, but less prominent softening effect of the primary radiation than in the experiments with $\gamma$-rays. Besides X-ray scattering, Compton then also studied the properties of discrete X-ray spectra (Compton, 1921e, 1922a). Without any doubt, Arthur Compton could be considered in the early 1920s as one of the leading American experts in the field of X-rays physics, especially X-ray scattering. His reputation increased further because of a new, fine experimental work: in spring 1922 he showed the existence of total reflection of X-rays from glass and silvered surfaces and thus determined directly their index of refraction (Compton, 1922c). He was invited at that time to join the committee on the status of X-ray research of the Division of Physical Sciences of the National Research Council, consisting of William Duane (Harvard University), Bergen Davis (Columbia University), Albert W. Hull (General Electric Research Laboratory) and David Locke Webster (Stanford University), and he became engaged in preparing the report on X-ray scattering and secondary radiation.

Compton worked on his report during the summer of 1922, which he spent—like the previous year—as a visiting lecturer at the University of California at Berkeley. One of the first insights he obtained from the detailed analysis of the scattering data was that no model of the electron—including his extended electrons—seemed to fit both the X-ray and $\gamma$-ray observations. He made another observation when discussing the secondary $\beta$-spectrum, i.e., the electrons emitted from matter bombarded by X- or $\gamma$-radiation. The properties of this spectrum, especially the forward-backward asymmetry of the electron emission and the number of electrons and their velocities, suggested the existence of two types of photoelectrons: the first type was characterized by subsequent emission of fluorescent radiation, while the second type of electrons recoiled after scattering a quantum of energy, $h\nu$, of radiation of frequency $\nu$. Compton concluded: 'The evidence is thus consistent with the view that each photoelectron represents the removal of one quantum of energy from the primary beam, and that no other energy [of the radiation] is lost except perhaps through true scattering' (Compton, 1922d, p. 29).

Compton devoted a major part of the report to the subject of fluorescent secondary radiation. On one hand, he found that Barkla's characteristic $J$-series did not exist; on the other, he again emphasized the existence of his own 'fluorescent radiation,' which he had detected in his X- and $\gamma$-ray scattering investigations. In particular, he stated: 'Recent spectroscopic measurements by

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0155 -->

522 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

the writer show that the secondary rays have suffered a distinct change in wavelength ... According to the writer's absorption measurements [Compton, 1922b], over the range of primary rays from 0.7 to 0.025 [Å], the wavelength of the secondary X-rays at 90° with the incident beam is roughly 0.03 [Å] greater than that of the primary ray which excites it' (Compton, 1922d, pp. 16–17). Since this change in the wavelength of the primary radiation could not be explained by a Doppler effect of the scattering particles—in that case the electrons in the scattering material would have to move with velocities of the order of *c*, the velocity of light *in vacuo*—Compton concluded that either the scattered radiation was really fluorescent radiation, as he had assumed before, or that a new quantum hypothesis had to be made. He formulated the new hypothesis as follows:

> Let us suppose that each electron when it scatters X-rays receives a whole quantum of energy and reradiates the whole quantum in a definite direction. The momentum which the scattering electron receives from the radiation will then be $h\nu/c$ ... This will result in a velocity in the forward direction which will produce a Doppler effect as the scattered rays are observed at different directions. In addition, as the electron radiates a quantum of energy toward the observer, the conservation of momentum principle demands that the electron shall recoil with a momentum $h\nu'/c$, where $\nu'$ is the average frequency of the scattered radiation. For cases in which the resulting velocity of the electron is small compared with the speed of the light, it can be shown on this basis that the ratio of the average frequency of the rays scattered at 90° to that of the incident rays should be $1 - h/mc\lambda$. (Compton, 1922d, p. 18)

Since this expression accounted, for instance, quantitatively for the observed frequency change of the $K_{\alpha}$-line of molybdenum, Compton concluded: 'This close numerical agreement would suggest that we should consider scattering [of X-rays] as a quantum phenomenon instead of obeying the classical laws of electricity' (Compton, 1922d, pp. 18–19).

In the light of Compton's previous attitude the new hypothesis concerning the scattering of X-rays appeared to be very surprising. It meant that Compton was prepared to give up his conviction that secondary radiation, whenever it possessed a wavelength very different from that of the primary radiation (such that it could not be explained by the Doppler effect), had to be considered as fluorescent radiation. Instead he now proposed to use a quantum-theoretical description of radiation, in contrast to all earlier attempts to account for X-ray scattering on the basis of classical electrodynamics. This change of attitude also came rather suddenly, for Compton had not adhered thus far to quantum-theoretical considerations. For example, in his early papers on the specific heat of solids and related phenomena (Compton, 1915; 1916a, b), he had tried to replace the quantum hypothesis by Carl Benedicks' hypothesis of the agglomeration of atoms and molecules (Benedicks, 1913). Later, in the investigations of X-ray scattering and absorption he had tried to rescue classical electrodynamics at the expense of introducing the model of the extended electron. Only towards the end of the year 1921 had he thought of applying a quantum-theoretical

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0156 -->

V.1  The Proof of the Light-Quantum Hypothesis                                                                                              523

argument in order to explain the wavelength of secondary radiation obtained by scattering the $K_{\alpha}$-line of molybdenum by celluloid or aluminum at a scattering angle of 90°. He had remarked then:

> If we suppose that the incident X-ray beam ejects electrons moving forward [in the direction of the primary radiation] with a kinetic energy of $hc/\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the exciting ray, and if the ejected electron is oscillating at such a frequency that as observed in the direction of motion the wavelength is $\lambda$, on account of the Doppler effect the wavelength of the radiation at right angles with the primary beam will be very close to that of the fluorescent rays observed in these experiments. (Compton, 1922b, p. 268)

This argument, however, did not imply the use of the light-quantum hypothesis; it was rather based on the assumption that the electrons of the scatterer absorb from the primary radiation of frequency $\nu$ an energy quantum $h\nu$, and after this process emit secondary ‘fluorescent radiation.’ In the National Research Council report of October 1922 Compton picked up this argument and applied it also to the scattering of $\gamma$-rays. He now presented a detailed mechanism for the origin of secondary radiation, consisting of the following sequence of processes: first, an electron of the scattering atom absorbs from the primary radiation of frequency $\nu$ the energy $h\nu$ and obtains a momentum $h\nu/c$ in the direction of the incident radiation; second, the electron emits secondary radiation of the same frequency $\nu$; third, the secondary radiation, if viewed at an angle of 90°, possesses a frequency $\nu'$ due to the Doppler effect, given by the equation

$$\nu' = \nu\left(1 - \frac{v}{c}\right), \tag{275}$$

where $v (= h\nu / m_e c)$ is the velocity of the electron.$^{813}$

The above considerations on the role played by the Doppler effect in accounting for the frequency of secondary radiation encouraged Compton to replace the known expression for the mass-absorption coefficient, Eq. (274), by a more general one,

$$\frac{\mu}{\rho} = \frac{\sigma}{\rho} + \frac{\tau}{\rho} + \frac{\omega}{\rho} . \tag{276}$$

That is, he added a term, which he called the ‘momentum-absorption coefficient,’ in order to account for the momentum transfer from the primary radiation to the electrons of the scattering atoms. For the mass-scattering coefficient, $\sigma/\rho$, Compton had developed an explanation on the basis of classical electrodynamics by assuming a model of the extended electron. The fluorescent-scattering coefficient, $\tau/\rho$, could be explained in two different ways: either by assuming that

By putting $\theta_1 = 90^\circ$ and $\theta_2 = 0^\circ$ he found Eq. (275).

# Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

there existed slightly damped electronic oscillators in scattering atoms, having frequencies between the critical absorption frequency and infinity; or by employing quantum theory, especially Bohr's frequency condition. The first of these assumptions was used by Compton, while Louis de Broglie employed the second one to obtain a result in agreement with Compton's (L. de Broglie, 1921b).⁸¹⁴
Compton now proposed two alternative explanations, a classical and a quantum-theoretical one, also for the momentum-absorption coefficient, $\omega/\rho$, namely:

1. We may think of this energy [i.e., the energy of the absorbed radiation due to the term $\omega/\rho$ in the mass-absorption coefficient, $\mu/\rho$, Eq. (276)] as spent in exciting a form of general fluorescent radiation through the medium of secondary $\beta$-rays.
2. Or we may propose, on the quantum idea of scattering, that when an electron receives a quantum of $\gamma$-energy, the momentum of the quantum gives to the scattering electron a considerable momentum, so that the scattered energy is equal to the energy absorbed less the kinetic energy of recoil of the scattering electron. (Compton, 1922d, p. 45)

The two different possibilities to account for the absorption of X-rays in matter stimulated Compton to raise, in the final section of his report, the question about the nature of radiation. He noted that there were available two theories of radiation, the classical electromagnetic wave theory and the ‘quantum conception’ of radiation. Although the latter seemed to account for many features, Compton pointed out its main difficulty: the hypothesis that radiation occurred in entire multiples of energy-quanta $h\nu$, each having a directed momentum, did not represent properly the observed coherence and interference phenomena of X-rays; only the scattering processes yielding secondary radiation of larger wavelength demanded a quantum-theoretical interpretation. Such an interpretation, however, did not necessarily imply quanta of radiation; any reversible mechanism, through which the energy-quanta may be exchanged between radiation and the kinetic energy of the electrons, would explain the observations just as well. Compton concluded: ‘*There is no reason to question the application of the classical electrodynamics to the problem of scattering*’ (Compton, 1922d, p. 55).
The problem of the proper theoretical interpretation of the increase of wavelength of X-rays in the process of scattering continued to bother Compton, and he recalled later:

> I found at once that the change of wavelength that I observed for scattering at 90° was what should be expected if the scattering electrons were moving in the direction of the primary beam at about half the speed of light, which would mean that each electron had a momentum equal to that of a quantum of energy of the frequency of the primary X-rays. It was obvious, however, that not all the electrons in the

will be reduced in the same ratio as is the energy. Thus on the quantum theory we should expect the wavelength of the scattered X-rays to be greater than that of the incident rays. (Compton, 1923b, p. 485)

With the transfer of momentum from the radiation to the electron Compton could immediately explain the fact that the intensity of the radiation scattered in the forward direction was greater than that in the backward direction. For the frequency $\nu_{\theta}$ of the quantum of radiation scattered by the electron (of mass $m_e$) into an angle $\theta$ (with respect to the original direction) he then derived the equation

$$
\nu_{\theta} = \nu_0 \left(1 + 2\alpha \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}\right)^{-1}, \tag{277}
$$

with

$$
\alpha = \frac{h \nu_0}{m_e c^2}, \tag{277a}
$$

where $\nu_0$ denoted the frequency of the primary radiation. Equation (277) could also be written as an equation for the wavelength $\lambda$, i.e.,

$$
\lambda_{\theta} - \lambda_0 = \frac{h}{m_e c} (1 - \cos\theta), \tag{277'}
$$

which stated that the increase of wavelength did not depend on the wavelength $\lambda_0$ of the incident radiation. Due to the scattering process the electron received a recoil momentum $p_e$, where

$$
p_e = \frac{m_e \beta c}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}}, \tag{278}
$$

with

$$
\beta = \frac{v}{c} = 2\alpha \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{1 + (2\alpha + \alpha^2)\sin^2(\theta/2)}}{1 + 2(\alpha + \alpha^2)\sin^2(\theta/2)}. \tag{278a}
$$

Compton further calculated the angular distribution of the scattering intensity $I_{\theta}$, obtaining the result

$$
I_{\theta} = \frac{I_0 N e^4}{R^2 m_e^2 c^4} \frac{1 + \cos^2\theta + 2\alpha(1 + \alpha)(1 - \cos\theta)^2}{2\left[1 + \alpha(1 - \cos\theta)\right]^5}, \tag{279}
$$

with $I_0$ denoting the intensity of the incident radiation, $R$ the distance from

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0160 -->

(279), yielded an absorption coefficient for X-rays, which was smaller than the one derived from the classical theory by a factor $(1 + 2\alpha)^{-1}$. By checking all available data on X- and $\gamma$-ray scattering against his new theory Compton found a remarkable agreement, which left ‘but little doubt that the scattering of X-rays is a quantum phenomenon.’ Com

ing the matter in detail. Especially, a symposium on ‘The Reflection and Scattering of X-rays’ was arranged on the afternoon of 28 December, with Compton, Duane and Bergen Davis (of Columbia University) as speakers. As Compton recalled: ‘Having frequently repeated the experiments I entered the debate with confidence. But I was nevertheless pleased to find that I had support from P. A. Ross of Stanford and M. de Broglie of Paris, who had obtained photographic spectra showing results similar to my own’ (Compton, 1961, p. 818).$^{817}$ The debate led to Duane visiting Compton, who had meanwhile moved to Chicago, and examining his apparatus and inviting Compton to come to Harvard University to do the same. Compton noted: ‘The result was that neither of us could find the reason for the difference in the results of the two laboratories, but it turned out that the equipment I was using was more sensitive and better adapted than was Duane’s to a study of the phenomenon in question’ (Compton, 1961, p. 818).$^{818}$ The debate continued during the following year, ending only in December 1924, when Duane, together with his associate Samuel K. Allison, also obtained the Compton effect (Allison and Duane, 1925a, b). By that time the effect had been generally accepted by the physicists, especially because of certain theoretical considerations.

Before the publication of Compton’s paper in *Physical Review* (Compton, 1923b), there appeared an article by Peter Debye, entitled ‘*Zerstreuung von Röntgenstrahlen und Quantentheorie*’ (‘Scattering of X-rays and Quantum Theory’), in the issue of 15 April 1923 of *Physikalische Zeitschrift* (Debye, 1923). In it Debye, one of the leading experts in X-ray physics, discussed the question of the scattering of short-wavelength radiation by matter, especially the deviation of the observations from the predictions of the classical theory.$^{819}$ He emphasized four points: first, the fact that more secondary radiation appeared in the forward direction ($\theta = 0^\circ$) than in backward direction ($\theta = 180^\circ$); second, the forward radiation possessed shorter wavelength than the backward radiation; third, the total energy of the scattered radiation was smaller than the value obtained from the classical theory for mass scattering (i.e., the scattering with the coefficient $\sigma$); fourth, together with the scattered X-rays there appeared electrons at angles, which were smaller, the shorter the wavelength of the incident radiation. Debye noted that these four empirical facts could also be concluded from Arthur Compton’s National Research Council report, and remarked: ‘Therefore, I do

not wish to delay in presenting for discussion an explanation of the phenomena with the help of quantum theory, which occurred to me quite some time ago' (Debye, 1923, p. 162). This interpretation was based on the assumption that 'the classical electrodynamics also fails in the calculation of the radiation scattered by a free electron, which is subjected to the stimulus of primary radiation, and one must replace it by a quantum explanation' (Debye, 1923, p. 162). He then proposed to use the picture of an elementary process between a single free electron and 'needle radiation in the sense of Einstein,' obeying the laws of energy and momentum conservation. Thus he derived the same results as Compton, namely, Eqs. (277) and (278). From Eq. (277) he concluded, for instance, that with primary radiation of 0.708 Å the radiation scattered at an angle of $\theta = 90^\circ$ possessed a wavelength which was larger by about 33%, in agreement with Compton's observation on the scattering of the $K_\alpha$-line of molybdenum (Compton, 1922b). Debye further showed that the ratio of the energy of the scattered radiation according to his quantum theory of scattering over the energy determined on the classical theory might be written as a function $f(x)$, where $x = \lambda/\Lambda$ (where $\lambda$ denotes the wavelength of the incident radiation and $\Lambda = h/m_e c = 0.0243$ Å). The function $f(x)$ became 1 in the limit of very large $\lambda$, while for small values of $\lambda$ it was given by the expansion

$$f(x) = \frac{3}{2} x \left( \ln \frac{1}{x} - \frac{3}{4} + \cdots \right), \quad (280)$$

that is, it approached the value zero for infinite frequency of the primary radiation, as demanded by the $\gamma$-ray experiments.

In his paper, Debye did not suggest that the proposed quantum theory was necessarily the true theory of X-ray scattering. In his opinion it just represented an attempt to understand in detail the consequences for the description of the phenomena considered, 'by means of the sole utilization of the most general laws: "energy" and "momentum conservation"' (Debye, 1923, p. 166). In any case, it seemed to him worthwhile to test the new theory thoroughly by detailed experiments. He did not know that such tests were already on the way and that Arthur Compton was ahead of him in the solution of that problem.$^{820}$

During the winter semester 1922–1923 Arnold Sommerfeld lectured as Carl Schurz Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin, and there he came to know about Compton's results very soon. Already on 21 January 1923 he wrote to Niels Bohr: 'The most interesting scientific news I have learned in America is a work of Arthur Compton in St. Louis. According to it the wave theory of X-rays would finally have to be given up.' Sommerfeld added that, although he was himself not yet certain about the correctness of Compton's conclusion, he

Debye later acknowledged this fact without reservation and remarked that the effect should bear Compton's name only. (See Debye, AHQP Interview, 5 March 1962, p. 12.)

would like to draw Bohr's attention to the possibility that 'in this respect we may perhaps expect a very fundamental correction' (Sommerfeld to Bohr, 21 January 1923). At the time he wrote the letter to Bohr, Sommerfeld travelled from Wisconsin to California to give lectures at Pasadena, Berkeley, and other places. Wherever he went, he referred to Compton's work and its importance for the quantum theory. In this way P. A. Ross of Stanford University also became interested in the problem and began to work on it, confirming eventually the effect observed by Compton (Ross, 1923a, 1924). Sommerfeld also enthusiastically advocated Compton's results after his return to Germany. Several months later he reported to Compton: 'Your discovery of the change in wavelength of X-rays also occupies the scientific community in Germany most deeply. I met Einstein and Kossel in August, and we mainly discussed your effect' (Sommerfeld to Compton, 9 October 1923). Sommerfeld mentioned that the Compton effect had similarly attracted attention at the recent Bonn meeting of the German Physical Society.⁸²¹ And he remarked: 'In my book, on the fourth edition of which I am working, I have also introduced a section in the first chapter, entitled "Über die Quantenstruktur des Lichtes" [On the Quantum Structure of Light], and I have discussed "Doppler Effect and Compton Effect" in it' (Sommerfeld to Compton, 9 October 1923).

The news of the discovery of Compton effect also reached Hamburg. As Rudolph Minkowski recalled: 'Sommerfeld came back from a trip to the United States and told the story. That, of course, was a very exciting thing' (Minkowski, AHQP Interview, p. 15). In summer 1923 Wolfgang Pauli came to Hamburg, having taken several weeks' leave of absence from Copenhagen. In a letter to Niels Bohr, dated 16 July, he reported about a new work: 'In Hamburg I have basically finished some calculations on the thermal equilibrium between radiation and free electrons. I enjoyed [working on] this problem very much, and I would like to discuss with you a bit about the fundamental questions connected with it before publishing my considerations.' The questions, which Pauli wanted to discuss with Bohr, were indeed the fundamental ones in quantum theory. Already many years earlier Hendrik Lorentz, for example, had treated the problem of the equilibrium between temperature radiation and electrons having a Maxwellian velocity distribution at the first Solvay Conference: in his calculation he had not been able to establish the condition of thermal equilibrium (see Lorentz' report in Langevin and de Broglie, 1912). The recent investigations of Compton and Debye employing directed light-quanta stimulated Pauli to attack the problem again with the following assumption: free electrons and radiation interact with each other by means of reversible collisions between electrons and light-quanta, obeying the laws of conservation of energy and momentum. On 9 August 1923 the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Pauli's paper containing the proof of thermal equilibrium between electrons having a Maxwellian distribution and

V.1 The Proof of the Light-Quantum Hypothesis 531

radiation obeying Planck’s law (Pauli, 1923b). In order to obtain the desired result, however, Pauli had to make a special *Ansatz* for the quantity $F$ determining the probability of collisions per unit time, namely,

$$F = A\rho_{\nu} + B\rho_{\nu}\rho_{\nu'}, \tag{281}$$

where $\rho_{\nu}$ and $\rho_{\nu'}$ denoted the intensities of the radiation with frequencies $\nu$ and $\nu'$, i.e, the frequencies before and after the collision process, respectively, and $A$ and $B$ were the coefficients of Einstein’s radiation theory (Einstein, 1916d).$^{822}$ Pauli showed that in case the radiation satisfied Wien’s law, only the first term contributed to the probability $F$ (because one could then neglect the $\rho_{\nu}\rho_{\nu'}$-term in comparison with the $\rho_{\nu}$-term); for long wavelengths, however, i.e., in the limit of the Rayleigh–Jeans law, the second term became important, and Pauli interpreted it as being due to the interference fluctuations of classical waves. Pauli’s results stimulated Albert Einstein and Paul Ehrenfest, who learned about his work prior to publication. They succeeded in clarifying and generalizing Pauli’s treatment and submitted a note on ‘Zur Quantentheorie des Strahlungsgleichgewichts’ (‘On the Quantum Theory of Radiation Equilibrium’) in October 1923 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1923). In particular, Einstein and Ehrenfest discussed the ‘paradoxical’ second term in Eq. (281), ‘which implies that the number of the elementary processes of scattering occurring per unit time at an electron (which is at quasi rest) increases faster than being proportional to the radiation density $\rho'$ of frequency $\nu'$, which the radiation quantum possesses after being modified by the elementary process’ (Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1923, p. 301). This term, they concluded, followed immediately from a detailed consideration of all interaction processes between radiation and electrons, including the induced emission of light-quanta. Further, they generalized Pauli’s expression for $F$, Eq. (281), to cases in which the elementary processes (i.e., the collisions between electrons and light-quanta) involved more than two quanta of radiation (i.e., more than one incident and one scattered light-quantum).

The work of Compton and Debye also stimulated a different kind of theoretical investigation. Adolf Smekal of the University of Vienna found that the use of elementary processes between light-quanta and the electrons in atoms enabled him to derive an interesting result in the quantum theory of dispersion. In a note, submitted in September 1923 to *Naturwissenschaften*, he discussed a ‘new kind of quantum transitions’ occurring ‘under the influence of monochromatic radiation,’ which he called ‘translational quantum transitions’ (‘*Translationsquantenübergänge*’) and described as follows:

For each atom or molecule—which is in its *m*th quantum state with energy $E_m$ and possesses a translational velocity $v$, whose direction makes an arbitrary angle with the direction of the incident light—there exists a probability, $C_{m,\nu}^{n,\nu'}$, that it passes in

***

532 | Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

a unit of time—under the influence of radiation of a given frequency—from the *mth* into the *nth* quantum state, changes the direction and absolute value of its translational velocity (into $v'$), and emits simultaneously secondary radiation of frequency $\nu'$. (Smekal, 1923c. p. 874)

By requiring energy conservation he obtained a relation for $\nu'$, the frequency of the scattered radiation, that is,

$$\frac{Mv^2}{2} + E_m + h\nu = \frac{Mv'^2}{2} + E_n + h\nu', \tag{282}$$

where $M$ is the mass of the atom or molecule. Evidently, $\nu'$ could be either smaller or larger than $\nu$, depending on the other energy terms. In case the translational energy of the atom could be neglected, the same situation still occurred: especially, the frequency of the incident radiation would then be changed by $\nu_{mn}$ corresponding to a transition between two stationary states $(\nu_{mn} = (E_m - E_n)/h$, and $E_m \gtrless E_n)$. Five years later such scattering of radiation would be shown to exist experimentally (Raman, 1928). For the moment, however, Smekal’s calculation just provided an illuminating example of the fact that the Compton effect was taken rather seriously by the quantum physicists, and it helped them to consider a quantum theory of radiation. However, Compton’s discovery also caused difficulties: in particular, Niels Bohr became the spokesman of those who saw in the light-quantum interpretation of the Compton effect one of the greatest dangers for the future quantum theory. We shall discuss next Bohr’s reasons for that opinion and his attempt to interpret the Compton effect in a different way.

### V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation

Since the formulation of his quantum theory of atomic constitution in 1913, Bohr knew very clearly that the laws of classical electrodynamics could not be satisfied in two respects: first, the electrons in stationary states did not radiate; and, second, the frequency emitted by atoms had to be calculated according to the quantum-theoretical relation (118), ‘in obvious contrast to the ordinary ideas of electrodynamics’ (Bohr, 1913b, p. 7). Bohr was not the first to recognize the fact that for the proper description of quantum phenomena the laws of electrodynamics had to be abandoned: Albert Einstein and Hendrik Lorentz had pointed out, in connection with the derivation of Planck’s law of blackbody radiation, that the electrodynamics theory of radiation seemed to contradict any quantum hypothesis employed. In order to improve upon this situation, Einstein proposed in 1916 to re-establish the ‘uniformity of the theory’ by replacing ‘the electromagnetic–mechanical considerations’ in the derivation of Planck’s law ‘by quantum-theoretical considerations concerning the interaction of matter and radiation’ (Einstein, 1916d, pp. 318–319). He showed that the blackbody radiation law

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0166 -->

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 533

could indeed be obtained by considering a thermodynamic equilibrium between radiation and atoms, the latter having stationary states and obeying Bohr’s frequency condition, provided he made the following assumption: in the limit of infinitely increasing temperature the radiation density also becomes infinite, in agreement with the result on the classical theory. The detailed discussion of the processes establishing the equilibrium then led him to conclude that atoms seemed to interact with radiation (of frequency $\nu$) as if single atoms collided with light-quanta of energy $h\nu$ and directed momentum $h\nu/c$ (Einstein, 1916e). In spite of the success of the light-quantum hypothesis, however, Einstein was not completely satisfied and, at the end of his treatment, he remarked: ‘The weakness of the theory lies, on one hand, in the fact that it does not bring us closer to a connection with the undulatory theory, and, on the other hand, in the fact that it leaves the instant and direction of the elementary processes to “chance”’ (Einstein, 1916e, p. 61).

In the same year, 1916, Einstein’s equation for the photoelectric effect, Eq. (60), was finally completely verified through the experiments of Robert Andrews Millikan (Millikan, 1916a, b, c). Nevertheless people continued, as we have mentioned, to have doubts about the light-quantum hypothesis, from which the photoelectric equation had been derived, especially because one could not imagine that this hypothesis could provide a reasonable description of the interference phenomena observed with all kinds of radiation. Bohr also believed in the wave theory of radiation and continued to be acutely aware of the difficulties when combining the electromagnetic description of radiation with the theory of atomic structure. Thus, for instance, he remarked in his 1918 memoir on the quantum theory of line spectra: ‘We must assume that *the ordinary laws of electrodynamics cannot be applied* . . . without radical alterations’ (Bohr, 1918a, p. 6). However, he claimed at the same time that in the problem of calculating the stationary states of atoms the forces connected with the emission and absorption of radiation might be neglected against the Coulomb forces between the electrons and the nucleus: ‘Even if the theory of radiation must be completely altered, it is therefore a natural assumption that it is possible in such cases to obtain a close approximation in the description of motion of stationary states, by retaining only the latter forces’ (Bohr, 1918a, p. 6). Further he dealt in his memoir with certain specific problems of atomic radiation, notably the question of the intensity of spectral lines emitted by an atom by referring to the corresponding classical system. The establishment of such an analogy depended crucially on having a similar, or essentially the same, description of radiation both in quantum theory and the classical limit. Since there did not seem to be any smooth transition between the light-quantum theory and the electromagnetic theory, Bohr found it necessary to avoid any use of the former. This conservative attitude in radiation theory was reflected in particular by his treatment of the so-called selection rules and the polarization rules of atomic spectra.

In the 1918 memoir cited above, Bohr showed that the observed absence of transition lines between certain states of a given atom followed directly by

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0167 -->

534 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

applying the analogy argument, or correspondence principle, as he would call it later. Simultaneously and independently, Adalbert Rubinowicz arrived at a different derivation of the selection rules, based on ‘the fact that the laws of conservation of energy and angular momentum are satisfied for the system “atom + ether”’ (Rubinowicz, 1918a, p. 442). His derivation thus implied the assumption that the radiation emitted or absorbed by atoms possessed an angular momentum and that in the interactions between radiation and electrons the total angular momentum of radiation plus orbiting electrons always remained a constant quantity. With this assumption he succeeded not only in deriving the selection rules for allowed transitions between the stationary states of atoms (and molecules), but also to some extent the polarization of the emitted spectral line components, for example, in the case of Zeeman and Stark effects (Rubinowicz, 1918a, b). In a later paper, entitled ‘Zur Polarisation der Bohrschen Strahlung’ (‘On the Polarization of the Bohr Radiation’) and submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in January 1921, Rubinowicz completed the discussion of the polarization question by showing that the radiation emitted in transitions characterized by a constant azimuthal quantum number was always linearly polarized. For that purpose he treated the radiation formally like a mechanical system, whose energy might be quantized according to the rules of multiply periodic systems (Rubinowicz, 1921).$^{823}$

Bohr did not like Rubinowicz’ approach to the selection rules, nor his treatment of the polarization problem. He raised ‘fundamental objections’ in a paper, entitled ‘Zur Frage der Polarisation der Strahlung in der Quantentheorie’ (‘On the Problem of Polarization of Radiation in Quantum Theory’), which he submitted in June 1921 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Bohr, 1921b). Bohr again explained in detail the difficulties of the radiation problem in atomic theory, which consisted mainly in the fact that in atoms the emitted radiation was not connected—as in classical electrodynamics—with the motion of the electrons, but determined instead by the quantum-theoretical frequency condition. These difficulties had occurred already in the derivation of Planck’s law, for which there existed two essentially different ways, one proposed by Einstein (1916d) and the other by Peter Debye (1910), respectively. In Bohr’s opinion, Einstein’s derivation consisted in the general considerations concerning the probabilities of the emission and absorption processes of radiation by atoms and their balance with the heat radiation surrounding the atoms; the relations thus obtained passed over, in the appropriate limit, into the analogous classical ones and thus satisfied the correspondence principle. In Debye’s derivation, however, cavity radiation was represented by a superposition of standing waves, to which the same quantization rules had been applied as to a mechanical system of charged particles. The extension of this treatment to atomic theory, Bohr pointed out, ‘has also led to a conception of the radiation process that is of significance for the formal development of quantum theory, a conception according to which not the

***

V.2  The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation                                  535

atomic system alone is regarded as subject to quantization; rather, the atom together with the radiation in the surrounding cavity is considered as an entirety subject to “quantization” (Bohr, 1921b, p. 4). He continued:

> However, in order to agree with observations, it is necessary to assume that the coupling between the parts of the total system cannot be described by the conceptions of classical dynamics but is governed by laws which ensure that, in any exchange of energy between the atom and the radiation field, both will be in stationary states, before as well as after the process, an assumption which is quite analogous to the laws holding, according to the quantum theory, for collisions between atomic systems. (Bohr, 1921b, p. 4)

By the last remark Bohr meant that many empirical facts, such as the polarization rules for the radiation emitted by atoms, seemed to imply (for example, in the derivation of Rubinowicz, 1921) the use of the light-quantum hypothesis in its most extreme version: that is, one had to assume a special coupling of atoms and the radiation field, in which the collisions between electrons and quanta of radiation played a fundamental role.
Bohr evidently did not favour the light-quantum hypothesis, for it seemed to ruin his plans to build atomic theory on the basis of the correspondence principle. Thus, in his lecture on 27 April 1920 at the German Physical Society in Berlin, he remarked:

> I shall not here discuss the familiar difficulties to which the “hypothesis of light-quanta” leads in connection with the phenomena of interference, for the explanation of which the classical theory of radiation has shown itself to be so remarkably suited. Above all, I shall not consider the problem of the nature of radiation. I shall only attempt to show how it has been possible in a purely formal manner to develop a spectral theory, the essential elements of which may be considered as a simultaneous rational development of the two ways of interpreting Planck’s result [i.e., the law of blackbody radiation]. (Bohr, 1920, pp. 425–426; *Collected Works* 3, 1976, p. 244)

While Bohr avoided entering into the problem of radiation theory as much as possible in his talk, he took the opportunity of discussing it privately with Albert Einstein on that occasion. Einstein at that time was thinking again about the consequences of the quantum-theoretical absorption and emission process. Thus, a few months before Bohr’s visit to Berlin, he had written to Born:

> That business about causality causes me a lot of trouble, too. Can the quantum absorption and emission of light ever be understood in the sense of the complete causality requirement or would a statistical residue remain? I must admit that here I lack the courage of my convictions. But I would be very unhappy to renounce *complete* causality. (Einstein to Born, 27 January 1920)

Evidently Einstein, like Bohr, struggled with the problems of quantum-theoretical radiation. He even believed that the problem was more serious and difficult and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0169 -->

536 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

could not be overcome completely by methods such as the ones offered by the analogy or the correspondence principle. Still, it was good for Bohr to talk about his ideas and worries with Einstein. Several weeks later he thanked Einstein for the conversations. He wrote: ‘You don’t know how stimulating it was for me to have the opportunity, which I had hoped for since long, to hear personally your opinion about the problems I have been dealing with. I shall never forget our conversations on the way from Dahlem to your house, and I hope very much that when you visit us here there will be an opportunity to continue these conversations’ (Bohr to Einstein, 24 June 1920). However, Einstein’s visit to Copenhagen, which was planned and to which Bohr looked forward for continuing his discussions on the problems of quantum theory, did not take place. Both of them were invited to participate in the third Solvay Conference in Brussels in April 1921, but both were prevented from attending it and meeting again. Therefore, Bohr and Einstein were not able to exchange their views further for several years to come.824

Although Bohr was prevented by ill health from attending the Solvay Conference in 1921, he submitted a report ‘On the Application of the Quantum Theory to Atomic Problems,’ which was read by Paul Ehrenfest and published in the proceedings of the Conference (Bohr, 1923e). In this report he devoted a full section, §3, to ‘The Radiation Problem in Quantum Theory,’ which he began by stating:

> When now from the problem of principles underlying the description and fixation of the stationary states we turn again our attention to the *radiation process*, we see that the fundamental postulates of the quantum theory not only . . . involve that the process of emission and absorption of radiation cannot be described in detail on the basis of the classical theory of electrodynamics, but that the claim as to the constitution of radiation accompanying the process even excludes any immediate connection between the motion of the particles in the atom and the radiation, analogous to that exhibited by the emission of periodical disturbances in an elastic medium from a vibrating mechanical system. (Bohr, 1923e; English translation in *Collected Works* 3, 1976, pp. 372–373)

That is, instead of having the well-known connection between radiation and the motion of charged particles due to classical electrodynamics, one had to assume the processes of emission and absorption as governed by a foreign, if not incompatible law, which seemed to have no relation whatsoever to the dynamics of the system. The light-quantum hypothesis, which implied an ‘unrestricted

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 537

application of the notion of conservation of energy and momentum,’ Bohr remarked, did allow one to describe the atomic radiation, but it failed to account for any interference phenomenon. Hence he concluded:

> At present we do not possess any detailed picture of the mechanism of emission and absorption of electromagnetic radiation by atoms and the propagation of radiation through space. We shall see, however, how it is possible to trace a connection between the motion of an atomic system and the spectrum which, even if it must be essentially different from that which would follow from the classical electromagnetic theory, still preserves such features that it gives us hope of attaining a picture which includes the interpretation of the experimental evidence regarding atomic processes as well as the phenomena of interference of light waves, although the mechanism underlying this picture probably will involve radical departure from fundamental notions on which the foundation of physical theories have hitherto been sought. (Bohr, 1923e; *Collected Works 3*, 1976, pp. 374–375)

Concerning the nature of the ‘radical departure from fundamental notions,’ contemplated by Bohr, Ehrenfest—after visiting Copenhagen in late December 1921—wrote to Einstein: ‘If I am able to reproduce here his [Bohr's] opinion on these matters correctly, I might formulate it this way. He is much more willing to give up energy and momentum theorems (in their classical form) for elementary atomic processes, and to maintain them only statistically, than to “lay the blame on the aether”’ (Ehrenfest to Einstein, 17 January 1922; quoted after M. J. Klein, 1970a, p. 19).
The thought of resolving the difficulties of radiation theory in atomic physics by relaxing the laws of conservation of energy and momentum seemed to be a rather desperate step. After all, the physicists had learned in the past century to believe in the absolute validity of the conservation principles. Not only had a large number of phenomena found their explanation by assuming, especially, the fact that no energy can be created or lost in a process, but the existence of the conservation laws had been connected with fundamental symmetry properties of the physical space, which one was not willing to sacrifice easily. It was difficult to imagine that these well-established physical laws might break down, even on the atomic scale, because even the kinetic theory of gases had been built on the strict validity of energy and momentum conservation. On the other hand, nobody had been able to test the conservation laws directly on the atomic level. Thus the Viennese physicist Franz Exner, in a book on the foundations of science, could claim without running into contradiction with experiment that the known physical laws held only for the average state of many atoms, while for single atoms the laws of probability were valid (Exner, 1919, §93).<sup>825</sup>
The statistical assumptions seemed to play a role, as Einstein showed in 1916, in the description of blackbody radiation (Einstein, 1916d, e). While Einstein tried to minimize their influence, Bohr emphasized just these statistical features

538

in Einstein’s theory in order to establish a connection between atomic radiation and the undulatory waves known from classical electrodynamics (Bohr, 1918a). A little later Charles Galton Darwin reflected about the difficulties of quantum theory in general and suggested in an unpublished paper ‘that the most promis‑ing outlook for the reconciliation of our difficulties is to suppose that energy is not exactly conserved.’ He added: ‘Now, no one can doubt that energy is approximately conserved, but ordinary dynamical and electrical experiments only establish it statistically, and so really only put it on the same footing as the second law of thermodynamics.’ (See Jammer, 1966, p. 172.) At the same time he wrote to Niels Bohr that he considered ‘the case against conservation quite overwhelming’ (Darwin to Bohr, 20 July 1919). Bohr did not answer Darwin immediately, because his views on the problem were not yet quite settled.⁸²⁶ However, more than three years later he treated the radiation problem in detail in a paper, entitled ‘*Über die Anwendung der Quantentheorie auf den Atombau. I. Die Grundpostulate der Quantentheorie*’ (‘On the Application of Quantum Theory to Atomic Structure. I. The Fundamental Postulates of Quantum Theory’), which he submitted in the middle of November 1922 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* and which appeared about two months later (Bohr, 1923a).

In Chapter 3 of the new paper Bohr discussed in particular two possibilities for resolving the difficulties between the electrodynamic and the quantum‑theoretical descriptions: the light‑quantum hypothesis and what he called ‘the coupling principle.’ With respect to the light‑quantum hypothesis he again emphasized the ‘insuperable difficulties’ it encountered in accounting for the interference phenomena. He argued: ‘We can even maintain that the picture, which lies at the foundation of the hypothesis of light‑quanta, excludes in principle the possibility of a rational definition of the conception of a frequency ν which plays a principal part in this theory’ (Bohr, 1923a, p. 157; English translation in *Collected Works* 3, 1976, p. 492). And he concluded:

> The satisfactory manner in which the hypothesis reproduces certain aspects of the phenomena is rather suited for supporting the view, which has been advocated from various sides, that, in contrast to the description of natural phenomena in classical physics in which it is always a question only of statistical results of a great number of individual processes, a description of atomic processes in terms of space and time cannot be carried through in a manner free from contradiction by the use of conceptions borrowed from classical electrodynamics, which, up to this time, have been our only means of formulating the principles which form the basis of the actual applications of the quantum theory. (Bohr, 1923a, pp. 157–158; *Collected Works* 3, 1976, p. 492)

In the method of the ‘coupling principle,’ on the other hand, one tried to reach the goal of a simultaneous treatment of atomic structure and radiation by ignoring the propagation of radiation in free space. That is, one dealt only with
