V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 539

radiation enclosed by reflecting walls and formally applied to it quantum conditions, as Debye (1910) and Rubinowicz (1917a) had done previously. One could then consider the total system of atoms plus enclosed radiation and also study the transfer of energy between the parts, which depended on the coupling assumed. A special case of coupling implied that energy was only exchanged by elastic collisions between one quantum *hν* (of frequency *ν*) and an atom, satisfying energy and momentum conservation, and this case was equivalent to assuming the light-quantum hypothesis. Bohr, however, was mainly interested in the more general case of interaction, where ‘a formulation can be given . . . by connecting the concept of coupling with the considerations of probability and with the Correspondence Principle’ (Bohr, 1923a, p. 159; English translation, *Collected Works 3*, 1976, p. 493). He proposed to introduce the probability into the coupling mechanism in the following way:

> Just as in the classical electrodynamics the so-called force of reaction of the radiation conditions the immediate coupling between the field of radiation and the various harmonic components of the motion of the atom, so we shall assume that the probability of the occurrence of various processes of exchange between the atom and the enclosure [i.e., the radiation in the enclosure] is controlled by “latent” reactions of radiation, which answer to the harmonic components corresponding to the respective processes of transition. (Bohr, 1923a, p. 159; *Collected Works 3*, 1976, p. 493)

Since the various characteristic vibrations of the enclosure were independent, the atom did not interact simultaneously with all modes of the radiation. Bohr argued that for the purpose of calculating the stationary states of the atom, the interaction between the atom (or the electrical particles contained in it) and the enclosed radiation might be neglected. Nevertheless the coupling point of view provided ‘a point of access for understanding the relations which, notwithstanding the difference in principle between the two cases, exist between the probabilities of the radiative processes of transition in the undisturbed atom, and the probability of non-radiative process of transitions, which can be occasioned by electronic collisions’ (Bohr, 1923a, p. 160; *Collected Works 3*, 1976, p. 494).
From his analysis of the two above-mentioned methods, Bohr found that the ‘coupling principle’ allowed one not only to begin with a reasonable theory of the dispersion of light by atoms, but it also relaxed the strict validity of the laws of conservation of energy and momentum in the process of interaction between radiation and atoms. ‘As a result of the previous considerations [on the principles of atomic theory],’ Bohr remarked, ‘a general description of the phenomena, in which the laws of the conservation of energy and momentum retain in detail their validity in their classical formulation, cannot be carried through’ (Bohr, 1923a, p. 163; *Collected Works 3*, 1976, p. 497). He further regarded Einstein’s proof of directed light-quanta from a strict application of energy and momentum conservation (Einstein, 1916e) and Rubinowicz’ derivation of the selection rules by assuming angular momentum conservation (Rubinowicz, 1918a, b) as indicating ‘the incompleteness of our picture of atomic processes’ (Bohr, 1923, p. 164;

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0173 -->

540 &emsp; Chapter V &emsp; The Problems of Radiation Theory

*Collected Works 3*, 1976, p. 497). He concluded:

In connection with the general questions discussed in this chapter it may be pointed out here that in the application of the laws of conservation of energy and momentum, such as the one last mentioned [i.e., the derivation of the selection rules], which is often referred to as a bridge between the classical and the quantum theory, it is rather a question of a formal applicability of these laws to cases in which, according to the nature of the case, the differences in principle of the two theories do not come to light. (Bohr, 1923a, p. 165; *Collected Works 3*, 1976, pp. 498–499)

At the time when Bohr argued in favour of giving up strict conservation of energy and momentum in processes of interaction between atoms and radiation, he did not stand alone among the quantum physicists in holding this view. As we have mentioned, especially Darwin, who had contemplated the violation of energy conservation in atomic processes for years, published a note in *Nature*, in which he attempted to obtain a description of the dispersion of light by atoms on its basis (Darwin, 1922). On 9 December 1922, Erwin Schrödinger—in his inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich—spoke about Franz Exner’s idea that all phenomena of nature had to be described by statistical laws and that no absolute laws of nature and, therefore, also no absolute causal behaviour existed (Schrödinger, 1929). He concluded his lecture by claiming that the difficulties in atomic theory supported Exner’s views, and remarked: ‘I believe it to be more likely that the liberation from the deep-rooted prejudice of absolute causality will help us in overcoming the difficulties, rather than—on the contrary—the theory of the atom will finally prove the dogma of causality to be right, as if by accident’ (Schrödinger, 1929, p. 11). In disclaiming the existence of absolute casual laws, Schrödinger certainly went beyond the speculations of most quantum physicists. On the other hand, even Sommerfeld let the idea of relaxing energy conservation in the case of a single radiation phenomenon, that is, the idea that it ‘be valid only on the average for many processes,’ enter into the third edition of his *Atombau und Spektrallinien* in 1922.<sup>827</sup> Also Max Born and Werner Heisenberg, in their paper on phase relations in Bohr’s models of atoms and molecules—when discussing the difficulties of explaining dynamically the orientation of atoms in inhomogeneous magnetic fields (observed in the Stern–Gerlach effect)—stated: ‘We are inclined to assume a violation of the mechanical equations; the adjustments (of atomic axes and phases, respectively) will also occur without compensation in the case of non-adiabatic transitions. The conservation of energy and perhaps also of momentum will not be valid for individual processes’ (Born and Heisenberg, 1922a, p. 55).<sup>828</sup>

<sup>827</sup>The quote is from the English translation (p. 253) of the third edition of *Atombau und Spektrallinien* (1922d).
<sup>828</sup>In his first paper on the anomalous Zeeman effects, submitted in December 1921, Heisenberg had already assumed that a strict law—i.e., Rubinowicz’ principle stating that the angular momentum of the atoms changed by an amount $\pm h/2\pi$ when perpendicularly polarized radiation was emitted—was valid ‘only for the totality of the atoms’ (Heisenberg, 1922a, p. 281).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0174 -->

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 541

While these doubts concerning the application of conservation principles plagued several physicists who were particularly involved in atomic theory, Arthur Compton published the interpretation of his effect in terms of the light-quantum hypothesis, which definitely supported the laws of strict energy and momentum conservation in the processes of interaction between atoms and radiation (Compton, 1923b). This event, of course, seriously upset Bohr's version of the 'coupling principle.' As Oskar Klein recalled: 'We in Copenhagen were really unprepared for the Compton effect because we were rather far, the whole time, from taking Einstein's light-quanta seriously' (O. Klein, Conversations, p. 63). Bohr learned more about Compton's experimental results and theoretical conclusions on his visit to the United States; he went, for example, to the University of Chicago, where Compton had moved in fall 1923, and attended the meeting of the American Physical Society, 30 November to 1 December 1923.$^{829}$ He did not, however, go to the Christmas meeting at Cincinnati, where Arthur Compton and William Duane fought their battle on the Compton effect. Instead he received a report about it from Edwin C. Kemble of Harvard University, who wrote in a letter, dated 4 January 1924:

> You will be interested to know that many of those who went to the recent Cincinnati meeting of the American Physical Society inclined to belittle Compton's corpuscular theory came away with a very different feeling. In view of the evidence offered it was difficult to avoid the conclusions that the phenomena of changed wavelength is a real one. It would not be difficult to invent a form of wave theory that would account for Compton's observations and the recoil electrons of C. T. R. Wilson, but when I try to correlate those things with Einstein's discussion of the maintenance of the Maxwell distribution law in an absorbing gas [Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1923] it seems to me hopeless to try to hold on to the wave theory.$^{830}$

Kemble then added: 'Perhaps Dr. Slater's recent scheme for a combination of wave theory and corpuscular theory may solve our difficulties' (Kemble to Bohr, 4 January 1924). Kemble's letter reached Copenhagen shortly after John Slater had arrived there. Slater had immediately become deeply engaged in a collaboration with Niels Bohr and Hendrik Kramers on the radiation problem. Several weeks later Bohr reported to Albert A. Michelson, who had been his host during

---

his visit to Chicago:

> It may perhaps interest you to hear that it appears to be possible for a believer in the essential reality of the quantum theory to take a view which may harmonize with the essential reality of the wave theory conception even more clearly than the views I expressed during our conversation. In fact, on the basis of the correspondence principle it seems possible to connect the discontinuous processes occurring in atoms with the continuous character of the radiation field in a somewhat more adequate way than hitherto perceived. The essentially new idea involved has been suggested by Dr. Slater, a young and very promising American physicist who is at present studying at Copenhagen. I hope soon to send you a paper about these problems written in cooperation with Dr. Kramers and Dr. Slater. (Bohr to Michelson, 7 February 1924)

John Clarke Slater, the young man of whom Kemble and Bohr spoke, was born on 22 December 1900 at Oak Park, Illinois. He had studied at the University of Rochester from 1916 to 1920 and at Harvard University from 1920 to 1923 and had obtained his doctorate with a thesis on the properties of alkali halides at high pressure under the supervision of Percy W. Bridgman (Slater, 1924b).<sup>831</sup> Having learned quantum theory from the courses of Edwin Kemble and private study, he had become interested in atomic and radiation theory. He had acquired familiarity with the actual status of the problems of atomic structure and with Bohr’s approach to these problems based on the correspondence principle and had closely followed the controversy between Compton and Duane on the Compton effect. As he recalled later: ‘I remember the controversy pretty well . . . We all said: “Duane is a nice man, he is doing many fine things, we will just keep quiet.” I never believed that Duane was right. I had always assumed that, of course, Compton was right, and I think that most of us assumed the same thing . . . We didn’t talk about it very much because of politeness to Duane’ (Slater, AHQP Interview, First Session, p. 22). This general interest in quantum theory motivated him to apply for a fellowship to go to Europe to continue his studies, and he selected Copenhagen as the place to do research.<sup>832</sup> In order to increase his chances, he tried two possibilities, the Sheldon Traveling Fellowship of Harvard University and the Scandinavian American Fellowship. ‘I took the Harvard Fellowship,’ he recalled, ‘and then after I got the fellowship, I learned that Bohr was going to spend the first half year in the United States’ (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 23). Slater, therefore, decided to spend a couple of months at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.

Slater arrived at Cambridge in September 1923. At the Cavendish, Joseph John Thomson, Ernest Rutherford and Francis Aston were around; he enjoyed being at the Laboratory and attended the colloquia there. Since he was interested

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation

543

in theory, Ralph Fowler looked after him.<sup>833</sup> He attended several courses of lectures, including one by Rutherford on elementary atomic structure. He found the lectures of Ebenezer Cunningham on electromagnetic theory especially interesting. ‘He had written a book which I had read carefully,’ Slater recalled. ‘He was thinking rather out of the ordinary electromagnetic theory, and it happened that what he was thinking was tying in with what I was interested in, because I was trying my best to tie together the photons [i.e., light-quanta] and the waves’ (Slater, AHQP Interview, First Session, p. 28). He had already thought in America about the possibility of connecting together the wave theory and the light-quantum theory. As he recalled: ‘A number of scientists—W[illiam] F[rancis] G[ray] Swann, among others—had suggested that the purpose of the electric field was not to carry a continuously distributed density of energy, but to guide the photons in some manner. This was the point of view which appealed to me, and during my period at the Cavendish Laboratory in the fall of 1923, I elaborated on it’ (Slater, 1975, p. 9).

Slater started from the observation that in electromagnetic theory the bright and dark fringes in an interference pattern or a diffraction pattern corresponded to high and low energy densities, respectively. In the light-quantum theory he interpreted the energy density as determining the probability of finding light-quanta at a given space-point, in agreement with the correspondence principle. However, in applying these considerations to the radiation emitted by atoms, he encountered a difficulty: according to Bohr one assumed that the spectral lines were emitted instantaneously, but the observed sharpness of the lines demanded—in agreement with the relation, $\Delta \nu \cdot \Delta t \sim 1$ (where $\Delta \nu$ is the width of the spectral lines and $\Delta t$ the time of emission), which Slater had learned from Michelson’s textbook *Light Waves and Their Uses*—that the atoms radiated during a finite period of time. Slater concluded: ‘The situation thus appeared to me perfectly clear. It must be that all the time an atom is in an excited state, it must be emitting electromagnetic waves of the frequencies corresponding to transitions to lower states which would be allowed by Bohr’s theory’ (Slater, 1975, p. 10). In order to describe the propagation of radiation in electromagnetic theory, he tried to construct a vector, which corresponded to the velocity of a light-quantum, and he recalled:

> Cunningham in his book actually had a vector which had some of those properties [Cunningham, 1915]. I played around with his vector quite a good deal to see if it would work, and it would not. People since then have discovered the fact that you cannot define a quantity that transforms like a vector out of Poynting’s vector and the energy density. Well, I found this too and I gave this up and decided that you could not set up a real vector field that was guiding the photons [i.e., light-quanta]. (Slater, AHQP Interview, First Session, p. 29)

***

<sup>833</sup> At that time Fowler was mainly interested in problems of statistical mechanics; he did not interact much with Slater scientifically and left him to pursue his own ideas.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0177 -->

544 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

However, he soon found a way out of this difficulty, which he described as follows:

> What I wanted to do was perfectly straightforwardly to have a wave and to have a photon. And by then I decided you could only have a statistical connection between them because you couldn't set up a vector to represent the photon [in electromagnetic theory]; that you would have the intensity of the wave governing the probability of finding the photon there. And I wanted to have the wave emitted during the stationary state so as to get it emitted over a long enough period so that it would have a suitable spectral distribution. (Slater, *loc. cit.*, p. 30)

When Slater presented these ideas on the width of spectral lines in Cambridge, people listened to him politely, but he did not stimulate any active interest.$^{834}$ The situation was very different in Copenhagen, where he soon went from Cambridge.
Slater's original intention had been to spend his full fellowship year in Copenhagen. It was only Bohr's absence until Christmas that made him change his plans; then, however, he came over to Denmark. In preparing the details of his arrival in Copenhagen, he wrote a letter to Hendrik Kramers. He announced that he would arrive on 21 December 1923 and also mentioned briefly some 'speculations on quantum theory' which he had made for explaining dispersion and other phenomena. He wrote:

> I have been going on with that [i.e., thinking about the problems of quantum theory connected with radiation], and came some weeks ago to the rather surprising conclusion that the only possible way of getting a consistent explanation was in the direction of *Lichtquanten*. Of course, the quanta can't travel on a straight line with the speed of light; but it seems possible to suppose that there is an electromagnetic field, produced not by the actual motions of the electrons but by the motions with the frequency of the possible emission lines (or, in an impressed field, of possible absorption lines), and amplitudes determined by the correspondence principle; the function of this field being to determine the motion of the quanta. If this motion is determined by the condition that Poynting's theorem shall hold over an average taken over a long period of time, definite paths are described (roughly by the lines tangent to Poynting's vector), and the probability of moving along these paths is such, for example, as to account for interference, many quanta being led to the bright spots in the field. (Slater to Kramers, 8 December 1923)

These remarks excited Kramers' curiosity—Kramers was concerned at that time with the problem of dispersion of light by atoms—and he looked forward to Slater's arrival. Slater was invited by the Bohrs to Christmas dinner, and on this occasion he had a good opportunity to talk about his work. As he recalled: 'I told him [i.e., Bohr] about my ideas, and he felt that these were fine.' But Bohr

***

Nevertheless he thanked Fowler in a later paper for guidance in his theoretical work (Slater, 1925b, p. 278); he felt that 'I ought to thank Fowler wherever I had a chance to do it' (Slater, AHQP Interview, First Session, p. 29).

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation
**545**

also had some reservations with respect to involving the light-quanta; therefore, he told Slater that certain ideas appeared to him to be too definite. ‘Bohr said: “We cannot have this exact conservation. We must not think specifically about the photons. We don’t have photons like that”’ (Slater, AHQP Interview, First Session, p. 30). Bohr wanted to make the light-quantum concept as vague as possible, and Kramers followed Bohr completely in that endeavour. Over fifty years later, Slater summarized the situation as follows:

> While at the Cavendish Laboratory in the fall of 1923 I had talked over the ideas with Fowler, who liked them, and had put them on paper not only in memoranda of my own, but in a letter to Kemble. As soon as I discussed them with Bohr and Kramers, I found them enthusiastic about the idea of the electromagnetic waves emitted by oscillators during the stationary states—they at once coined the name “virtual oscillators” for them. But to my consternation I found that they completely refused to admit the real existence of the photons. It had never occurred to me that they would object to what seemed like so obvious a deduction from many types of experiments. The result was that they insisted on our writing a joint paper in which the electromagnetic field was described as having a continuously distributed energy density whose intensity determined the probability of transition of an atom from one stationary state to another. One had then to assume only a statistical conservation of energy between the continuously distributed energy density in the electro-magnetic field and the quantized energy of the atoms. They grudgingly allowed me to send a note to *Nature* indicating that my original idea had included the real existence of the photons, but that I had given that up at their instigation. (Slater, 1975, p. 11)

Slater’s letter to *Nature*, dated 28 January 1924, appeared as a note entitled ‘Radiation and Atoms’ in the issue of 1 March 1924 (Slater, 1924a). In it he formulated the essential points he had in mind. Especially, he explained the crucial idea involved, namely, that atoms in stationary states exhibit a certain ‘activity,’ which gives rise to a ‘virtual field of radiation.’ He commented on the origin of this idea at the end of his note: ‘The idea of the activity of the stationary states presented here suggested itself to me in the course of an attempt to combine the elements of the theories of electrodynamics and of light-quanta by setting up a field to guide discrete quanta, which might move, for example, along the direction of Poynting’s vector.’ And he added immediately: ‘But when the idea with that interpretation was described to Dr. Kramers, he pointed out that it scarcely suggested a definite coupling between emission and absorption processes which light-quanta provide, but rather indicated a much greater independence between transition processes in distant atoms than I perceived’ (Slater, 1924a, p. 308). Not only did Kramers influence the writing of Slater’s note to *Nature*, so did Bohr. Especially, he helped Slater in formulating the introductory sentence as: ‘Any atom may, in fact, be supposed to communicate with other atoms all the time it is in a stationary state, by means of a virtual field of radiation, originating from oscillators having the frequencies of possible quantum transitions and the function of which is to provide for statistical conservation of energy and momentum by determining the probabilities for

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0179 -->

quantum transitions' (Slater, 1924a, p. 307). Thus the concept of statistical conservation laws sneaked into Slater's note.$^{835}$

At the end of his letter to *Nature*, Slater remarked: 'The subject [of the letter] has been discussed at length with Professor Bohr and Dr. Kramers, and a joint paper with them will shortly be published in the *Philosophical Magazine*, describing the picture more fully, and suggesting possible applications in the development of the quantum theory of radiation' (Slater, 1924a, p. 308). The paper thus introduced bore the title 'The Quantum Theory of Radiation'; the authors submitted it in January 1924 and it appeared in the May issue of the *Philosophical Magazine* (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924).$^{836}$ 'The paper with Bohr and Kramers,' Slater reported to Van Vleck a little later, 'was got out of the way the first six weeks or so [of Slater's stay at Copenhagen]—written entirely by Boh

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 547

the known difficulties of radiation theory within the framework of atomic theory. He remarked:

> The essentially new assumption introduced in §2 that the atom, even before a process of transition between two stationary states takes place, is capable of communication with distant atoms through a virtual radiation field, is due to Dr. Slater. Originally his endeavour was in this way to obtain a harmony between the physical pictures of the electrodynamical theory of light and the theory of light-quanta by coupling transitions of emission and absorption of communicating atoms together in pairs. It was pointed out by Kramers, however, that instead of suggesting an intimate coupling between these processes, the idea just mentioned leads rather to the assumption of a greater independence between transition processes in distant atoms than hitherto perceived. The present paper is the result of a mutual discussion between the authors concerning the possible importance of these assumptions for the elaboration of the quantum theory, and may in various respects be considered as a supplement to the first part of a recent treatise by Bohr [Bohr, 1923a], dealing with the principles of the quantum theory, in which several of the problems dealt with here are treated more fully. (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 786)

The embedding of Slater's idea of virtual oscillators into Bohr's fundamental principles of atomic theory might indeed account for most of the changes, which Bohr and Kramers made and about which Slater afterwards complained so bitterly. Bohr evidently stuck fully to the conviction that the theory of light-quanta contradicted for all time the undulatory features of radiation. Hence he commented on the light-quantum hypothesis:

> Although the great heuristic value of this hypothesis is shown by the confirmation of Einstein's predictions concerning the photoelectric phenomenon, still the theory of light-quanta can obviously not be considered as satisfactory solution of the problem of light propagation. This is clear even from the fact that the radiation “frequency” $\nu$ appearing in the theory is defined by experiments on interference phenomena which apparently demand for their interpretation a wave constitution of light. (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 787)

Of course, Bohr admitted, certain consequences of the light-quantum hypothesis somehow led to the fundamental frequency condition in the quantum theory of atomic structure. The latter theory, however, did not provide a description of the details of the mechanism underlying the process of transition between two stationary states. Bohr concluded: ‘At the present state of science it seems necessary, as regards the occurrence of transition processes, to content ourselves with considerations of probability’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 788). Such probability considerations had been introduced by Einstein in 1916, and they had played a crucial role in the recent discussion of the temperature equilibrium between free electrons or atoms and radiation, carried out by Pauli and by Einstein and Ehrenfest. In spite of the inclusion of probability considerations, the quantum-theoretical description of radiation phenomena had to represent a ‘natural generalization’ of the classical, electrodynamical description, as was ‘evident from the condition that in the limit, where we consider processes

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0181 -->

548 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Problems of Radiation Theory

which depend on the statistical behaviour of the large number of atoms, and which involve stationary states where the difference between neighbouring stationary states is comparatively little, the classical theory always leads to conclusions in agreement with experiment’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 789). In Bohr’s opinion the correspondence principle accounted completely for the relation established thus far between the classical and the quantum theory of radiation. However, the difficulties to account, say, for the ‘time interval in which the emission of radiation connected with the transition takes place . . . has strengthened the doubt . . . whether the detailed interpretation of the interaction between matter and radiation can be given at all in terms of a causal description in space and time of the kind hitherto used for the interpretation of natural phenomena’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 790).

In section two of the paper, Slater’s ideas on the radiation of atoms, as modified by the considerations of Kramers, were discussed. Thus the authors, i.e., Bohr and Kramers, began by saying: ‘We will assume that a given atom in a certain stationary state will communicate continually with other atoms through a time-spatial mechanism which is virtually equivalent with the field of radiation which on the classical theory would originate from the virtual harmonic oscillators corresponding with the various possible transitions to other stationary states’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 790). The authors further assumed that the occurrence of transition processes (absorption and emission) in the given atom and in the atoms ‘with which it is in mutual communication’ were connected ‘by probability laws which are analogous to those which in Einstein’s theory hold for the induced transitions between stationary states when illuminated by radiation’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 791). They interpreted the ‘spontaneous’ transitions of Einstein as ‘induced by the virtual field of radiation which is connected with the virtual harmonic oscillators conjugated with the motion of the atom itself,’ and the ‘induced’ transitions as arising ‘in consequence of the virtual radiation in the surrounding space due to other atoms’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 791). Such an interpretation, the authors concluded, implied a change in the usual space-time picture of the radiation processes, especially because the occurrence of a certain transition in a given atom not only depended on its initial state (as in the usual picture) but also on the states of the atoms with which the given atom ‘communicated’ through the virtual radiation field. While this conclusion was in accord with Slater’s original ideas (concerning the linewidths of radiation emitted by atoms), the following assumption went beyond them. The authors declared: ‘As regards the occurrence of transitions [in atoms], which is the essential feature of the quantum theory, we abandon . . . any attempt at a causal connexion between the transitions in distant atoms, and especially a direct application of the principles of conservation of energy and momentum, so characteristic for the classical theories’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 791). That is, strict conservation principles should be applied only to collisions between the atoms, where the forces arising from the interaction between radiation and matter (atoms or electrons) could be neglected against the electrostatic forces of attraction and repulsion between the atoms involved in the collision.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0182 -->

V.2 The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation  
549

Besides the assumption of the statistical conservation of energy and momentum for atomic processes involving absorption and emission of radiation, a second, to some extent related, assumption was proposed by the authors, an assumption which could again be motivated by the correspondence principle. According to the classical theory of radiation, distant atoms should not exert upon each other an *instantaneous* influence. Therefore, Bohr and Kramers demanded that ‘an induced transition in an atom is not directly caused by a transition in a distant atom for which the energy difference between the initial and final stationary state is the same’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 792). That is, the processes of emission and absorption in distant atoms must be regarded as being statistically independent.

The authors were fully aware of the fact that so far no empirical tests existed of the two assumptions, namely, the statistical energy and momentum conservation and the statistical independence of radiation processes in distant atoms. However, they claimed that their new theory of radiation did not contradict any available information and, in fact, allowed one, without ‘any departure from the electrodynamic theory of light as regards the propagation of radiation in free space,’ ‘to establish a consistent and fairly complete description of the general optical phenomena accompanying the propagation of light through a material medium, which accounts at the same time for the close connexion of these phenomena with the spectra of the atoms of the medium’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, pp. 793–794). They presented the outline of such a consistent description in the last two sections of their paper.

In section three, Bohr, Kramers and Slater discussed what they called the ‘capacity of interference of spectral lines,’ i.e., the ability of a given spectral line, originating from an atom which undergoes a transition from one stationary state to another, to interfere with itself. They claimed that the sharpness (linewidth) of the spectral lines and the ‘capacity of interference’ had to be related in atomic theory, and further that the sharpness of a spectral line was determined by the accuracy with which the energies of the initial *and* the final states of the atoms could be defined. The fact that both states contributed then established the observed ‘reciprocity’ existing in ‘the constitution of a line when appearing in an emission and in an absorption spectrum’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 795), in agreement with Kirchhoff’s law of the emission and absorption of radiation in thermal equilibrium.⁸³⁸

Finally, in section four, Bohr, Kramers and Slater treated several phenomena that were connected with the dispersion of light by atoms, for example, the strong absorption of radiation by monatomic vapours or the scattering of light by free atoms. In their description of these phenomena, they attempted to retain—in

spite of the discontinuous character of the transition processes in atomic theory
—‘an element of continuity similar to that exhibited by the classical electro-
dynamical theory of the propagation of light through media’ (Bohr, Kramers and
Slater, 1924, p. 797). Therefore they interpreted the so-called anomalous disper-
sion, as well as the occurrence of fluorescent radiation (from the absorption of
radiation by atoms and molecules) as arising from the interference of the
incident radiation with ‘secondary spherical wavelets set up by each of the
illuminated atoms’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 798). The authors also discussed the Compton
effect, which Arthur Compton and Peter Debye had previously explained on the
basis of the light-quantum theory including strict energy and momentum conser-
vation in the process of scattering of individual light-quanta by individual
electrons (bound in atoms). In contrast to Compton and Debye’s interpretation,
Bohr, Kramers, and Slater proposed to consider the scattering of radiation by
electrons ‘as a continuous phenomenon to which each of the illuminated elec-
trons contributes through the emission of coherent secondary wavelets’ (*loc. cit.*,
p. 799). In this process the atom acted as if it were under the influence of a
‘virtual’ radiation field having the quantum-theoretical transition frequencies.
That is, when the incident radiation fell on an atom, the electrons in it behaved
as if they oscillated with the frequencies of the virtual field and not with the
frequencies derived from atomic theory. The authors were, of course, aware that
their interpretation contradicted the familiar (classical) conceptions, but argued:
‘In view of the fundamental departures from the classical space-time description,
involved in the very idea of virtual oscillators, it seems at the present state of
science hardly justifiable to reject a formal interpretation as that under consider-
ation as inadequate’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924, p. 799). On the contrary,
they found their interpretation to be ‘unavoidable’ in order to account for the
observed phenomena, the description of which seemed to imply a wave concep-
tion of radiation. The new interpretation would also account for the Compton
effect, provided one assumed ‘that the illuminated electron possesses a certain
probability of taking up in a unit time a finite amount of momentum in any
given direction’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 799). This assumption, which replaced in quantum
theory the continuous transfer of momentum from radiation to the electron due
to classical theory, led to a statistical conservation of momentum. And this
assumption, the authors pointed out, was also consistent with the earlier treat-
ments of statistical equilibrium between radiation and matter by Pauli (1923b)
and Einstein and Ehrenfest (1923).

The same interpretation, as given for the Compton effect, could be shown to
work—at least in principle—also for the dispersion of light by atoms, a phenome-
non which Smekal had proposed to treat earlier on the basis of the light-quantum
hypothesis (Smekal, 1923c).<sup>839</sup> In conclusion, Bohr, Kramers and Slater de-

V.2  The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation                                                                                   551

monstrated—by treating the emission of electromagnetic waves from a (macroscopic) antenna in accordance with their ideas—that the new radiation theory indeed passed over into Maxwell’s electrodynamics in the classical limit. They claimed, in particular, that the ‘oscillation of the electricity’ in the antenna produced ‘a (virtual) radiation field which through probability laws again induces changes in the motion of the electrons which may be regarded as continuous’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 801)—continuous because of the smallness of the energy differences in the atom as compared to the radiation energy in the antenna. Then also ‘the “virtual” character of the radiation field, which at the present state of science seems so essential for an adequate description of atomic phenomena, automatically loses its importance in a limiting case ..., where the field, as regards its observable interaction with matter, is endowed with all attributes of an electromagnetic field in classical electrodynamics’ (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, p. 802). That is, in the classical limit the ‘virtual’ radiation field becomes transformed into a ‘real’ radiation field.

For Niels Bohr and his associates the new quantum theory of radiation thus formulated meant a major step forward towards a consistent theory of all atomic phenomena because it enabled one for the first time to treat the problem of atomic radiation in all respects without leaving the basis of the correspondence principle. Besides this enormous progress in principle, the theory led to important practical applications. The Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory not only justified the use made thus far of the mechanical methods of calculating the stationary states of atoms, it also provided an adequate tool to calculate the influence of radiation on the motion of the electrically charged particles in atoms and thus on atomic structure. The hope thus arose among a number of physicists that one could now successfully attack several problems of atomic theory, which had previously presented serious difficulties. One such problem was the dispersion of light by atoms, and with respect to it Bohr, Kramers and Slater referred (*loc. cit.*, p. 797, footnote) to a note of Kramers, in which a quantitative theory was outlined and which was to appear very soon in *Nature* (Kramers, 1924a). Because of such prospects a very strong optimism prevailed at Bohr’s Institute since the beginning of 1924. Werner Heisenberg, who visited Copenhagen in March of that year, also became infected by this optimistic mood and he transmitted it to Göttingen and Max Born. A few weeks later Born wrote to Bohr:

> I wish to tell you how happy I feel about the turn in radiation theory, which you have given to this problem. Just before I left Göttingen, Heisenberg visited me and reported about your ideas. We have, of course, also discussed similar ideas before, but you have hit upon the decisive point: namely, the correlation of *two* resonators (of an emission and an absorption resonator) of the same frequency with both the end-states involved in a “quantum jump.” With it, as I have convinced myself, all contradictions indeed disappear. Above all, the transition becomes independent of the time, and emission and absorption of radiation occur in the stationary states. Although I have only the brief oral report of Heisenberg, I am convinced that your new theory has hit upon the right thing and also represents in a sense the final answer to these problems; it constitutes the rational extension of the classical

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0185 -->

552 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

conceptions of radiation to discrete elementary processes. (Born to Bohr, 16 April 1924)

Like Born, Erwin Schrödinger also reacted positively towards the Copenhagen radiation theory. He felt especially attracted by the statistical aspects of the theory, which agreed so well with the ideas of his former teacher Franz Exner on the probabilistic description of microscopic phenomena.$^{840}$ On 24 May he sent an enthusiastic letter to Bohr indicating his approval. At the same time, however, he criticized the use of the notion of ‘virtual radiation,’ and commented:

> Which then is the “real” radiation if not the one which “causes” the transitions, i.e., gives rise to transition probabilities? Moreover, no other type is at all assumed. Indeed, from a purely philosophical point of view one might even dare to doubt as to which of the two electron systems possesses a higher degree of reality: the “real” one, describing the stationary orbits, or the “virtual” one, representing the virtual radiation and dispersing the incident virtual radiation. (Schrödinger to Bohr, 24 May 1924)

Schrödinger also reviewed and advocated the new radiation theory in an article, entitled ‘Bohrs neue Strahlungshypothese und der Energiesatz’ (‘Bohr’s New Radiation Hypothesis and the Conservation of Energy’) and published in *Naturwissenschaften* in September 1924 (Schrödinger, 1924d). Especially, he drew attention to the ‘most exciting’ idea it contained, namely, the violation of energy and momentum conservation. Schrödinger also estimated the magnitude of possible energy violations in atomic process, but did not find them to be ‘dangerous’; that is, the energy fluctuations calculated from the assumption of statistical energy conservation were considerably below those obtained from the thermal motion. Hence he concluded that ‘the new formulation of radiation processes from this point of view is not in contradiction with the experience made thus far’ (Schrödinger, 1924d, p. 724).$^{841}$

Schrödinger’s clear stand in favour of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory pleased Bohr very much because the support came from outside the

$^{840}$Schrödinger had been concerned with Exner’s ideas already earlier—see his inaugural lecture at the University of Zurich quoted above—and he had mentioned them again in a paper dealing with the degeneracy in gases from the point of view of quantum theory, which was published in January 1924 (Schrödinger, 1924a). Further Schrödinger discussed the problems of radiation theory, especially of the equilibrium between light and acoustic radiation, in other papers at that time (Schrödinger, 1924b, c).

$^{841}$Schrödinger found, however, that the statistical conservation laws may lead to difficulties with the validity of the thermodynamic laws; especially, the statistical energy fluctuations in a finite system would grow in the course of time and could be made small only if the system were enlarged. (See Schrödinger, 1924d, p. 724.)

Among Kramers’ papers is contained an essay, entitled ‘Über eine mögliche Bedeutung des Versagens des Energieprinzips bei Atomprozessen’ (‘On a Possible Significance of the Failure of the Energy Principle in Atomic Processes’). In it Kramers argued that Schrödinger’s energy fluctuations do not play any role in the realistic situations of physics; he further claimed that $\overline{\Delta E}$, the average of the deviations from energy conservation, remained basically zero for all times because a possible constant increase of $\overline{\Delta E}$ could be compensated easily by a slight change of the dynamics of the systems under consideration.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0186 -->

V.2  The Bohr–Kramers–Slater Theory of Radiation 553

Copenhagen circle.^842  Schrödinger especially liked the assumption of the statistical conservation laws, which John Slater had only reluctantly adopted. In fact, Slater would soon after leaving Copenhagen and returning to Harvard turn away from the joint radiation theory of 1924 and again emphasize the light-quantum aspects in his later papers (Slater, 1925a, b).^843  The proposed violation of conservation laws, as well as the opposition to the light-quantum concept, aroused Albert Einstein to action. In a popular article, entitled ‘*Das Komptonsche Experiment*’ (‘The Compton Experiment’) which appeared in the *Berliner Tageblatt* on 20 April 1924, i.e., before the publication of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory in a scientific journal, Einstein argued: ‘The positive result of Compton’s experiment proves that radiation behaves—not only with respect to energy transfer, but also with respect to collision interactions—as if it consisted of projectiles of energy’ (Einstein, 1924a). Several days later he wrote to Max Born: ‘Bohr’s opinion about radiation theory is of great interest to me. But I should not want to be forced into giving up strict causality without defending it more strongly than I have done so far’ (Einstein to Hedwig and Max Born, 29 April 1924). In a letter to Paul Ehrenfest, dated 31 May 1924, Einstein summarized his criticism by listing five major points in which he disagreed with the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory: first, nature seemed to respect the strict validity of conservation principles; second, a cavity—having totally reflecting walls, when filled with temperature radiation—would show, according to the Copenhagen radiation theory, a Brownian motion which increases with time; third, any fundamentally statistical behaviour of nature, i.e., any violation of causality in microscopic processes, was unacceptable; fourth, in addition to ‘virtual electric fields’ also ‘virtual acoustic fields’ had to exist (for example, in a solid); fifth, the process of normal dispersion of light by atoms (without any transformation of the frequencies, etc.) could be described only very indirectly by the new quantum theory of radiation.^844  
 Einstein repeated his main objections against the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory

 ^842 To the Copenhagen circle belonged Oskar Klein, then at Ann Arbor, Michigan. In a letter to Bohr, Klein remarked that he was ‘enraptured by the beautiful and simple solution of so many apparent paradoxes’ (O. Klein to Bohr, 30 June 1924).  
 ^843 Slater stayed at Harvard until 1930 (instructor, 1924–1926; assistant professor, 1926–1929; associate professor, 1929–1930). In 1929 he was a Guggenheim Fellow at the University of Leipzig. Then he joined the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (1930–1951) as professor of physics and head of the physics department and was then appointed Institute Professor of Physics (1951–1966); upon retirement from M.I.T., he went as research professor of physics and chemistry to the University of Florida at Gainesville (1966–1976). Slater died on 25 July 1976 at Sanibel Island, Florida.  
 ^844 Einstein discussed the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory in a talk given at the Prussian Academy of Sciences on 24 April 1924 (Einstein, 1924b). Since the paper of Bohr, Kramers and Slater had not yet appeared in print, one must assume that Einstein saw the manuscript or the proof-sheets before publication. Rudolf Ladenburg, who listened to Einstein’s talk, reported about it to Copenhagen:  
His [Einstein’s] opinion was not negative; he declared the new formulation to be consistent and logical and not directly in contradiction with any facts; in his opinion one had to stick in any case to the mechanism of the wave theory. However, he emphasized forcefully the logical difficulties of the theory, of the “pre-stabilized harmony,” which is brought in by the fundamental introduction of probability in place of causality. (Ladenburg to Kramers, 8 June 1924)

Nevertheless Bohr remained unshaken in the belief that the new radiation theory was essentially correct and that a physical reality could not be ascribed to the light-quanta. He used to argue that ‘Even if Einstein sends me a cable that now an irrevocable proof of the existence of light-quanta had been found, the message cannot reach me, because it has to be transmitted by electromagnetic waves’ (Heisenberg, Conversations p. 169). Einstein, on the other hand, was convinced that ‘the “free” [“*losen*”] quanta cannot be dispensed with’ (Einstein to Ehrenfest, 17 July 1924). In his opinion, progress had to be sought in an improved theory of light-quanta, perhaps along the lines indicated in a recent paper by Satyendra Nath Bose (Bose, 1924a).

## V.3 Bose’s Light-Quantum Statistics and Its Extension to Gas Theory

During the first fifteen years of its existence the light-quantum hypothesis was applied only to a few selected problems: the derivation of Planck’s law of blackbody radiation (Einstein, 1906c, 1916e), the explanation of the photoelectric effect (Einstein, 1905b) and the description of the production of X-rays (Stark, 1909b). A really universal theory combining the usual radiation phenomena and these quantum phenomena on the basis of the light-quantum concept appeared to be impossible, because the existence of interference effects seemed to prevent it. Indeed, all the processes involving the propagation of light, its reflection and diffraction could be described perfectly by the assumption that radiation consisted of transverse electromagnetic waves, and one could not imagine any method of dealing with them as well by a nonundulatory hypothesis. By late 1922, however, the situation had changed drastically. Compton recognized that the shift in the wavelength of X-rays, if scattered by atoms, could be derived only by assuming the existence of radiation in the form of light-quanta, which collide with the electrons in atoms in elementary processes (Compton, 1923a, b). While he did not believe in the reality of the Compton effect, William Duane of Harvard University suggested the existence of another light-quantum effect in 1923, with the help of which he explained what he called ‘abnormal reflection’ of X-rays by crystal lattices (Duane, 1923).

It had been discovered about a decade earlier that X-rays were reflected from crystal lattices, provided the relation

$$2d \sin \theta = n\lambda \tag{283}$$

was satisfied between integral multiples (\(n\)) of the wavelength \(\lambda\) of X-rays, the angle of incidence \(\theta\) (i.e., the angle between the direction of the incident X-rays and the normal to the plane of the crystal) and the lattice constant \(d\) (W. L.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0188 -->

V.3 Bose’s Light-Quantum Statistics and Its Extension to Gas Theory
555

Bragg, 1913a, b). In spring 1922 George Lindenberg Clark and William Duane found a different kind of reflection: the crystal also reflected rays not satisfying Eq. (283), i.e., rays having wavelengths which coincided with those of discrete X-rays characteristic of the substances composing the crystal lattice (Clark and Duane, 1922). Clark and Duane continued their experiments in the following year (Clark and Duane, 1923a); they then confirmed this surprising anomalous reflection in later experiments (Clark and Duane, 1923b). Since it could not be described by the wave theory, Duane proposed in a note, communicated in March 1923 to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, a solution, consisting of ‘an attempt to formulate a theory of reflection of X-rays by crystals, based on quantum ideas without reference to interference laws’ (Duane, 1923, p. 158). He assumed that the radiation was composed of quanta having energy $h\nu$ and directed momentum $h\nu / c$, and that in the process of reflection energy and momentum were transferred from light-quanta to matter such that energy and momentum were conserved.$^{845}$ Further he assumed the validity of the quantum condition,

$$ \int_0^d p \, dq = nh, \tag{284} $$

where $p$ denoted the momentum transferred, $d$ the lattice constant, $n$ an integer, and $h$ Planck’s constant. With these assumptions he obtained from momentum conservation the equation

$$ \frac{h\nu}{c} \cdot 2 \sin \theta = \frac{nh}{d}, \tag{285} $$

which agreed with Bragg’s equation (283).$^{846}$

Thus far Duane had just reproduced the case of normal reflection with his quantum ideas without involving any interference argument. However, in the case of the anomalous reflections of the X-rays having the characteristic wave-length of one of the substances composing the lattice, he argued that the situation was more complex: ‘Here we must consider that a certain amount of the energy of the incident ray goes to produce the emission of an electron from an atom with a certain velocity and we must take into account the transfer of

---
$^{845}$ Because of the large mass of the crystal lattice, Duane neglected the energy transfer and worked only with momentum conservation.

$^{846}$ Duane treated the case in which the direction of the incident light was parallel to one plane of a three-dimensional lattice (whose (main) directions were at right angles to each other); that is, he considered the reflection of X-rays by a two-dimensional lattice, with lattice constants $a$ and $b$. Hence he had to use two quantum conditions of the type of Eq. (284); but one of the conditions yields in the case of reflection the equation

$$ \frac{h\nu}{c} [\cos \theta - \cos(-\theta)] = \frac{n'h}{b}, $$

which could be satisfied only by taking $n' = 0$.

momentum to the atom and the emitted electron, as well as to the crystal' (Duane, 1923, p. 161). In doing so, he arrived at equations 'which may be interpreted as meaning that the characteristic radiations came off from the crystal in directions approximating to those directions which obey the laws of defraction by the crystal' (Duane, 1923, p. 162). That is, the anomalous reflection nearly, but not fully, satisfied Bragg's law, Eq. (283).

Duane's theory of the reflection of X-rays was taken up by Arthur Compton. In a paper, submitted to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* in October 1923, he argued that one might replace Duane's two assumptions, the light-quantum hypothesis and the quantum condition, Eq. (284), by one general quantum postulate (Compton, 1923f). This postulate could be formulated as the equation

$$\bar{p} = \frac{\int p \, dq}{q_1} = \frac{nh}{q_1} + \gamma, \qquad (286)$$

where $p$ and $q$ denoted the dynamical variables of the system under consideration, $\bar{p}$ the displacement average of the momentum, and $q_1 \ (= \int dq)$ the displacement necessary to bring the system back to its original condition. The constant $\gamma$ represented a minimum average momentum corresponding to the zero-point energy. Applying Eq. (286) to a beam of plane waves of wavelength $\lambda$, evidently $q_1$ was equal to $\lambda$. Hence the momentum of the beam in the direction of propagation was $\bar{p}$, i.e.,

$$\bar{p} = \frac{nh}{\lambda} + \gamma, \qquad (286')$$

and its energy was $\bar{p}c$. Since, from experiments on the photoelectric effect the energy of the beam turned out to be $h\nu$, the constants $n$ and $\gamma$ had to assume the values 1 and 0, respectively; or the light-beam's momentum was

$$\bar{p} = \frac{h}{\lambda} \ . \qquad (286'')$$

Similarly, Compton applied the quantum condition to the uniform (translational) motion of a crystal lattice, as well as to the passage of radiation through a crystal. He thus found equations describing the diffraction of light, i.e., equations relating the cosines of the angle of incidence and the angle of deflection, the lattice constants and wavelength, which were 'exactly those obtained on the theory of interference for the angles at which the ray of wavelength $\lambda$ may be diffracted by a crystal' (Compton, 1923f, p. 361).<sup>847</sup>

Although he had built on Duane's theory, Compton abandoned a part of the light-quantum hypothesis in his note on the diffraction of radiation by crystals.

<sup>847</sup> Compton had assumed the incident radiation to consist of infinite wave trains. Gregory Breit showed, however, that this restriction could be removed (Breit, 1923a). Further, Paul S. Epstein and Paul Ehrenfest extended Compton's quantum-theoretical treatment of diffraction of light by crystals to lattices having only finite extension (Epstein and Ehrenfest, 1924).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0190 -->

V.3 Bose’s Light-Quantum Statistics and Its Extension to Gas Theory 557

Thus he remarked at the end of his paper: ‘Attention may be called to the fact that the quantum conception of diffraction is far from being in conflict with the wave theory. In fact we were able to quantize the incident radiation only in view of the fact that it repeats itself at regular space intervals. Thus even from the quantum viewpoint electromagnetic radiation is seen to consist of waves’ (Compton, 1923f, p. 362). On the other hand, Compton’s colleague from Washington University, St. Louis, George Eric MacDonnell Jauncey stuck to a pure light-quantum theory in nearly all his publications on the scattering of X-rays.<sup>848</sup> For example, Jauncey provided a detailed ‘Corpuscular Quantum Theory of the Scattering of X-rays by Light Elements,’ including a formula for the intensity distribution as a function of the scattering angle, in a paper published in *Physical Review* in September 1923 (Jauncey, 1923).<sup>849</sup> A little later he treated the scattering of polarized X-rays from the point of view of the corpuscular radiation theory; he found that, in contrast to J. J. Thomson’s classical wave theory, for X-rays of short wavelength the polarizing angle—i.e., the scattering angle which gave completely polarized secondary rays from unpolarized primary rays—was shifted from 90° to smaller values (Jauncey, 1924a, c).<sup>850</sup> Finally, he calculated on the same theory the width of discrete X-rays, when modified by the Compton effect (Jauncey, 1924d), as well as the width of the unmodified line (Jauncey, 1925).

From the interaction between radiation and matter, which was responsible for such phenomena as the Compton effect and the photoelectric effect, certain typical quantum properties of radiation could be deduced. However, there existed the phenomenon of blackbody radiation, in which the nature of light should be revealed much more clearly. In principle, the blackbody radiation of a given temperature should be considered as a system of pure radiation because the additional resonators—as assumed by Planck in the derivation of the energy distribution law of cavity radiation (Planck, 1900f)—or the atoms—as assumed later by Einstein for the same purpose (Einstein, 1916d)—merely served to establish a well-defined temperature in the radiation. The question, therefore, arose whether the observed blackbody radiation, described by Planck’s law,

Jauncey was born on 21 September 1888 in Adelaide, Australia. He studied science at the University of Adelaide, obtaining his B.S. in 1910. He went to America in 1914 and continued his studies at Lehigh University, taking his M.A. in physics in 1916. He became an assistant professor of physics at Washington University, St. Louis, in 1921, associate professor in 1924 and full professor in 1930. Jauncey worked primarily on problems of X-ray scattering. He was associate editor of *Physical Review* from 1926 to 1928. Jauncey died on 19 May 1947 at St. Louis.

<sup>849</sup> The previous year Jauncey had discussed the scattering of X-rays by crystals on the basis of the classical theory (Jauncey, 1922). In December 1923 he showed how the experimental deviations from Bragg’s law of reflection of X-rays could be explained on the basis of a classical theory of Charles Galton Darwin (Jauncey, 1924b).

<sup>850</sup> Jauncey confirmed this conclusion qualitatively in an experiment, in which X-rays were scattered by paraffin (Jauncey and Stauss, 1924a, b).

558 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

allowed one to determine the nature of radiation directly, without any reference to the interaction between radiation and matter. Einstein was the first person who tried to answer this question: in early 1909 he found from an analysis of the energy and momentum fluctuations in blackbody radiation that radiation must exhibit both undulatory and light-quantum features (Einstein, 1909a). Then, in a paper submitted in October of the following year, Peter Debye attacked the reverse question: he proposed a derivation of Planck's law based on the concept of electromagnetic modes and avoided the use of resonators (Debye, 1910). For this purpose he calculated the number, $N_\nu$, of transverse radiation modes having frequencies in the interval, $\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$, existing in a cubic cavity of length $l$; he obtained the result

$$N_\nu d\nu = \frac{8\pi l^3 \nu^2}{c^3} d\nu. \quad (287)$$

By endowing each mode at temperature $T$ with the average energy $\bar{\epsilon}_\nu$,

$$\bar{\epsilon}_\nu = \frac{h\nu}{\exp(h\nu / kT) - 1} , \quad (288)$$

Planck's law followed for the energy density $\rho_\nu (= N_\nu / l^3)$.
The crucial step in Debye's derivation was to justify Eq. (288) by a probability consideration. Debye assumed that $w_\nu$, the probability of distributing $N_\nu f_\nu$ quanta of energy $h\nu$ among $N_\nu$ modes, was given by the relation

$$w_\nu = \frac{(N_\nu d\nu + N_\nu f_\nu d\nu)!}{(N_\nu d\nu)! (N_\nu f_\nu d\nu)!} . \quad (289)$$

Evidently the average energy per oscillator, $\bar{\epsilon}_\nu$, was given by the product $f_\nu h\nu$. Debye then determined the unknown function $f_\nu$ in the following way. He calculated the maximum ($w_\nu^{\text{max}}$) of the probability $w_\nu$, Eq. (289), under the constraint of constant energy (i.e., $\rho_\nu l^3 = \text{const.}$, $\rho_\nu$ being the energy density of radiation of frequency $\nu$). The product $k \ln w_\nu^{\text{max}}$ then represented the equilibrium entropy $s_\nu$ of the radiation. Finally, he used the definition of the entropy ($ds_\nu / d\rho_\nu = T^{-1}$), and thus obtained

$$f_\nu = \left[ \exp \left( \frac{h\nu}{kT} \right) - 1 \right]. \quad (290)$$

With $f_\nu$ given by Eq. (290), he immediately obtained the expression for $\bar{\epsilon}_\nu$, Eq. (288).
In his paper Debye defined the probability in radiation theory, Eq. (289), 'analogously to Planck' (Debye, 1910, p. 1430). He did not investigate the consequences of this definition on the nature of radiation because in his opinion the quantum hypothesis ($\epsilon_\nu = h\nu$) had nothing to do with the radiation itself, but

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0192 -->

only determined the energy transfer from one mode to another. Later authors tried to motivate the existence of the Planck–Debye definition of probability. For example, Ladislas Natanson derived it by taking the distribution of $n$ ($= N_{\nu} f_{\nu}$) energy quanta $h\nu$ among $N_{\nu}$ receptacles of energy, of which $N_0$ had the energy 0, $N_1$ the energy $h\nu$, $N_2$ the energy $2h\nu, \ldots, N_p$ the energy $ph\nu$ ($N_{\nu} = \sum_{i=0}^{p} N_i$) (Natanson, 1911).$^{851}$ However, he did not give any physical interpretation for this description. Two years later, Mieczysław Wolfke proposed to use the idea of 'light-atoms' ('$Lichtatom$,' Wolfke, 1913a, p. 1123) for the systematic derivation of Planck's law in a series of papers (Wolfke, 1913a, b; 1914a).$^{852}$ But G. Krutkow, then at Leyden, claimed that with independent 'light-atoms' one would arrive, not at the probability definition, Eq. (289), but at the probability leading to Wien's law (Krutkow, 1914a).$^{853}$ To Krutkow's criticism Wolfke replied that his 'light-atoms' were *independent* of each other as far as their *existence* was concerned, but they were not *spatially independent* of each other' as in Einstein's light-quantum theory (Wolfke, 1914b, p. 309).$^{854}$

In a paper communicated to the Amsterdam Academy on 31, October 1914, Paul Ehrenfest and Heike Kamerlingh Onnes also came to the same conclusion after giving a simple derivation of Planck's combinatorial formula, which agreed with the probability definition, Eq. (289), of Debye (Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes, 1914).$^{855}$ In an appendix to their paper, they also carefully analyzed the difference between Einstein's hypothesis of '*quanta independent of each other*' and Planck's energy-quanta: 'The difference between Planck and Einstein consists therein that the latter assumes the existence of mutually independent energy-

---

$^{851}$ Natanson thus found for $w_{\nu}$, the expression $(N_{\nu}! / \prod_{i=0}^{p} N_i!)$, which could be rewritten as the right-hand side of Eq. (289).

Ladislas (Władysław) Natanson (1864–1937) studied at St. Petersburg, Cambridge, Dorpat and Graz (where Boltzmann then was). He became a docent at the Jagiellonian University, Cracow, in 1891 and professor of theoretical physics two years later. Initially Natanson was mainly interested in thermodynamics and the kinetic theory of gases. Later on he turned to the theory of electrons and the optical properties of matter. In his last years he pursued the investigation of the basic principles of geometrical optics. He retired from his Cracow chair in 1937.

$^{852}$ M. Wolfke (1883–1947) studied at the Universities of Liège, Paris and Breslau (with Rudolf Ladenburg). During World War I he was *Privatdozent* at the *Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule*, Zurich. In 1921 he was appointed professor of physics and head of the physics department at the Technical University, Warsaw. Wolfke first concerned himself with the problem of optical instruments (e.g., he developed a cadmium–mercury lamp). In his Warsaw time he shifted his interest to low temperature physics and twice visited the cryogenic laboratory at Leyden. During the second visit, in 1928, he discovered the two states of helium together with Willem Hendrik Keesom.

$^{853}$ Wolfke had also considered the relation between his theory of 'light-atoms' and the usual undulatory theory of radiation; he had assumed in particular that 'the light-atoms are formed out of the continuous electromagnetic field, especially when the radiation density falls below a given limiting value' (Wolfke, 1914a, p. 4).

$^{854}$ Krutkow and Wolfke continued the debate in 1914 without presenting really new arguments (Krutkow, 1914b; Wolfke, 1914c).

$^{855}$ Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes considered the probability of the distribution of $N_0, N_1, N_2 \ldots$ (with $\sum_{i=0} N_i = N$) resonators among the 'energy steps' $0, \epsilon (= h\nu), 2\epsilon, \ldots$, with the total energy $P\epsilon (= N_{\nu} f_{\nu} \epsilon)$, arriving at the probability
$$w_{\nu} = \frac{(N - 1 + P)!}{P! (N - 1)!}.$$

560 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

quanta also in empty space, the former only in the interior of matter, in the resonators’ (Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes, 1914; English translation, p. 872). Hence, due to Einstein the number of possibilities of distributing $P$ quanta among $N_1$ or $N_2$ space cells, respectively, were related as $N_1^P$ to $N_2^P$, while Planck claimed it to be $(N_1 - 1 + P)!/(N_1 - 1)! P!$ to $(N_2 - 1 + P)!/(N_2 - 1)! P!$. Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes therefore noted: ‘Planck does not deal with $[P]$ really mutually free [independent] quanta $\epsilon$... The real *object which is counted* remains the number of all different distributions of $N$ resonators over the energy grades [levels] $0, \epsilon, 2\epsilon, \ldots$, with a given total energy $P\epsilon$’ (Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes, *loc. cit.*, p. 873). For example, for $P = 3$ and $N = 2$, Einstein had to count $2^3 = 8$ possibilities, I,..., VIII, of distributing three identical quanta, A, B, C, among two space cells, 1 and 2, as given by the table:

|   | I | II | III | IV | V | VI | VII | VIII |
|---|---|----|-----|----|---|----|-----|------|
| A | 1 | 1  | 1   | 1  | 2 | 2  | 2   | 2    |
| B | 1 | 1  | 2   | 2  | 1 | 1  | 2   | 2    |
| C | 1 | 2  | 1   | 2  | 1 | 2  | 1   | 2    |

However, according to Planck, one would count cases II, III and V as only one possibility because in all these cases the resonator 1 assumed the energy $2\epsilon$ and the resonator 2 the energy $\epsilon$; similarly, cases IV, VI and VII would count as one possibility because in them the resonator 1 assumed the energy $\epsilon$ and the resonator 2 the energy $2\epsilon$. Hence Planck would find only four different possible distributions. Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes concluded: ‘*Planck’s formal device* (distribution of $P$ energy-elements $\epsilon$ among $N$ resonators) *cannot be interpreted in the sense of Einstein’s light-quanta*’ (Ehrenfest and Kamerlingh Onnes, *loc. cit.*, p. 873).$^{856}$

Several years later Wolfke returned to the question of the spatial dependence of ‘light-atoms’ in a paper, entitled ‘*Einscheinsche Lichtquanten und räumliche Struktur der Strahlung*’ (‘Einstein’s Light-Quanta and the Spatial Distribution of Radiation’) and submitted in May 1921 to *Physikalische Zeitschrift* (Wolfke, 1921). In this paper Wolfke separated the energy density of blackbody radiation, $\rho_\nu$, belonging to a given frequency, into ‘partial radiations thermodynamically independent of each other’ (‘*voneinander thermodynamisch unabhängige Teilstrahlungen*’, Wolfke, 1921, p. 376), by expanding it into a sum

$$ \rho_\nu = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \rho_n = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3} \exp\left(-\frac{nh\nu}{kT}\right). \tag{291} $$

Then the partial radiations had the entropy densities $s_n$,

$$ s_n = - \frac{k\rho_n}{nh\nu} \left( \ln \frac{c^3 \rho_n}{8\pi h\nu^3} - 1 \right) \quad (i = 1, 2, \ldots). \tag{292} $$

$^{856}$ That Planck’s radiation law could be obtained only by assuming ‘an association of quanta into double quanta, etc.,’ had been argued already by Abram Joffé of St. Petersburg in a talk given on 27 September 1910 at the Russian Physical Society (Joffé, 1911, p. 550).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0194 -->

V.3  Bose’s Light-Quantum Statistics and Its Extension to Gas Theory                                                                                      561

From Eq. (292) he obtained for $S - S_0$, the entropy change of the partial radiation of type $\rho_n$ and energy $E_n$ when condensed from the initial volume $V_0$ $(= E_n/\rho_n)$ to the smaller volume $V$, the result

$$S - S_0 = \frac{kE_n}{nh\nu} \ln \frac{V}{V_0} . \tag{293}$$

Translated in terms of probabilities—$W_n = (V/V_0)^{E_n/nh\nu}$—Eq. (293) could be interpreted to mean that ‘the cavity radiation, looked at from the point of view of Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis, consists of light-molecules $h\nu, 2h\nu, 3h\nu, \dots$, which are mutually independent in space’ (Wolfke, 1921, p. 378). Wolfke argued that

> *with growing radiation density there occurs an association of light-quanta into increasingly complex molecules, until finally—for very high radiation densities satisfying the Jeans–Rayleigh formula—the quanta agglomerate to form a continuous distribution in space, [while] on the other hand, with decreasing radiation density the radiation continuum dissociates in simpler and simpler light-molecules, until it ultimately dissolves into discrete light-atoms. (Wolfke, 1921, p. 378)*$^{857}$

The assumption of ‘light-molecules’ accounted for the properties of blackbody radiation, but it also led to a new question. What mechanism caused the independent light-quanta or ‘light-atoms’ to agglomerate into ‘light-molecules’? Didn’t one have to assume then the existence of a specific interaction between the light-quanta? However, nobody had any idea about the nature of this interaction. Then, on 2 July 1924, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* received an article, entitled ‘*Plancks Gesetz und Lichtquantenhypothese*’ (‘Planck’s Law and the Light-Quantum Hypothesis’) in which the author, a certain Mr. Bose from Dacca University, India, proposed a derivation of the energy distribution law for blackbody radiation based on Einstein’s original concept of light-quanta without invoking composite ‘light-molecules’ (Bose, 1924a). Albert Einstein, who revealed himself as the translator of Bose’s paper from English into German, pointed out in a note at the end of the paper that: ‘Bose’s derivation of Planck’s formula appears to me to be an important step forward. The method used here gives also the quantum theory of an ideal gas, as I shall show elsewhere. (A. Einstein)’ (Bose, 1924a, p. 181). Who was this Mr. Bose, and how did it come about that an unknown man from distant India had found the solution of a problem which had existed for so long?

Satyendra Nath Bose was born on 1 January 1894 in Calcutta, the son of an employee in the Executive Engineering Department of East Indian Railways.$^{858}$

***

$^{857}$ Further evidence on the formation of composite light-quanta, or ‘light-molecules,’ was presented by Louis de Broglie (1922a, b) and Walther Bothe (1923e).

$^{858}$ Bose’s father, Surendranath Bose, was a trained accountant and held several responsible posts. He was interested in mathematics and science and became one of the founders of a modest chemical and pharmaceutical company. He enjoyed reading philosophy and literature as well. Satyendra Nath was the eldest son; he had six younger sisters. (See the detailed biography of S. N. Bose: Mehra, 1975b.)

After passing high school in 1909, Bose entered Presidency College, Calcutta, enrolling in science courses. Presidency College had excellent teachers, among them the chemist P. C. Ray and the physicist Jagadish Chandra Bose, and was attended by able students. Bose’s contemporary was Megh Nad Saha, who became his friend.859 Bose took the examination for the B.Sc. degree in 1913, and the examination for M.Sc. in mixed mathematics (consisting of astronomy, dynamics, hydrodynamics and several mathematical topics) of Calcutta University in 1915, standing first in both examinations—with Saha in the second place.860 Following their master’s degree examination, Bose and Saha continued their studies in physics and applied mathematics at the newly established University College, Calcutta.861 Although only limited European scientific literature and few advanced books were available at the Calcutta libraries due to war conditions, they obtained effective help from P. J. Brühl, an Austrian instructor at the Bengal Engineering College.862 ‘He possessed a good collection of advanced texts and journals of physics in German. He had Planck’s *Theorie der Wärmestrahlung*, Laue’s *Das Relativitätsprinzip*, as well as papers on quantum theory and relativity,’ Bose recalled. ‘Since Saha and I had learned some German, we were glad to borrow these things from Brühl. Saha chose to study first thermodynamics, statistical mechanics and spectroscopy, while I decided upon electromagnetism and relativity’ (Bose, Conversations, quoted in Mehra, 1975b, p. 120). Thus Bose and Saha, who were teaching advanced courses in the

859 The students at Presidency College had close relations with each other. They had a great interest in the *Swadeshi* (patriotic) movement, which was opposed to the partition of Bengal (declared by Lord Curzon in 1905).
M. N. Saha was born on 6 October 1893 in Seoratali, Dacca District. He studied at Dacca College from 1909 to 1911 and at Presidency College, Calcutta from 1911 to 1915, receiving his M.Sc. degree from the latter in 1915. In 1916 he joined the University College as lecturer. He spent the years from 1919 to 1921 at the Universities of London and Berlin with a scholarship from the University of Calcutta. On his return to India, he became professor of theoretical physics at Presidency College, Calcutta, in 1921; two years later he moved to Allahabad University. In 1927 he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society. In 1938 he returned to Calcutta University as head of the physics department. In 1951 he was elected to the Indian Parliament as an independent member. He died on 16 February 1956 in New Delhi.
Saha’s first important contribution to physics was his work, performed at Imperial College, London, under Alfred Fowler, on thermal ionization of atoms (Saha, 1920). Later he published papers on spectroscopic problems and on nuclear physics, on the propagation of electromagnetic waves in the ionosphere and on radio waves escaping from the sun. As he grew older, he turned more and more to questions of education, industrialization and national planning. He was instrumental in the establishment of the Institute of Nuclear Physics, Calcutta.

860 Although Bose was hindered in his studies by very weak eyesight, he made up for it by a keen intelligence and sharp memory.

861 University College, a part of Calcutta University, was founded in 1914 by Sir Asutosh Mookerji, a judge of the High Court and Vice Chancellor of Calcutta University, with the help of large donations from wealthy people. Bose and Saha approached him with the request to start postgraduate courses; he gave them scholarships to undertake advanced study and research and allowed them to use his own large collection of books on mathematics and physics. As Bose recalled later: ‘I borrowed from him Gibbs’ book [*Elementary Principles of Statistical Mechanics*: Gibbs, 1902] from which I learned about phase space and statistical mechanics’ (Bose, Conversations, quoted in Mehra, 1975b, p. 120).

862 Presidency College, Calcutta, used to subscribe to the *Philosophical Magazine*.

Department of Mathematics since 1917, gradually became acquainted with the more recent status of physics.

After the end of World War I a new source of information opened for them: Debendra M. Bose was appointed to the second endowed chair of physics in Calcutta University, the Rash Behari Ghosh Professorship.$^{863}$ He had been interned in Berlin from 1914 to 1918 and now brought with him many new German publications, such as Planck’s *Festschrift* of 1918, which had been published in the *Naturwissenschaften*.$^{864}$ ‘He gave me Planck’s *Thermodynamik* to read, and I greatly appreciated the logical manner in which Planck deduced the whole of thermodynamics from a limited number of postulates,’ Bose remembered five decades later. ‘We were anxious to learn. Saha could read German fairly well without any help, but I tried to go ahead by doing translations on my own and having them checked by D. M. Bose’ (Bose, Conversations, quoted in Mehra, 1975b, p. 122). At that time the news from Arthur Stanley Eddington’s solar eclipse expedition and the general enthusiasm for Einstein’s relativity theory also reached India. Bose and Saha saw the need for first-hand information and published a collection of papers on relativity in their own translations from German into English: Saha translated Einstein’s paper on special relativity (Einstein, 1905d) and Hermann Minkowski’s paper on the fundamental equations of electromagnetic phenomena in moving bodies (Minkowski, 1908), while Bose translated Einstein’s paper on general relativity (Einstein, 1916c).$^{865}$ Besides

A little later the German collection of papers on relativity, entitled ‘*Das Relativitätsprinzip*’ (fourth edition), was translated into English by W. Perret and G. B.
