V.4 The Phase Waves Associated with Matter 591

small proper mass? There is the objection that the velocity of light would depend on the frequency. However, if the proper mass is extremely small, the dependence will be extremely feeble’ (L. de Broglie, Conversation with F. Kubli, quoted in Kubli, 1971, p. 63). Especially, one had to think of possible effects of the mass of the light-quantum on astronomical observations. These observations seemed to admit a mass below $10^{-45}$ g, but, because of the role of the velocity $c$ in special relativity, de Broglie put the limit still lower. He explored further consequences of the light-quantum mass in his second communication to the Academy of Sciences in Paris, entitled ‘*Quanta de lumière, diffraction et interférences*’ (‘Light-Quanta, Diffraction and Interference,’ L. de Broglie, 1923b).$^{904}$

In this note de Broglie introduced a new description of the wave phenomena, which he had associated with the material particles: he spoke of just one wave motion. But with each light-quantum, for instance, he associated a group of waves having the ‘group velocity’ $v_g$, the same velocity as the massive light-quanta had; the phase velocity of the waves, however, was $c^2/v$, the velocity of propagation of the fictive wave motion, which he now called ‘the phase wave’ (L. de Broglie, 1923b, p. 549). The phenomenon of diffraction, de Broglie continued, implied that the light-quanta did not move in a straight line. Hence one had to replace the usual principles of particle dynamics by the following postulate: ‘At each point of this trajectory, a free particle follows in uniform motion the *ray* of its phase wave, that is (in an isotropic medium), the normal to the surfaces of equal phase’ (L. de Broglie, 1923b, p. 549). With the help of this postulate de Broglie formulated mathematically the conviction, at which he had arrived in summer, that light-quanta and electrons should be considered as particles and waves at the same time. According to the new postulate, he claimed that the motion of the quantum-theoretical particles agreed with the one derived from the usual dynamics of mass-particles (determined by the principle of least action) or of geometrical optics (determined by Fermat’s principle). De Broglie asserted: ‘But if the particle has to pass through a slit, whose dimensions are small in comparison with the wavelength of the phase wave, its trajectory will bend in general like the ray of a diffracted wave’ (L. de Broglie, 1923b, p. 549).$^{905}$ Thus he predicted the diffraction of light atoms ‘however small their number’; that is, any moving particle would be diffracted under suitable conditions. Especially, an electron beam going through a slit would do so, and de Broglie added: ‘It is in this direction that one must look for the experimental confirmation of our ideas’ (L. de Broglie, 1923b, p. 549).

De Broglie interpreted the phase wave as ‘guiding the propagation of the energy’; their very existence allowed him to perform ‘the synthesis of the waves

***

$^{904}$ When he submitted the note of 10 September 1923, de Broglie had already obtained the main result of his second note, for he announced: ‘As of today, we are in a position to explain the phenomena of diffraction and interference by taking into account the light-quanta’ (L. de Broglie, 1923a, p. 510).

$^{905}$ De Broglie stated that in the process of diffraction the momentum of the light particles will not be conserved because they might transfer momentum to the atoms at the border of the slit.

592 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

and the quanta’ (‘la synthèse des ondulations et des quanta,’ L. de Broglie, 1923b, p. 549). The new dynamical description included the previous point dynamics (and its relativistic generalization) as well as geometrical and wave optics. With its help de Broglie now explained the interference patterns in the following way. He assumed that every atom possessed a probability of absorbing a light-quantum, and this probability was determined by the vector describing the phase wave of the light-quantum. If a light-quantum was emitted by an atom, its phase wave tried to establish phase coherence with the phase waves of the light-quanta emitted by other, neighbouring atoms. Hence he concluded that the phase waves of all or many light-quanta emitted by atoms had a tendency to coincide, thereby giving rise to a coupling of the light-quanta, which seemed to result in the formation of ‘light-molecules’—as had been noticed in the analysis of blackbody radiation. Returning to the problem of diffraction, he assumed that the passage of ‘light-atoms’ through a slit was guided by their phase waves. The phase waves were then responsible for the bright and dark fringes emerging in the space behind the slit. Thus the same diffraction pattern should be established as in the wave theory of light, no matter how small the intensity of the incident radiation might be.

In his third note of October 1923, entitled ‘Les quanta, la théorie cinétique des gaz et le principe de Fermat’ (‘Quanta, the Kinetic Theory of Gases and Fermat’s Principle’), de Broglie finally looked at the description of the properties of gases from the point of view of the phase-wave theory (L. de Broglie, 1923c). He declared that his main goal in this work was the justification of Max Planck’s assumption concerning the elementary phase-space regions associated with each atom. For this purpose he considered that with each atom (of proper mass $m_0$ and velocity $v$) was associated a *group of phase waves*, having the *phase velocity* $c^2/v$, frequency $(m_0c^2/h)(1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ and the *group velocity* $v$. Then he made the following assumption: ‘The state of the gas will be stable only if the waves corresponding to all the atoms form a system of stationary waves’ (L. de Broglie, 1923c, p. 630). That is, he took over the treatment, which Lord Rayleigh and especially James Jeans had applied to radiation in thermal equilibrium: they had considered the stationary modes in a given volume.$^{906}$ De Broglie also took over Jeans’ method of counting the number of stationary waves of a given frequency interval, $\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$, contained in a unit volume; he found this number to be $n_{\nu} d\nu$, where

$$n_{\nu} d\nu = \frac{4\pi}{v(c^2/v)^2} \nu^2 d\nu = \frac{4\pi v}{c^4} \nu^2 d\nu. \qquad (324)$$

By substituting the relation between $\nu$ and $w$, the kinetic energy of the gas atoms

---
$^{906}$ James Jeans had applied such a treatment in several papers around 1910 (e.g., Jeans, 1910) as well as in his report at the first Solvay Conference in 1911, which Louis de Broglie knew in detail.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0226 -->

V.4  The Phase Waves Associated with Matter                                                              593

(i.e., $h\nu = w + m_0c^2$), he rewrote Eq. (324) as

$$n_{\nu} d\nu = \frac{4\pi}{h^3} m_0^2 c (1 + \alpha) \sqrt{\alpha(\alpha + 2)} \ dw, \qquad (324')$$

where $\alpha = w/m_0c^2$. Now each wave could transport either zero, or one, or several atoms, their number being determined by the canonical (temperature) distribution. Hence the number of atoms, connected with the phase wave of energy $h\nu$ and having kinetic energy in the interval $w$ and $w + dw$, in a volume element of the six-dimensional phase space became

$$dn_w = (\text{const.}) \frac{4\pi}{h^3} m_0^2 c (1 + \alpha) \sqrt{\alpha(\alpha + 2)} \cdot \frac{\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n \exp(-nh\nu/kT)}{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \exp(-nh\nu/kT)} \ dw \ dx \ dy \ dz. \qquad (325)$$

For small values of $\alpha$, i.e., in the nonrelativistic approximation, all terms except the first in the sum in the numerator on the right-hand side might be neglected, and de Broglie rediscovered Planck's result for gas atoms.$^{907}$ In the case of light-quanta, however, $\alpha$ was always large; hence one had to sum over all terms on the right-hand side of Eq. (325).

At the end of his short paper, de Broglie reformulated his ideas in a still more accurate manner. He assumed that a phase wave was associated with any particle, being in phase with the particle at any space-point and having its frequency and velocity determined by the energy and velocity of the particle. These phase waves should especially have the property that: 'The rays of the phase waves coincide with the trajectories [which are] dynamically possible' (L. de Broglie, 1923c, p. 632). In a situation with variable dispersion—for example, in the case where light-quanta were diffracted by a dispersive medium—de Broglie claimed that the rays of the phase wave must be described by the (optical) principle of Pierre de Fermat, which he formulated as the condition for the path integral extending between two space points, that is,

$$\delta \int \frac{v \ dl}{(c^2/\nu)} = \delta \int \frac{m_0 v}{h \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} \ dl = 0. \qquad (326)$$

$^{907}$He found, in particular,

$$dn_w = \text{const.} \frac{4\pi}{h^3} m_0^{3/2} \sqrt{2w} \exp(-\frac{w}{kT}) \cdot dx \ dy \ dz.$$

(See, for instance, Planck, 1921b, Section 132.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0227 -->

594 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

Fermat’s principle coincided with Pierre de Maupertuis’ principle of least action. ‘The fundamental link which unites the two great principles of geometrical optics and of dynamics is thus also brought clearly to light,’ de Broglie concluded proudly. He further pointed out that certain among the dynamically possible trajectories of quantum-theoretical trajectories are distinguished as being ‘in resonance with the phase wave’ (L. de Broglie, 1923c, p. 632). Thus, for instance the Bohr orbits of electrons were such resonance trajectories; they were determined by the fact that the integral over the closed path, $\oint v \, dl/(c^2/v)$, took an integral value.

With the three communications to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, in fall 1923 Louis de Broglie had presented the main ideas of his unified dynamics of light-quanta and atoms. De Broglie was confident enough about his results that he submitted them also in English in a paper, entitled ‘A Tentative Theory of Light Quanta’ and published in the *Philosophical Magazine* (L. de Broglie, 1924a).<sup>908</sup> At the end of the paper, which appeared in the February issue, de Broglie summarized his results as follows:

In the present paper it is assumed that the light is essentially made up of light-quanta, all having the same extraordinarily small mass. It is shown mathematically that the Lorentz–Einstein transformation joined with the quantum relation leads us necessarily to associate motion of body and propagation of wave, and that this idea gives a physical interpretation of Bohr’s analytical stability conditions. Diffraction seems to be consistent with an extension of Newtonian Dynamics. It is then possible to save both the corpuscular and the undulatory characters of light, and, by means of hypotheses suggested by the electromagnetic theory and the correspondence principle, to give a plausible explanation of coherence and interference fringes. Finally, it is shown why quanta must take a part in the dynamical theory of gases and how Planck’s law is the limiting form of Maxwell’s law for the light-quanta gas. (L. de Broglie, 1924a, p. 457)

He claimed that though the ideas may be criticized and undergo further changes in the future, the ‘real existence of light-quanta’ should not be doubted. ‘Moreover,’ he stated finally, ‘if our opinions are received, as they are grounded on the relativity of time, all the enormous evidence of the “quantum” will turn in favour of Einstein’s conceptions’ (L. de Broglie, 1924a, p. 457).

One of the changes, which de Broglie found appropriate to introduce later on, was the systematic relativistic formulation of the relation between the energy of the particle and the frequency of the wave. He suggested the first steps already in a postscript added in proof to his paper in the *Philosophical Magazine* (L. de Broglie, 1924a, pp 457–458). There he defined a four-dimensional vector $O_{\mu}$,

<sup>908</sup>De Broglie’s paper was communicated to the *Philosophical Magazine* by Ralph Fowler. C. D. Ellis, a guest from Cambridge, who had worked with Maurice de Broglie in Paris in 1923 on the photoelectric effect, had encouraged de Broglie to write the paper and had corrected the translation. We should mention here that Louis de Broglie had already presented an outline of his ideas earlier in *Nature*, in a letter entitled ‘Waves and Quanta,’ dated 12 September and published in the issue of 13 October 1923 (L. de Broglie, 1923d).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0228 -->

V.4 The Phase Waves Associated with Matter 595

whose time component was equal to the frequency $\nu$ of the phase wave divided by $c$, and whose space components were the components of a vector of magnitude $\nu$ over the phase velocity (or $\lambda^{-1}$) drawn along the ray of the phase waves. He connected this four-dimensional phase vector to the four-momentum vector $J_{\mu} (= (W/c, p_x, p_y, p_z))$ of the particle by the equation

$$J_{\mu} = h 0_{\mu} \quad (\mu = 0, 1, 2, 3). \tag{327}$$

He presented this relation again in his note ‘Sur la définition générale de la correspondance entre onde et mouvement’ (‘On the General Definition of the Correspondence between Wave and [Particle] Motion’), submitted in the beginning of July 1924 to the Academy of Sciences, Paris (L. de Broglie, 1924b). Especially, he considered in it how the phase wave propagated (i.e., in the direction normal to the plane of equal phases) and how the motion of the phase wave was related to the motion of the particle. Thus he arrived at the equations

$$E = h \nu \quad \text{and} \quad p = \frac{h \nu}{v_{\text{ph}}} = \frac{E}{v_{\text{ph}}}, \tag{327'}$$

where $p$ denoted the momentum of the particle at a given point in the direction of the tangent to its trajectory, and $v_{\text{ph}}$ the phase-wave velocity in the same direction (which was also the direction of the ray of the phase wave). With the help of the Hamiltonian equation of motion, he also proved that $v$, the velocity of the particle, was equal to $v_g$, the group velocity of the phase wave, because

$$v = \frac{dx}{dt} = \frac{\partial W}{\partial p} = \frac{\partial \nu}{\partial (\nu/v_{\text{ph}})} = v_g. \tag{328}$$

At that time, in summer 1924, Louis de Broglie received some support from his Paris colleague Léon Brillouin in dealing with the light-quantum theory. Brillouin studied the reflection and refraction of radiation in a note, presented by his father to the Academy of Sciences in Paris on 19 May 1924, and showed that the usual behavior of radiation (i.e., the behaviour due to classical electrodynamics) could be obtained by applying Maupertuis' principle of minimum action to light-quanta (L. Brillouin, 1924). In the course of this investigation he also found the second Eq. (327').$^{909}$ De Broglie himself returned to the problem of interference in fall 1924. In a note, communicated to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, on 17 November 1924, he

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0229 -->

596 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

theory (L. de Broglie, 1924c)—in which de Broglie showed that the correspondence between the transition frequencies of atoms and the classical radiation frequencies could be deduced from the dynamics of the phase waves connected with the electrons in the neighbouring orbits of higher quantum numbers—were the last ones which de Broglie published in 1924. During the same year, however, he also completed his doctoral thesis, an important piece of work bearing the title ‘*Recherche sur la théorie des quanta*’ (‘Investigations on the Theory of Quanta’) (L. de Broglie, 1924e, 1925).

As de Broglie remarked many years afterwards, he began to write the thesis immediately after publishing the three notes in *Comptes Rendus* in September and October 1923 (L. de Broglie, Conversations).<sup>910</sup> In summer 1924 he had completed the work and had it printed (L. de Broglie, 1924e), so that it was ready for his doctoral examination, which was held on 25 November 1924 at the Sorbonne. The thesis was also published in the January–February 1925 issue of *Annales de Physique* (L. de Broglie, 1925). In his thesis Louis de Broglie attempted to present a systematic and logical report on the results, which he had obtained during the previous years. He organized the material in an historical introduction, seven chapters and one appendix. By the time de Broglie began to write the thesis, he was already thirty-one years old and had pondered about the problems for over ten years. The historical introduction described the perspective in which he wished to place his own studies: namely, the development of the main physical theories since the Renaissance, in a line with the principal ideas created by such men as Newton, Maupertuis, Hamilton, Maxwell, Boltzmann and Gibbs in mechanics, as Fermat, Huygens and Fresnel in optics, as Volta, Ampère, Faraday, Maxwell and Lorentz in electrodynamics, as Lorentz, FitzGerald and Einstein in relativity theory, and as Planck and Einstein in quantum theory. After describing the results of quantum theory, he pointed to the main problems and difficulties which had remained in this theory: namely, the fundamental nature of the quantum conditions of Bohr and Sommerfeld and the simultaneous corpuscular and undulatory nature of radiation, which seemed to have renewed the historic debate between Newton and Huygens. He concluded:

> In short, the moment seems to have arrived to try to make an effort with the goal of uniting the corpuscular and the undulatory points of view and thus penetrating a bit into the real nature of quanta. This is what we have done recently, and the main goal of the present thesis is to present a more complete treatment of the new ideas which we have proposed, of the successes to which they have led, and also of the many gaps they still contain. (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 30)

<sup>910</sup> Léon Brillouin, in his interviews for the *Archives for the History of Quantum Physics*, recalled that de Broglie had begun to compose his thesis already in 1920 and that the printing took a long time. He probably had in mind the earlier versions of the thesis; after all, de Broglie had started to think about his thesis before World War I.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0230 -->

V.4 The Phase Waves Associated with Matter

597

In Chapter **One** de Broglie discussed the phase wave and its properties. He introduced the energy–frequency relation (314) and derived from it the existence of the wave motions with the two frequencies $\nu$ and $\nu_1$, given by Eqs. (318) and (319); by requiring agreement of the phases of the two waves at all times, he arrived at the phase wave, as he had shown in his notes of 1923 (L. de Broglie, 1923a, b, c). He showed, in particular, that one could connect two velocities of propagation with the phase wave, the so-called phase velocity and group velocity (denoting the velocity of groups of phase waves), and proved the equality of the group velocity and the velocity of the particle, with which the phase waves were associated. (See the content of the paper, L. de Broglie, 1924a, discussed above.)

The hypothesis of the phase wave connected with all material particles enabled de Broglie, in Chapter **Two**, to enter into an analysis of two fundamental dynamical principles: the principle of Maupertuis and the principle of Fermat. Although they had been used earlier to describe different phenomena of mechanics and optics, respectively, de Broglie demonstrated that both could be applied alternatively to describe the dynamics of just one object: the quantum-theoretical particle. For this purpose he first formulated Maupertuis' principle of particle dynamics as

$$\delta \int_{A}^{B} \sum_{i=1}^{f} p_i \, dq_i = 0, \tag{329}$$

where $p_i$ and $q_i$ ($i = 1, \dots, f$) denoted the momentum and position variables of a given system (of $f$ degrees of freedom) and the integral extended from the initial state (position) A to the final state B. For a relativistic particle the principle read

$$\delta \int_{P}^{Q} \sum_{\mu=0}^{3} J_{\mu} \, dx^{\mu} = 0 \quad (\mu = 0, 1, 2, 3), \tag{329'}$$

where $J_{\mu}$ is the four-momentum of the particle and $P$ and $Q$ are two points in the four-dimensional space. Second, he wrote Fermat's principle, Eq. (326), similarly in the relativistic form,

$$\delta \int_{P}^{Q} \sum_{\mu=0}^{3} 0_{\mu} \, dx^{\mu} = 0, \tag{326'}$$

where the phase-wave four-vector $0_{\mu} = (\nu / c, -(\nu / v_{\text{ph}}) \cos(x, \mathbf{l}), -(\nu / v_{\text{ph}}) \cos(y, \mathbf{l}), -(\nu / v_{\text{ph}}) \cos(z, \mathbf{l}))$, where $\mathbf{l}$ denoted a position vector in the three-dimensional space (hence $|\mathbf{l}| \cos(x, \mathbf{l}) = l_x, |\mathbf{l}| \cos(y, \mathbf{l}) = l_y, |\mathbf{l}| \cos(z, \mathbf{l}) = l_z$) describing the direction of the ray of phase waves. Now he assumed the validity of the quantum-theoretical equation (327) connecting the particle's four-momentum vector $J_{\mu}$ with the phase-wave vector $0_{\mu}$. Comparing then, the content of the two dynamical principles, he concluded: 'Fermat's principle applied to the phase

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0231 -->

598  
Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

wave is identical to Maupertuis’ principle applied to the [moving] particle; the dynamically possible trajectories of the particle are identical with the possible rays of the wave’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 56).

In the following chapters de Broglie drew certain consequences from his dynamical theory of quanta. Thus, in Chapter Three, he studied the stability of electron orbits in atoms, and presented in some detail the ideas contained in his note of 10 September 1923 to the Academy of Sciences, Paris (L. de Broglie, 1923a). Especially, he showed how the quantum condition for multiply periodic systems followed from the assumption that the electrons in atoms were accompanied by phase waves. When the electron moves in a closed orbit, de Broglie argued, its phase wave should behave analogously to a wave of a fluid in a closed channel of finite length $l$. A stationary situation will exist in the channel filled with the fluid only in the case of ‘resonance,’ i.e., when an integral multiple of the wavelength of the fluid motion, $n\lambda$, is equal to $l$. De Broglie now imposed the same resonance condition on the phase wave of the electron in the atom, writing it in a form involving the integral of Fermat’s principle ($\int dl/\lambda$ with $\lambda = v_{\text{ph}} / v$) as

$$ \oint \frac{v}{v_{\text{ph}}} dl = \frac{l}{\lambda} = n, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots , \qquad (330) $$

where the line integral on the left-hand side extended over the closed path of the electron in the atom. By applying the relation between Fermat’s and Maupertuis’ principles—i.e., by replacing the integral, $\oint (v/v_{\text{ph}}) dl$, up to a constant factor by the integral, $m_0 \oint v_g dl$, de Broglie arrived at Bohr’s quantum condition for the circular orbits in the hydrogen atom. Finally, he proved that, in the case of a multiply periodic system the resonance condition for the phase wave led to several quantum conditions: for that purpose he first showed that the sum of the phase integrals had to be an integral multiple of Planck’s constant $h$ (see, e.g., Eq. (323)); the phase-wave resonance condition then implied that each individual phase integral became an integral multiple of $h$.

In Chapter Four, de Broglie treated the problem of the relativistic hydrogen atom. There occurred a special difficulty in that problem, for one did not know how to distribute the electrostatic energy between the hydrogen nucleus and the electron. De Broglie, therefore, proposed to assign to the electron an effective mass, $m_e - \alpha P / c^2$, and to the nucleus an effective mass, $M - (1 - \alpha) P / c^2$, with $-P$ denoting the potential energy, $m_e$ and $M$ the rest masses of the electron and the hydrogen nucleus, respectively, and $\alpha$ a constant between 0 and 1. He estimated the maximal effect caused by the change of the electron’s rest mass on $R$, the Rydberg constant of the hydrogen atom, as calculated from the method due to Bohr; he found $\delta R / R \sim 10^{-5}$, a correction which was several orders of magnitude smaller than the usual corrections (due to the motion of the nucleus) considered so far. Neglecting the mass correction, de Broglie then applied his resonance condition, Eq. (330), to the relativistic hydrogen atom and obtained

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0232 -->

V.4  The Phase Waves Associated with Matter
599

the equation

$$\frac{2\pi m_e \omega (R + r)^2}{\sqrt{1 - (M / (m_e + M))(v^2 / c^2)}} \left( 1 - \frac{\omega R}{v} \right) = nh, \quad (331)$$

where $\omega$ is the angular velocity and $v (= (R + r)\omega)$ the velocity of the centre of mass of the system, which he assumed to move on a circle of radius $R + r$ ($r$ and $R$ being the radii of the motions of the electron and the nucleus, respectively). In the nonrelativistic limit ($v \ll c$), the condition (331) passed over into the one used by Bohr in 1913 (i.e., $2\pi m_e (M / (M + m_e)) \omega (R + r)^2 = nh$, see Bohr, 1913d).

In Chapter Five, de Broglie presented his theory of light-quanta, which he assumed to be—as in his previous publications (L. de Broglie, 1922b, 1924a)—particles having an extremely small mass $m_0$ and, in contrast to electrons (which he pictured to be spherically symmetric objects), possessing ‘an axis of symmetry corresponding to the polarization’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 77).<sup>911</sup> They should propagate with a frequency-dependent velocity $v$, where

$$v = c \sqrt{1 - \frac{m_0^2 c^4}{h^2 \nu^2}} . \quad (332)$$

From the known measurements of the velocity of propagation of radio waves having wavelengths of several kilometres, de Broglie concluded that the mass of the light-quanta had to be less than $10^{-44}$ g. Then he discussed several results of the wave theory of radiation and compared them with the ones found from the new theory, especially the Doppler effect and the reflection from a mirror; in all cases no difference showed up. Further, the same relation between the pressure of blackbody radiation and its energy density (i.e., $p = \frac{1}{3} \rho$) could be obtained as in classical theory. Finally he treated qualitatively the phenomena of interference and coherence of radiation and demonstrated that Bohr’s frequency condition of atoms was consistent with his theory.

De Broglie devoted the following Chapter Six to problems of the interaction of X- and $\gamma$-rays with matter. After discussing the classical theories of Joseph John Thomson and Peter Debye describing the passage of radiation through matter, and the light-quantum theories of Arthur Compton and Debye describing the Compton effect, he proposed a generalization of the Compton–Debye theory by treating the collision of light-quanta with electrons having a finite initial energy. To the individual collision processes, involving a light-quantum of initial frequency $\nu_1$ and an electron of initial velocity $v_1$, he applied the laws of energy and momentum conservation and found for $\nu_2$, the frequency of the scattered

***

<sup>911</sup> De Broglie proposed to consider the light-quantum like a ‘doublet of the electromagnetic theory,’ without specifying this concept further; he just noted that he expected a profound modification of the electromagnetic theory in the future (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 77).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0233 -->

600 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; **Chapter V &nbsp; The Problems of Radiation Theory**

light-quantum, the equation

$$
\nu_2 = \nu_1 \frac{1 - (\nu_1/c)\cos\theta_1}{1 - (\nu_1/c)\cos\phi + (2h\nu_1/m_ec^2)\sin^2(\theta/2)\sqrt{1 - v_1^2/c^2}} , \tag{333}
$$

where $\theta_1$ and $\phi$ denoted the angles between the directions of the incident and outgoing light-quanta and the initial velocity of the electron, respectively, and $\theta$ the angle of the scattered light-quantum with respect to the incident one. In the case of the zero initial velocity of the electron ($v_1 = 0$), de Broglie rediscovered the Compton–Debye formula for the frequency of the scattered light-quantum, while in the case of negligible Compton effect ($h\nu_1/m_ec^2 \ll 1$) he confirmed the result from the classical scattering of X-rays, i.e., the Doppler effect.

In the final Chapter Seven, de Broglie developed the statistical mechanics of quantum-theoretical objects (light-quanta and atoms). After reporting the main results of classical kinetic gas theory and Planck's theoretical extensions of them, he showed that certain modifications were brought into the description by taking into account the hypothesis of phase waves and relativistic effects. The concept of the phase waves, he declared, demanded a new interpretation of the statistical equilibrium of gases. Thus he stated: 'We are naturally led to consider—as in the conception of blackbody radiation developed by Mr. Jeans—the phase waves constituting the stationary systems (that is, which resonate within the dimensions of the cavity) as being the only stable ones; they alone enter into the investigation of thermodynamic equilibrium' (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 110). That is, he assumed that in the gas there existed systems of stationary phase waves having phase velocities ($c^2/v$) of the order of $9 \times 10^{15}$ cm/s for gas atoms with thermal velocities ($v$) of the order of $10^5$ cm/s. These phase waves then established a certain coherence in the behaviour of quantum-theoretical gas atoms, in spite of the fact that they (i.e., the atoms) could move in space in a rather irregular way. For nonrelativistic velocities of the gas atoms the wavelength $\lambda$ of the phase waves followed from the equation

$$
\lambda = \frac{c^2/v}{m_0c^2/h} = \frac{h}{m_0v} , \tag{334}
$$

where $m_0$ is the rest mass of the gas atoms. If an atom of the gas was allowed to move a linear distance $l$, the resonance condition implied that an integral multiple of $\lambda$ be equal to $l$; as a consequence, the thermal velocity of the gas atom would also assume a value that is an integral multiple of $v_0 = h/m_0l$. By applying this consideration to a gas contained in a three-dimensional volume, de Broglie reproduced the results of his earlier paper on the quantum theory of gases (L. de Broglie, 1923c). He also discussed again the theory of blackbody radiation and concluded that the phase-wave hypothesis implied a general statistical dependence of quantum-theoretical particles. He gave the following reason: 'If two or several atoms possess phase waves which superpose exactly,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0234 -->

V.4  The Phase Waves Associated with Matter  

601  

and thus one can say that they are transported by the same wave, then their motions cannot be considered as being entirely independent of each other; hence these atoms should not be treated as independent objects in the calculus of probability’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 116). That is, the phase wave, if associated with several atoms, gave rise to a certain coherence of their motions.  

Since the elementary object in statistical mechanics thus appeared to be the stationary phase wave, de Broglie had to define the concept of an elementary stationary phase wave. He did so by constructing a stationary wave from the superposition of two waves of the same frequency $\nu$, the same wavelength $\lambda$, and the same phase constant $\phi_0$, propagating in opposite directions, say by adding $\sin[2\pi(\nu t - x/\lambda + \phi_0)]$ and $\sin[2\pi(\nu t + x/\lambda + \phi_0)]$. In light-quantum theory, then, an elementary stationary wave was defined as such a superposition, where the frequency was chosen from a given infinitesimal interval $\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$. Each elementary stationary phase wave could now transport $0, 1, 2, \dots$, etc., ‘light-atoms’ of frequency $\nu$. By applying, at a given temperature $T$, a canonical distribution to the light-quanta, de Broglie found that the number of light-quanta described by an elementary stationary phase wave could be obtained from Eq. (325). This equation then yielded Planck’s radiation formula. Further, he derived Einstein’s expression for the energy fluctuation of blackbody radiation.$^{912}$  

Finally, in an appendix, de Broglie examined a special difficulty of the massive light-quantum hypothesis. If one calculated the velocity of light-quanta having frequencies below $\nu_0 = m_0c^2/h$ from Eq. (332), it turned out to have an imaginary value. In order to avoid such an undesirable consequence, he proposed to associate with a particular phase wave a mass $\mu_0$, dependent on the number of light-quanta it described simultaneously; on taking $\mu_0 = m_0$ for one light-quantum and $\mu_0 = 0$ for an infinite number of light-quanta, the difficulty disappeared. He admitted that, ‘the preceding hypothesis somewhat destroys the simplicity of the conception of “quanta of light,”’ but argued that ‘this simplicity surely cannot be entirely maintained if one would like to find an accord between the electromagnetic theory and the discontinuity revealed by the photoelectric phenomena’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 124). In any case, he added finally: ‘It must be acknowledged that the real structure of radiant energy still remains very mysterious’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 125).  

With his thesis, Louis de Broglie had tried to formulate consistently all of his ideas about what he considered to be the essentials of quantum theory. These essentials implied the existence of finite, discrete ‘isolated bits of energy’ (‘morceau isolée d’énergie,’ L. de Broglie, 1925, p. 69), which had been introduced by Planck and Einstein, and the necessity of which had been emphasized by Henri Poincaré in his last essays (Poincaré, 1912a, b).$^{913}$ From the very beginning  

$^{912}$ The grouping of light-quanta achieved by stationary waves demanded that the energy density of blackbody radiation, $\rho_\nu d\nu$, should be written as $\sum_{p=1}^{\infty} n_{p,\nu} (ph\nu) d\nu$ and the energy fluctuation, $\overline{\epsilon^2}$, as $\sum_{p=1}^{\infty} n_{p,\nu} (ph\nu)^2 d\nu$, with $n_{p,\nu} = (8\pi h\nu^2/c^3) \exp(-ph\nu/kT)$.  

$^{913}$ As we have mentioned earlier, L. de Broglie had read Poincaré’s books and articles in the beginning of his studies, and they had influenced his later choice to study science.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0235 -->

602 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Problems of Radiation Theory

of his involvement in quantum theory, de Broglie had adopted Einstein’s light-quantum hypothesis and had looked for some sort of unification of the dynamical description of light-quanta with that of atoms and electrons. This unification, which he had achieved by endowing the light-quantum with a mass, and considering it as a particle moving with relativistic velocity, had enabled him to approach the fundamental question posed by Henri Poincaré already at the first Solvay Conference in 1911: Can one construct a suitable dynamics of quanta? De Broglie had succeeded in doing so by inverting the method, through which Einstein had obtained the light-quantum; that is, he had associated with all material particles a wave motion. This phase-wave hypothesis allowed him indeed to formulate the principles of a new, quantum-theoretical dynamics describing particles and light-quanta. While the applications of the new dynamics seemed to reproduce all the good results derived so far in quantum theory, he was aware that he had not answered an important question concerning the physical interpretation of his theory. ‘I have intentionally left quite vague the definitions of the phase wave and the periodic phenomenon, as well as of the light-quantum,’ de Broglie noted in concluding his thesis, and added: ‘The present theory should therefore be considered rather as a scheme whose physical content is not fully defined, than as a consistent doctrine which is definitely established’ (L. de Broglie, 1925, pp. 127–128).

The principal results of de Broglie’s doctoral thesis had become known in France (especially through the publication of his earlier notes in the *Comptes Rendus*) even before he formally presented it. After all, members of the Academy of Sciences of Paris, such as the experimentalists Jean Perrin and Henri Deslandres had communicated these notes. Perrin was also the chairman of the committee which examined Louis de Broglie at the Sorbonne on 25 November 1924; the other three members were the mathematician Élie Cartan and the physicists Charles Victor Mauguin and Paul Langevin. They all found that the candidate gave an elegant presentation of his ideas and defended his thesis quite well. Langevin, who had formally supervised and accepted the thesis, emphasized in his report on it—besides the originality of the thoughts—the fact that de Broglie had been capable ‘of having pursued with remarkable mastery an effort aimed at overcoming the difficulties which encumbered the physicists’ (Langevin, quoted in Tonnelat, 1966, p. 28). In spite of the good impression which de Broglie left on the members of the committee, and in spite of the fact that his scientific work was well known, he did not entirely convince his examiners of his ideas.<sup>914</sup> As Mauguin recalled nearly thirty years later:

> At the time of the defence of the thesis, I did not believe in the physical reality of the waves associated with the particles of matter. Rather I regarded them [the

***

<sup>914</sup> Francis Perrin, son of Jean Perrin, recalled later: ‘I think Mauguin and my father had looked through the paper, before the thesis was expounded. Langevin had thoroughly studied it and probably my father had spoken with Langevin, maybe, already before the day of the exposition of the paper’ (F. Perrin, AHQP Interview, 12 January 1963, p. 2).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0236 -->

V.4  The Phase Waves Associated with Matter                                                         603

waves] as very interesting objects of imagination, which allowed one—for the first time—to avoid the completely empirical character of the quantization rules, providing the latter with a simple, almost familiar, interpretation analogous to the laws of vibrating strings. (Mauguin, 1953, p. 434)

Nevertheless they let de Broglie pass the examination.
Francis Perrin described many years later the main difficulty, which had stood in the way of the acceptance of the phase-wave hypothesis, as follows:

> At that time Louis de Broglie had spoken of the fact that when an electron hits a target it gives X-rays and so we are more or less used to this transformation of particles into waves. But it was obvious that the wavelength of the X-rays connected with an electron [in the production of X-rays by electron impact] was quite different from the wavelength associated by de Broglie to the particle itself. So this argument of this easy production of waves by collision and transformation of momentum into production of X-rays was not at all a good connection between waves and matter particles. (F. Perrin, AHQP Interview, 12 January 1963, p. 2)

Another question concerned the experimental consequences following from the assumption of the matter waves. As Francis Perrin recalled: ‘At the *soutenance de thèse* [defence of the thesis] my father asked de Broglie if there could be some real experimental verification of his ideas. And Louis de Broglie stated at that time that maybe diffraction of particles through very narrow slits could be observed and show the existence of waves associated with the particles’ (F. Perrin, *loc. cit.*, p. 1). After the doctoral examination de Broglie tried to persuade the experimentalists to investigate the problem. He recalled later one of these efforts: ‘I suggested to Mr. Dauvillier—who was a very skillful experimenter, well versed in electronics at that time—to attempt the experiment, but being absorbed in other researches he did not do it’ (L. de Broglie, Conversations; AHQP Interview, 7 January 1963, p. 6).

Paul Langevin was not so much bothered about the direct experimental consequences. He rather admired the theoretical consistency of de Broglie’s idea about matter waves. As Francis Perrin recalled later, Langevin remarked at that time: ‘It is really this intrinsic invariance relation of the formulation of relativity which seems to me very coherent and true in showing that it is something [fundamental]’ (F. Perrin, *loc. cit.*, p. 1). Langevin’s opinion was shared by Albert Einstein, whom he considered to be a very high authority. Louis de Broglie recalled Einstein’s involvement with pleasure:

> I had my thesis typed and had naturally given one copy to Mr. Langevin, so that he could prepare his oral report of it. One day Mr. Langevin wrote to me—or telephoned—and said: “I spoke to Einstein about your thesis and it interested him; he would like to have a copy, do you have a typewritten one?” I told him: “Yes, luckily I had three copies made, and I do have one.” Well, I sent him a copy, which he forwarded to Einstein. (L. de Broglie, Conversations; AHQP Interview, 7 January 1963, p. 7)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0237 -->

604 | Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

Einstein’s reaction was very favourable, and he wrote to Langevin: ‘He [de Broglie] has lifted a corner of the great veil’ (‘*Er hat eine Ecke des großen Schleiers gelüftet*,’ Einstein to Langevin, 1924; quoted by Kubli, 1971, p. 28). Einstein wrote in greater detail to Hendrik Lorentz about de Broglie’s work: ‘A younger brother of the de Broglie known to us [i.e., Maurice] has made a very interesting attempt to interpret the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantization rules (Paris Dissertation, 1924). I believe that it is the first feeble ray of light to illuminate this, the worst of our physical riddles. I have also discovered something that supports his construction’ (Einstein to Lorentz, 16 December 1924). Einstein’s very positive and friendly interest in de Broglie’s work convinced Langevin of its value. Einstein, however, did more: he advocated de Broglie’s ideas in his second communication to the Prussian Academy on the quantum theory of an ideal gas; he showed that the phase-wave hypothesis supported the quantum statistics of S. N. Bose and himself, thus providing another evidence of the correctness of Louis de Broglie’s ideas (Einstein, 1925a). Einstein’s paper then served to acquaint many physicists outside France with de Broglie’s work. We shall discuss the important consequences of Einstein’s involvement in the next section.

### V.5 The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925

The early 1920s had brought forth an increasing concern on the part of the physicists with the problems of radiation theory. Several dozens of papers appeared each year, especially after the discovery of the Compton effect, dealing with the peculiar quantum effects of radiation. The description of radiation ranged from a purely classical one—in which one tried to account for ‘needle radiation’ by constructing very concentrated pulses from the electromagnetic wave theory (Oseen, 1922), or by obtaining completely new types of solutions of Maxwell’s field equations (Bateman, 1923)—to the extreme light-quantum point of view.$^{915}$ Quite a few studies were devoted to clarifying, for example, the question of whether the motion of light-quanta was directed, as Einstein had assumed, or not. Thus Gregory Breit treated the Brownian motion of a resonator in equilibrium with blackbody radiation and showed that the radiation need not be emitted unidirectionally, provided it was not strictly monochromatic (Breit, 1923c).$^{916}$ Other authors concerned themselves with the dimension, i.e., the

***

$^{915}$ Among the attempts to derive the typical quantum effects of radiation without explicitly introducing any quantum hypothesis, one should also count the work of H. Tetrode, Albert Einstein and Kornel (Cornelius) Lanczos, who investigated generalized field theories of electricity and matter (Tetrode, 1922; Einstein, 1923d; Lanczos, 1925b).

$^{916}$ Later discussions on the directedness of light-quanta occurred in the papers of Ralph de Laer Kronig (1924) and Edmund Stoner (1925a), who pleaded the case for unidirectional light-quanta. On the other hand, Pascual Jordan in his thesis tried to explain the quantum-theoretical interaction between radiation and matter without assuming a directed emission of radiation from atoms (Jordan, 1924).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0238 -->

V.5 The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925

spatial extension of light-quanta.$^{917}$ The nature of radiation was thus a favourite subject of discussion among the physicists in the mid-1920s.

In the beginning of 1925 these efforts had led to several different proposals to describe radiation in connection with atomic theory. First, there was Einstein's original light-quantum theory of 1905, according to which radiation of frequency $\nu$ assumed the form of individual, statistically independent and concentrated energy packets of size $h\nu$ and—as later required—a directed momentum $h\nu/c$; this theory perfectly explained the Compton effect (Compton, 1923b, Debye, 1923) and to some extent the equilibrium between radiation and matter (Pauli, 1923b; Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1923). Second, there existed the light-quantum theory of Satyendra Nath Bose, in which the author had modified the statistical behaviour of light-quanta; it yielded immediately Planck's law of blackbody radiation without further assumptions (Bose, 1924a). Third, there was available the light-quantum theory of Louis de Broglie, in which the light-quanta possessed a small mass and an associated phase wave (L. de Broglie, 1923a, 1924a, 1925); as a consequence the light-quanta could not be considered in all situations as statistically independent particles.$^{918}$ Fourth, there existed a number of theories which completely avoided the light-quantum concept, and in which one sought to explain the observed quantum effects of radiation—such as the photoelectric effect or the Compton effect—by a peculiar coupling of classically described radiation and matter, whose structure was determined by quantum theory: the most well-known theory of this type was the one of Niels Bohr, Hendrik Kramers and John Slater, which implied that energy and momentum conservation should be valid only on the statistical average, i.e., in processes in which a large number of atoms participate, but not in individual atomic processes (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924).$^{919}$ Fifth, and finally, there were the—so far preliminary—attempts to describe radiation in a modified classical field theory of electrodynamics (see, e.g., Tetrode, 1922; Bateman, 1923), or of electrodynamics and matter (see, e.g., Einstein, 1923d).

$^{917}$Especially, Leonard Salomon Ornstein of Utrecht and his student Herman Carel Burger tried to obtain, in a series of papers (Ornstein and Burger, 1924a, b, c), information on the 'sphere of action' ('*Wirkungssphäre*') of light-quanta by considering the interaction of radiation and electrons. Ornstein and Burger claimed that only with extended light-quanta—whose radius they found to be of the order of their wavelength—would one arrive at Planck's law of blackbody radiation, a conclusion which was contradicted by Wolfgang Pauli (1924b). Erich Marx of Leipzig then attempted to derive the result of Ornstein and Burger from the classical electron theory by calculating the emission of radiation from electrons having the 'oscillation volume' ('*Schwingungsvolumen*'); he thus arrived at about the same dimension of the light-quanta as given by Ornstein and Burger (Marx, 1924).

$^{918}$A very different concept of a massive light-quantum, to which some aspects of the classical radiation theory were attached, was proposed by Frank W. Bubb; after analyzing the photoelectric effect and the production of X-rays, he suggested that the light-quantum possessed a vector property, which derived from classical electrodynamics (Bubb, 1924).

$^{919}$Among the same class of theories one may also count the proposal of Arthur Compton to obtain the results of William Duane's theory of the reflection of X-rays from crystals by using a general quantum postulate to describe the situation (Compton, 1923f; see our discussion in Section V.3).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0239 -->

606
Chapter V  The Problems of Radiation Theory

The opinions among the physicists concerning the various radiation theories differed widely. While many of those who worked on the theory of atomic structure felt sympathetic toward the theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater, others, like Einstein, Pauli and Sommerfeld opposed it vigorously.⁹²⁰ Thus Sommerfeld stated in the fourth edition of *Atombau und Spektrallinien*, published in 1924, that 'Bohr rejects the extreme quantum structure of light more definitely than we permit ourselves to do' (Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. 59). Pauli, who, for a short time, after a visit to Copenhagen in spring 1924, had been won over to support the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory, turned completely against it in the fall of the same year. At the 88th *Naturforscherversammlung*, which took place in Innsbruck from 21 to 27 September 1924, he had encountered a number of physicists, especially Einstein, who shared his doubtful attitude, and a few days later he wrote to Bohr about Einstein’s and his own objections against the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory. Einstein was convinced, as Pauli wrote, that the statistical energy conservation in atomic processes would lead to systematic violations of the first law of thermodynamics in the course of time; that the conservation of energy and momentum was satisfied for all known elementary processes; and that ‘the wave properties of light come about as a secondary, indirectly produced effect’ (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924). Pauli stated that he himself did not believe, in the first place, in a specific consequence of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory: namely, the implication that there existed two types of resonance (or fluorescence) radiation, one type emitted by excited atoms and the other type emitted by nonexcited atoms. ‘I am firmly convinced,’ he wrote, ‘that nothing in reality corresponds to this distinction, and that, in principle, there exists no experiment which allows one to separate the parts contributed by the excited and the unexcited atoms, respectively’ (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924).⁹²¹ In Pauli’s opinion, the two types of radiation, if they existed, would also contradict the correspondence principle, and he said:

> Therefore (i.e., on account of the connection with the classical theory) I do not believe in a reasonable possibility to distinguish between Compton jumps and the real quantum jumps in a given line. The scattering processes connected with frequencies lying within or outside the frequencies of a spectral line are distinguished only by the *average* time of duration of the atom in the excited state. For a state far removed from the excited state, this time is of the order of the period of oscillation (Compton process); however, for the spectral line it is of the order of $10^{-8}$ sec (real quantum jump). Since these are *average* duration periods, there exists no possibility of distinguishing between two types of processes in the spectral line. (Pauli to Bohr, 2 October 1924)

---
⁹²⁰ The physicists, who favoured the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory included Max Born, Erwin Schrödinger, Rudolph Ladenburg and Gustav Mie.

V.5 The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925
607

Although many physicists criticized the fact that in the radiation theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater energy and momentum were not strictly conserved, they did not subscribe necessarily to a light-quantum theory. Moreover, not enough time had yet elapsed for physicists in general to become familiar with the new statistical concepts of the Indian physicist S. N. Bose, albeit they had been advocated by Einstein, and one did not think much of—or did not read—the papers of Louis de Broglie in the *Comptes Rendus*. Thus there prevailed a certain freedom of opinion; many physicists interested in the radiation problem developed their own points of view, either on the basis of the light-quantum concept or of classical wave theory.${}^{922}$

While the speculations about possible radiation theories ran high, experiments were lacking which could decide between them. Einstein, as we have mentioned earlier (in Section V.1), had devised such an experiment in 1921, but it failed to give the desired result. Two years later Georg Joos proposed to prove the existence of directed light-quanta by observing the flashes caused by the impact of $\alpha$-particles on a scintillation screen (Joos, 1923).${}^{922a}$ A test of another property of quantized radiation, namely, the concentration in small spatial regions, was proposed—also in 1923—by George Paget Thomson, son of J. J. Thomson; he studied the interference properties of the $H_\beta$-line emitted by moving hydrogen canal rays after passing through two consecutive slits, but observed no deviation predicted on the basis of the classical wave theory (G. P. Thomson, 1923).${}^{923}$ Since at that time the Compton effect stood clearly in favour of the light-

---
${}^{922}$Among those, who discarded the light-quantum theory completely, belonged James Jeans (Jeans, 1924). In order to avoid the light-quantum he constructed, for example, in his Rouse Ball Lecture on 11 May 1925, a different method to yield the Compton effect formula, Eq. (277), except that the factor multiplying $\sin^2(\theta/2)$ was not exactly $2h\nu_0/m_e c^2$ (Jeans, 1926). At about the same time, Joseph John Thomson developed a peculiar model of radiation: based on his earlier idea of tubes of electric force, he constructed a vortex-ring model of the light quantum; he even obtained with suitable assumptions the quantum-theoretical energy for the vortex light-quantum (Thomson, 1924). Thomson's model was further discussed by Edmund T. Whittaker, who developed a proper mathematical description of it (Whittaker, 1926), and by Thomson himself, who used it to account for the Compton effect (Thomson, 1925). While Jeans, Thomson and Whittaker applied quantum theory only to determine certain factors in their calculations, F. Russell Bichowski of Johns Hopkins University proposed (in a talk at the Washington meeting of the American Physical Society at the end of December 1924) to modify Maxwell's equations by using quantum-theoretical terms; thus he managed to preserve an undulatory description even when having quantum-theoretical energy packets (Bichowski, 1925).

${}^{922a}$Much earlier, Geoffrey Ingram Taylor had performed another important experiment, which seemed to decide at that time clearly in favour of the classical wave theory of light (Taylor, 1909). He had studied the interference pattern arising from the passage of light of very low intensity—such that the incident light ray should consist only of few quanta according to the light-quantum theory—through two slits; and he had found an interference pattern identical with the one observed with light of strong intensity.

${}^{923}$A similar experience was made three years later by Einstein, who proposed to investigate the coherence properties of the radiation emitted by canal rays, in order to find out whether they could be described by classical electrodynamics or not (Einstein, 1926a). Then Joos analyzed Einstein's suggestion and pointed out that it would not allow one to arrive at any decision (Joos, 1926). Einstein agreed with Joos' conclusion later (Einstein, 1926b), and finally the experimental investigation of Emil Rupp also confirmed the result (Rupp, 1926b).

quantum hypothesis, the experimental situation appeared to be very confusing. Evidently, radiation exhibited some properties of the light-quantum, but one could ask the question whether the assumption of directed light-quanta really corresponded to reality. Many people thought that perhaps a closer analysis of the Compton effect might provide the key for a decision about the true nature of radiation. Then, in summer 1923 two authors published peculiar cloud-chamber photographs exhibiting a new type of tracks caused by the passage of X-rays through air. One of them was Charles Thomson Rees Wilson, who had just perfected his cloud-chamber method for operation at small time intervals; he interpreted the new tracks as recoil electrons in the Compton effect (C. T. R. Wilson, 1923).^924 Shortly before Wilson's paper appeared in the *Proceedings of the Royal Society*, the *Zeitschrift für Physik* published a two-page note of Walther Bothe, entitled ‘*Über eine neue Sekundärstrahlung der Röntgenstrahlen*’ (‘On a New Secondary Radiation of X-Rays,’ Bothe, 1923b).^925 Bothe thought at first that the new type of secondary radiation (manifesting itself in the cloud-chamber tracks) consisted of hydrogen ions; in a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 9 November 1923, he recognized them—like Wilson—as recoil electrons from the

^924 C. T. R. Wilson was born on 14 February 1869 at Glencorse near Edinburgh. He was educated at Owens College, Manchester, from 1884 to 1888 (where he took mainly biology because he wanted to become a physician) and at the University of Cambridge (1888–1894, where he changed to chemistry and physics; 1895–1896, M.A. in 1896). In 1895 he joined the Cavendish Laboratory. Five years later he was made a Fellow of Sidney Sussex College and University Lecturer at Cambridge. He became Reader of Electrical Meteorology in 1918 and Jacksonian Professor of Natural Philosophy in 1925 at Cambridge University. Wilson retired in 1934; he died on 15 November 1959 in Carlops, near Edinburgh.

Starting from the observation of the optical phenomena seen when the sun shone on the clouds surrounding the hilltop, especially the coloured rings surrounding the sun (coronas) or surrounding the shadow cast by the hilltop or observer on mist or clouds, which he duplicated in the laboratory (in early 1895), Wilson developed the cloud chamber to demonstrate the tracks of ionizing radiations (X-rays in 1895, α- and β-particles in 1911). He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society already in 1900 and received the Hughes Medal (1911), the Royal Medal (1922) and the Copley Medal (1935) of the Royal Society. He shared with Arthur Compton the 1927 Nobel Prize in Physics.

^925 Walther Wilhelm Georg Bothe was born on 8 January 1891 at Oranienburg, near Berlin. He studied physics at the University of Berlin from 1908 to 1912. In 1913 he joined the *Physikalisch-Technische-Reichsanstalt*, where he remained until 1930 (1913–1920, assistant; 1920–1927, scientific member; 1927–1930, a supervisory position). He obtained his doctorate under Planck in 1914. Bothe spent a year as a prisoner of war in Siberia during World War I (he returned from Russia in 1920). He became *Privatdozent* at the University of Berlin in 1925; he was promoted to an extraordinary professorship in 1929. Then, in 1930, he was called to an ordinary (i.e., full) professorship at the University of Gießen; in 1932 he succeeded Philipp Lenard as professor of physics and director of the institute of physics and radiology at the University of Heidelberg. In 1934 he became director of the physics institute at the *Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für medizinische Forschung* in Heidelberg, a position which he kept until his death. Simultaneously, he was honorary professor (1934–1946) and ordinary professor (1946–1957) at the University of Heidelberg.

Bothe worked on various problems of experimental and theoretical atomic and nuclear physics. After contributing to the clarification of the properties of radiation (mainly in collaboration with Hans Geiger), he turned to study cosmic rays (with Werner Kolhörster) and nuclear processes. In Heidelberg he built a cyclotron in the 1930s. During World War II he worked on the theory of neutron diffusion. For his pioneering work on the coincidence method, and the discoveries he made with it, he was awarded—together with Max Born—the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics. Bothe died in Heidelberg on 10 February 1957.

609

Compton effect (Bothe, 1923d). He investigated the phenomenon further with the ionization method (Bothe, 1923f).
At that time Bothe was very interested in finding evidence for a non-wave-like behaviour of radiation. For this purpose he especially analyzed the photoelectric effect theoretically (Bothe, 1923c) and experimentally (Bothe, 1924b), and also concerned himself with the properties of cavity radiation (Bothe, 1923e) and the equilibrium of radiation with matter (Bothe, 1924a).<sup>926</sup> On the basis of all this work he also turned into a strong supporter of the light-quantum interpretation of the Compton effect.
The experiments of Wilson and Bothe could not be considered as a complete verification of the light-quantum hypothesis. In his second paper on the recoil electrons, Bothe admitted: ‘The confirmation of Debye’s quantum theory is not exact; for this purpose it would be especially necessary to use monochromatic X-rays’ (Bothe, 1923f, p. 253).<sup>927</sup> Although Wilson, for the explanation of his recoil electrons, referred to Compton’s theoretical ideas (Compton, 1922d), the question remained open whether his results could not be described just as well by the theory of Charles Galton Darwin, according to which the incident radiation was scattered like a spherical wave in all directions (Darwin, 1922). In order to decide between Darwin’s theory and the light-quantum theory (of Compton and Debye), Arthur Compton and John Charles Hubbard (of New York University) proposed to analyze the maximum energy of the recoil electrons and the relative number of observed recoil electrons to photoelectrons. They arrived at the following result: ‘Both from the standpoint of the experimental evidence and from internal consistency of the theory *we therefore seem forced to the conclusion that each quantum of scattered X-rays is emitted in a definite direction*’ (Compton and Hubbard, 1924, p. 449). Compton and Hubbard’s conclusion in favour of the light-quantum theory was based on counting the number of recoil electrons producing a track of given length in the cloud chamber. That is, they made a statistical evaluation of the data and were not able to exclude, say, the theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater. For that purpose one had to observe the scattering process involving individual electrons and radiation. Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger announced the programme for such an experiment in a short note, entitled ‘*Ein Weg zur experimentellen Nachprüfung der Theorie von Bohr, Kramers und Slater*’ (‘A Method of Testing Experimentally the Theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater’), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 7 June 1924 and published shortly afterwards (Bothe and Geiger, 1924).
Bothe and Geiger opened their note with the remark:

According to the conceptions held so far concerning the process of scattering (Compton, Debye), one might think of an experimental arrangement by means of

610 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

which the simultaneous appearance of a scattered radiation quantum and its associated recoil electron can be detected. Let $h\nu$ be the primary and $h\nu'$ the secondary radiation quantum and $e$ the recoil electron. If one places in each of the two paths of $h\nu'$ and $e$ a device that counts numerically, then both of them will be activated simultaneously. According to the most recent views of Bohr, Kramers and Slater such a time-dependent connection should not exist. (Bothe and Geiger, 1924, p. 44)

Bothe and Geiger claimed that such an experiment seemed to be feasible with the help of two counters, of which one registered the recoil electron and the other the scattered radiation. Admittedly, the number of counts in the second chamber was small, because only the scattered radiation passing through it would give rise to a count. ‘This, however, does not have any significance,’ they argued, ‘if one only succeeds in deciding whether there exists at all a statistical dependence between the two sequences of counts.’ Hence one had to construct an apparatus which allowed one to decide clearly whether the two counts coincided or not. If, however, there existed ‘with certainty a dependence between the two series of counts,’ any statistical interpretation of energy and momentum conservation must be excluded (Bothe and Geiger, 1924, p. 44).

The idea of testing the consequences of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory had occurred to Walther Bothe, who had followed the literature on radiation theory carefully. In order to perform the crucial experiment, however, he secured the help of Hans Geiger, then director of the radiation laboratory of the *Physikalisch-Technische-Reichsanstalt*. Geiger had pioneered the methods of counting radioactive particles during his Manchester years with Ernest Rutherford; in 1913 he had developed a particularly suitable instrument, the needle counter, to register $\alpha$- and $\beta$-particles (Geiger, 1913).$^{928}$ This so-called Geiger counter, therefore, enabled one also to detect even X-rays because of their ionization property—for they created electrons, which caused a discharge in the gas (air) filling the volume of the counter; thus it was *the* tool to investigate both the recoil electrons and the scattered radiation in the Compton effect. Thirty years later Bothe described the experimental setup in the following words:

> Our arrangement consisted of two needle counters, past the common front wall of which, without touching it, swept a beam of X-rays. The X-ray beam travelled in a hydrogen atmosphere; the Compton processes occurred in the one counter which indicated the recoil electrons, whereas only the scatter[ed] quanta were able to penetrate into the other counter and actuated it by electron release with very much lower probability. The readings of both counters were recorded side by side on a moving paper chart. This way we succeeded after a few failures to establish the

$^{928}$The needle counter consisted of a cylindrical metallic vessel, in the centre of which—isolated from the vessel—a needle-shaped wire was mounted. A charged particle passing through the apparatus then caused a discharge between the needle and the vessel (which was charged to a potential of about 1200 V).

accuracy of any temporal "coincidence" between the two pointer readings as being $10^{-4}$ sec. Film consumption however was so enormous that our laboratory with the films strung up for drying sometimes resembled an industrial laundry. (Bothe, Nobel Lecture, 1954; Bothe, 1964, p. 272)

The Bothe–Geiger experiment soon yielded a result. On 15 January 1925 Max Born wrote to Niels Bohr: "The other day I was in Berlin. There everybody was talking about the result of the Geiger–Bothe experiment, which decided *in favour* of light-quanta. Einstein was exultant."<sup>929</sup> He added, however, that he was not yet completely convinced and also that the experimentalists "themselves do not still regard their results as being final" (Born to Bohr, 15 January 1925). Three months later the experimentalists *were* sure, and on 18 April 1925 Bothe and Geiger sent a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, in which they gave a preliminary report on the outcome of the experiment. They stated:

> Under ideal experimental conditions, according to Compton and Debye, with each *hν*-count [in counter 2] there should occur simultaneously an *e*-count [in counter 1]. In reality, due to the unavoidable imperfect experimental conditions, one could expect only one coincidence for every 10 *hν*-counts, as extra experiments actually showed. On the other hand, coincidences should practically be excluded according to Bohr's views [i.e., the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory]. The experiments yielded one coincidence per 11 counts approximately, after deducting the counts expected purely accidentally . . . Our experiments, therefore, decide in favour of the older conception [i.e., the light-quantum theory]. (Bothe and Geiger, 1925a, p. 441)<sup>930</sup>

They gave a report on the details of the experiment in a paper, entitled "Über das Wesen des Comptoneffekts; ein experimenteller Beitrag zur Theorie der Strahlung" ("On the Nature of the Compton Effect; An Experimental Contribution to the Theory of Radiation"), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 25 April 1925 and published in the issue of 12 June 1925 (Bothe and Geiger, 1925b). In this paper Bothe and Geiger concluded with all the necessary clarity:

> The experiments described here are not in agreement with Bohr's interpretation of the Compton effect . . . However, not only with respect to the Compton effect, but also in general, the result obtained above seems to present very great difficulties for Bohr's new radiation theory, because the interpretation of the Compton effect has been connected by Bohr, Kramers and Slater most closely with the statistical view of energy and momentum conservation, on which this new theory is based. One must therefore reasonably well assume that the concept of the light-quantum

<sup>930</sup> The main reason for the success of the experiment was the fact that Bothe and Geiger were able to determine the coincidences sharply; for this purpose they had reduced the dead time of the counter from $10^{-2}$ s to $10^{-3}$ s and the accuracy of the measurement to $10^{-4}$ s.

possesses a higher degree of reality than admitted in this theory. (Bothe and Geiger, 1925b, pp. 662–663)<sup>931</sup>

Shortly after the publication of the Bothe–Geiger paper in *Zeitschrift für Physik*, there appeared a paper in the *Physical Review* of September 1925; it bore the title ‘Directed Quanta of Scattered X-rays’ and its authors were Arthur H. Compton and Alfred W. Simon, then a National Research Fellow at the University of Chicago (Compton and Simon, 1925c). Compton and Simon had investigated experimentally a problem—which had been mentioned already in November 1923 by William Francis Gray Swann of Yale University in a conversation with Niels Bohr and Arthur Compton—i.e., the question how the individual scattered X-rays were connected with the recoil electrons. With the help of a cloud chamber they had photographed both the scattered X-rays and the recoil electrons. In the introduction of their paper, Compton and Simon summarized their results by stating: ‘Of the last 850 plates, 38 show both recoil tracks and *β*-tracks [produced by scattered X-rays]. The angles projected on the plane of the photographs were measured and it was found that in 18 cases, the direction of the scattering is within 20° of that to be expected if the X-ray is scattered as a quantum so that energy and momentum are conserved during the interaction between the radiation and the recoil electron’ (Compton and Simon, 1925c, p. 289). This number, they argued, was four times larger than what would be expected if the scattered radiation proceeded in expanding waves. Hence they concluded: ‘These results do not appear to be reconcilable with the view of the statistical production of recoil and photoelectrons proposed by Bohr, Kramers and Slater. They are, on the other hand, in direct support of the view that *energy and momentum are conserved during the interaction between radiation and individual electrons*’ (Compton and Simon, 1925c, p. 299).<sup>932</sup>

The experiments of Bothe and Geiger and of Compton and Simon, which demonstrated beyond doubt the strict energy- and momentum-conserving coupling of light-quanta and electrons in the Compton effect, were considered generally to be an ultimate disproof of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation. Thus even Bohr, who had been informed by Hans Geiger in a letter, dated 17 April 1925, of the final result of the Bothe–Geiger experiment, remarked in a letter to Ralph Fowler: ‘Just in this moment I have received a letter from Geiger, in which he tells, that his experiment has given strong evidence for

<sup>931</sup>At the end of their third paper, Bothe and Geiger proposed another experiment to check the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory *versus* the light-quantum theory: if a substance is excited by incident radiation to emit fluorescence radiation, and one analyzes the fluorescence radiation in two separated parts of space, then one should register—according to the classical theory—coincidences of the radiation in the separated space volumes; in the light-quantum theory such coincidences would not occur. Bothe carried out the experiment, again using two Geiger counters, and observed that no coincidence happened (Bothe, 1926).

<sup>932</sup>Compton and Simon had started their experiment already a year earlier. They first reported their preliminary results at the American Physical Society meeting in Ann Arbor, 28–29 November 1924 (Compton and Simon, 1925a). Then they published a paper containing the content of the talk in the March 1925 issue of the *Physical Review* (Compton and Simon, 1925b).
