V.5  The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925  613

the existence of a coupling in the case of the Compton-Effect. It seems that there is nothing else to do than to give our revolutionary efforts as honourable a funeral as possible' (Bohr to R. Fowler, 21 April 1925). Pauli's reaction was much happier, and he wrote to Hendrik Kramers: 'At any rate, I consider it to be enormously lucky that the view of Bohr, Kramers and Slater has been refuted so quickly by the beautiful experiments of Geiger and Bothe as well as the recently published [results] of Compton' (Pauli to Kramers, 27 July 1925). The physicists accepted the new situation that energy and momentum were indeed conserved in processes of interaction between radiation and electrons. However, this did not mean that everybody immediately accepted the light-quantum hypothesis. Especially, Bohr and his collaborators still remained skeptical.$^{933}$ After all, the light-quantum theory suffered from its own difficulties. It was evident, from the numerous investigations of Einstein, Wolfke, Louis de Broglie and Bothe, that the light-quanta could not be considered as independent objects in the sense of statistical mechanics, and this lack of mutual independence seemed to lead to a serious conceptual problem. The problem had several aspects: it included the question of the indistinguishability of individual light-quanta and of electrons or atoms, as well as the relation between particles and waves.

As long as atoms and radiation were treated by means of classical mechanics and electrodynamics, respectively, the problem whether individual atoms of one type could be distinguished or not did not play an important role. However, this situation changed with the advent of quantum theory, in which the methods of statistical mechanics were applied to heat radiation. In the derivation of the law of blackbody radiation, Planck had considered the statistical distribution of $N$ indistinguishable energy packets $h\nu$ among $P$ distinguishable resonators in a cavity: that is, in counting the number of possibilities to obtain a given distribution of energy, Planck had not worried about which of the $N$ energy packets was taken by a given resonator (Planck, 1900f). Later authors, like S. N. Bose, who interpreted the energy packets of Planck as light-quanta, had taken over the assumption of indistinguishability in the case of the light-quanta (Bose, 1924a). In the early extensions of the quantum theory to gases—calculating, for example, the chemical constant of atoms and molecules—Otto Sackur and H. Tetrode had also assumed individual atoms and molecules of one type to be indistinguishable (Sackur, 1911, Tetrode, 1912); and Planck had done the same in his theory of the monatomic gas (Planck, 1916b). This procedure then stimulated a controversy in the early 1920s. In a paper on the 'Deduction of the Dissociation Equilibrium from the Theory of Quanta and a Calculation of the Chemical Constant Based on This,' communicated in February 1920 to the Amsterdam Academy of Sciences, Paul Ehrenfest and his student Viktor Trkal analyzed the previous derivation of chemical constants and concluded: 'It is not an accident that it is always the same point that remains obscure in these theories, viz., how an expression of the $N^{-N}$ (Sackur) or $(N!)^{-1}$ (Tetrode) can be forced into the

$^{933}$ Gustav Mie, for example, developed a modified form of the Bohr-Kramers-Slater theory, in which energy and momentum were fully conserved as in the light-quantum theory (Mie, 1925a, b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0247 -->

614

Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

“thermodynamic probability $W$” in order to obtain an admissible value for the entropy’ (Ehrenfest and Trkal, 1920, pp. 162–163). That is, they criticized the fact that Sackur and Tetrode, as well as Planck, had always divided the expression calculated for the probability of a distribution of atoms or molecules among the elementary phase-space regions by a factor $N!$, $N$ being the number of identical particles considered.

Paul Ehrenfest, who had been a student of Ludwig Boltzmann’s and knew the statistical methods very well, could not agree with the above step. Therefore, he and Trkal evaluated, e.g., the probability for a mixture of gases, consisting of $N_1$ molecules of type 1, $N_2$ molecules of type 2, etc., without dividing the final result by the product of factors $N_1!$, $N_2!$, etc. They observed that their method did not change the previous results concerning the equilibrium distribution in gases, whose molecules can dissociate into two or more atoms. However, the chemical constant of the molecules was determined by the chemical constant of the atoms only up to an additive constant. This fact in turn did not worry Ehrenfest and Trkal because they claimed that the additive constant led to no physical implication, provided one used the entropy-probability relation in the form

$$S_{\mathrm{I}} - S_{\mathrm{II}} = k \ln \frac{W_{\mathrm{II}}}{W_{\mathrm{I}}} \qquad (335)$$

that is, one only considered the entropy differences accompanying the transitions between two states I and II.

Ehrenfest and Trkal’s paper, of which a shortened version was published in *Annalen der Physik* (Ehrenfest and Trkal, 1921), stimulated a response from Planck. In an article, submitted in October 1921 also to *Annalen der Physik*, he argued that Ehrenfest’s criticism was not justified (Planck, 1922a). To prove his assertion, Planck considered a system (a model) of $N$ gas molecules and calculated its entropy due to the procedure of Ehrenfest and Trkal; he found that in this way ‘one obtains each elementary region of the gas model not once but $N!$ times, because due to the similarity of the atoms two states of the model—which are distinguished only insofar as two or several atoms have exchanged their coordinates or momenta—are physically completely identical’ (Planck, 1922a, p. 371). Thus one had to introduce the quotient $N!$ in the expression for the probability.

Planck’s method of counting identical particles in quantum statistical mechanics also helped to resolve a puzzle that had existed in kinetic gas theory for a while, the so-called ‘Gibbs’ paradox.’ J. Willard Gibbs, in the last paragraph of his *Elementary Principles of Statistical Mechanics*, had considered two adjacent volumes, separated by a removable wall and filled with a gas of the same type under the same conditions (of temperature and pressure); if the gas in the two volumes was allowed to mix, he had claimed, its entropy would not change, as would happen in the case of two different gases. The paradox consisted in the observation that the entropy increase, caused by the diffusion of different molecules into the adjacent volume, disappeared suddenly when one replaced the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0248 -->

V.5 The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925  
615  

different molecules by molecules of the same type. Then Walter Schottky pointed out in a paper, submitted in October 1920 to *Physikalische Zeitschrift*, that Gibbs' paradox should not be considered as a real problem in physics since one could not transform molecules of one type *continuously* into molecules of another type (Schottky, 1921). However, there still remained a question about the mixing of two identical gases: if the same gas in the two volumes was not under the same conditions, i.e., their respective molecules possessed different velocity distributions, then the entropy would increase in the diffusion process; if the velocity distributions were the same, the entropy would not change. How could one explain this fact? Planck addressed himself to the peculiar problem of Gibbs' paradox in his note '*Über die freie Energie von Gasmolekülen mit beliebiger Geschwindigkeitsverteilung*' ('On the Free Energy of Gas Molecules Having Arbitrary Velocity Distribution'), which he communicated to the Prussian Academy in March 1922 (Planck, 1922b). He showed that the paradox was removed in quantum theory in the following way: If one started with two adjacent volumes containing molecules of *very different velocity distributions* and then combined the two volumes, then the diffusion process would cause the entropy to increase; if, however, one considered the diffusion process in the case that the velocity distributions in the two originally separated volumes were only a little different, such that two molecules in the volumes 1 and 2 had velocities $v_1$ and $v_2$, lying within a small, but finite interval, $v$ and $v + \Delta v$—the finiteness of the interval comes about because of the finiteness of the elementary phase cells—then the entropy would remain constant, due to the fact that *two neighbouring molecules having velocities in the interval $v$ and $v + \Delta v$ must be regarded as not being distinguishable from each other*.  

Planck based his detailed discussion of Gibbs' paradox on his treatment of the quantum theory of monatomic gases of 1916 (Planck, 1916b). In a paper presented to the Prussian Academy in February 1925, he developed a new approach to gas theory (Planck, 1925a).<sup>934</sup> As he argued in the introduction to the paper, the new approach was necessitated by the result of the Stern–Gerlach experiment, which implied that there existed preferred paths in the phase space, in contrast to his earlier assumption. Planck took the new situation into account and found for $F$, the free energy of a gas consisting of $N$ atoms of mass $m$ in a volume $V$ at temperature $T$, the expression

$$
F = -kTN \ln \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \exp\left[ -\sigma(n - \alpha)^{2/3} \right], \tag{336}
$$

where

$$
\sigma = \frac{h^2}{2mkT} \left( \frac{3N}{4\pi eV} \right)^{2/3} \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \leqslant \alpha \leqslant 1, \tag{336a}
$$

---

<sup>934</sup> In the years between 1922 and 1925 Planck returned again and again to problems of statistical mechanics: thus he treated the statistics of heat radiation in three papers (Planck, 1923b, c; 1924a) and statistical aspects of Bohr's atomic theory in another paper (Planck, 1924b).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0249 -->

616 Chapter V The Problems of Radiation Theory

$k$ being Boltzmann's constant, $h$ Planck's constant, and $e$ the base of natural logarithm. From Eq. (336) the laws of monatomic gases followed immediately. Thus, for small values of $\sigma$ (for a gas under normal conditions, $\sigma$ is of the order of $10^{-4}$), Planck derived the equation of state,

$$pV = kTN \left[ 1 - \frac{(\alpha - \frac{1}{2})h^3 N}{(2\pi m k T)^{3/2} eV} \right]. \quad (337)$$

Hence for $\alpha = \frac{1}{2}$ the same equation of state resulted as on the classical theory, while for $\alpha = 0$ and $\alpha = 1$ (the latter corresponded to the case of no zero-point energy) deviations showed up. For large values of $\sigma$ only the first term ($n = 1$) contributed to the sum in the expression for the free energy (Eq. (336)); and for $\sigma = \infty$ a zero-point pressure of $p_0 = (h^2/3m)(3/4\pi e)^{2/3} N^{5/3}(1 - \alpha)^{2/3}$ was obtained, together with the entropy zero, in agreement with Nernst's theorem.

In deriving his new gas theory, Planck emphasized the assumption that each quantum cell ('*Quantenzelle*,' Planck, 1925a, p. 50) associated with a gas consisting of $N$ identical atoms was represented by $N!$ elementary cells of size $h^3$ in phase space ('*Urzellen*') because a permutation of two atoms having different points in phase space did not affect the (macroscopic) state of the gas. This was the same assumption, which had entered into his earlier quantum theory of monatomic gases, and which Ehrenfest and Trkal had attacked later. In summer 1925 Erwin Schrödinger discussed the implication of Planck's assumption in a paper, which was communicated by Planck to the Prussian Academy (Schrödinger, 1925d).$^{935}$ Schrödinger analyzed the different definitions of the entropy of an ideal gas and came to the interesting conclusion that Planck's assumption concerning the indistinguishability of atoms of the same type led 'almost *inevitably* to that definition of the entropy for the ideal gas, which recently A. Einstein [1924c; 1925a, b] and soon afterwards, apparently independently, A. Schidlof [1924] tried to introduce, based on a type of statistics which—on first inspection—looks rather strange' (Schrödinger, 1925d, pp. 436–437). To prove his assertion, Schrödinger argued as follows: If the atoms could be permuted, without consequences for the probability and the entropy of a given state, then it did not suffice to divide the number of possible realizations of that state, calculated by the classical method, just by $N!$—as Planck had done; rather, one had to count each distribution of atoms among phase cells (where $N_1$ were in cell 1, $N_2$ in cell 2, etc.) only once, independent of the possibilities of representing it by different permutations of the atoms.$^{936}$ Only for higher temperatures, when all $N_i$ were either 0 or 1, could Planck's procedure of dividing by $N!$ be justified, and then Einstein's and Planck's theories would coincide.

$^{935}$Schrödinger, in a previous paper on the degeneracy of gases, had supported the point of view taken by Ehrenfest and Trkal (Schrödinger, 1924a).

interval) and $z_\nu ( = (8\pi\nu/c^3)V\Delta\nu)$ is the corresponding number of quantum cells in the volume $V$. And he found the result,

$$\frac{\overline{\epsilon_\nu^2}}{n_\nu^2} = \frac{1}{n_\nu} + \frac{1}{z_\nu} , \tag{339}$$

for the energy fluctuation $\overline{\epsilon_\nu^2} ( = \overline{(E_\nu\Delta\nu - \overline{E_\nu\Delta\nu})^2} )$.

Einstein interpreted the fact that an equation similar to Eq. (339) described the energy fluctuation of an ideal monatomic gas as follows:

> The square of the average relative fluctuation of the molecules is composed additively of two terms. Only the first of these would be present if the molecules were independent of each other. To it is added the contribution of the average square fluctuation, which is totally independent of the average molecular density and is determined only by the elementary region $\Delta E [= E_\nu\Delta\nu]$ and the volume. One can interpret it, also in the case of gases, by associating with the gas a radiation phenomenon in a suitable manner and computing its interference fluctuations. (Einstein, 1925a, p. 9).⁹⁴⁰

This interpretation, Einstein continued, connected to the idea developed by Louis de Broglie in a ‘very remarkable work’—Einstein referred to de Broglie’s doctoral thesis (1924e)—i.e., to the assumption that with each material particle (atoms, molecules, electrons) a scalar wave field should be associated. After outlining the main properties of de Broglie’s phase waves, Einstein went on to say: ‘I have convinced myself by calculation that $1/z_\nu$ is the average square fluctuation of this wave field, insofar as it corresponds to the energy region $\Delta E [= E_\nu\Delta\nu]$ investigated above’ (Einstein, 1925a, p. 10). The wave motion connected with atoms and molecules then did resolve Gibbs’ paradox, as Einstein concluded:

> In order that two wave trains can interfere appreciably, they must have almost the same $v$ [group velocity] and $\nu$ [the frequency of the phase wave]. The wave fields associated with two gases having markedly different molecular masses cannot, therefore, interfere with each other appreciably. From this one may conclude that, on the theory presented here, the entropy of a gas mixture adds up exactly as on the classical theory, at least so long as the molecular weights of the components are somewhat different from each other. (Einstein, 1925a, p. 10)

The radiation described by the theories of de Broglie and Einstein did not have the properties of usual wave radiation. Paul Ehrenfest pointed out an important difference in a paper, entitled ‘*Energieschwankungen im Strahlungsfeld oder Kristallgitter bei Superposition quantisierter Eigenschwingungen*’ (‘Energy Fluctuations in a Radiation Field or a Crystal Lattice with Superposed Quan-

V.5 The Status of the Radiation Problem in 1925
619

tized Eigenoscillations’) and submitted in August 1925 to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Ehrenfest, 1925a). Ehrenfest treated there the question whether the radiation described by the statistics of Bose and Einstein was the same as the one obtained from a superposition of characteristic vibrations or eigenoscillations in a cavity, whose energy was quantized. Einstein, in his discussion of the energy fluctuations occurring in blackbody radiation, had assumed that the entropy of radiation in a large volume $V$ could be obtained by adding up the entropies in the partial volumes, $V_1, V_2, \dots$, etc. (Einstein, 1909a). He also made the same assumption of entropy addition in his new statistical theory (Einstein, 1925a). Now, in the wave theory of radiation, Max von Laue had shown that entropy addition did not hold in the case that radiation in several—or all—parts of a volume was coherent (Laue, 1906; 1907a, b). Consequently, Leonard Salomon Ornstein and Frits Zernike had claimed in a paper, contributed in 1919 to the Amsterdam Academy of Sciences, that the radiation considered by Einstein did not correspond to a superposition of quantized eigenoscillations in a cavity (Ornstein and Zernike, 1919). In 1925 Ehrenfest supported this conclusion by a detailed calculation. He first calculated the energy fluctuations of radiation consisting of a superposition of quantized eigenoscillations in a cavity, i.e., of eigenoscillations endowed with the average energy (at a given temperature) according to Planck’s law. By comparing the result with Einstein’s Eq. (339), he found that the two did not agree in the first term: that is, the ‘light-quantum’ fluctuation term in the case of superposition of eigenoscillations took on for the partial volumes, $V_1, V_2, \dots$, the same value as for the total volume $V$, in contrast to what Einstein had derived.$^{941}$ Hence Ehrenfest concluded that in the theory of black-body radiation (described by Planck’s law) it was necessary to give up one of the two assumptions: either the independence of the entropies in different parts of space (which allowed one to apply the addition theorem), or the superposition of the eigenoscillations in the cavity containing equilibrium radiation. Ehrenfest, in summer 1925, preferred to retain the first assumption, but Frits Zernike proposed to formulate the result of the energy fluctuation calculation rather as: ‘The energy fluctuations of radiation, therefore, do not provide any argument for or against the light-quanta’ (See Ehrenfest, 1925b, p. 316.)

Although many physicists had become familiar with the light-quantum concept and the statistical theory of Bose and Einstein, as well as with Louis de Broglie’s phase-wave theory of light and matter, the quantum-theoretical properties of radiation still remained mysterious to them.$^{942}$ Another aspect of the

---

$^{941}$In Einstein’s Eq. (339), the first term was always proportional to the inverse of the average number of light-quanta contained in the volume considered; hence this term was always larger in the partial volumes, $V_1, V_2, \dots$, than in the total volume $V$.

$^{942}$In 1925 a few physicists began to concern themselves with the light-quantum theory of Bose, Einstein and de Broglie. For example, Adolf Smekal showed that the new statistics could be considered as a special case of a more general quantum statistics, the results of which were compatible with the laws of thermodynamics (Smekal, 1925b). Alfred Landé, on the other hand, studied the problem of statistical independence of light-quanta, and claimed that statistical independence could be assumed provided the light-quanta possessed certain coherence properties (Landé, 1925c).

unified description of radiation and matter had also not been clarified: how far did the undulatory phase-wave field of electrons, atoms and molecules correspond to reality? Einstein declared in January 1925: ‘This wave field—whose physical nature is still dark—must be detectable in principle by means of the diffraction phenomena corresponding to it’ (Einstein, 1925a, p. 10).$^{943}$ And he went on to claim that a beam of molecules passing through a hole of small dimension $d$ in a screen, where $d$ was comparable with the wavelength $\lambda$ ($= h/mv$, with $m$ and $v$ denoting the mass and velocity of the molecules in the beam, and $h$ Planck’s constant), should exhibit diffraction phenomena. Now the wavelength of gas molecules under usual conditions (of temperature and pressure) was extremely small; however, for hydrogen and helium atoms at low temperatures the thermal velocity could be made so small that $\lambda$ became of the order of the diameter of the molecules. As a consequence one would expect unusually large scattering angles, not compatible with the usual particle dynamics, if a beam of such molecules collided with other molecules. These large-angle scattering processes, then, would lead to a reduction of the mean free path of the molecules and give rise to an unexpectedly fast decrease of the viscosity of the gas in the neighbourhood of the temperature for which $\lambda$ coincided with the diameter of the molecules. Einstein finally proposed to explain earlier viscosity measurements by Paul Günther (1920) by means of the phase-wave hypothesis (Einstein, 1925a, p. 11). Einstein’s theoretical demonstration of the wave properties of hydrogen and helium molecules at low temperatures was followed within a few months by another, even more direct one: Walter Elsasser at Göttingen showed that the so-called Ramsauer effect should be interpreted on the basis of de Broglie’s theory. In order to understand the significance of Elsasser’s proposal, let us remind ourselves here of the story of the Ramsauer effect and the previous attempts to interpret it.

At the 86th *Naturforscherversammlung* at Bad Nauheim in September 1920, Carl Ramsauer, then a senior assistant of Philipp Lenard in Heidelberg, gave a talk on some of his recent results, entitled ‘Über den Wirkungsquerschnitt der Gasmoleküle gegenüber langsamen Elektronen’ (‘On the Cross Section of Gas Molecules Against Slow Electrons,’ Ramsauer, 1920).$^{944}$ Ramsauer had begun to

$^{943}$ In Einstein’s paper, ‘diffraction phenomena’ (*Beugungserscheinungen*) was erroneously printed as ‘the phenomena of motion’ (*Bewegungserscheinungen*).

$^{944}$ Carl Wilhelm Ramsauer was born on 6 February 1879 at Osterburg, Oldenburg. He studied physics from 1897 to 1903 at the Universities of Munich, Tübingen, Berlin and Kiel, receiving his doctorate at the University of Kiel in 1903. Then he worked at the Imperial Torpedo Laboratory, Kiel, and as an assistant at the Universities of London and Breslau. In 1907 Lenard offered him the position of an assistant at his institute in Heidelberg, and Ramsauer stayed there—interrupted by the years of World War I—until 1921, when he became professor of physics at the *Technische Hochschule*, Danzig. In Danzig, starting from nothing, he established a reputable physics laboratory. After seven years in Danzig, he was asked by the *Allgemeine Elektricitätsgesellschaft* (A.E.G.), Berlin, to head their newly installed research laboratory (1928–1945). After World War II Ramsauer joined the *Technische Hochschule*, Berlin (where he had been honorary professor since 1931) as full professor and director of the physics institute. He retired in 1955 and died soon thereafter, on 24 December 1955 in Berlin.

Ramsauer, who pioneered the field of electron and proton collisions with gas molecules, served as president of the German Physical Society in the difficult years during World War II.

work on this problem already before World War I, when he had developed a suitable method of measuring the velocity of slow electrons very accurately by deflection in a homogeneous magnetic field (Ramsauer, 1914).$^{945}$ Then, after the war, he carried out his experiment, employing the following procedure: a constant magnetic field guided the electrons of a given velocity along a circular orbit, which was defined by several slits through which the electrons could pass; a chamber filled with gas was placed surrounding the orbit of the electrons; the intensity of the electron beam was measured before and after the gas chamber was introduced, and thus the absorption cross section was obtained. By filling the chamber with several different gases, such as hydrogen, helium, nitrogen and argon, Ramsauer found a surprising result, which he stated in his talk at Bad Nauheim as follows: ‘According to the initial measurements of Lenard, argon shows a completely normal behaviour even for electrons having [energies down to] 10 [electron-] volts . . . However, while [the cross sections of] other gases—as far as they have been investigated up to now—approach a constant value with the decreasing velocity of the [electron] beam, the cross section of argon becomes extraordinarily small’ (Ramsauer, 1920, p. 578). From this anomalous behaviour of argon, which a colleague of Ramsauer at Heidelberg, Hans Ferdinand Mayer, confirmed independently in his doctoral thesis (Mayer, 1921), Ramsauer concluded that ‘in this phenomenon one is observing the free permeability of the argon atom for slowest electrons’ (Ramsauer, 1920, p. 578). Ramsauer published the details of his investigations in a paper submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in September 1920 (Ramsauer, 1921a). He continued to work on these questions, presenting further results in several papers during the following years. Thus he systematically studied the cross sections, especially of the other noble gases, helium, neon, krypton and xenon (Ramsauer, 1921b, 1922, 1923). In spring 1923 he finally summarized the results in the following statement: ‘All noble gases (He, Ne, A, Kr, X), in contrast to the other gases investigated up to now (like H$_2$, N$_2$, CO$_2$), show the common peculiarity that, for decreasing electron velocity, the cross sections reach a maximum and then drop again’ (Ramsauer, 1923, p. 351).

Ramsauer’s results on noble gases were substantiated by other experimentalists, for example, by Rudolph Minkowski and Hertha Sponer (Minkowski and Sponer, 1923; Sponer, 1923).$^{946}$ Minkowski also observed a similar, but weaker,

Then he spent a year at Göttingen. He joined the University of Hamburg (assistant, 1922–1926; *Privatdozent*, 1926–1931; extraordinary professor, 1931–1935). In 1935 he went to the United States and became a staff member at Mt. Wilson Observatory (1935–1948) and then jointly at Mt. Wilson and Mt. Palomar Observatories (1948–1960). During 1960–1961 he was a visiting professor at the University of Wisconsin, and in 1961 he joined the University of California at Berkeley as a research astronomer (until 1965). Minkowski died in Berkeley on 4 January 1976.

Stimulated by Franck, Friedrich Hund worked out a theory to describe this effect in his doctoral thesis (Hund, 1923).$^{948}$ Hund started in his work from the idea that an electron penetrating into an atom would not be deflected according to the laws of classical electrodynamics, but would obey some quantum condition. In the course of the interaction with the atom the electron would lose a certain amount of energy, which would be radiated away. The correspondence principle then required that the probability that an electron loses energy while passing through an atom should become negligible for small electron velocities.$^{949}$

Hund’s theory accounted more or less for the observations of cross sections of noble gases, as Minkowski and Sponer confirmed in their review article on this topic, entitled ‘*Über den Durchgang von Elektronen durch Atome*’ (‘On the Passage

of Electrons through Atoms’) and written for *Die Ergebnisse der exakten Naturwissenschaften, Volume 3* (Minkowski and Sponer, 1924). In that article, Minkowski and Sponer also connected the Ramsauer effect with the results that had been obtained on reflecting electrons from metallic surfaces. Clinton Joseph Davisson and Charles Henry Kunsman had studied the situation by using electrons having kinetic energies up to 1500 eV and different metals; they had measured, in particular, the dependence of the intensity of the reflected electron beam on the angle of reflection, finding in the intensity versus reflection-angle curves one or several maxima of the intensity (Davisson and Kunsman, 1921; 1922a, b; 1923).⁹⁵⁰ Davisson and Kunsman interpreted their results with the help of an idealized atomic model, consisting of a positively charged nucleus and one or more electron shells bearing negative charge. Thus they were able to explain the qualitative features; e.g., they showed that the magnesium data could be described fairly well by assuming that the electrons were concentrated on one shell, while the data for platinum required the assumption of several shells situated at certain distances from the nucleus (Davisson and Kunsman, 1923). Their model agreed vaguely with the picture derived from Bohr’s theory of atomic structure. However, for small electron velocities the model predicted large energy losses for the electron when passing through the atom, even a complete absorption. ‘This consequence,’ commented Minkowski and Sponer in their review article, ‘evidently contradicts the empirical facts openly. Hence one must expect from the beginning that on the basis of the validity of [classical] electrodynamics a description of the processes in the case of small [electron] velocities cannot be achieved and that it is necessary, therefore, to apply restrictions to electrodynamics in order to remain in agreement with experience’ (Minkowski and Sponer, 1924, p. 79). Both the Ramsauer effect and the reflection of slow electrons, therefore, suggested a deviation from the usual dynamical laws, a deviation, which occurred in particular in elastic collisions of low energy electrons with atoms. This was the situation before Elsasser came in.

Walter Elsasser had joined Franck's Institute in early 1925 as a doctoral candidate.⁹⁵¹ He wanted to become an experimentalist, although he had also become interested in theory—especially in Munich, where he had attended Arnold Sommerfeld’s lectures and seminars. Thus, besides trying to work on the research topic Franck had assigned to him, he followed the theoretical literature and attended the Seminar on ‘The Structure of Matter,’ which was directed at that time by Max Born. As Elsasser recalled later:

> I distinctly remember one of the earliest presentations in this seminar, by a student of Born’s named Fritz Hund . . . The subject of that particular seminar was an experiment by two Americans, Davisson and Kunsman, that had been reported in the *Physical Review* of 1923 . . . Hund told us that Max Born had developed some ideas to explain the phenomenon and that Born had asked him, Hund, to study the matter more closely. (Elsasser, 1978, pp. 59–60)

Born’s idea was to exploit the assumption, which had been used already by Davisson and Kunsman, that the maxima and minima in the intensity of the reflected electrons were caused by the shell structure of atoms. Hund, in his talk in the Seminar, did not present any details of such a calculation; and Elsasser did not think about the problem for some time. But then, as he remembered, he came back to it in the following way:

> One day, in May 1925, I found in the library two recent papers by Einstein on the effect of quantum theory upon gases . . . Einstein had shown that certain gases did not behave like assemblies of particles, the way most particles do, but they did in other respects behave like assemblies of waves; these additional effects might yet be observed . . . Einstein then quoted a thesis of Louis de Broglie that had just been published. (Elsasser, 1978, pp. 60–61)

Elsasser became curious about de Broglie’s thesis and he was happy to find a copy in the library.⁹⁵² He recalled:

obtained the Debye–Scherrer rings, similar to those observed in X-ray scattering, when electrons of several $10^{4}$ eV were allowed to pass through thin foils of celluloid (Thomson and Reid, 1927).$^{956}$  
One may ask why the confirmation of what Elsasser had suggested in July 1925 had to wait for such a long time. Why, for example, did James Franck not support Elsasser—when he knew that he was not an experienced experimentalist —more effectively? Perhaps the reason lay in the general attitude taken by the physicists in Göttingen. As Heisenberg recalled:  

> At least Franck . . . started to propagate the idea of matter waves. Born, in some way, was very skeptical and said: “Well, that’s too odd. That’s absurd. That now the electron which we can see in a cloud chamber is to be a wave—what do you mean by that?” Then, of course, the discussion came to the Compton effect where we *see* that kind of absurdity—we have to have light-quanta as well as waves. (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 244; also AHQP Interview)  

That is, in summer 1925 the connection between matter and waves appeared to be still a vague talk; people assumed that there might be some truth in it, but they did not dare to have more definite opinions. Similarly, the situation of radiation theory was also not clear. Only several months later would decisive progress take place: Erwin Schrödinger, after concerning himself with Einstein’s gas theory (Schrödinger, 1926b), would come out with a new kind of quantum theory based on the wave concept in a series of papers (Schrödinger, 1926c, d, e, f). His work would then stimulate the experimentalists to test Louis de Broglie’s phase-wave theory of matter. But these events belong to a later chapter in the development of quantum mechanics.  

$^{956}$We shall discuss the story of the discovery of matter waves later on.

# Chapter VI
# New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

In Chapters IV and V we have discussed the difficulties of the standard Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, which had arisen since 1922 in the detailed investigation of several important problems. In this chapter we shall deal with certain specific developments, which occurred mainly in 1924 and 1925 and seemed to open the path to a more satisfactory description of spectroscopic data, namely: the dispersion-theoretic approach to atomic theory; the new organization of electron groups in atoms and, associated with it, a new principle, later called the exclusion principle; and, finally, the concept of electron spin.

The dispersion-theoretic approach developed from the endeavour to obtain the correct theory of the dispersion of light by matter, whose atoms were described by Bohr's theory of atomic structure. After several attempts since 1913 had failed, Rudolf Ladenburg was the first to derive in 1921 a quantum-theoretical formula. This formula was extended and completed in early 1924 by Hendrik Kramers. And Kramers' dispersion formula became the prototype of many further quantum formulae, which allowed one to describe properties arising from the interaction of atoms with radiation, such as the width of spectral lines or the energy loss of charged particles passing through matter. The quantum-theoretical dispersion formula thus developed into a general scheme, a scheme formulated with the help of a peculiar mathematical method: according to it the dynamical equations of the old atomic theory, which were differential equations, were transformed into difference equations. Since the dispersion approach played the principal role in the discovery of quantum mechanics, which we shall discuss in Volume 2, we restrict ourselves in what follows to outlining the prehistory of Kramers' dispersion formula and to sketching in brief the problems of atomic structure to which this approach could be successfully applied.

While Bohr and his associates put their hopes in an extended use of the correspondence principle, other prominent quantum physicists—including Arnold Sommerfeld and Wolfgang Pauli—had serious doubts about the further usefulness of this principle in atomic theory. They argued, in particular, that the correspondence principle could hardly account for the numerical relationships exhibited by the data. In the description of data, ratios of small integral numbers occurred frequently; these ratios seemed to be connected with the peculiar organization of electrons in stable orbits, which was not explained by the existing atomic theory nor by any correspondence argument. From the analysis of chemical and spectroscopic data, J. D. Main Smith and Edmund Stoner derived

261

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0262 -->

630 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

in 1924 a group arrangement of electrons in the stable states of atoms, different from the one which had hitherto been assumed by Bohr on the basis of his theory of the periodic system of elements. Wolfgang Pauli then explained the Main Smith–Stoner scheme as a consequence of a new principle. This principle, which came to be called the exclusion principle, determined the number of electrons in orbits having the same energy (i.e., equivalent orbits).

In connection with the exclusion principle, Pauli introduced a new quantum number of the electron, to which he refused to give a physical interpretation. However, George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit, supported by the analysis of further data—such as was provided by the anomalous Zeeman effects and the fine structure of spectral lines—proposed in November 1925 to interpret this quantum number as representing, when multiplied by $h/2\pi$, the *intrinsic* angular momentum of the electron. Although the concept of the intrinsic angular momentum, or spin, did not solve all the difficulties of the theory of multiplets and of the anomalous Zeeman effects, it enabled the spectroscopists to order satisfactorily most of the available, relevant spectroscopic data. Hence the concept of spin, together with the exclusion principle, both of which had not been anticipated on the basis of any principle of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, represented an important extension of it. If to the theory so extended one added the dispersion-theoretic approach, a modified Bohr–Sommerfeld theory seemed to arise, which represented another step towards *the* future quantum theory of atomic structure.

## VI.1 The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach

The dispersion of light when passing through matter without getting fully absorbed, i.e., the variation of the refractive index $n$ (which denotes the ratio of the velocity of light *in vacuo* to the velocity of light in matter) with the wavelength, always played an important role in the history of optics since the times of Isaac Newton. After the undulatory theory of light won over the corpuscular view in the beginning of the nineteenth century, Augustin Louis Cauchy proposed an explanation of the dispersion phenomenon, based on the assumption that matter consisted of molecules having finite distances from each other (Cauchy, 1836). According to his theory the refractive index $n$ increased with decreasing wavelength $\lambda$ of the light—$n$ was approximately proportional to $\lambda^{-2}$—in agreement with the data on what was later called ‘normal’ dispersion. When studying the spectrum obtained from the transmission of light through a prism filled with iodine vapour, F.-P. Le Roux discovered an inversion of the usual order of colours, i.e., blue light was deflected more strongly than red; he called this phenomenon ‘anomalous dispersion’ (Le Roux, 1862). A closer investigation of anomalous dispersion yielded the following result: the phenomenon was always observed with radiation having wavelength around an absorption line of the dispersive medium; then the refractive index reached very high values for

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0263 -->

VI.1  The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach 631

wavelengths slightly larger than that of the absorbed line, while for shorter wavelengths it was reduced to a low value. The first general description of dispersion, based on the electromagnetic theory of light, was provided by James Clerk Maxwell in an investigation, published in the Cambridge Mathematical Tripos Examination of 1869: he employed the idea that the dispersing matter was constituted of molecules, which might be displaced by the traversing radiation (Maxwell, 1869). Similar treatments were given by other authors, who also obtained formulae for the refractive index $n$ similar to the one of Maxwell's, i.e.,

$$n^2 - 1 = \frac{\text{const.}}{\nu_0^2 - \nu^2}, \tag{340}$$

where $\nu_0$ denoted a natural frequency (absorbed or emitted) of the molecules, $\nu$ the frequency of the incident light, and the constant in the numerator on the right-hand side of Eq. (340) depended on the density of the dispersive medium. In 1892 Hendrik Lorentz finally developed the electron theory of dispersion of light on the assumption that matter, in which the light was dispersed, consisted of molecules, each of which contained an elastically bound electron (Lorentz, 1892a). The electric field of the incident radiation ($\mathbf{E}$) shifted the electron from its equilibrium position, giving each molecule an induced electric moment. By solving the equation of motion of the electron in the presence of the radiation, Lorentz derived a formula for the dielectric constant $\epsilon$ (where $\epsilon$ represented the constant of proportionality in the relation $\mathbf{P} = \epsilon\mathbf{E}$, connecting the polarization vector $\mathbf{P}$ of the medium with the electric field $\mathbf{E}$), namely,

$$\frac{\epsilon - 1}{\epsilon + 2} = \frac{1}{3\pi} \frac{N e^2 / m_e}{\nu_0^2 - \nu^2}, \tag{341}$$

with $N$ denoting the number of dispersion electrons (having charge $e$ and mass $m_e$) per unit volume (cm$^3$) having the characteristic frequency $\nu_0$ (determined by the force binding the electron in the molecule). Because of the relation, $\epsilon = n^2$, this equation had the same structure as the old dispersion Eq. (340): indeed, for a medium of not too high density, such that $\epsilon \approx 1$, Eq. (341) passed over into Eq. (340) with const. $= N e^2 / \pi m_e$.

Although the dispersion theory of Lorentz applied originally only to nonconducting materials, Paul Drude succeeded in extending it to describe the dispersion of electromagnetic waves in metals (Drude, 1900a, 1904). In a series of papers, published between 1902 and 1905, Max Planck completed the classical theory of dispersion of electromagnetic radiation by insulators and conductors; he especially connected the damping effect of the incident radiation—for which Lorentz had introduced a velocity-dependent term, $\gamma v$, in the equation of motion of the (bound) electron—with the energy radiated away by the oscillating electron (Planck, 1902b). Thus he was able to calculate the quantity $\gamma$, which corresponded to the width of the characteristic absorption (or emission) line having the frequency $\nu_0$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0264 -->

632 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

After the advent of Bohr’s atomic model, the physicists had to attack the problem of developing a quantum theory of the dispersion of light by matter. That is, they had to show how atoms, in which electrons moved on stationary orbits around a nucleus, behaved under the action of incident radiation and influenced it. The first to tackle the problem was Peter Debye (Debye, 1915a). He treated the dispersion of light by hydrogen molecules in which the two electrons moved with the same frequency on one circular orbit.$^{957}$ By solving, as Lorentz had done in the classical case, the equations of motion for the rotating electrons in the external electric field (provided by the electromagnetic radiation falling on the hydrogen molecules), Debye obtained an equation for the refractive index $n$, which had the same structure as Eq. (341). An important point in his result was, however, that as the characteristic frequency $\nu_0$ there occurred the frequency possessed by the rotating electrons. Shortly afterwards Arnold Sommerfeld applied Debye’s method to treat the dispersion of light in gases whose molecules had an axial symmetry (Sommerfeld, 1915d). These molecules could be described in Bohr’s theory as being constituted of several nuclei, with an arbitrary number of electrons moving in a circular orbit around an axis in the molecule. Again, Sommerfeld obtained a dispersion formula having the same structure as the classical equation (341), namely,

$$n^2 - 1 = \frac{e^2}{\pi m_e} \sum_{k=1}^{3} \frac{NC_k/3}{\nu_{0k}^2 - \nu^2}, \quad (341')$$

where $NC_k$ is the number of dispersion electrons (per cm$^3$) having the frequency $\nu_{k0}$, $k = 1, 2, 3$. $^{958}$

In principle, the dispersion formulae of Debye and Sommerfeld seemed to be acceptable, for they yielded the observed dependence of the refractive index on the frequency of the dispersed radiation. The question remained, however, whether only the general structure of the dispersion equation, or also its details could be confirmed. Debye and Sommerfeld had assumed particular models of the molecules, based on Bohr’s theory of molecular constitution. If these models represented the truth, the data should be used to determine the parameters of the models, say the characteristic frequencies of the electrons. Different investigations of that kind revealed that the situation was far from being satisfactory. For example, Clinton Joseph Davisson compared the data on the dispersion of light by hydrogen and helium molecules with the theoretical values calculated on the basis of Bohr’s models; he claimed that the dispersion data confirmed the hydrogen model but not the helium model (Davisson, 1916). A year later

***

$^{957}$Debye used a model for the hydrogen molecule, in which two electrons rotated on a circular orbit (lying in the plane between the two nuclei, perpendicular to the line joining them) of diameter $1.05 \times 10^{-8}$ cm with angular velocity $\omega = 2\pi\nu_0 = 4.21 \times 10^{16}$ s$^{-1}$. His formula described the data on the dispersion of light of small frequencies by hydrogen gas.

$^{958}$An anisotropically bound electron possessed three characteristic frequencies. Thus for isotropically bound electrons, i.e., $C_k = 1$ ($k = 1, 2, 3$), Eq. (341') would pass into Eq. (341).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0265 -->

VI.1  The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach 633

Sommerfeld showed that the dispersion data did not confirm the models for oxygen and nitrogen molecules similar to Bohr's hydrogen model, i.e., models in which several electrons—four in the case of $\text{O}_2$ and six in the case of $\text{N}_2$—moved with the same frequency in one circular orbit lying in the middle plane of the molecule, perpendicular to the line joining the two nuclei; he concluded, therefore, that the molecules had a constitution different from the one hitherto assumed (Sommerfeld, 1918a).

Thus the results of these investigations, in which quantum theory was first applied to the problem of describing the dispersion of radiation by molecules, remained rather inconclusive. One could cite several reasons to explain the unsatisfactory situation. The most important reason was that quantum-theoretical arguments were used only at one place, namely, to determine the parameters of the molecular model, but not also for determining the frequencies of the characteristic lines absorbed and emitted by the atomic systems. These characteristic frequencies, $\nu_0$, had played a crucial role in the classical dispersion formula, Eq. (341). In Debye and Sommerfeld's quantum formulae—see, e.g., Eq. (341')—the frequency of rotation of electrons in the circular orbit had replaced the characteristic frequencies of the molecules. However, these frequencies differed from the absorption frequencies of the molecules. Hence their treatment could not be considered as being the correct quantum theory of dispersion, and the above-mentioned difficulties with the molecular models had to be expected. In order to arrive at a more consistent description, one had to connect—as in the classical theory of Lorentz, Drude and Planck—the phenomenon of dispersion with the phenomena of absorption and emission of radiation. The first step in that direction was taken by Rudolf Ladenburg in 1921. Before discussing this contribution, however, we must report briefly on an investigation in classical theory, which Ladenburg undertook many years earlier and which was closely connected with his quantum-theoretical treatment of the dispersion of light by atoms.

When he came to the University of Breslau in 1907, Ladenburg started a series of studies to test the available description of the dispersion of light.$^{959}$ Especially, he computed—together with Stanislaw Loria—the number $N$ of dispersion

***

$^{959}$Rudolf Walther Ladenburg was born in Kiel on 6 June 1882. He studied physics from 1900 to 1906 at the Universities of Heidelberg (1900–1901), Breslau (1901), and Munich (1902–1906), obtaining his doctorate under W. C. Röntgen in Munich in 1906. Then he spent a year at the University of Cambridge, before joining (in 1907) the University of Breslau as assistant to Otto Lummer. At Breslau he became *Privatdozent* in 1909 and *Extraordinarius* in 1921. (During World War I he worked at the *Artillerie-Prüfungskommission* in Berlin.) In 1924 Fritz Haber invited him to become director of the physics department at the *Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Physikalische Chemie und Elektrochemie* in Berlin. In 1931 he succeeded Karl T. Compton as professor of physics at Princeton University. He died in Princeton on 3 April 1952.

Stimulated by the theoretical investigations of Hendrik Lorentz and Woldemar Voigt, Ladenburg worked at first on optical and magneto-optical phenomena connected with the electron theory of matter; then he turned to deal with the phenomena of dispersion of light by atoms. Later on, in the United States, he studied the production cross sections of neutrons, and after World War II he investigated supersonic phenomena.

proposed a different method to find the number of electrons contributing to the
dispersion of light in a unit volume of a given gas (Ladenburg, 1914). He
measured the total energy absorbed per unit time by a unit volume of the gas
from incident radiation of frequencies in the neighbourhood of an absorption
frequency $\nu_0$ of the gas; he divided this quantity by the energy, $S_{\text{el}}$, absorbed or
emitted per second (on the basis of classical electrodynamics) by a single electron
resonating with the same frequency; the quotient then had to be the number of
dispersion electrons. Now, due to Planck's theory, $S_{\text{el}}$ was obtained from the
equation

$$S_{\text{el}} = \frac{\overline{U}_{\text{el}}}{\tau} , \quad \text{(342)}$$

where $\overline{U}_{\text{el}}$ denoted the average energy of the oscillating electron and $\tau$, i.e.,

$$\tau = \frac{3m_{e}c^{3}}{8\pi^{2}e^{2}\nu_{0}^{3}} , \quad \text{(342a)}$$

denoted what was later called the 'decay-time' ('*Abklingzeit*,' see Ladenburg,
1921a, p. 452), that is, the time in which the amplitude of an oscillating electron
emitting radiation of frequency $\nu_0$ was reduced by radiation damping to the *e*th
part (*e* being the base of natural logarithm).$^{960}$ In this way Ladenburg deter-
mined the number of dispersion electrons per cm$^3$ in the case of the emission of
the sodium *D*-line by sodium vapour, obtaining the result that about 40 electrons
contributed to the emission of the line out of 100 sodium atoms (Ladenburg,
1914, p. 779). His result agreed completely with what he had expected.
Nearly seven years after this classical treatment of the number of dispersion
electrons, Ladenburg returned to the same problem in quantum theory. In a
paper, entitled '*Die quantentheoretische Deutung der Zahl der Dispersions-

VI.1 The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach 635

sion Electrons') and submitted in February 1921 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, he showed how to adapt his classical method to calculate the number of dispersion electrons in the absorption region to the quantum theory of atomic structure (Ladenburg, 1921a). The key idea had been provided by Einstein's treatment of the absorption and emission coefficients of atoms and molecules (Einstein, 1916d). According to it the total energy emitted per second by $N_k$ atoms, when passing from a stationary state $k$ to a state $i$, was given by the relation

$$S_{ki} = N_k h \nu_{ki} (a_{ki} + b_{ki} \rho_{ki}), \quad (343)$$

where $a_{ki}$ and $b_{ki}$ denote the Einstein coefficients of spontaneous and induced emission of an atom, describing the probability of the emission of a spectral line with frequency $\nu_{ki} (= (W_k - W_i)/h, W_k$ and $W_i$ being the energies of the stationary states), and $\rho_{ki}$ the density of blackbody radiation having the same frequency $\nu_{ki}$. In thermal equilibrium—and Ladenburg, like Einstein, considered the atoms in thermal equilibrium with heat radiation—the emitted and absorbed energy per second ($S_{\text{absorbed}} = N_i h \nu_{ki} b_{ik} \rho_{ki}$) had to balance each other; hence Eq. (343) could be replaced by

$$S_{ki} = N_i \frac{g_k}{g_i} a_{ki} \frac{c^3}{8 \pi \nu_{ki}^2} \rho_{ki}, \quad (343')$$

where $g_k$ and $g_i$ represent the statistical weights of the states $k$ and $i$, respectively. Now Ladenburg claimed that $S_{ki}$ had to be interpreted as the product $N S_{\text{el}}$, with $S_{\text{el}}$ given by Eq. (342) and $N$ denotes the number of electrons which contribute to the emission of absorption of the radiation. For $N$ he then obtained the quantum-theoretical expression

$$N = N_i \frac{g_k}{g_i} \frac{m_e c^3}{8 \pi^2 e^2 \nu_{ki}^2} a_{ki}. \quad (344)$$

The immediate goal, which Ladenburg had in mind in 1921, was to make use of the measurements of the energy absorbed by the atoms in layers of gases or vapours from the radiation penetrating through them in order to determine the probability coefficients of the atoms involved. He admitted that this procedure could be questioned because of the fact that a quantum theory of anomalous dispersion did not yet exist and he had to take over the classical dispersion formula, Eq. (340). However, he noted: 'Surely one will be able to describe it [i.e., the quantum theory of dispersion] with the help of the idea that the molecules, which are taken by the incident radiation from a state $i$ into a state $k$, possess an altered electric moment and react back through it upon the radiation. The electric fields arising from neighbouring atoms or from other causes (e.g., the electric field of the incident light itself) create, besides the states $i$ and $k$, other altered states $i', i'', \dots$ and $k', k'', \dots$ (Stark effect)' (Ladenburg, 1921a, p. 455). On this assumption, Ladenburg argued, the quantum theory of dispersion of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0268 -->

636 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

radiation by atoms would lead to more or less the same dispersion formula as the classical theory, with the damping constant (i.e., \(1/\tau\), the inverse of the quantity \(\tau\) in Eq. (342a)) being determined by a sum of the absorption coefficients \(a_k = a_{ki} + a_{kj} + \dots\), associated with all possible transitions from a given stationary state \(k\).

The new quantum-theoretical expression for the number of dispersion electrons enabled Ladenburg to interpret the available observations on anomalous dispersion and the magneto-rotation polarization (in the presence of an external magnetic field) of hydrogen and alkali lines. Thus, for example, from the observed intensity ratio of the sodium \(D\)-doublet (\(N_2 : N_1 = 2 : 1\)), he derived the result that the \(2p_2\)-state of the atom should occur twice as often as the \(2p_1\)-state (Ladenburg, 1921a, b).\(^{961}\) In the following years Ladenburg continued to perform the experiments on absorption and dispersion of radiation in Breslau and received in their interpretation the assistance of the theoretician Fritz Reiche, who had come from Berlin.\(^{962}\) The two of them described the results of their own and other investigations in a review article published in the Bohr issue of *Naturwissenschaften* (Ladenburg and Reiche, 1923). In their article, Ladenburg and Reiche presented the foundations and applications of the quantum theory of dispersion of light by atoms that had been achieved hitherto. Thus, for instance, they formulated the condition under which the quantum-theoretical expression (344) was valid—namely, that the ratio of \(\rho_\nu\) and \(8\pi h\nu^3 / c^3\) was small compared to 1. And, by comparing the quantum-theoretical and classical expressions for \(N\), they established the relation between Einstein’s emission coefficients, \(a_{ki}\), and the classical damping constant \(\tau^{-1}\), i.e.,

\[ a_{ki} = \frac{1}{\tau} f_{ki}, \tag{345} \]

where \(f_{ki}\) was a numerical factor which determined the coupling strength of the quantum-theoretical transition, i.e., how many of the series electrons in the atom contributed to the spectral line considered. Further, they gave an interpretation

\(^{961}\)Rudolf Ladenburg and his student Rudolph Minkowski also studied the sodium doublet themselves; they measured the magnetic rotation of the plane of polarization of radiation in the vicinity of the doublet frequency (Ladenburg and Minkowski, 1921). Minkowski further investigated whether the presence of other gases had an influence on the magneto-rotation of the sodium lines (Minkowski, 1922).

\(^{962}\)F. Reiche was born in Berlin on 4 July 1883. He studied physics at the Universities of Munich (1901–1902) and Berlin (1902–1907), obtaining his doctorate in Berlin under Max Planck in 1907. Then he joined Otto Lummer in Breslau, but returned to Berlin in 1912. In 1913 he became *Privatdozent* in theoretical physics at the University of Berlin. In 1918 he accepted a position at the *Kaiser-Wilhelm-Institut für Physikalische Chemie und Elektrochemie* in Berlin; three years later he was called to the University of Breslau to take up the chair of theoretical physics (succeeding Erwin Schrödinger). From 1934 to 1935 he was a visiting professor at the German University of Prague. On his return to Germany he remained without a position. In 1941 he emigrated to the United States, where he worked at several colleges (including the City College, New York) until he became an adjunct professor at New York University in 1946. Reiche retired in 1958 and died on 14 January 1969 in New York.

Reiche worked in numerous fields of theoretical physics, including the problems of optics, paramagnetism and X-ray spectroscopy. In later years he investigated the problems of supersonic flow and electromagnetic theory.

VI.1  The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach
637

of the quantum-theoretical dispersion mechanism by claiming that the dispersion of radiation by atoms could be described by the action of (classical) ‘equivalent oscillators’ (‘*Ersatzoszillatoren*’, *loc. cit.*, p. 590), whose electric moment was given by the (classical) electric moment of an electron oscillating with the same frequency multiplied by the factor $N/N_i$. If several electrons in an atom had the same characteristic frequency, the number of dispersion electrons increased accordingly. Ladenburg and Reiche concluded their report by stating:

> If we survey the field of scattering and dispersion, discussed here, in its entirety, then we must admit that we indeed do not know the real mechanism by which an incident wave acts on the atoms and that we cannot describe the reaction of the atoms in detail . . . . Still, on the basis of the observed phenomena, we believe that we should obtain—as a final result of the action of radiation of frequency $\nu$ on atoms—an effect, which is not essentially different from the one produced by such a wave on classical oscillators: secondary wave trains arise, having the same frequency $\nu$ and the same phase as the incident wave. (Ladenburg and Reiche, 1923, p. 597)

Any deviation of the observed behaviour from the classical dispersion theory, Ladenburg and Reiche continued, could be perfectly described by the quantum-theoretically modified expression, Eq. (344), for the number of dispersion electrons. This expression took into account correctly the transition probabilities as well as the statistical weights of the stationary states.

As for a possible mechanism of the quantum-theoretical dispersion, Ladenburg and Reiche referred to a note of Charles Galton Darwin, published in the issue of *Nature* of 23 December 1922 (Darwin, 1922). In this note Darwin had suggested the following picture: if a radiation wave, represented by its wave vector $E_x$ (polarized in the $x$-direction), strikes an atom, there exists a probability equal to $A_l(\partial E_x/\partial t)dt$ that in the time interval $dt$ the atom will be excited to emit spherical waves of frequency $\nu_l$ and amplitude $a_l \exp(-\lambda_l t)\cos(2\pi\nu_l)$, where $A_l$, $a_l$, $\lambda_l$ (the ‘damping’ factor) and $\nu_l$ depend only on the motion of the atom. Considering an incident wave of frequency $\nu$, Darwin had derived the following equation for the index of refraction $n$:

$$\frac{3(n^2 - 1)}{n^2 + 2} = \sum_l \frac{1}{\pi} \frac{c^2 N A_l a_l}{\nu_l^2 - \nu^2} . \qquad (346)$$

He noticed that, for $NA_l a_l$ equal to $N_l e^2/m_e c^2$, Eq. (346) nearly coincided with the classical dispersion formula, Eq. (341). In addition, it agreed with Ladenburg’s result, Eq. (344), for the number of dispersion electrons if one properly related Darwin’s quantities $A_l$ and $a_l$ to Einstein’s coefficients $a_{ki}$. A special feature of Darwin’s theory was that it connected a wave-theoretical description with certain aspects of the light-quantum theory: since the dispersion equation, Eq. (346), did not determine the amplitude of the scattered wave, Darwin had to do so by adding the extra condition that the atom can emit radiation only in energy packets $h\nu_l$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0270 -->

638 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

Darwin’s theory stimulated the interest of Niels Bohr. Bohr had known for many years that the theory of dispersion of radiation by atoms and molecules, as developed by Debye and Sommerfeld in 1915, had failed to account for essential facts.$^{963}$ But he had not been able to attack the dispersion problem himself, for his theory of atomic structure seemed to offer no means of approaching it. Thus he had avoided entering into the discussion of dispersion for nearly a decade. Even in his paper on the fundamental postulates of quantum theory, submitted in November 1922 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, Bohr still stressed the difficulties hindering the progress towards a consistent quantum theory of the dispersion of light. There he remarked: ‘It seems necessary, in order to account for the phenomena of reflection and dispersion, to assume that an atom reacts on the field of radiation just as a system of electrified particles in the classical theory — in other words, that the atom forms the starting point for a secondary wave train which stands in a coherent phase relation with the original field of radiation.’ However, this necessity conflicted with the observation that ‘it is an immediate consequence of the requirements typical to the quantum theory for the stability of the stationary states, that the reaction of the atom to the influence of a field of radiation in general cannot even approximately be calculated according to the classical theory’ (Bohr, 1923a; English translation, Bohr, 1976, p. 495). The conflict between the classical and the quantum-theoretical description showed itself in the fact that the characteristic frequencies of the radiation emitted or absorbed by atoms were not connected in any simple way with the motion of the electrons in the normal state of the atom. Hence Bohr claimed that the reaction of the atom on being subjected to incident radiation arises from ‘an unknown mechanism which is answerable for the emission of radiation on the transition between stationary states’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 496). That mechanism, he argued, had also to take into account that ‘the real absorption [of radiation by atoms] does not merely consist in a uniform decrease in the energy of the wave train [of the incident light], but in an exchange of energy, governed by discontinuous laws, between individual atoms and the field of radiation’ (Bohr, *loc. cit.*, p. 496).

According to Bohr, in a quantum-theoretical description of the dispersion of light by atoms there would not exist any phase coherence between the absorbed and the reemitted radiation, as was exhibited in the phenomenon of resonance radiation. Therefore he criticized, in a footnote in his paper quoted above, Darwin’s picture of the dispersion process — which established a certain phase relation between incident and emitted radiation — as being ‘scarcely reconcilable with the assumption of a finite duration of the existence of excited atoms’ and encountering ‘apparently insuperable difficulties when it tries to take account of the phenomena of dispersion in very weak illumination’ (Bohr, 1923a; English translation, Bohr, 1976, p. 497, footnote). Bohr concluded: ‘The complete inde-

VI.1  The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 639

pendence of the observed phenomena of dispersion on the intensity of the light might rather call for an explanation of these phenomena in which . . . an essential feature is a close agreement with the continuous, non-statistical conceptions of classical theory' (Bohr, loc. cit., p. 497). That is, he advocated a theoretical description of the interaction of light with atoms, in which the phenomena of resonance radiation were treated in a different way from those of the dispersion of light, the latter being accounted for by a theory closely related to the classical one.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Bohr's hesitation in accepting Darwin's proposal was partly motivated by his hostile reaction towards the light-quantum concept around 1923. In those days he considered any reference to the light-quantum as signifying an obstacle to the progress of atomic theory because the concepts of the light-quantum and the correspondence principle appeared to be irreconcilable. The problem of the dispersion of light by atoms could, therefore, not be really approached at the quantum level in Copenhagen before the arrival of a new idea connecting the quantum-theoretical description of atomic structure and the classical description of radiation. This idea was provided by John Slater's 'virtual field of oscillators' connected with the atoms, which we have discussed in Section V.2. The very existence of the virtual field of radiation, having the quantum-theoretical frequencies of the atoms, then allowed Bohr and his associates to generalize the proposal of a quantum theory of radiation, which Ladenburg had made in 1921. The radiation theory, developed by Bohr, Kramers and Slater on Slater's idea, brought into the description of the dispersion phenomena the necessary discontinuity which Bohr had emphasized in his paper of November 1922 (Bohr, 1923a): that is, the statistical energy and momentum conservation and the statistical coupling of neighbouring atoms provided a suitable mechanism to relax the coherence—existing in classical radiation theory—between the incident radiation and the resonance radiation emitted by the atom, while it still allowed the dispersed radiation having a frequency far below the characteristic frequencies of the atom to be in phase with the incident radiation. Hendrik Kramers, Bohr's closest associate, thus succeeded in constructing a quantum theory of the dispersion of light by atoms on the principles of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Kramers, since the time he worked on his thesis on the intensities of spectral lines (Kramers, 1919), had been interested in problems related to the interaction of light with atoms. One could even consider the question of the intensities of spectral lines as a part of the dispersion problem.⁹⁶⁴ Also in his paper of November 1923 on the absorption of X-rays by atoms and the continuous X-ray spectra, Kramers had treated a problem which could be connected to the dispersion phenomena (Kramers, 1923d). At about the same time he thought of generalizing the dispersion-theoretic approach of Ladenburg so as to include the dispersion of light by atoms, when the latter were in excited states, and he

640 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

obtained a formula which seemed to describe the situation.$^{965}$ After completing the joint paper with Bohr and Slater on the new radiation theory, Kramers felt safe to publish his dispersion formula in a letter, dated 25 March 1924, which appeared in the issue of 10 May of *Nature* (Kramers, 1924a).$^{966}$

Kramers started his letter, entitled 'The Law of Dispersion and Bohr's Theory of Spectra,' by saying: 'It is well known that a consistent description of the phenomena of dispersion, reflection and scattering of electromagnetic waves by material media can be given on the fundamental assumption that an atom, when exposed to radiation, becomes a source of secondary wavelets, which are coherent with the incident waves' (Kramers, 1924a, p. 673). This assumption, underlying the classical dispersion theory, led to a formula for the amplitude $\mathbf{P}$ of the secondary wavelets having the frequency $\nu$, that is,

$$\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{E} \sum_l f_l \frac{e^2}{m_e} \frac{1}{4\pi^2 (\nu_l^2 - \nu)} . \tag{347}$$

In other words, the induced electric moment $\mathbf{P}$ should be proportional to the electric field (strength $\mathbf{E}$), multiplied by a sum over terms, each of which involves a characteristic frequency, $\nu_l$, of the electrons bound in the atom. The $f_l$ denoted constants determining the coupling strength of the electron oscillation associated with the frequency $\nu_l$.$^{967}$ Kramers continued: 'In Bohr's theory of spectra, the picture of electrons which are elastically bound inside the atom is abandoned, and for it is substituted a picture according to which an atom exhibiting an absorption line of frequency $\nu_l$ is capable of performing under the influence of the illumination a transition from the state under consideration to a stationary state the energy content of which is $h\nu_l$ greater' (Kramers, 1924a, p. 673). This absorption of radiation of a discrete frequency could then be interpreted, on the basis of the correspondence principle, as being caused by a certain harmonic oscillation component of the motion of the atom. Kramers proposed to establish what he called an 'adequate description of the activity of the atoms regarding their interaction with radiation,' guided by the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of

VI.1 The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach 641

radiation in the following way: first, the picture of the quantum-theoretical dispersion mechanism is essentially the same as the classical one; second, the quantum-theoretical relation between $\mathbf{P}$, the induced electric moment, and $\mathbf{E}$, the electric vector of the incident radiation, had to be formulated consistently with the theory of atomic structure and the mutual influence of atoms on one another.$^{968}$ Since the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory, underlying the new dispersion theory, had not yet yielded definite mathematical equations, Kramers put forward ‘a very simple expression for $\mathbf{P}$, which fulfills the condition claimed by the correspondence principle, that, in the region where successive stationary states of an atom differ only comparatively little from each other, the interaction between the atom and the field of radiation tends to coincide with the interaction to be expected on the classical theory of electrons’ (Kramers, 1924a, p. 673).

By the ‘very simple expression’ Kramers meant a dispersion formula, which he had obtained by generalizing Ladenburg’s result *before* the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory had been formulated. Especially, he had considered an atom having the (Einstein) emission coefficients $A_1^e, A_2^e, \dots$, and the absorption coefficients $A_1^a, A_2^a, \dots$; that is, the probability of an atom to make a spontaneous transition to a state of lower energy, associated with the emission of radiation of frequency $\nu_j^e$, was $A_j^e, j = 1, 2, \dots$, while the probability for the absorption of frequency $\nu_i^a$ was $A_i^a, i = 1, 2, \dots$. Assuming, for the sake of simplicity, that the statistical weights of all states of the atom had the same value, and that the atom was so oriented in space that the vectors $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ were parallel, Kramers then proposed the following equation for the ratio $P/E$ (with $P$ and $E$ the magnitudes of the vectors $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{E}$):

$$ \frac{P}{E} = \sum_i A_i^a \tau_i^a \frac{e^2}{m_e} \frac{1}{4\pi^2 ((\nu_i^a)^2 - \nu^2)} - \sum_j A_j^e \tau_j^e \frac{e^2}{m_e} \frac{1}{4\pi^2 ((\nu_j^e)^2 - \nu^2)} . \quad (348) $$

In Eq. (348), the quantities $\tau_i^a$ and $\tau_j^e$ denoted the analogues of the classical decay- (or damping-) times, i.e.,

$$ \tau_i^a = \frac{3 m_e c^2}{8 \pi^2 e^2 (\nu_i^a)^2} \quad \text{and} \quad \tau_j^e = \frac{3 m_e c^2}{8 \pi^2 e^2 (\nu_j^e)^2} . \quad (348a) $$

Kramers’ dispersion formula, Eq. (348), generalized the previous formulas—of Ladenburg and Darwin—by including the additional second term which contributed to the dispersion of light by atoms only in the case of excited atoms, which were able to emit spontaneously radiation of frequency $\nu_j^e$. Kramers interpreted the two terms as follows: ‘In the final state of the transition the atom acts as a “positive virtual oscillator” of relative strength $+f [= +A_i^a \tau_i^a]$; in the initial state it acts as a negative virtual oscillator of strength $-f [= -A_j^e \tau_j^e]$’ (Kramers,

1924a, p. 674). Although the concept of the ‘negative dispersion’ was not familiar, Kramers emphasized that it ‘exhibits a close analogy with the “negative absorption” which was introduced by Einstein, in order to account for the law of temperature radiation on the basis of quantum theory’ (Kramers, 1924a, p. 674). While in the case of atoms in the ground state, Eq. (348) agreed with the result of Ladenburg, which had already been confirmed by experiment, Kramers admitted that ‘the experiments at hand scarcely allow testing the complete formula in a more general case’ (Kramers, 1924a, p. 674).⁹⁶⁹ In favour of his complete formula he argued, however, that *only by taking into account the negative dispersion* would one be able to obtain—in the correspondence limit of high quantum numbers and transitions between neighbouring states of the atoms—the classical equation (347) from the quantum-theoretical equation (348).

Kramers’ dispersion equation, though it lacked experimental confirmation thus far, was regarded by most quantum physicists as an important advance. Max Born in Göttingen and Richard Becker in Berlin—in papers submitted in June (Born, 1924b) and July 1924 (Becker, 1924) to *Zeitschrift für Physik*—also concerned themselves with the quantum theory of dispersion, starting from roughly the same physical ideas as Kramers and arriving at the same dispersion formula. Becker attempted to formulate mathematically the content of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation and derived Eq. (348) on its basis. Born, on the other hand, started from the perturbation-theoretic scheme for multiply periodic systems, which he had developed earlier with Wolfgang Pauli (Born and Pauli, 1922). According to this theory, the induced electric moment $\mathbf{P}$ of an atom was a first-order perturbation effect, given by the equation

$$ \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{p}^{(1)} = \sum_k \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}^{(0)}}{\partial J_k^0} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w_k^0} - \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}^{(0)}}{\partial w_k^0} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial J_k} \right), \tag{349} $$

where $\mathbf{p}^{(0)}$ denoted the electric moment of the unperturbed system (in the direction of the electric field) described by the action-angle variables $J_k$ and $w_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$, and $S_1$ the first-order correction to the action function $S$. Since both quantities $\mathbf{p}^{(0)}$ and $S_1$ were supposed to be multiply periodic—e.g., $|\mathbf{p}^{(0)}| = \sum_{\tau_k} C_\tau \exp\{2\pi i w_k^0 \tau_k\}$—$\mathbf{P}$ could be expressed in classical electrodynamics as

$$ \mathbf{P} = -\mathbf{E} \sum_k \sum_{(\nu\tau)>0} \tau_k \frac{\partial}{\partial J_k} \left[ \frac{2|C_{\tau_k}|^2 (\nu\tau)_k}{(\nu_k \tau_k)^2 - \nu^2} \right], \tag{350} $$

⁹⁶⁹ It still took some time before the negative term in the dispersion formula, Eq. (348), was verified. Thus Ladenburg remarked at the end of his review on dispersion phenomena, published in December 1926 in *Naturwissenschaften*: ‘Above all it is desirable to prove the effect of “negative dispersion” in the quantum-theoretical dispersion formula by choosing appropriate experimental conditions’ (Ladenburg, 1926b, p. 1213). About a year later he reported about the first experimental indication of the influence caused by negative dispersion: when discussing the data on anomalous dispersion from hydrogen atoms in the region of $H_\alpha$- and $H_\beta$-lines, he noticed that the observed ratio of oscillator strengths, $f_\alpha/f_\beta$, did not agree exactly with the result calculated without the negative dispersion term (Carst and Ladenburg, 1928, p. 192).
