VI.1 The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach 643

with **E** denoting the periodic incident electric field ($\mathbf{E} \propto \cos(2\pi\nu t)$) and $\nu_k\tau_k$ the harmonics of the frequencies $\nu_k, k = 1, \dots, f$, of the system. Born now proposed to replace the classical expression for **P** by a quantum-theoretical one due to the following prescription: any differential quotient of a classical variable $\Phi$ with respect to an action variable $J$ becomes a difference quotient in quantum theory, namely,

$$ \frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial J} \rightarrow \frac{\Phi(n + \tau) - \Phi(n)}{\tau h}, \qquad (351) $$

where $n + \tau$ and $n$ were the quantum numbers of two stationary states of the system under consideration. By applying the prescription (351) to Eq. (350), Kramers' dispersion Eq. (348) was obtained, if one identified $\nu_k\tau_k$ with the absorption and emission frequencies, $\nu_i^a$ and $\nu_j^e$, and put the absolute squares of the amplitudes, $|C_{\tau_k} C_{-\tau_k}|$, proportional to the absorption and emission coefficients, $A_i^a$ and $A_j^e$. $^{970}$

Born’s procedure for obtaining quantum-theoretical results by rewriting classical results with the help of the replacement prescription (351) was immediately accepted by Kramers. In a second letter to *Nature* on 'The Quantum Theory of Dispersion,' dated 22 July 1924 and published in August, he emphasized the principal aspects of the quantum theory of dispersion: first, the notion of 'virtual oscillators,' which 'does not mean the introduction of any hypothetical mechanism, but is meant only as a terminology suitable to characterize certain main features of the connexion between the description of optical phenomena and the theoretical interpretation of spectra'; second, the fact that the quantum formula (348) contained only quantities which allowed a 'direct physical interpretation on the basis of the fundamental postulates of the quantum theory of spectra and atomic constitution' (Kramers, 1924b, p. 311). $^{971}$ In fall 1924 Kramers extended, together with Werner Heisenberg, his dispersion formula to describe also the situation in which the frequency of the radiation changed by discrete amounts, $\pm \nu_{qu}$, where $\nu_{qu}$ denoted the transition frequencies of the dispersing atoms (Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925). $^{972}$

The progress in dispersion theory achieved since early 1924 opened up a new fruitful period of atomic theory. A great number of problems involving the

interaction of matter with radiation now became accessible to a quantum-theoretical description.$^{973}$ The range of these problems extended from the intensity of spectral lines of atoms and molecules—with or without external electric and magnetic fields—to the energy losses of charged particles in their passage through matter. Suddenly the quantum physicists saw everywhere atomic phenomena that seemed to be related to dispersion phenomena, to which the same theoretical methods could be applied as to the scattering of light by atoms.

In the case of certain phenomena the concept of virtual oscillators already provided the explanation of the observed facts. The question of the width of the spectral lines was one of these.$^{974}$ Now, the classical electron theory led to a linewidth given by the inverse of the quantity $\tau$, Eq. (342a).

Another property of spectral lines, which had thus far not been possible to describe satisfactorily in atomic theory, was their intensity. In classical electrodynamics the intensity of radiation emerging from an accelerated charge followed immediately from its (the charge's) electromagnetic field. Thus, for example, for an oscillating electron—and an electron moving in an elliptical orbit around a nucleus could be represented by an oscillating electron—the intensity depended only on the amplitude and the frequency of the oscillation. In Bohr's quantum theory of atomic structure, classical electrodynamics had failed. Neither the frequency of the emitted radiation was given by the motion of the electron nor the intensity of the lines could be related to it: the intensity rather depended on the probability for the electrons to occupy the initial state involved in the transition, and on the tendency or probability of the initial state to pass over into the final state. The first of these probabilities—i.e., the probability to occupy a given state—was not a simple quantity either because it also depended on the statistical weight of the state.

In the early years of Bohr's theory there did not really exist a reliable method of calculating the intensities of spectral lines. Nevertheless the theoreticians tried. The first to develop some detailed ideas about the question was Arnold Sommerfeld: he suggested that the intensity depended on the number of possibilities to obtain a given spectral line by means of transitions between different states; that is, the intensity was just proportional to number of transitions between the two orbits involved in the emission of the line under investigation. Further, he claimed that very eccentric orbits were less probable than the circular ones belonging to the same principal quantum number (Sommerfeld, 1916b). Although Sommerfeld was able to describe the data on the intensities of spectral lines and their components—e.g., the relativistic or Stark components—at least qualitatively, Niels Bohr did not like his ideas. In his 1918 memoirs Bohr put forward a different explanation by claiming that a close relation existed between the radiation emitted by electrons moving in Kepler orbits on the classical theory and the radiation emitted by atoms, provided transitions between neighbouring states of high quantum numbers were involved (Bohr, 1918a). Hendrik Kramers then quite successfully calculated on the basis of Bohr's analogy or correspondence argument the intensities of hydrogen lines, especially of their Stark and Zeeman components (Kramers, 1919). In evaluating the frequencies, $\nu_{qu}$, and the amplitudes, $A_{qu}$, of the spectral lines, he took averages of the corresponding classical expressions between the initial and final orbits of the electrons in the atom, i.e.,

$$\nu_{qu} = \frac{1}{h} \int_0^1 \delta W_\lambda \qquad (353a)$$

Born and Van Vleck's papers provided the tools for calculating the intensities of spectral lines of arbitrary atoms and molecules, whether external fields were present or absent. Did they describe the available wealth of spectroscopic data consistently? Of particular interest for the theory of atomic structure at that time appeared to be the measurements on the intensity ratios of multiplets, which were carried out at the experimental institute of the University of Utrecht under the direction of Leonard Salomon Ornstein.<sup>977</sup> He had started to work on the problem, together with his collaborators like Herman Carel Burger and Hendrik Berend Dorgelo, in 1922.<sup>978</sup> The Utrecht experimentalists used the photographic techniques as others had done before, but achieved a more reliable determination of the intensity ratios of neighbouring spectral lines by the following method: the intensity of the stronger line was weakened by placing a substance of known absorbing power between the emitting atoms and the photographic plate (Dorgelo, 1923). This method could then be extended to measure the intensity ratios of lines having rather different frequencies, provided the sensitivity of the photographic plates for radiation of varying frequencies had been determined with the help of a standard lamp—emitting spectral lines of known intensity having frequencies within the interval under consideration (Dorgelo, 1924; Ornstein, 1925).
The first results found in Utrecht by these methods indicated that the intensity ratios of multiplet components were independent of the conditions of the excitation; they could be represented in good approximation by the quotient of two small integers, such that the intensity ratio of the alkali doublet components was given by the value 2 : 1, and the intensity ratio of the alkaline-earth triplet components was given by the values $\frac{5}{2} : \frac{3}{2} : \frac{1}{2}$ (Dorgelo, 1924).<sup>979</sup> Sommerfeld, on

Even without using these model-dependent assumptions, Heisenberg proved that the sum of the intensities of all components of a multiplet, associated with the same initial state, was proportional to the statistical weight (i.e., the inner quantum number) of this state; thus he derived one of Burger and Dorgelo’s sum-rules (Heisenberg, 1925a, p. 619). At the turn of the year from 1924 to 1925 the study of the intensity ratios and of ‘sum-rules’ à la Burger and Dorgelo occupied many physicists.980

While the successful description of intensity ratios for the individual components of line multiplets required extra model assumptions—which could be justified partly on the basis of new principles, such as Pauli’s exclusion principle—the sum-rules just reflected a general property of the series electrons in atoms, as was shown independently by two physicists, Willy Thomas in Breslau and Werner Kuhn in Copenhagen. Thomas, who had worked for some time under the direction of Fritz Reiche on the problem of dispersion electrons, discovered that the sum of the oscillator strengths entering into Kramers’ dispersion formula, Eq. (348), was equal to the degree of periodicity *s* of the system, or

$$\sum_i f_i^a - \sum_j f_j^e = s, \tag{355}$$

where $f_i^a = 3 A_i^a \tau_i^a$ and $f_j^e = 3 A_j^e \tau_j^e$ (Thomas, 1925a).981 Thomas also claimed that the *f*-sum represented, ‘multiplied, if necessary, by the ratio of weights [of the states involved in the transition] and a factor which takes into account the spatial averaging, the number of “dispersion electrons” per atom’ (Thomas, 1925a, p. 627). In a joint paper with Fritz Reiche, Thomas discussed the theoretical implications of the result, and they concluded that ‘the total number of dispersion electrons per atom, which are associated with a stationary state, is equal to *s*/3 (i.e., $\frac{1}{3}$ times the degree of periodicity)’ (Reiche and Thomas, 1925, p. 515). Werner Kuhn arrived at the same result by taking the limit of high frequency $\nu$ ($\gg \nu_i^a, \nu_j^e$) for the incident radiation in Kramers’ dispersion formula and by putting the result equal to the high-frequency limit of the classical dispersion formula, Eq. (347); he obtained the sum-rule

$$\sum f_i = 1, \tag{355'}$$

for the case of hydrogen, where $f_i$ denotes the oscillator strengths—being positive

650 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

or negative—i.e., $f_i = A_i^a \tau_i^a$ or $- A_i^e \tau_i^e$ (Kuhn, 1925a).$^{982}$ Kuhn then explored the experimental values of the $f$-sums (which Kuhn called $p$-sums) in the cases of thallium, cadmium and sodium absorption lines (Kuhn, 1925b; 1926a, b, c). He thus found values for the sums, which sometimes were larger than unity and which allowed conclusions about the electronic structure of atoms. Altogether the intensity sum-rules confirmed the new concepts in dispersion theory and the theory of atomic structure very well.

As we have seen, the dispersion of light by atoms constituted one example of a general class of quantum phenomena determined by the interaction of radiation and matter. In a programmatic essay, entitled 'Über die Wirkung von Atomen bei *Stößen*' ('On the Action of Atoms in Collisions') and submitted by the end of March 1925 to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, Niels Bohr discussed another example: the passage of charged particles through matter (Bohr, 1925a). Experiments on the scattering of charged particles, like electrons and $\alpha$-particles by atoms, had revealed the structure of atoms in the first two decades of the twentieth century. Especially, Rutherford had formulated his model of the nuclear atom on the basis of his investigations of the collisions between $\alpha$-particles and heavy atoms (Rutherford, 1911a, b). A little later, the experiments on the impacts of electrons on atoms—performed by James Franck and Gustav Hertz (1914b)—had confirmed Bohr's theory of the stationary states of atoms. While the scattering of $\alpha$-particles with atomic nuclei had been described satisfactorily with the help of the laws of classical electrodynamics, the understanding of the inelastic electron–atom collisions required the use of quantum laws in order to account for the transfer of discrete energy-quanta to atoms. In spring 1925 Niels Bohr proposed a general approach to all quantum-theoretical scattering problems, based on the following ideas. He first suggested that the collision processes between electrons and atoms that were usually considered—i.e., those processes which implied the excitation of the atoms—exhibited a property which he called reciprocity ('Reziprozität,' Bohr, 1925a, p. 142). By reciprocity he denoted the fact, observed earlier by Oskar Klein and Svein Rosseland (1921), that to each inelastic collision between atoms and electrons, in which energy was transferred to the atom, there existed the inverse reaction, i.e., an atom–electron collision ('collision of the second kind'), in which a discrete amount of energy was transferred from the atom to the electron, leaving the atom in a final state of lower energy without emission of radiation ('radiationless collision'). The reciprocity property was not, in Bohr's opinion, shared by the processes between radiation and atoms, such as the dispersion of light, which were described by Kramers' dispersion formula, Eq. (348).

The two rather different kinds of processes, i.e., those having the reciprocity property and those not having it—only in the first ones did the mechanical laws of energy and momentum conservation hold, while in the latter the conservation

VI.1 The Dispersion-Theoretic Approach

651

laws held statistically—should represent, as Bohr suggested, the limiting cases of quantum-theoretical scattering processes. ‘In the case of other collision phenomena,’ Bohr remarked, ‘we must be prepared to accept a more complicated description as being necessary, in which neither a purely mechanical formulation nor a correspondingly simple quantum formulation [as in the dispersion formula] can be applied’ (Bohr, 1925a, p. 143). To give an example of such a scattering process, Bohr referred to the observations of the energy losses suffered by fast electrons in matter. If the velocity of the electrons was large enough, so that the duration of the collision between the electron and an atom could be considered small in comparison with the period of the electron motions in the atom, the effect was satisfactorily described by classical theory (Bohr, 1913a; Fowler, 1925b). But in substances consisting of heavy atoms the periods of the bound electrons were very small, and the energy transfer from the electrons to the atoms could not be accounted for anymore by classical mechanics; as a consequence a description involving quantum-theoretical probability arguments had to be used.$^{983}$ In this context Bohr quoted the work of Max Born and James Franck dealing with the quantum theory of molecules (Born and Franck, 1925a, b). In it, Born and Franck had proposed the following process for the formation of a diatomic molecule: when two atoms A and B collide, a ‘quasi-molecule’ of higher energy and finite lifetime is created, which can decay into the stable molecule AB only if the excess energy is taken away by a third atom (three-body collision). This process of formation of molecules contradicted in several respects Bohr’s previously assumed picture of atomic and molecular constitution: i.e., the quantization of the electron motions came prior to the quantization of the motion of the two nuclei. Hence Bohr interpreted it as an example of an ‘irreciprocal’ phenomenon, because the molecule thus arising ‘would not, as far as the oscillations and rotations of the nucleus are concerned, be uniquely associated with the relative motion of the atoms before collision, and the final result of the process might at present only be describable with the help of probability laws’ (Bohr, 1925a, p. 153).

Less than three weeks after the submission of his paper, Bohr learned that Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger had proved the existence of strict energy and momentum conservation in the Compton effect (Bothe and Geiger, 1925a). Therefore, the separation between quantum-theoretical scattering processes exhibiting ‘reciprocity’ and those which did not had broken down. Bohr wrote a long addendum to his paper, in which he withdrew his concept of an ‘irreciprocal process’; instead he now spoke of processes in which the usual ‘space-time pictures’ failed (Bohr, 1925a, pp. 156–157).

$^{983}$ Still, Bohr argued that the description would not be exactly the same as on the quantum theory of dispersion. Therefore, he refuted a theory proposed by Enrico Fermi a few months earlier (Fermi, 1924b). In it Fermi had replaced the effect of electrons on atoms by the effect of a radiation field—constructed by a superposition of harmonic fields giving the electromagnetic field of the moving electrons—on the atoms.

652 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

The falsification of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation, though it hit Bohr’s concepts of the quantum theory seriously, did not render useless the main results achieved with the help of the dispersion-theoretic approach. The physicists were not sure, after all, of the extent to which the dispersion formulae actually implied the idea of statistical energy and momentum conservation. Thus they continued to extend the application of the dispersion methods, including Born’s discretization prescription (351), and even tried to describe nonperiodic phenomena, such as the scattering of electrons by atoms and molecules (Born and Jordan, 1925a; Born, Jordan and Nordheim, 1925; Nordheim, 1926). In summer 1925, Bohr himself and Hendrik Kramers gave lectures at the sixth Scandinavian Mathematical Congress, in which they presented the dispersion-theoretic approach, characterizing it as an important achievement in the description of atomic phenomena (Bohr, 1925b; Kramers, 1925b).

VI.2 Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells

The year 1923, in which the failures of atomic models to account for the energy states of the helium atoms and the anomalous Zeeman effects were confirmed, represented a low point in the development of atomic theory. These serious difficulties did not, however, stop the experimental and theoretical research in spectroscopy. On the contrary, a boom of new investigations followed in the next few years, for the physicists were determined to crack the puzzles of atomic structure by exploring the finest details of line and band spectra with improved apparatus and intricate model considerations. Numerous centres devoted to spectroscopy at various places in Europe, in the United States, and even in Japan, provided new results. Among these places let us mention here the National Bureau of Standards in Washington, D.C., where William F. Meggers had directed the spectroscopy section since 1920, having as associates such men as Paul Darwin Foote, Fred Loomis Mohler and Otto Laporte; or the California Institute of Technology, where Robert Andrews Millikan, as director of the Norman Bridge Laboratory, had established the pursuit of spectroscopy as an important discipline; or the Physical Institute at the Imperial University, Tokyo, where Hantaro Nagaoka had carried on his research on the anomalous Zeeman effects since the beginning of this century, partly assisted by Toshio Takamine. Important contributions also came from the old and new centres in Europe: thus James Franck continued with his students the tradition founded by Woldemar Voigt and Carl Runge in spectroscopy in Göttingen; in Tübingen Friedrich Paschen and Ernst Back worked on the complex structure and the anomalous Zeeman effects; at the Potsdam Observatory Walter Grotrian carried out measurements of absorption spectra; in London Alfred Fowler, since 1907 at the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0285 -->

VI.2  Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells  
653

Imperial College of Science and Technology, explored various spectroscopic questions, occasionally assisted by John Robert Strutt, eldest son of Lord Rayleigh (John William Strutt, the third Baron Rayleigh); at Niels Bohr’s Institute in Copenhagen, Hans Marius Hansen and Sven Werner investigated specific problems suggested by Bohr; Manne Siegbahn’s institutes in Lund (before 1923) and Uppsala (after 1923) and Maurice de Broglie’s private laboratory in Paris remained particularly active in X-ray spectroscopy; and in Utrecht, Leonard Salomon Ornstein with Herman Carel Burger and Hendrik Berend Dorgelo concentrated on the measurements of the intensities of spectral lines.

Everywhere at these places the physicists improved the experimental techniques and extended their applications to investigate new spectra. For example, as we have already mentioned, Ornstein and his associates developed a precision method for measuring the line intensities; James Franck and his collaborators in Göttingen and Gustav Hertz in Eindhoven perfected the electron–atom collision method and detected with it the energy states of an increasing number of atoms and molecules; as we shall see later in this section, Robert Andrews Millikan and Ira Sprague Bowen in Pasadena, California, worked on a method to obtain the ultraviolet spectra of lighter elements. The indefatigable experimental efforts of Ernst Back in Tübingen to examine the details of the Paschen–Back effects of complex atoms have been described earlier (in Section IV.4). A variety of different techniques to excite spectral lines were employed: the lines could be observed in emission and absorption spectra, they could be excited by incident radiation, in flames and electric discharges or by electron impact. For example, Christian Füchtbauer in Tübingen developed a method to obtain the entire spectrum of an atom: a tube filled with mercury vapour was exposed to the light from a strong mercury lamp; the mercury atoms of the vapour then passed, on absorbing radiation of wavelengths 2537 Å (an intense line emitted by the mercury lamp), into the excited energy state $2p_1$; in this state the atoms (of the vapour) were also able to absorb other lines contained in the spectrum of the illuminating mercury lamp, and thus could assume successively higher energy states until finally they became ionized; then by the capture of an electron the ionized atom emitted, in cascade-like transitions, a complete spectrum of lines (Füchtbauer, 1920). Füchtbauer applied his technique not only to measure the frequency and the intensity of the series lines, but also to determine the decay-times of the excited states of atoms (Füchtbauer and Joos, 1920, 1922). Another way of bringing atoms into certain excited states, which could not be reached by normal methods (like raising the temperature of the gas containing the atoms), was proposed by James Franck and his student Günther Cario: in gas vapours at high pressure they excited transitions in one type of atoms by collisions of the second kind with atoms of another type (‘sensibilisierte Fluoreszenz,’ Cario and Franck, 1923, p. 202). By varying their methods, the physicists discovered hitherto unobserved lines, or they were able to determine the frequencies and intensities of already known lines with greater accuracy.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0286 -->

654  Chapter VI  New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

Simultaneously with the experimental investigations, there proceeded the organization of the new spectroscopic data. In spite of the recognizable failure of the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantum theory of atomic structure, the physicists still interpreted all data by applying its principles. In particular, they used the frequencies of the spectral lines to derive the energy terms of a given atom.⁹⁸⁴ For this purpose they assumed the absolute validity of the combination principle.⁹⁸⁵ However, the combination principle did not suffice to establish an ordering of the terms in many-electron atoms due to the complexity of their line spectra: one needed, in addition, extra model assumptions leading to the quantum numbers which fully characterized the stationary states. Although these model assumptions—which we have discussed in Section IV.4, and which introduced in the first place the inner quantum number *j*, besides the principal quantum number *n* and the azimuthal quantum number *k*—could not be justified on the basis of the known quantum theory of atomic structure and, therefore, had to be regarded as constituting empirical rules, they enabled the physicists to disentangle completely the energy terms of several atoms. Thus Hilde Gieseler succeeded in the case of the chromium atom (Gieseler, 1924)⁹⁸⁶; Otto Laporte devoted himself to the analysis of the iron spectrum (Laporte, 1924a, b)⁹⁸⁷; Karl Bechert and Ludwig August Sommer did the same with the vanadium spectrum (Bechert and Sommer, 1925)⁹⁸⁸; finally, Miguel Catalán and Karl Bechert analyzed the cobalt spectrum (Catalán and Bechert, 1925).⁹⁸⁹ Like the states of these enormously complex atoms, the states of other interesting atomic objects were also investigated: as, for example, the states of ionized lithium, which should resemble the states of the helium atom. Hermann Schüler performed this task in Tübingen and Potsdam between 1924 and 1926: he found two systems of terms, corresponding to the ortho-helium and parhelium systems (Schüler, 1924, 1925, 1926).
The actually observed spectral lines were determined not only by the stationary states of the atom under investigation; the number of possible combinations between two such states was rather restricted by the so-called selection rules, which had been proposed in 1918 by Adalbert Rubinowicz (1918a, b) and Niels Bohr (1918a, b). These selection rules, which originally applied only to the azimuthal quantum number, were extended in the 1920s to the inner quantum

VI.2 Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells 655

number for the purpose of describing multiplet spectra and their anomalous Zeeman effects, and they worked perfectly well. Nevertheless, it had been known for some time that there existed exceptions to the selection rules. In 1915 John Koch of Göteborg, Sweden, had discovered what he called a new series in a spectrum of ionized helium (Koch, 1915). Then Johannes Stark and his associates investigated the situation more closely and found that the new, anomalous lines were emitted by the neutral helim atom and they appeared only when strong electric fields were present (Stark, 1918). In the language of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory the lines could be explained by the transitions $2p-m p$, $2s-m d$, and $2s-m s$ ($m=3,4,5$, etc.), which implied the changes $\Delta k=0,2,0$ of the azimuthal quantum number $k$. Similar emission lines, for which the selection rule ($\Delta k=1$) was violated, were observed later on in the case of alkali elements. A theoretical explanation of a possible failure of the $\Delta k=1$ rule had been given already in 1918 by Niels Bohr: he had pointed out that in a perturbed atomic system, 'in addition to the main probabilities of such transitions for the original system, there will . . . exist small probabilities of new transitions' (Bohr, 1918a, p. 35). Since an electric field might cause a perturbation in the atoms, the facts observed by Stark and others followed immediately. However, in the April 1922 issue of *Philosophical Magazine* there appeared a note of Paul Foote, William F. Meggers and Fred L. Mohler, describing the excitation of some lines of the arc spectrum of potassium in a new type of discharge tube (Foote, Meggers and Mohler, 1922). They claimed that in their experiment no perturbing influence had been exerted by electrostatic fields on the potassium atoms, but still selection-rule-violating lines had occurred.

Niels Bohr, whose theory seemed to be at stake, immediately wrote a letter (dated 11 April 1922) to *Philosophical Magazine*, in which he argued that in the new discharge tubes ions could be formed and accumulate in certain regions and 'already a rough calculation makes it very probable that the fields due to neighbouring ions and free electrons, to which the emitting atoms have been subject, have been of the order of magnitude claimed by the quantum theory for the appearance of new lines with the intensity observed' (Bohr, 1922a, p. 1116). Bohr's explanation was contradicted by Snehamoy Datta, then at Alfred Fowler's spectroscopic laboratory at Imperial College, London, who urged in a letter published in the issue of *Nature* of 8 July 1922 that he had obtained lines connected with selection-rule-violating transitions also as absorption lines; that is, the lines were absorbed by the atoms of cold vapours, in which no free electrons or charged particles existed, which could be responsible for a perturbing electric field (Datta, 1922a). Still there was a way to understand Datta's result: for the observation of the absorption spectra the density of atoms must be very high, hence the absorbing atoms should not be considered as unperturbed free systems. While Datta claimed that this way out of the difficulty was not confirmed by more detailed investigations of some forbidden lines of the mercury atom (Datta, 1922b), experiments at Bohr's Institute in Copenhagen seemed

to support it. Hans Marius Hansen, Toshio Takamine and Sven Werner also
observed the mercury spectrum: they observed several new lines when an
external field was applied; and they studied the conditions under which the line
of wavelength $2270 \text{ \AA}$—corresponding to the transition from a metastable state
(discovered earlier in electron collision experiments: Franck and Einsporn, 1920)
to the ground state— was excited and concluded that this line must be stimulated
by rapidly changing electric forces from neighboring atoms and ions because
external electric and magnetic fields did not influence its occurrence (Hansen,

The combination principle and the selection rules provided the most impor-
tant assumptions for the task of ordering the overwhelming amount of spectro-
scopic data. The final confirmation of these two assumptions (or rules) by the
new data in turn convinced the physicists that they represented fundamental
aspects of the correct atomic theory of the future. However, the combination
principle and the selection rules did not determine the electronic structure of an
atom, whose spectral lines were analyzed with their help. For that purpose one
rather investigated detailed energy considerations in certain mechanical models
of the atom. That is, for a given atom, having a given nucleus and a given
number of electrons, one calculated or estimated the energy of electrons in the
stable orbits admitted by the quantum conditions. The most difficult part in the
calculation of energy (on the basis of classical mechanics) was—as we have
discussed in Section III.4—to take into account satisfactorily the effect of the
mutual interaction of the electrons in the atom. The theoreticians frequently
employed approximations in the evaluation of the electron–electron interaction:
as, for instance, the one provided by the picture of the penetrating orbits.
According to this picture, which had been proposed by Alfred Landé, Niels Bohr
and Erwin Schrödinger, one calculated the energy of a given electron orbit by
separating it into an outer part, lying outside the orbits of the other electrons,
and an inner part, in which the electron dives into the region occupied by the
inner electrons of the atom (see Schrödinger, 1921; Bohr, 1921e). Erwin Fues
developed this approach and applied it especially to calculate the energy states of
non-hydrogen-like atoms, such as the sodium atom (Fues, 1922a, b; 1925).⁹⁹¹

VI.2 Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;657

Another point of interest in the mechanical energy calculations constituted the so-called relativistic corrections. Sommerfeld’s pioneering proposal of 1915 to compute the fine structure of the hydrogen spectral lines by considering the fact that the electrons in Kepler orbits around the nucleus move with relativistic velocities was examined critically in the early 1920s. Precision experiments were carried out, for example, by Ernst Gehrcke and his collaborator Ernst Lau.^(992,993) Gehrcke and Lau presented the first results on the fine structure of the hydrogen Balmer lines, obtained with the help of the Lummer–Gehrcke interference method, at the *Naturforscherversammlung* in Bad Nauheim in September 1920 (Gehrcke and Lau, 1920). After carefully measuring the intensity distribution in the doublets, $H_\alpha$, $H_\beta$, and $H_\gamma$, Gehrcke and Lau arrived in their paper, submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in June 1921, at the conclusion: ‘It is remarkable that the absolute value of $\Delta v$ [i.e., of the doublet separation] comes out in the measurements to be smaller by 25% than calculated according to Sommerfeld’s theory of fine structure’ (Gehrcke and Lau, 1921a, p. 575). Gehrcke and Lau repeated this result in a talk at the Jena meeting of the German Physical Society in September 1921 (Gehrcke and Lau, 1921b).

The attack on the relativistic interpretation of the hydrogen fine structure alarmed Sommerfeld, although he knew that Hendrik Kramers had explained in his thesis that a smaller doublet separation might follow if a perturbing electric field acted on the atom (Kramers, 1919, pp. 577–578). After all, Gehrcke had been connected previously with the movement directed against Einstein’s relativ- supervised by Sommerfeld at the University of Munich. Then he joined the *Technische Hochschule*, Stuttgart, where he became *Privatdozent* in 1924. In 1929 he was invited to a professorship at the *Technische Hochschule*, Hanover. In 1934 he moved to Breslau, occupying a joint professorship at the University of Breslau and the *Technische Hochschule*, and in 1943 he went to the *Technische Hochschule* in Vienna. After World War II he returned to Stuttgart and served (from 1947) as professor of theoretical physics at the *Technische Hochschule*. Fues worked on many topics of theoretical physics, especially atomic structure, wave mechanics, and solid state physics.

^(992) E. Gehrcke was born on 1 July 1878 at Berlin. He studied physics at the University of Berlin (1897–1901), obtaining his doctorate with a thesis under Emil Warburg (1901). In 1901 he joined the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*, becoming in 1926 the director of its optical department, a position which he kept until 1946. (Simultaneously, he was *Privatdozent*, 1904–1921, and professor, 1921–1946, at the University of Berlin.) In 1946 he went to the University of Jena as director of the Institute for Physiological Optics, and four years later he returned to East Berlin to the *Deutsches Amt für Materialprüfung*. In 1953 he became director of the optical department of the *Amt für Maß und Gewicht*. He died on 25 January 1960 at Hohen-Neuendorf.
Gehrcke contributed to the experimental techniques of interference spectroscopy (e.g., he developed with Otto Lummer the Lummer–Gehrcke method), to physiological optics and to the physics of gaseous discharges.

^(993) E. Lau was born on 7 March 1893 at Brünn, Moravia. At an early age he went to Berlin, where he attended school and studied (theology, philosophy, psychology and physics) at the University of Berlin. After his military service during World War I he obtained his doctorate at the University of Berlin with a thesis on a topic of physiological optics in 1920. Then he joined the optics department of the *Physikalisch-Technische Reichsanstalt*; there he directed the radiation laboratory from 1929 to 1945. Shortly after World War II he established an optical laboratory in East Berlin, which became in 1948 the *Institut für Optik und Feinmechanik* and later developed into the *Institut für Optik und Spektroskopie*, Berlin-Adlershof. He died on 17 February 1978 in East Berlin. Lau contributed to a variety of optical problems, ranging from spectroscopy to photography and physiological optics.

Walther Bothe did not agree with the interpretation of the fine-structure data in terms of the rigid electron hypothesis. In a letter to *Naturwissenschaften*, dated 28 November 1922, he argued that the Gehrcke–Lau results should not be considered as a ‘refutation of the special relativity theory and confirmation of the absolute theory,’ but as demonstrating the fact that ‘the conditions for the

$^{994}$ Gehrcke belonged to the earliest promoters of the antirelativity movement. In summer 1920 Paul Weyland established in Berlin a ‘German Scientists’ Study Group for the Preservation of Pure Science’ (*‘Arbeitsgemeinschaft deutscher Naturforscher zur Erhaltung reiner Wissenschaft’*), which fought against Albert Einstein’s relativity theory. On 24 August 1920 the *Arbeitsgemeinschaft* held a meeting in Berlin’s Philharmonic Hall, at which Weyland and Gehrcke addressed a large gathering. Max von Laue reported about this meeting to Sommerfeld as follows:

> Yesterday we had here one of the 20 announced protest meetings against relativity theory. An “*Arbeitsgemeinschaft deutscher Naturforscher*,” led by a Mr. Weyland, has taken charge of them, after the matter had been introduced several weeks ago through an article of Mr. Weyland in the *Täglichen Rundschau*. The article and yesterday’s speech of Mr. Weyland were on the same level: Einstein was called a plagiarist, and those who support relativity theory were called partisans of Dadaism. (This word was really used.) And the most incredible thing is that people with scientific reputations, like [Philipp] Lenard and [Maximilian] Wolf of Heidelberg, offer themselves to give lectures in such company. Yesterday Gehrcke spoke after Weyland; and although he rehashed the old arguments, his calm, impersonal way of discussing was a relaxation after Weyland, who can compete with the most unscrupulous demagogues. (Laue to Sommerfeld, 25 August 1920)

Laue added in his letter to Sommerfeld that he, together with Walther Nernst and Heinrich Rubens, had sent a letter for publication to all major Berlin newspapers protesting against the antirelativity movement. Sommerfeld found soon afterwards that the Heidelberg astronomer M. Wolf had not really joined the Weyland group.

applicability of the special relativity theory are not present here'; the behaviour of the electron should be determined rather by ‘its intrinsic forces,’ about which one did not know anything (Bothe, 1923a, pp. 45–46). A year later Ernst Lau, in a review of the status of the fine-structure problem—published in the *Physikalische Zeitschrift*—discussed all available measurements, especially the possible errors of the determination of the doublet separation and the details of the intensity distribution of the lines (Lau, 1924). After a thorough evaluation of the data Lau concluded again that the observed frequency differences were appreciably smaller than those predicted on the basis of Sommerfeld’s fine-structure theory.$^{995}$ It occurred to him that Bothe’s attempt to account for the deviation from the relativistic theory by assuming the fine structure of the lines to arise from unknown inner forces of the electron had to be rejected because the ‘actual hydrogen lines are simpler than predicted by Sommerfeld’s theory’ (Lau, 1924, p. 65). In support of this conclusion, Lau referred to the fact that the relativistic theory of the hydrogen energy states had run into further difficulties: ‘The more recent investigations on the Zeeman effect of Balmer lines have yielded the unequivocal result that these lines exhibit an anomalous Zeeman effect. Because of this the hydrogen doublet must be seen in close analogy to the alkali lines, a fact which is of the greatest importance for the further development of the theory’ (Lau, 1924, p. 65).

Peter Erochin, a student of Woldemar Voigt’s in Göttingen, had already drawn attention—in a paper published in 1913—to the possibility that hydrogen lines might exhibit an anomalous Zeeman effect: he had observed the transition of the $H_{\alpha}$-doublet in magnetic fields of growing field strength first into a broad single line and finally into a triplet (Erochin, 1913). Nearly ten years later Otto Oldenberg in Munich studied the situation again, obtaining the following results: for weak fields each component of the $H_{\alpha}$-doublet was separated in a normal Zeeman triplet, with a parallel component of unchanged frequency and two shifted perpendicular components; but for strong fields the Zeeman patterns of the doublet changed into the Zeeman pattern of a singlet line (Oldenberg, 1922). Karl Försterling and Gerhard Hansen confirmed these results by measurements of even greater accuracy in the case of $H_{\alpha}$- and $H_{\beta}$-doublets (Försterling and Hansen, 1923). Serious consequences seemed to follow from the above observations: if the hydrogen lines really exhibited an anomalous effect, the relativistic theory of the hydrogen atom broke down. However, there still existed a way out: the anomalous behaviour of the Balmer lines in a magnetic field could originate from some extra perturbation effect, and then one had to discuss the relative strength of this perturbation effect versus the perturbation effects from the magnetic field and the relativistic motion of the electron. Such a possibility had been discussed already by Hendrik Kramers in 1920, when he had treated the influence of electric fields on the relativistic fine structure of hydrogen lines

Still, however, the anomalous Zeeman effect of Balmer lines could be caused by perturbative forces other than the ones arising from electric fields.

The situation was even more complex in the other example of the relativistic effect, which Sommerfeld had given in 1916: the X-ray doublets (Sommerfeld, 1916c). Sommerfeld's interpretation had been used with success to explain the X-ray data in the late 1910s and early 1920s, especially by Walther Kossel, Gregor Wentzel and Sommerfeld himself (see Sections III.3, III.4, and III.5). For a closer analysis the X-ray frequencies had been organized into two types of doublets, the so-called 'relativistic doublets' and the 'screening doublets,' the nomenclature being connected with their supposed origin from the relativistic correction to the energy of the moving electron, on one hand, and from the influence of the groups of inner electrons on the states of the electron involved in the emission of X-ray lines, on the other. Formally, the energy terms derived from the X-ray spectra were described by three quantum numbers: for instance, $L(2, 1)$ denoted a state with principal quantum number $n = 2$, and two 'azimuthal' quantum numbers $k_1 = 2$ and $k_2 = 1$. In this notation the relativistic $L$-doublets, deduced from the X-ray spectra, were connected with the pair of states, $\{L(2, 1), L(2, 2)\}$, and the screening doublets with the pair of states, $\{L(1, 1), L(2, 1)\}$; that is, the relativistic doublets constituted states with the same quantum number $k_1$, screening doublets with the same quantum number $k_2$. This notation for energy terms, together with the selection rules—i.e., $\Delta k_1 = +1$ and $\Delta k_2 = +1$ for strong lines, and $\Delta k_1 = -1$ and $\Delta k_2 = 0$ for weak lines—worked perfectly in the analysis of X-ray spectra (see, e.g., Wentzel, 1923c; Coster, 1923; Nishina, 1925). And yet, Alfred Landé criticized it severely in a paper, entitled 'Zur Theorie der Röntgenspektren' ('On the Theory of X-Ray Spectra') and received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 12 June 1923 (Landé, 1923b). Landé was mainly interested in the origin of the so-called 'anomalous' X-ray states having different quantum numbers, $k_1$ and $k_2$, for which he proposed and discussed two possible explanations: (a) the state was caused by removing an $n_{k_1}$-electron from the atom, or (b) by removing an $n_{k_2}$-electron.$^{996}$ While the term data did not allow one to decide between possibilities (a) and (b), the selection rules and the term multiplicities spoke in favour of (a). Landé cited another evidence in favour of (a): if one assumed the anomalous X-ray level to be obtained by the removal of an $n_{k_1}$-electron, then the electron groups in the atom would rearrange themselves so as to leave one electron in a state with azimuthal quantum number $k = k_1$; this electron would behave like a series electron in the alkali atoms, i.e.,  

$^{996}$ Landé assumed, of course, the usual explanation for the occurrence of X-ray states, i.e., the removal of electrons from the interior of atoms. The removal of an $n_{k_1}$-electron means that an electron with principal quantum number $n$ and azimuthal quantum number $k_1$ was removed from the neutral atom. Then, by the capture of an electron from the outer states of the atom an X-ray line would be emitted.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0293 -->

661

it would occur in two different energy states due to the interaction with the angular momentum of the $K$-electrons constituting the core.$^{997}$

Landé found the relation between the states involved in the emission of X-rays and the states of the alkali atoms responsible for the optical spectra very satisfactory, for it enabled him to suggest an interpretation for the quantum numbers $k_1$ and $k_2$ of the X-ray states: $k_1$ should be put equal to the azimuthal quantum number, and $k_2$ equal to the inner quantum number $j$ of the atom. With this identification the X-ray levels $K(1,1)$, $L(1,1)$, $L(2,1)$ and $L(2,2)$ corresponded simply to $1s$, $2s$, $2p_2$ and $2p_1$ levels, respectively. As a consequence the observed X-ray level separations could be related to the corresponding optical level separations: for example, the term difference between a normal state, $n (k, j = k)$, and an anomalous state, $n (k, j = k - 1)$, corresponded to the term difference of the optical doublets in Na, Mg$^+$, Al$^{++}$, etc. From the relation of optical to X-ray doublets it followed, in turn, that in optical doublets—as in the so-called X-ray doublets—the separations should increase for atoms and ions of increasing atomic number $Z$ like $(Z - \sigma)^4$, where $\sigma$ is the screening constant. By analyzing the data in question along these lines, Landé found that ‘in favour of the alternative (a), and especially for the relation between optical and relativistic X-ray doublets, can be cited not only the *multiplet structure* and the *selection rules* of X-ray terms, but also the *interval rules* cannot be regarded *a priori* as an obvious counter-argument’ (Landé, 1923b, p. 396). In other words, coarse estimates seemed to confirm the common origin of optical doublets and X-ray doublets.

Such a common origin had been proposed already several years earlier by Arnold Sommerfeld, when he tried to explain the lithium doublet as a relativistic doublet (Sommerfeld, 1916b, Part II, Section 11). In the 1920s the first physicists to point out an analogy between optical and X-ray spectra were Louis de Broglie and Alexandre Dauvillier; they established, for instance, the correspondence between the X-ray $L$-doublet—i.e., $L(2,1)$ and $L(2,2)$ in our notation—and the optical doublet lines.$^{998}$ Then Landé stepped in and generalized these ideas. However, unlike Sommerfeld he believed that both term doublets arose from the coupling of the angular momenta of the atomic core and the series electron (or the electron responsible for the emission of the X-ray lines). His interpretation resulted, therefore, in a slightly different assignment of quantum numbers to the X-ray states than assumed by Sommerfeld and others before him. For example, in the case of the $L$-states—$L(1,1)$, $L(2,1)$ and $L(2,2)$—one had so far taken the principal and the azimuthal quantum numbers to be $n_k = 2_1$, $2_1$ and $2_2$ (see

He argued again that the selection rules and the multiplicity of terms favoured his theory. On the other hand, the fact that the doublet separations were proportional to $(Z - \sigma)^4/n^3$—as predicted on the relativistic theory ($n$ being the principal quantum number)—did not necessarily rule out all nonrelativistic theories. Landé proved this point by calculating the doublet separation according to what he called the ‘magnetic theory of the optical doublets’ (Landé, 1924a, p. 94). That is, he considered the separation of optical doublets as being caused by the different positions of the core in the atom. Hence the term separation was proportional to $\Delta m$, where $\Delta m$ was the difference of the components of the core’s angular momentum (in the direction of the angular momentum of the series electron) in units of $h/2\pi$, and the strength of the magnetic field, $|\mathbf{H}|$, created by the series electron (of mass $m_e$ and charge $e$ moving in an $n_k$-orbit) was given by

at the California Institute of Technology, independently of Alexandre Dauvillier and Louis de Broglie and Alfred Landé.$^{1000}$ On coming to Pasadena, California, in 1921, Millikan had started the exploration of the spectra emitted by light elements—from hydrogen to aluminum—in the extreme ultraviolet region (Millikan, 1921a). Working with a hot spark between two electrodes as a tool for exciting the line spectra and large gratings for measuring the frequency, Millikan and Bowen observed lines of wavelengths down to 136 Å (Millikan and Bowen, 1924a). They investigated elements up to copper in the periodic table (Millikan and Bowen, 1924a), including especially highly ionized elements, such as doubly ionized boron, triply ionized oxygen, or quadruply ionized nitrogen (Millikan and Bowen, 1924b). Their investigations not only resulted in an enormous accumulation of new, hitherto unknown data, but allowed in addition important hints concerning its systematic organization. Thus, after reporting the separation of the doublet components of the $2s–2p$ transitions in lithium, ionized beryllium, doubly ionized boron and triply ionized carbon (i.e., atoms and ions having the same number of electrons but different nuclear charges), whose wavelengths ranged from 6707.85 Å to 1548.26 Å, Millikan and Bowen stated: ‘The doublet separation . . . not only increases as the fourth power of the effective nuclear charge [i.e., the nuclear charge minus the screened off charges due to the $K$-electrons], but its numerical value is closely predicted by the relativity, or regular, doublet law’ (Bowen and Millikan, 1924b, p. 263). In a further paper, Millikan and Bowen confirmed this conclusion in several other cases: as, for example, in atoms and ions having three $L$-electrons (boron, ionized carbon, doubly ionized nitrogen and triply ionized oxygen) or having one $M$-electron—from sodium to fivefold ionized sulphur (Bowen and Millikan, 1924c). At the same time they showed that the irregular $L$-doublet, which had been first discovered by Gustav Hertz in the X-ray $L$-series (Hertz, 1920), and which corresponded to the $L(1, 1)$ and $L(2, 1)$ states, occurred also in the ultraviolet and optical regions in the case of atoms with lower atomic numbers; that is, the same law, which described the X-ray doublet,

$$\sqrt{\nu_1} - \sqrt{\nu_2} = \text{const.}, \qquad (359)$$

also accounted for the ultraviolet and optical doublets arising from the same types of states in homologous atomic systems (with the same number of electrons), such as $\text{Li, Be}^+, \text{B}^{++}, \text{C}^{+++} \text{ and } \text{Ni}^{+++++}$. Millikan and Bowen noted:

$^{1000}$ I. S. Bowen was born on 21 December 1898 at Seneca Falls, New York, and studied physics at the California Institute of Technology with Millikan. In 1931 he became professor of physics at Caltech, and in 1946 director of Mt. Wilson Observatory and two years later also of Mt. Palomar Observatory. For his pioneering work on the analysis of spectra and the identification of spectra of astronomical objects (e.g., the explanation of the ‘nebulium’ lines as those emitted by ionized oxygen), he received numerous honours, including the 1942 Henry Draper medal, the 1946 Potts medal, and the 1949 Rumford medal (of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences). Bowen also designed many powerful instruments for astronomical research and was responsible for the installation of the 200-in. reflecting telescope at Mt. Palomar. He died in Los Angeles on 6 February 1973.

664 \ Chapter VI \ New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

‘The behavior, then, of the irregular doublet is beautiful confirmation of the conclusion arrived at from the behavior of the relativity doublet that both of the doublet laws first discovered in the X-ray field [i.e., Sommerfeld’s relativistic doublet law and Eq. (359)] *are equally applicable to the whole optical region*’ (Bowen and Millikan, 1924c, p. 216).

Millikan and Bowen summarized the main theoretical consequences of their experimental studies of ultraviolet line doublets already in a paper, entitled ‘Some Conspicuous Successes of the Bohr Atom and a Serious Difficulty,’ which was published in the September 1924 issue of *Physical Review* (Millikan and Bowen, 1924b). As ‘conspicuous successes of the Bohr atom’ they interpreted the fact that the same laws applied to optical and X-ray spectra. At the same time certain consequences of the unified description of optical and X-ray spectra caused a ‘serious difficulty’ in the existing atomic theory. Especially, the quantum numbers determined by comparing optical and X-ray spectra for the X-ray levels did not seem to be consistent with the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. For example, one had to associate the $L(2, 1)$ and $L(2, 2)$ states with the quantum numbers $n_k = 2_2$, instead of associating $L(2, 1)$ with $n_k = 2_1$ and $L(2, 2)$ with $n_k = 2_2$, as would be required on the relativity theory (Landé, 1923b). Millikan and Bowen now added empirical support to this argument: the $L(2, 1)$ and $L(2, 2)$ states of doublet-lines-emitting atoms and ions possessed the same screening constant $\sigma$, while $L(1, 1)$ and $L(2, 1)$ possessed different $\sigma$; three states with azimuthal quantum number $k = 2$ seemed to be present in the case of triplet atoms and ions, such as $\text{Be}$, $\text{B}^+$, $\text{C}^{++}$, etc., while the relativity theory allowed just two states with $k = 2$. Millikan and Bowen now claimed:

> The only way in which it appears to be possible to avoid the foregoing serious difficulties is to throw overboard altogether the relativity explanation of the “relativity doublet” and to assume that the amazing success of this relativity formula . . . is not due at all to differences in the shapes of elliptical and circular orbits, as postulated by the relativity theory of doublet separations, but that there is some other cause which by mere chance leads exactly to this relativity formula without actually necessitating relativity conceptions. (Millikan and Bowen, 1924b, p. 224)

They argued, however, that the quantitative success of the relativity theory in explaining the doublet separations spoke against giving up the old theory completely. An alternative possibility remaining in the game consisted in an ‘abandonment of Bohr’s interpenetration ideas and with them the practice of assigning azimuthal quantum numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 etc. to $s$, $p$, $d$, $f$, etc. terms’ and to admit orbits having the same shape (i.e., the same azimuthal quantum number $k$), but widely different screening constants $\sigma$, a possibility, which ‘would seem to require the introduction of a dissymmetry not heretofore contemplated into atomic models’ (Millikan and Bowen, 1924b, p. 228).

Millikan and Bowen spoke, in their paper just mentioned, of ‘two horns of a dilemma’ (*loc. cit.*, p. 228) when addressing the problem of either abandoning the relativity interpretation or Bohr’s conceptions of atomic constitution. Previously,

666                                                          Chapter VI  New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

C-atom, in particular, has been removed in a satisfactory way. According to Stoner, the shells in the interior of the atom must be further subdivided; the number of electrons in the subgroups of atomic shells become different from each other and are determined by the formal rules of the inner quantum numbers; and the constitution of atoms is still tighter than associated hitherto with the structure of the X-ray spectra. (Sommerfeld, 1924d, p. VI)

Edmund Clifton Stoner submitted the results, referred to by Sommerfeld, from Cambridge in a paper, entitled 'The Distribution of Electrons among Atomic Levels'; it was submitted to *Philosophical Magazine* in July 1924 and appeared in the October issue of the same year (Stoner, 1924).<sup>1003</sup> Stoner gave the motivation for his theoretical investigation in the introduction by stating:

The scheme for the distribution of electrons among the completed sub-levels in atoms proposed by Bohr [see, e.g., Bohr, 1921e] is based on somewhat arbitrary arguments as to symmetry requirements; it is also incomplete in that all the sub-levels known to exist are not separately considered. It is here suggested that the number of electrons associated with a sub-level is connected with the inner quantum number characterizing it, such a connection being strongly indicated by the term multiplicity observed for optical spectra. (Stoner, 1924, pp. 719–720)

Stoner started from Landé's organization of X-ray levels as dependent on the principal quantum number $n$, the azimuthal quantum number $k$ and the inner quantum number $j$, i.e., $n(k, j)$ (see Landé, 1923b). He then drew attention to the difficulties arising in this scheme—that it did not agree with the relativity interpretation for such term pairs as $L(2, 1)$ and $L(2, 2)$—as well as its advantages —that it established a relation with the optical spectra. And he referred to a proposal of Louis de Broglie and Alexandre Dauvillier, who had tried to obtain a more consistent description of the situation by assuming a larger number of subgroups of electrons in atoms than Bohr had done (L. de Broglie and Dauvillier, 1924; Dauvillier, 1924). Louis de Broglie and Dauvillier had introduced several months earlier the following subgroups of electrons in completed *K-*, *L-*, *M-* and *N*-levels: $K(2)$; $L_3(2), L_2(2), L_1(4)$; $M_6(2), M_5(2), M_4(4), M_3(2), M_2(4), M_1(4)$; $N_{10}(2), N_9(2), N_8(4), N_7(2), N_6(4), N_5(4), N_4(2), N_3(4), N_2(4), N_1(4)$. (The numbers in brackets represent the maximum numbers of electrons in the subgroup under consideration.) The separation in subgroups deviated from Bohr's earlier one of 1921, but could be justified by measurements of the

He studied at Cambridge University from 1918, obtaining his B.A. in 1921 and continuing his research work at the Cavendish Laboratory (obtaining his doctorate under E. Rutherford in 1925). In 1924 he went as Lecturer to the University of Leeds. In 1927 he was appointed Reader; in 1939 he was appointed to the newly instituted chair of theoretical physics, and in 1951 to the Cavendish Chair in Physics, also at Leeds. He retired in 1963. Stoner did pioneering work on the magnetic properties of matter, on which subject he wrote three books, the first being *Magnetism and Atomic Structure* (1926). In the laboratory connected with the Cavendish Chair he worked on problems of electron band structure in metals. Stoner had been elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1937. VI.2 Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells 667

absorption coefficients of X-rays by matter consisting of atoms of given elements (Dauvillier, 1924); it also explained the relative intensities of the X-ray spectral lines more satisfactorily than Bohr's theory (L. de Broglie and Dauvillier, 1924). A difficulty arose, however, with respect to the number of subgroups: the absorption experiments revealing the number of X-ray edges, as well as the experiments on excitation by electron impact or incident radiation, yielded fewer levels than assumed by L. de Broglie and Dauvillier, namely, not more than 5 *M*-levels and about 7 *N*-levels (see, e.g., Ross, 1923b; Robinson, 1923). Stoner considered the latter evidence together with the results of the description of multiplet spectra and the anomalous Zeeman effects and noted: 'The experiments thus support the view that for Röntgen spectra, as for optical doublet series, the number of sub-levels characterized by different *j*'s into which a given *K*-level subdivides is restricted to two' (Stoner, 1924, p. 721).

Working with the above hypothesis, Stoner proposed a new classification exhibiting two features: first, 'the number of electrons in each completed level is equal to double the sum of the inner quantum numbers as assigned, there being in the *K*, *L*, *M*, *N* levels, when complete, 2, 8(2 + 2 + 4), 18(2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 6), 32, . . . electrons'; second, 'the number of electrons associated with each sub-level separately is also equal to double the inner quantum number' (Stoner, 1924, p. 722). This classification immediately explained the ground-state structure of the atoms of noble gases: in helium the *K*-level with inner quantum number $j = 1$ is occupied by two electrons; in neon, in addition to the completed *K*-shell (with two electrons), the *L*-shell is occupied with two (for the $L(K = 1, j = 1)$ state) plus two (for the $L(2, 1)$ state) plus four (for the $L(2, 2)$ state), i.e., with eight electrons; in argon one has also the *M*-level occupied with ten (four for the $M(3, 2)$ state and six for the $M(3, 3)$ state), hence there are altogether eighteen electrons, etc. Stoner's classification, of course, deviated from Bohr's. In Bohr's theory of the periodic system the form of the orbit had played the crucial role: thus, for instance, in the *L*-levels, one distinguished only between the $n_k = 2_1$- and $2_2$-orbits, and assumed that both types had to be occupied (in a complete shell) by four electrons each. For obtaining these occupation numbers of the $n_k$-levels, Bohr had used detailed energy considerations in the case of competing orbits, and from such considerations it followed occasionally that the maximum occupation number of a given $n_k$-state was different for atoms with different atomic numbers: especially, the inner sublevels of elements having higher atomic numbers could be filled by more electrons than were present in a complete level of an element having a lower atomic number. In contrast to that, Stoner's scheme was characterized by the fact that 'inner sub-groups [i.e., states with given principal and inner quantum numbers, $n$ and $j$] are completed at an earlier stage, subsequent changes being made by simple addition of electrons to outer sub-levels without reorganization of the groups as a whole' (Stoner, 1924, p. 724).

The crucial role in the new organization of the inner atomic structure was assumed by the inner quantum number, which Sommerfeld had postulated and which had been used to classify line multiplets and the anomalous Zeeman

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0300 -->

**668** \quad **Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory**

components of many-electron atoms. The similarity of the optical and the X-ray spectra justified to some extent the application of the inner quantum number in the description of the inner structure of atoms. Although so far no unique physical interpretation had been given of the inner quantum number—Sommerfeld’s original interpretation of it as the spatial quantum number determining the spatial orientation did not identify it clearly enough for atoms with many electrons—Stoner’s scheme seemed to establish the inner quantum number further as an independent and fundamental quantum number in atomic structure. From the fact that $2j$ electrons could be in a complete subgroup denoted by the index $j$, Stoner concluded that in the subgroup up to $2j$ equally probable states existed.

In the last section of his paper, Section 7, Stoner reported the evidence supporting the proposed electron distribution in atoms. First of all, he quoted the information derived from the relative intensity of X-ray lines. Assuming this intensity was—more or less—proportional to the number of electrons in the levels involved in the transition, he derived from the fact, that the $K_{\alpha_2}$-line of several metals (such as iron, copper, etc.) was about half as intense as the $K_{\alpha_1}$-component, the consequence that in the $L(2, 2)$-state (which was assumed to be involved in the $K_{\alpha_1}$-transition) twice as many electrons existed as in the $L(2, 1)$-state (which was involved in the $K_{\alpha_2}$-transition). That is, the intensity ratio proved the new electron distribution to be the correct one rather than Bohr’s (according to which a different intensity ratio, either 3:1 or 1:1 would be expected). He found a similarly positive result from the other available intensity data.$^{1004}$ Second, Stoner quoted the data on the ionic paramagnetism of the third-period elements, from $\text{K}^+$, $\text{Ca}^{++}$, . . . to $\text{Cu}^+$, as confirming his views on the systematic occupation of the $M(3, 2)$- and $M(3, 3)$-levels in the atoms of successive elements in the periodic system of elements. As we have mentioned earlier, the building-up of the electron groups in Bohr’s theory was connected with a complete reorganization of the whole $M$-group, which made the observed regularity in the number of Bohr magnetons—according to observation this number increased in steps of unity from 0 to 5 (for $\text{Mn}^{++}$ and $\text{Fe}^{+++}$ with 23 electrons) and then decreased in the same steps to 0 (for $\text{Cu}^+$ with 28 electrons)—very difficult to explain. Third, the chemical properties of the elements could be accounted for by the new scheme as well as by Bohr’s theory. Since these properties depended basically on the arrangement of the outer electrons, in which both schemes agreed, Stoner had to examine only the few exceptions in which they did not. Thus he found, for example, that the chemical compounds of

$^{1004}$The absorption data, which had already been used by L. de Broglie and Dauvillier, also agreed with Stoner’s scheme. According to a formula found by Louis de Broglie (1922a), the absorption coefficient for an X-ray line of frequency $\nu$ was proportional to the number of electrons in the initial state of the transition. For the ratio of the numbers of electrons in the levels $L(2, 2)$, $L(2, 1)$ and $L(1, 1)$, respectively, Dauvillier had obtained the ratio 62 : 41 : 35 (Dauvillier, 1924). Harold Robinson deduced approximately the same result from his investigation of secondary corpuscular rays ejected from several metallic surfaces upon incidence of primary X-rays of characteristic frequencies (Robinson, 1923).

**VI.2 Atomic Structure and the Problem of Closed Electron Shells** \quad **669**

phosphorus spoke in favour of his atomic structure: phosphorus was usually pentavalent, due to the five outer $M$-electrons, but could also be trivalent because of the three less strongly bound $M(2, 1)$- and $M(3, 1)$-electrons.$^{1005}$

The case of the carbon atom was especially interesting. Bohr had assumed that its four outer electrons were bound in equivalent $2_1$-orbits, which were arranged tetrahedrally, while Stoner now assumed two electrons to be in $2_1$-orbits and the other two electrons in $2_2$-orbits. However, in the new scheme the tetravalence of carbon could also be explained: the tetrahedral symmetry had to be attributed not to the four outer electrons, ‘but to the four “vacant places” [i.e., those in the $L(2, 2)$-state] which would have to be filled up for it to attain a complete [noble gas] configuration’ (Stoner, 1924, p. 735). In any case, Stoner’s organization was perfectly consistent with Alfred Fowler’s $C^+$-spectrum. Thus Stoner concluded confidently: ‘Evidence based on consideration of intensities of X-ray lines, absorption of X-rays, chemical and magnetic properties, and optical spectra is discussed and shown to give considerable support to a distribution of the kind put foward’ (Stoner, 1924, p. 736).

Stoner’s reorganization of electron groups in atoms seemed to answer many questions that had accumulated against Bohr’s theory of the periodic system of elements. Still, as we have mentioned, Stoner was not the first to abandon Bohr’s theory; already Louis de Broglie and Alexandre Dauvillier had done so. Even the particular arrangement proposed by Stoner had been expounded earlier by the chemist J. D. Main Smith of Birmingham University in a series of notes in the journal *Chemistry and Industry* (*Journal of the Society of Chemical Industry*), the first of which appeared in the issue of 28 March 1924 (Main Smith, 1924a). Main Smith had combined the observation that nearly all X-ray levels were doublets with a large amount of chemical data, and arrived at the conclusion that the electrons occupying $L$-, $M$-, $N$-, etc., levels in atoms fell into more subgroups than Bohr had assumed (see also Main Smith, 1924b, c). He had proposed to determine the number of electrons in each subgroup by twice the value of a quantum number, which corresponded to the inner quantum number; thus he had obtained the same numbers of electrons in closed subgroups as Stoner did several months later.$^{1006}$

Although Main Smith used partly the same arguments as Stoner, his papers were not noticed by physicists, because they did not read the journal where they appeared. However, Main Smith also presented his results in an elaborated form with all available chemical evidence for the electronic structure of atoms in his book, entitled *Chemistry and Atomic Structure*, which appeared in October 1924 (Main Smith, 1924d). This book was then cited by Arnold Sommerfeld in a paper ‘Zur Theorie des periodischen Systems,’ published in the 1 January 1925 issue of

Nevertheless Main Smith felt that his contribution was not properly acknowledged, and in a letter to the editor of *Philosophical Magazine* he directed 'attention to the fact that the distribution of electrons in atoms characterized by the sub-groupings 2; 2, 2, 4; 2, 2, 4, 4, 6; 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6, 8 did not originate with Mr. E. Stoner, as within recent months various papers published in your journal have suggested' (Main Smith, 1925, p. 878). After referring to his first paper of 28 March 1924 and his book of October 1924, Main Smith concluded: 'I do not suggest that Mr. Stoner's work was not independent, but in view of the foregoing there can be no question of my priority in the matter of this electronic distribution in atoms. On the Continent and in America my priority is acknowledged, but in my own country my work has failed even to be cited in your magazine' (Main Smith, 1925, pp. 878–879).

The work of Edmund Stoner, however, was quickly recognized by the quantum physicists because he fully justified it on the basis of known data and had managed to resolve several difficulties in interpreting the data on the Bohr theory of atomic structure.$^{1007}$ Among those who read Stoner's paper, belonged Dirk Coster, the expert on X-ray spectra in Groningen. He wrote to Niels Bohr about it on 7 December 1924: 'I regret very much that I have no occasion at the moment to discuss a matter with you or Kramers which interests me very much, namely Stoner's paper on the distribution of electrons in groups.' He added that, in spite of 'the actually rather doubtful justification' one should consider the proposed scheme seriously because it seemed 'that it is actually possible to build up an electron group in such a way that one gets Stoner's sub-groups' (Coster to Bohr, 7 December 1924). The available empirical data did not yet allow, in Coster's opinion, a 'decision with certainty,' but he hoped to obtain more information soon in order to decide between the two competing organizations (see the citation of Coster's letter in Bohr, 1977, p. 41). In his reply, Bohr admitted that he immediately 'understood the formal beauty and simplicity of his [Stoner's] classification of the levels,' but that 'from a quantum-theoretical point of view, it cannot mean a final solution of the problem, since we do not yet possess any possibility of connecting the classification of levels in a rational manner with a quantum-theoretical analysis of electron orbits' (Bohr to Coster, 10 December 1924; quoted in Bohr, 1977, p. 41). Bohr was very hesitant to accept a final solution of the problem before the character of the doublets was fully clarified in theory.

Bohr's reservation towards the new ideas in atomic theory may be easily understood in view of the uncertain theoretical and experimental situation at that

time.$^{1008}$ Stoner himself knew about this situation; hence he tried to assemble further evidence in favour of his scheme through an investigation of the spectroscopic magneton numbers of ions. In a paper, which contained the supporting data and appeared in the June 1925 issue of *Philosophical Magazine*, he showed that his new organization of electrons in subgroups made it possible to describe satisfactorily the observations on the multiplet structure of atoms as well as the ionic magnetic moments obtained from an analysis of the spectra (Stoner, 1925b).$^{1009}$ He added a note in proof, stating: ‘In a recent paper on the connexion between the completing of electron groups in atoms with the multiplet structure of spectra, Pauli has discussed in detail, with important conclusions, several questions closely related to those considered here’ (Stoner, 1925b, p. 1309). With this remark Stoner referred to the most important development of his scheme by Wolfgang Pauli.

**VI.3 The Rule for Equivalent Electrons:**
**Pauli’s Exclusion Principle**

Pauli had since long considered the correct distribution of electrons in atoms as an important problem of atomic theory, and he had been aware of the fact that Bohr’s theory of the periodic system did not solve the problem. ‘The weakness of the theory is,’ he had written to Sommerfeld already on 6 June 1923, ‘that it does not provide any explanation for the values 2, 8, 18, 32, . . . of the length of periods, because one cannot derive definite conclusions as to where exactly the periods are closed.’ In Pauli’s opinion this weakness could not be removed on the basis of the fundamental principles of Bohr’s theory; the failure of classical mechanics—i.e., of an essential part of the fundamental principles of atomic theory—which was reflected by the unsuccessful calculation of the stationary states of the helium atom and by the inability (of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory) to explain the phenomena of the anomalous Zeeman effects, made it obvious that the known difficulties of the existing theory could not be resolved by a slight modification of the assumptions or equations that had been used so far. New

$^{1008}$Bohr remained reserved even in later years, as shown by his article on the ‘Atom’ for the *Encyclopedia Britannica* (Bohr, 1926b). There he represented roughly the Main Smith–Stoner sub-groups, but added that ‘a full theoretical treatment of the problem cannot be obtained from considerations based only on the simple picture of central orbits’; instead, he expressed the hope that ‘the idea that the electron itself has magnetic properties may give the clue to the interpretation of the empirical rules governing the number of electrons in the group structure of the atom’ (Bohr, 1926b, p. 266).

$^{1009}$Stoner presented his results in more detail in a book, *Magnetism and Atomic Structure*, which appeared a year later (Stoner, 1926). It should be noted that Stoner referred to the work of Main Smith in his paper in a manner that was fair. In connection with the new electron scheme, he stated: ‘I have since found that the distribution had already been proposed, primarily on the basis of chemical arguments, by Main Smith. (See *Chemistry and Atomic Structure*, 1924.) It is very satisfactory that two different lines of attack should have led to the same conclusions’ (Stoner, 1925b, p. 1296, footnote).

He was soon promoted to *Privatdozent*, and as the topic of his inaugural public lecture he chose ‘*Quantentheorie und periodisches System der Elemente*’ (‘Quantum Theory and Periodic System of Elements’).$^{1010}$ Later, in his Nobel lecture, Pauli recalled:

> Very soon after my return to the University of Hamburg, in 1923, I gave there my inaugural lecture as *Privatdozent* on the periodic system of elements. The contents of this lecture appeared very unsatisfactory to me, since the problem of the closing of the electron shells had been clarified no further. The only thing that was clear was that a closer relation of this problem to the theory of multiplet structure must exist. I therefore tried to examine again critically the simplest case, the doublet structure of the alkali spectra. According to the point of view then orthodox, which was taken over by Bohr in his . . . lectures in Göttingen, a non-vanishing angular momentum of the atomic core was supposed to be the cause of this doublet structure. (Pauli, 1948, p. 133)

Towards the end of the year 1923 Pauli concerned himself with a different problem: the heat conduction in solid bodies (see Pauli to Kramers, 19 December 1923). He continued to work on this problem in early 1924, and in a letter to Bohr, dated 11 February 1924, he reported: ‘About my own work I cannot report much at the moment. With the problem of heat conduction in solids I have still not succeeded completely, but I hope to finish it before long.’$^{1011}$ He added: ‘In any case, it has been very good for me that I took leave of atomic theory for some time. Later, perhaps very soon, I will return to it with fresh forces’ (Pauli to Bohr, 11 February 1924). Pauli, who spoke in the same letter to Bohr about the problems of atomic theory, such as the anomalous Zeeman effects—‘with which I have tormented myself in vain and which are much too difficult for me’—indeed hoped for a fresh start. But he soon realized that the problems of atomic theory were more difficult than he had anticipated. Thus he wrote again to Bohr: ‘In contrast to the point of view, which you still had last fall, I now believe that also
