$^{1055}$ Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck assumed that the helium spectrum consisted of singlets and doublets.

We should mention that a proposal similar to Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck’s on the hydrogen and helium spectra was made by John Slater in a paper, submitted on 16 November 1925 to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* (Slater, 1925d). Further, Arnold Sommerfeld and Albrecht Unsöld wrote a paper on the spectrum of hydrogen, which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 6 February 1926; their scheme also coincided formally with the earlier one of Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck (Sommerfeld and Unsöld, 1926).

700 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

summer of 1925. Especially, they concentrated more and more on the mysterious four quantum numbers, which Pauli had introduced earlier that year. 'I only remember the discussion with George [Uhlenbeck], where I tried to explain the Pauli principle to him, that there are four quantum numbers, and one quantum number is always a half,' Goudsmit said later (Goudsmit, AHQP Interview, 6 December 1963, p. 16), and Uhlenbeck completed the report by recalling: 'It came one afternoon ... It was always this question of the four quantum numbers, and I still remember that I said, "If there are four quantum numbers, there must be four degrees of freedom ... And if there are four degrees of freedom, then there must be some kind of internal motion"' (Uhlenbeck in Goudsmit, AHQP Interview, 7 December 1963, pp. 4–5). What happened next? On an afternoon at the end of September 1925, Uhlenbeck proposed to connect Pauli's fourth quantum number of the electron with a dynamical degree of freedom of the electron. Although Goudsmit had been concerned with the fourth quantum number earlier—he had even developed a modification of Pauli's scheme, in which the fourth quantum number always assumed the values $\pm \frac{1}{2}$ for arbitrary terms (Goudsmit, 1925b, pp. 795–796)—he had never tried to give an interpretation to it as a fourth degree of freedom.$^{1056}$ For Uhlenbeck, who knew classical statistical mechanics very well, the situation was clear, and he argued: 'Since (as I had learned) each quantum number corresponded to a degree of freedom of the electron, the fourth quantum number must mean that the electron had an additional degree of freedom—in other words, the electron must be rotating' (Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 46). Goudsmit found Uhlenbeck's proposal rather nice because with the intrinsic angular momentum of the electron of magnitude $\frac{1}{2} h/2\pi$ everything fell into place. As Goudsmit recalled:

After his remark about the spin [i.e., the intrinsic rotation of the electron], we recognized immediately that it was now completely clear why $m_s$ [i.e., the quantum number replacing Pauli's $m_1$ in Goudsmit's scheme] was always $\frac{1}{2}$ or $-\frac{1}{2}$. Further we saw that all Zeeman splittings could be explained if one assigned to the electrons a magnetic moment of an entire Bohr magneton [i.e., of $eh/4\pi m_e c$]. Besides it became clear that the spin agreed completely with our new interpretation of the hydrogen [spectrum]. (Goudsmit, 1965, p. 450)$^{1057}$

It was not so clear, however, whether the new hypothesis did not lead into serious difficulties, and why—though it was an obvious consequence of Pauli's scheme—it had not occurred in literature before. Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck were, therefore, a little suspicious, and they tried to investigate further the conse-

VI.4 The Discovery of Electron Spin 701

quences that followed from the assumption of an intrinsic angular momentum of the electron. Thus, for example, Goudsmit asked Uhlenbeck in a postcard—sent from Amsterdam, where Goudsmit still worked part-time in Zeeman’s Institute—whether the gyromagnetic ratio of a charged particle did not depend on its linear extension. In any case, the two of them did not plan at first to publish anything about their hypothesis, for they felt it was too speculative. At that moment Ehrenfest, who had been informed about the idea, interfered; he encouraged and helped his assistants. When, for instance, Uhlenbeck showed him Goudsmit’s above-mentioned postcard, he drew his attention to an old paper of Max Abraham on the magnetic properties of the extended electron (Abraham, 1902b). Uhlenbeck studied this paper very carefully, then applied Abraham’s theory to his problem and was satisfied to find that if the electron possessed only surface charge, the gyromagnetic ratio indeed turned out to be $e/m_e c$, which corresponded to a $g$-factor of 2; it was exactly this result which the spectroscopic data demanded. With that result in hand, Uhlenbeck recalled, ‘Ehrenfest told us to write a short modest letter to *Naturwissenschaften* and to give it to him’ (Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 47). Since the $g$-factor calculation rested on an application of Abraham’s nonrelativistic electron model, Ehrenfest added the remark: ‘And then we shall ask Mr. Lorentz’ (‘*Und dann werden wir Herrn Lorentz fragen*,’ Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 47).

Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit composed the note requested by Ehrenfest. They first described the well-known atomic core–series electron model or Landé’s vector model of 1923 (see our discussion of it in Section IV.4), with all its complications, extra rules and difficulties: i.e., Pauli’s demonstration that the (noble gas) core could not have nonzero magnetic moment; the disagreement with the ‘construction’ or ‘building-up principle’ (‘*Aufbauprinzip*’); the failure to provide the correct ground states in the case of several many-electron atoms. Then Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit referred to the removal of these difficulties if one assigned, with Pauli, four quantum numbers to the electron; but they also drew attention to the fact that Pauli’s scheme did not explain the relativistic X-ray doublets and the alkali spectra, unless one assumed a rather hypothetical ‘non-mechanical duplicity.’ The latter assumption might be avoided, however, if one re-interpreted the four quantum numbers of the electron slightly: while $n$, $k$ and $j$ (or the $n$, $K$ and $J$ in Landé’s vector model) retained their previous meanings in Landé’s vector model (as principal, azimuthal and inner quantum numbers), Uhlenbeck proposed to connect $R$ (or $2m_1$ of Pauli) with an ‘intrinsic rotation of the electron.’ This re-interpretation, they argued, would be perfectly consistent with the spectroscopic data, provided one could prove that the gyromagnetic factor of the electron was indeed 2, as suggested by the calculation from Abraham’s model, and provided one could obtain the correct formula for the ‘relativistic’ doublets.

Ehrenfest, just as he had promised Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, wrote immediately to Lorentz, informing him about the problem of his students (Ehrenfest to Lorentz, 16 October 1925). Hendrik Lorentz at this time was retired, but he still

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0334 -->

702 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

gave lectures every Monday morning at Leyden. Following Lorentz’ next Monday morning lecture—it was 19 October—Uhlenbeck approached him personally on the matter. ‘Lorentz was very kind and interested, although I got the idea that he was rather skeptical,’ Uhlenbeck recalled fifty years later. ‘He said that he would think about it and that we should talk again the next Monday’ (Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 47). The following Monday, Lorentz brought a stack of papers filled with detailed calculations, from which Uhlenbeck just understood that there were serious problems. For example, the surface velocity of the rotating electron came out to be ten times the velocity of light *in vacuo*. Thus Uhlenbeck got the impression that ‘if one extended the Abraham calculation properly as Lorentz had apparently done, then our picture of quantized rotation of the electron could not possibly be reconciled with classical electrodynamics’ (Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 47). Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit immediately went to Ehrenfest and told him that the idea contained in the note for *Naturwissenschaften* was nonsense, and that it would be better not to publish it. But to his surprise Ehrenfest answered that he had sent off the note quite a while ago, and that it would appear in print pretty soon. Ehrenfest comforted the perplexed authors by remarking: ‘You are both young enough to be able to afford a stupidity like that’ (‘*Sie sind beide jung genug um sich eine Dummheit leisten zu können*,’ Ehrenfest, quoted by Uhlenbeck, 1976, p. 47). The short note of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit was published a few weeks later (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925).$^{1058}$

The note of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit initiated a quick response: on 21 November 1925, just the day after its publication, Werner Heisenberg from Göttingen wrote to Goudsmit—whom he knew quite well—stating his essential agreement with the idea of the rotating electron but asking how he had got rid of the factor 2 in the doublet formula.$^{1059}$ This difficulty had not been noticed by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit because they had not tried to calculate the doublet formula.$^{1060}$ In fact they did not even know how to proceed with the calculation. Fortunately, a little afterwards Albert Einstein came to Leyden and provided the necessary hint. He suggested that the calculation should be made in the coordinate system in which the electron was at rest. By performing the calculation Uhlenbeck found that there was indeed a difficulty about the factor 2 in the doublet formula.

The negative result was, however, soon balanced by the response which the Uhlenbeck–Goudsmit hypothesis received from Einstein and Niels Bohr, who

$^{1058}$Ehrenfest had asked Goudsmit to invert the alphabetical order of names, i.e., put Uhlenbeck’s name first. As Goudsmit recalled: ‘Since I had already published several papers on spectra, he [Ehrenfest] feared that the readers might remember my name and forget Uhlenbeck’s, and, after all, it was Uhlenbeck who had thought of the spin’ (Goudsmit, 1965, p. 451).

$^{1059}$Heisenberg then worked in the following months—as did Pauli—on the problem of the factor 2 in the quantum-mechanical formalism. We shall discuss this point in detail in Volume 3 on matrix mechanics. (See Volume 3, Sections V.1 and V.5.)

$^{1060}$In the note in *Naturwissenschaften*, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit had mentioned only the difficulty with the faster-than-light velocity of the rotating electron accoring to Abraham’s theory (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925, p. 954, footnote 2).

704 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

While Pauli—and, to a lesser extent, Heisenberg—struggled with the difficulties arising from the hypothesis of the magnetic electron, Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck made rapid progress by using it to organize the complex spectra. In a paper, which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 27 November 1925, they developed a vector model of the atom, in which they attributed to each orbiting electron, besides the angular momentum vector $\mathbf{K}$, another vector $\mathbf{R}$ of magnitude $\frac{1}{2} (h/2\pi)$ (Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck, 1926). Although they did not introduce explicitly ‘the quantized rotating electron’ in the main text of the paper, they mentioned in an addendum that the vector $\mathbf{R}$ should be interpreted as the intrinsic angular momentum of the electron (Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck, 1926, p. 625).$^{1064}$ In any case, the new vector scheme enabled them to discuss all possible couplings between the ‘quantum vectors’ that might occur in atoms, provided one could describe the atoms as being constituted of an ion with angular momentum vectors $\mathbf{K}_1$ (for the orbital motion) and $\mathbf{R}_1$ (for the intrinsic motion) and an electron with $\mathbf{K}_2$ and $\mathbf{R}_2$. For example, the two vectors associated with the ion, on one hand, and the series electron, on the other, would add up to two resultants, $\mathbf{J}_1 = \mathbf{K}_1 + \mathbf{R}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}_2 = \mathbf{K}_2 + \mathbf{R}_2$, respectively, and the coupling of $\mathbf{J}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}_2$ would then yield the term energy (i.e., the correction to the energy of the Kepler orbit); or, the momenta $\mathbf{K}_1$ and $\mathbf{K}_2$ could add up to the resultant $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{K}_1 + \mathbf{K}_2$, and similarly the momenta $\mathbf{R}_1$ and $\mathbf{R}_2$ to $\

manner, which helped to remove some of the difficulties which existed in Sommerfeld’s relativistic theory. Thus Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit noted:

> In particular the new theory explains at once the occurrence of certain components in the fine structure of the hydrogen spectrum and the helium spark spectrum which according to the old scheme would correspond to transitions where *K* remains unchanged. Unless these transitions could be ascribed to the action of electric forces in the discharge which would perturb the electronic motion, their occurrence would be in disagreement with the correspondence principle, which only allows transitions in which the azimuthal quantum number changes by one unit. In the new scheme we see that, in the transitions in question, *K* will actually change by one unit and only *J* will remain unchanged. Their occurrence is, therefore, quite in conformity with the correspondence principle. (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1926, p. 264)

Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit immediately pointed out in their letter to *Nature* that the new scheme also explained the X-ray doublets fully: the doublets formerly called ‘screening’ doublets were pairs of states having the same angular momentum *J* and different quantum number *K*, hence the two states corresponded to electron orbits, which penetrated to different distances from the nucleus; the so-called ‘relativistic’ doublets, however, were now characterized by the same value of the quantum number *K*, but in the two terms the orientation of

VI.4 The Discovery of Electron Spin
707

the spin axis relative to the orbital plane was opposite, hence they ‘may more properly be termed “spin” doublets’ (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1926, p. 265). Also the analogy between the X-ray and the optical doublets could be understood because the optical doublets were spin-doublets like the relativistic doublets in the X-ray spectra. Finally, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit addressed themselves in a qualitative way to the anomalous Zeeman effects, claiming that the introduction of the magnetic electron did indeed fully account for the observed violation of Larmor’s theorem.

Some of the same questions, e.g., the explanation of the relativistic doublets of X-ray spectra and of the anomalous Zeeman effects on the basis of the hypothesis of the magnetic electron, were treated by F. Russell Bichowski and Harold Urey in a paper, which they communicated to the *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, where it appeared in the issue of February 1926 (Bichowski and Urey, 1926).$^{1069,1070}$ Bichowski and Urey referred to Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit’s note in *Naturwissenschaften* and applied the conception of the magnetic electron to calculate explicitly the double separation due to different relative orientations of the electron’s magnetic moment and the orbit. Thus, by assuming the magnetic moment to be $(e/2m_ec) \cdot (h/2\pi)$—i.e., *half as big* as the value assumed by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit—they obtained the same expression as on the relativistic theory. While this result fitted the alkali doublets and the X-ray doublets, it seemed to Bichowski and Urey to be incompatible with the fine structure of the hydrogen lines: because in that case, they claimed, one had to take a superposition of Sommerfeld’s relativistic separation (the relativistic doublet) plus the separation of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, arising from the interaction of the magnetic moment of the electron with the internal field.$^{1071}$

Like Bichowski and Urey, also Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit had trouble describing the fine structure of the hydrogen lines. The reasons, however, were different.

$^{1069}$Francis Russell Bichowski was born on 19 February 1889 at San Gabriel, California. He became director of the Naval Research Laboratory, Anacostia, D.C., in 1927. He died in 1951.

$^{1070}$Harold Clayton Urey was born on 29 April 1893 at Walkerton, Indiana. After working as a school teacher from 1911 to 1914, he studied chemistry at the University of Montana (1914–1917), receiving his B.Sc. in 1917 and served as instructor there (1919–1921). Then he continued his studies at the University of California at Berkeley (1921–1923), receiving his doctorate under A. R. Olsen and G. N. Lewis in 1923. He spent the academic year 1923–1924 with Bohr in Copenhagen on a fellowship of the American–Scandinavian Foundation. On his return to America he became an associate in chemistry at Johns Hopkins University (1924–1929). Then he went to Columbia University as an associate professor (1929–1934), becoming a full professor (1934–1945). In 1945 he moved to the University of Chicago, becoming Martin A. Ryerson Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at the Institute for Nuclear Studies (1952–1958), and finally, in 1958, he joined the University of California at San Diego.

Harold Urey worked on absorption spectra and the structure of atoms and molecules, on the separation of isotopes, and on questions related to the origin of the solar system. For his discovery of the heavy hydrogen isotope, he received the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

$^{1071}$As Bichowski and Urey pointed out, the theory of the magnetic electron solved a difficulty that had existed before in Heisenberg’s theory of the alkali doublets (Heisenberg, 1922a). According to this theory the energy order of the $p_1$ and $p_2$ terms came out the wrong way (see Breit, 1923b); in the new scheme, however, the sign of the $p_1-p_2$ term difference was opposite to that in the previous scheme.

708 Chapter VI New Methods and Concepts in Atomic Theory

Bichowski and Urey had simply suppressed the factor 2 in the doublet formula by assuming a normal gyromagnetic factor, i.e., $g = 1$, for the magnetic electron. Of course, this assumption could not be correct in view of the anomalous Zeeman effects. Therefore, the treatment of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit had to be preferred, although their hope that a ‘closer study of quantum mechanics and perhaps also of questions concerning the structure of the electron’ might contribute to the ‘final solution’ of the entire complex of problems (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1926, p. 265) received no justification during the following months. The solution came from an unexpected source: in a letter to *Nature* from Copenhagen, dated 20 February 1926, Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas dealt with ‘The Motion of the Spinning Electron’ (Thomas, 1926).
Thomas, who came to Copenhagen in fall 1925 as Isaac Newton Student from Cambridge, participated in the discussions of Bohr and Kramers—which were going on in late 1925 and early 1926—concerning the difficulty with the factor 2 in the spinning electron model.$^{1072}$ After Bohr explained the coupling of the spin and the tranformed electric field of the nucleus and the resulting discrepancy, Thomas naïvely suggested: ‘Well, why didn’t people work that out relativistically,’ to which Kramers replied that, ‘that will only make a small correction’ (Thomas, AHQP Interview, 10 May 1962). But Thomas did not really believe in what Kramers said and, being familiar with general relativity from Arthur Stanley Eddington’s lectures at Cambridge, he thought about using it in the present problem. In particular, he remembered the calculation of the general relativistic effects on the moon’s nodes, which was contained in Eddington’s book on *The Mathematical Theory of Relativity* (Eddington, 1923b). Thomas consulted the book and adapted the method to his needs, and within three days he found the answer: the reasoning which had led to Eq. (365) was erroneous because in transforming the atomic system, consisting of a moving electron and a nucleus at rest, to a system, consisting of an electron at rest and a moving nucleus, one had neglected an important effect. This effect arose from the acceleration of the electron, and it reduced the inner magnetic field $\mathbf{H}_i$ entering in Eq. (365). In particular, Thomas found that the angular velocity $\omega$ of the intrinsic rotation of the electron was not $(- e / m_e c^2)(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{v})$—$(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{v})$ being the vector product of the electric field $\mathbf{E}$ (acting on the electron) and the velocity $\mathbf{v}$ of the electron—but rather

$$
\omega = \frac{-e}{m_e c} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{v}) - \frac{1}{2c^2} (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{f}), \tag{367}
$$

---
$^{1072}$ L. H. Thomas was born on 21 October 1903 in London. He studied physics at the University of Cambridge from 1921 to 1925. He received his B.A. in 1924. During the winter of 1925–1926 he spent several months in Copenhagen as Isaac Newton Student. On his return to Cambridge, he completed his doctorate in 1927. From 1927 to 1929 he was an 1851 Exhibition Scholar at Cambridge. Then he went to the United States, where he joined Ohio State University: assistant professor (1929–1930), associate professor (1930–1936), and full professor of physics (1936–1943). In 1946 he became a member of the senior staff at Watson Scientific Laboratory in New York City; in 1950 he was appointed as a professor of physics at Columbia University.
Thomas contributed to questions of the structure of atoms and molecules and to the use of computing machines in scientific problems.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0341 -->

VI.4  The Discovery of Electron Spin

where $\mathbf{f}$ was the acceleration of the electron. Since $\mathbf{f}$ was given in the first approximation by the Lorentz force on the electron, i.e., by the expression $(-e/m_e)\mathbf{E}$, he arrived at the result

$$\omega = - \frac{e}{2m_e c} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{v}). \quad (367')$$

Since $\omega$ gave, apart from the factor $2\pi$, the doublet separation, $\Delta\nu$, in the Uhlenbeck-Goudsmit model of the magnetic electron, Thomas had indeed provided the factor $\frac{1}{2}$, which was necessary in order that Eq. (365) agree with the empirical data.

The above calculation, which Thomas presented in greater detail in a paper published in the *Philosophical Magazine* (L. H. Thomas, 1927), immediately convinced Niels Bohr. It made the way clear for the satisfactory description of the fine structure of hydrogen lines and the anomalous Zeeman effects, which was achieved soon afterwards in a quantum-mechanical calculation by Werner Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). And soon there followed other applications of the rotating electron hypothesis, which established the spin as a firm property of the electron.$^{1073}$ Only Pauli hesitated. For several weeks he doubted—as we shall discuss in Volume 3, Section V.5—the correctness of Thomas' calculation; then, after accepting it, he tried to incorporate the electron spin into the deeper quantum-mechanical description of the electron.$^{1074}$ Within this formalism Bohr would be able to show (Bohr, 1932) to Pauli's great satisfaction, 'that the electron spin cannot be measured by classically describable experiments (as, for instance, deflection of molecular beams [of electrons] in external electromagnetic fields) and must therefore be considered an essentially quantum mechanical property of the electron' (Pauli, 1948, p. 134). Apart from these fundamental questions, which remained to be clarified in later years on the basis of wave mechanics, the conception of electron spin had indeed ended in large part the sorrows of atomic theory.

$^{1073}$ We shall discuss some of these applications in Volume 3, Chapter V.

$^{1074}$ When, ultimately, Pauli accepted the correctness of Thomas' calculation and thus the concept of electron spin, he wrote to Bohr: 'Now all that remains for me is to *capitulate completely*' (Pauli to Bohr, 12 March 1926). To Goudsmit he wrote: 'I am writing to you today to tell you, first of all, that I have meanwhile—on the basis of recent reports from Copenhagen—finally come to the conviction that I was wrong in my objections against Thomas and that his relativistic consideration can be cast in a perfectly correct and unobjectionable form. The problem of fine structure is thus really satisfactorily explained now' (Pauli to Goudsmit, 13 March 1926).

# Epilogue

We had begun the foregoing account of the pre-quantum-mechanical development of quantum and atomic theory with a prologue outlining the principal fields of nineteenth-century physics that led to the discovery of quantum theory. Now, after the review of the first twenty-five years of work on this development, it would seem desirable to give a summary of the status—i.e., the achievements as well as the difficulties—of the field at the very moment when a new development set in: the discovery of quantum mechanics. We shall give this status report by discussing three points: First, how—in the mid-1920s—did the physicists look at the development of quantum theory? Second, how did they represent the knowledge of quantum physics in books and reviews? Third, what did they think about the future of the field, or in which direction did they expect to obtain further progress?

In 1921 Fritz Reiche, a former student of Max Planck’s, published a book called ‘*Quantentheorie: Ihr Ursprung und ihre Entwicklung*’ (Reiche, 1921). In this book, an extended version of his earlier article with the same title for the *Planckheft* of *Naturwissenschaften* (Reiche, 1918b), Reiche dealt with the historical development of the quantum theory from 1900 to 1920, which he organized into nine chapters: I. The Origin of the Quantum Hypothesis; II. The Failure of Classical Statistics; III. The Development and the Ramifications of the Theory; IV. The Extensions of the Doctrine of Quanta to the Molecular Theory of Solid Bodies; V. The Intrusion of Quanta into the Theory of Gases; VI. The Quantum Theory of the Optical Series—The Development of the Quantum Theory of Several Degrees of Freedom; VII. The Quantum Theory of Röntgen Spectra; VIII. Phenomena of Molecular Models; IX. Outlook. What Reiche’s book did not include—the enormous amount of work performed on the theory of atomic structure and spectra since 1920—was discussed in many special reviews of this field. Thus by 1925 people interested in the quantum theory possessed a fair knowledge of its development. We shall outline the main points of this knowledge in the following.

In a rational organization of the development of quantum theory between 1900 and 1925, one may consider two periods of about equal length, during which different problems and aspects concerned the quantum physicists: the period from 1900 to 1912, when the quantum concept was founded; and the period from 1913 to 1925, when the quantum theory was mainly used to describe the structure of atoms and molecules. Although the phenomena, which had been recognized originally as quantum problems, continued to be treated in later years

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0343 -->

712

Epilogue

as well and occasionally yielded important new insights, the above-mentioned shift in the quantum-theoretical development must be considered as being remarkable. However, practically no problem of quantum theory found its final solution before 1925; in all cases, smaller or larger puzzles and difficulties remained. It did happen though that the unresolved part of a given problem combined with a new problem, giving rise to a more serious and fundamental difficulty, which had then to be removed by applying deeper physical concepts or more refined mathematical methods.

When we look back on the years between 1900 and 1912, we notice in particular the discovery of several quantum concepts, all characterized by the same constant of nature—the Planck constant $h$: the quantum of energy and of action in 1900; the quantum of light in 1905; the quantum of phase space in 1906; and other quanta connected with certain physical and chemical properties of matter, such as the specific heat of solids and gases or the binding energy of molecules, in later years. During that time only a few physicists concerned themselves with the problems of quantum theory: Max Planck, Albert Einstein, Johannes Stark, Walther Nernst, and later Peter Debye, Arnold Sommerfeld, Joseph Larmor and William Henry Bragg, determined with their contributions the beginning and the growth of quantum physics. Simultaneously with the recognition of an increasing number of quantum phenomena another phase of the development started after 1905. It emerged from the completion of what were later called the ‘classical’ theories, i.e., the canon of theories ranging from classical mechanics, Maxwell’s electrodynamics including electron theory and special relativity, to the Maxwell–Boltzmann–Gibbs statistical mechanics. In the course of their detailed and fundamental investigations some concerned scientists —in the first place, Hendrik Lorentz, Albert Einstein and Max Planck—came to an important and surprising conclusion: it was impossible to derive, for instance, the law governing the energy distribution in blackbody radiation on the basis of classical theory; new concepts were needed to account for the characteristic quantum discontinuity. The clear recognition of the failure, or at least of the insufficiency of classical dynamics to describe the quantum phenomena, stood—besides the presentation of the various physical topics that were connected with the quantum of action—in the centre of the discussions at the first Solvay Conference in October 1911. This conference, held in Brussels at the initiative of Ernest Solvay and Walther Nernst, brought together distinguished European scientists to discuss for the first time the problems of quantum theory, and it contributed crucially to the propagation of the quantum concept in the following decade.

The beginning of the next important period of development in quantum theory can be fixed accurately: in July 1913 Niels Bohr published the first part of his memoir on the constitution of atoms and molecules, including a theory of the hydrogen spectrum (Bohr, 1913b). With it quantum theory gained an enormous field of application: this was the electronic and nuclear structure of atoms and molecules, which was responsible, in the first place, for the characteristic line

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0344 -->

**Epilogue**  
**713**  

spectra absorbed and emitted by atomic systems, and was closely related to the observable physical and chemical properties of matter. The importance of the quantum theory of atomic structure, the new branch of quantum theory which evolved from Bohr's pioneering work, must be seen in two facts: first, the theory enabled the physicists to construct mechanical models of atoms and molecules, consisting of the known charged particles (i.e., electrons and nuclei); second, these mechanical models could be tested in detail by comparing their consequences with the great wealth of known or soon available data. The quantum theory of atomic structure then dominated the following dozen years of research in quantum physics.  

It is possible to subdivide the years from 1913 to 1925 again into two phases.¹⁰⁷⁵ During the first phase, from 1913 to 1918, the principles of the quantum theory of atomic structure, or the so-called Bohr–Sommerfeld theory, were firmly established: these were the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems (i.e., the dynamical theory of conditionally periodic systems—made up of electrons and nuclei—plus quantum conditions), the adiabatic hypothesis and the correspondence principle. In the second phase, from 1919 to 1925, the physicists concentrated their investigations to a large extent on an immensely skillful use of the models and principles for explaining the—mostly spectroscopic—data. The number of people contributing to quantum theory increased vastly: the older, established professors of theoretical and experimental physics were soon joined by many students who were eager to work in the new and, as it appeared, revolutionary field of science. The more or less complete interruption of university life during World War I in many European countries, especially England, France and Germany, made young people particularly susceptible to new ideas and thus served as a decisive stimulus in the postwar growth of quantum theory.  

In 1925, after the development of a quarter of a century, quantum theory could be rightly regarded as an integral part of established physics. Moreover, it represented the field in which the greatest amount of research activity took place. Not only was quantum theory taught at most universities in regular courses, but theoreticians and experimentalists at many institutes—notably at the centres in Copenhagen, Munich, Göttingen, Cambridge and Leyden in Europe, as well as at selected places in the United States of America and Japan—devoted their work entirely to the quantum problems. Gifted young researchers contributed more original papers on these problems to scientific journals than was customary for research students to do (on other problems) in earlier times. One of the conspicuous features in the development of quantum physics, especially after 1920, was the large percentage of theoretical works among the published papers. This was due to several reasons: among them the often depressing economic  

¹⁰⁷⁵ Two phases may also be seen in the first period of the development of quantum theory: during the first phase, from 1900 to about 1906, the existence of quanta was discovered; while during the second, from 1906 to 1912, detailed applications of the quantum theory were proposed and the discontinuous nature of the quantum-theoretical description became evident.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0345 -->

714 Epilogue

conditions in some countries, which prevented the installation and use of expensive apparatus in university laboratories, or the large number of students, who could not be employed at the existing laboratories that were much too small in size. However, in spite of this important role of theory, the many decisive contributions to quantum and atomic physics from one particular experimental field should not be forgotten: the contributions from X-ray investigations. The great period of X-ray physics began in 1912 with the discovery of X-ray interference from crystals. The interference patterns (of von Laue, Friedrich and Knipping or of the Braggs—which we discussed in Section I.7) allowed the physicists not only to study the atomic structure of crystals or the electronic structure of atomic systems, but also provided a method of measuring X-ray wavelengths exactly. Thus X-ray spectroscopy began and the data on X-ray absorption and emission spectra soon gave decisive hints about the structure of atoms. X-ray spectroscopy provided major empirical support of Bohr’s theory of the periodic system of elements of 1921, and it also caused its revision in 1924. Moreover, the study of the scattering of X-rays by atoms led to the discovery of the Compton effect, which yielded decisive evidence concerning the quantum nature of radiation and its interaction with the charged constituents of matter.

Although after 1913 the majority of the quantum physicists worked on problems of atomic structure, interest in the typical quantum phenomena of earlier years did not disappear. For example, the question of the nature of radiation received continuous attention during all these years, and also the application of quantum theory to explain the chemical binding of atoms in molecules was discussed again and again.$^{1076}$ Sometimes these questions on old quantum problems as, for instance, the specific heat of solids, just served to enlighten particular details of the problem that had already been understood in principle; that is, they then allowed one to describe the phenomena a little more accurately without contributing to further progress in quantum theory. Still the variety of problems treated with the help of quantum concepts in the 1910s and 1920s made it clear that quantum theory was not limited to describing atomic structure and spectroscopic data.

In the middle of the 1920s quantum physics represented a flourishing field of science. An uninterrupted, even steadily increasing flow of papers—both on experimental and theoretical questions of quantum theory—occupied a growing number of pages in the leading physics journals, such as *Zeitschrift für Physik*, *Philosophical Magazine* and *Physical Review*. At the same time several broad reviews and treatises on the entire range of quantum physics, or large parts of it, written by experts from different parts of the scientific world, became available. As a consequence, the older literature, for example James Jeans’ *Report on Radiation and the Quantum Theory* (Jeans, 1914b) or Arnold Sommerfeld’s *Atombau und Spektrallinien* (1919), received keen competition. Let us briefly mention and compare some of the books and booklength reviews published

**Epilogue**  
715  

between 1924 and 1926: Jeans’ *Report on Radiation and the Quantum Theory* (second edition, Jeans, 1924), Alfred Landé’s *Die neuere Entwicklung der Quantentheorie* (Landé, 1926d) and Wolfgang Pauli’s article on *Quantentheorie* in the Geiger–Scheel *Handbuch der Physik* (Pauli, 1926b) covered a wide range of quantum phenomena; Max Born’s *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* (Born, 1925), Sommerfeld’s *Atombau und Spektrallinien* (Fourth Edition, Sommerfeld, 1924d), Edmund C. Stoner’s *Magnetism and Atomic Structure* (Stoner, 1926), and John H. Van Vleck’s *Quantum Principles and Line Spectra* (Van Vleck, 1926c) dealt with atomic structure and line spectra.¹⁰⁷⁷  

All the books and reports mentioned above presented a wealth of experimental data and their explanation on the basis of quantum theory to the interested readers, whether they were professors and students working on quantum problems or other scientists interested in the results obtained from recent research work. Of course, each of these publications addressed a slightly different public. Thus Landé gave a brief recapitulation of the main quantum problems and of the recent advances for those who already had some knowledge of quantum theory. His book included chapters on (i) quantum theory of radiation, (ii) atoms with one electron, (iii) atoms with several electrons, (iv) atomic magnetism, (v) band spectra and molecular binding, (vi) quantum theory of solids and gases, (vii) methods of quantization, and (viii) application to the hydrogen spectrum. In contrast to Landé, Jeans had a wider class of reader in mind when he revised his old report. He retained the organization and main parts of his 1914 review, but omitted the material which appeared to be unnecessary ten years later (such as the defensive statements about why it was necessary to introduce quantum concepts). He added a few topics, which meanwhile had become important, such as the Stark effect, the adiabatic hypothesis and the correspondence principle. With these changes Jeans tried to modernize his previous report. Although he treated the most recent problems of the theory of atomic structure and spectral lines rather sketchily, he succeeded in presenting—as the reviewer of the second edition of Jeans’ *Report on Radiation and the Quantum Theory* remarked in *Nature*—‘an admirable summary of those parts of the quantum theory which are now really established’ (*Nature* **113**, issue of 17 May 1924, p. 702).  

Unlike Jeans, who after 1910 had not worked himself on quantum problems and who viewed the development of quantum theory with the attitude of a distant, though sympathetic, observer, the authors of the other books and reports mentioned above were deeply immersed in the recent investigations of the atomic theory themselves. This was evident in the case of Arnold Sommerfeld, the old master of spectroscopic theory, who had prepared the fourth edition of *Atombau und Spektrallinien*—as we have mentioned in Section VI.2—in order to present a

These books and reports also served, of course, as useful introductions to quantum and atomic theory for many physicists.

complete description of all available spectroscopic data on the basis of Bohr’s theory of the periodic system of elements. Landé, on his part, devoted ample space in his *Die neuere Entwicklung der Quantentheorie* to discussing the theory of line multiplets and the associated Zeeman effects, to which he had contributed greatly; still he also treated such topics as the radiation theory (wave versus light‑quantum problem), the theory of the magneton (i.e., the magnetic moments of atoms and ions), the constitution of molecules and band spectra, and quantum statistics including quantum gas theory. Compared to Jeans, Landé and Sommerfeld, Stoner restricted his attention—as reflected in the title of his book—to one particular aspect of atomic theory: the magnetic properties of atoms. He had himself made an important contribution to this subject (see Section VI.2). In support of his treatment of the magnetic properties of atoms, Stoner gave—at various places in his book—summaries of the relevant parts of the existing theory of atomic structure. As Peter Kapitza noted in a review of Stoner’s book, these (explanatory) passages could be ‘regarded as only a means of recalling certain facts with regard to electrodynamics and the quantum theory to the mind of the reader who is already acquainted with them’ (Kapitza, 1927, p. 810).  

Among the remaining books in the above list, two dealt explicitly—as stated in their titles—with the theory of atomic structure and line spectra: they were Van Vleck’s report for the National Research Council, completed in August 1925 and published in March 1926, and Max Born’s book containing his lectures on atomic mechanics (given in winter semester 1923–1924), with a preface dated November 1924, published in spring 1925. Pauli’s article on the quantum theory appeared in *Volume 23* of the *Handbuch der Physik*. The long article of 278 printed pages constituted the first chapter of this volume; the other chapters (of the same volume, entitled ‘*Quanten*’) were written by Rudolf Ladenburg (Chapter Two: Review of the Methods for Measuring Planck’s Constant), Walther Bothe (Chapter Three: Absorption and Dispersion of X‑rays), Helmuth Kuhlenkampff (Chapter Four: Continuous X‑ray Spectra), Peter Pringsheim (Chapter Five: Emission of Spectra Stimulated by Incident Radiation), Walter Noddack (Chapter Six: Photochemistry), and James Frank and Pascual Jordan (Chapter Seven: Excitation of Quantum Jumps by Collisions). Since other articles, published in different volumes of the Geiger–Scheel *Handbuch*, already covered the statistical applications of quantum theory, quantum chemistry, molecular structure and band spectra, and the mathematical methods of quantum theory, Pauli was able to restrict himself in his article to discussing the following topics: in Section I, the general principles of quantum theory; in Section II, the theory of spectra of one‑electron atoms; in Section **III**, the theory of spectra of many‑electron atoms. As a result of this peculiar organization the contents of Pauli’s review article overlapped more or less with what Born and Van Vleck treated in their respective books.  

In comparing the accounts of Born, Pauli and Van Vleck—all of which were over 250 printed pages long—one may immediately notice the similarity in the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0348 -->

Epilogue

717

organization. All authors devoted the earlier parts of their reviews—e.g., Section I of Pauli’s article, Chapters One and Two of Born’s book, and Chapters I to IV of Van Vleck’s report—to setting up the foundations of the quantum theory of atomic structure; then they treated one-electron atoms and several-electron atoms. However, within this general organization, each author presented the material according to his own taste and preferences. Thus, for instance, Born—after briefly mentioning the physical foundations of quantum theory (Introduction)—gave a detailed description of the classical Hamilton–Jacobi theory and its application to multiply periodic systems (Chapters One and Two). Then he treated one-electron atoms with or without external fields (Chapter Three), and finally he developed systematically the quantum-theoretical perturbation schemes for multiply periodic systems (Chapter Four). In general, Born restricted his efforts to discussing ‘the facts of atomic physics from the special viewpoint of the application of mechanical principles’ (Born, 1925, p. V). Since the application of these mechanical principles had been recognized in the previous couple of years (i.e., between 1922 and 1924) as leading to several fundamental failures—such as the failure in the calculation of the energy states of the helium atom, or in the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects, or in the crossed-field problem—Born cautiously called his *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* the ‘first volume’ of a series of books on the quantum theory that he intended to write. In particular, in the preface he announced a second volume dealing with ‘a higher approximation to the “final” atomic mechanics’ (Born, 1925, p. V).<sup>1078</sup>

In fall 1924 Born was very cautious about a more ‘final’ atomic mechanics. He argued that ‘at the moment one possesses only a few unclear hints about the type of deviations, which must be imposed upon the classical laws in order to explain atomic properties’ (Born, 1925, p. V), referring to Heisenberg’s recent theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg, 1924e), the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation (Bohr, Kramers and Slater, 1924) and Kramers’ dispersion theory (Kramers, 1924a, b). While Born did not discuss these matters in the *Vorlesungen*, the other authors devoted several sections to them. Thus Van Vleck not only wrote a chapter on ‘The Correspondence Principle for Intensities’ (Chapter IX), but also one on ‘Polarization, Dispersion, etc., in the Quantum Theory’ (Chapter X), ‘Half Quanta and the Anomalous Zeeman Effect’ (Chapter XII) and ‘Light-Quanta’ (Chapter XIII), all of them dealing with developments going beyond the limits of the old quantum theory of atomic structure. As a rule, Van Vleck presented the different topics of atomic theory as applications of the correspondence principle, and he made extensive use of what we have called (in Section VI.1) the dispersion-theoretic approach. He also described the standard quantum theory of multiply periodic systems (Chapters II, III and IV) and its use

***

<sup>1078</sup> Born indeed published a second volume, entitled *Elementare Quantenmechanik*, together with Pascual Jordan, several years later (Born and Jordan, 1930). It contained the final version of atomic mechanics in the form of matrix mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0349 -->

718 Epilogue

in one-electron problems (Chapter V), and devoted Chapter VIII to its failure (“The Apparent Non-Conformity of the Quantum Orbits to Classical Dynamics in Atoms with More than One Electron”).
Pauli was allowed—because of the organization of articles on quantum theory in the Handbuch der Physik—to omit from his review of quantum theory the discussion of the mathematical methods used in dealing with multiply periodic quantum systems. He just showed what results these methods had yielded in special examples of one- and many-electron atoms, and he stressed clearly where the methods had failed. The topics treated by Pauli and Van Vleck agreed almost completely: thus both authors wrote sections on the Compton effect and the problems of radiation theory; both concerned themselves in detail with the theory of line multiplets and the anomalous Zeeman effects; and, above all, both were not tired of pointing out the importance of the guiding role of the correspondence principle in atomic theory.
The accounts of Born, Pauli and Van Vleck—especially those of the last two—reflected the status of the quantum theory of atomic structure in the year 1925 most adequately. The reader could obtain from each report information about the successes and failures of the theory. None of the three authors tried to hide the failures. Thus Born concluded his book by referring to the breakdown of Bohr–Sommerfeld theory in the case of the helium atom and claimed that the old theory had to be transformed into a ‘discontinuous atomic mechanics’ in order to enable the physicists to describe properly the interaction of electrons in many-electron atoms (Born, 1925, p. 341). Van Vleck made similar remarks at the corresponding places in his report, while Pauli drew attention to the difficulties and failure of the old atomic theory already in the case of one-electron atoms.
Pauli, more than the other authors, had contributed to demonstrating the inconsistency of the Bohr–Sommerfeld quantum theory of atomic structure: he had calculated the energy states of the hydrogen molecule-ion in his doctoral thesis in 1921, without being able to reproduce the empirical data; he had analyzed the anomalous Zeeman effects in 1923 and found that they could not be described by the standard theory; and he had helped to demonstrate in 1924 that Bohr’s theory of the periodic system of elements, the most brilliant result obtained on the basis of the old principles, was incorrect. Finally, in April 1925, he had witnessed the experimental disproof of the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation, which had previously been thought to provide the foundation of the very successful dispersion-theoretic approach of Kramers, Heisenberg, Kronig and others. Evidently, atomic theory was in a mess, and Pauli expressed his desperation about its state in a letter to Ralph Kronig in Copenhagen by saying: ‘Physics at the moment is again very muddled; in any case, for me it is too complicated, and I wish I were a film comedian or something of that sort and had never heard anything about physics. Now I do hope nevertheless that Bohr will save us with a new idea. I beg him to do so urgently’ (Pauli to Kronig, 21 May 1925).
Now Bohr, of whom Pauli expected that he would save physics from its

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0350 -->

Epilogue

719

‘muddled’ situation in spring 1925 with a brilliant new idea, was in a similarly desperate mood as Pauli. The main reason was, of course, the fact that the experiment of Walther Bothe and Hans Geiger had just led to a result which seemed to destroy the entire scheme of atomic theory set up by Bohr during the previous two years in order to overcome the failures of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems. If these dark prospects turned out to be true, all the work done on atomic theory since 1913 would lose its value. In a letter to Ernest Rutherford, his former teacher and fatherly friend, Bohr wrote about ‘our present theoretical troubles which are of an alarming character indeed’ (Bohr to Rutherford, 18 April 1925). Never before had the difficulties appeared so forbidding to Niels Bohr, and never before had he been left without any glimpse of the theoretical understanding of the quantum phenomena as in these months of spring 1925.

When the quantum physicists tried to review in later times the development of quantum and atomic theory in the first half of the 1920s, they more or less unanimously characterized the years after 1922 (until the discovery of quantum mechanics) as years of a deep crisis of the existing theory. For example, Friedrich Hund in his *Geschichte der Quantentheorie*, after mentioning the success of Bohr’s theory of the periodic system of elements, stated: ‘But shortly afterwards one was more certain about the difficulties of this older quantum theory, hence in 1922 one spoke about a “crisis”’ (Hund, 1967, p. 95). Although the word ‘crisis’ may well be used to describe much of the situation in quantum theory in the years between 1922 and the advent of quantum mechanics in 1925, one does not find an explicit recognition of such a ‘crisis’ in the publications and scientific correspondence of the quantum physicists at that time. Of course, they realized the failures of their attempts to describe certain properties of atoms and molecules and stated them clearly. Thus Werner Heisenberg, at the end of his and Born’s unsuccessful helium calculations, remarked: ‘What a misery!’ (‘Es ist ein Jammer,’ Heisenberg to Pauli, 19 February 1923). And Pauli, on the failure of his efforts to explain the anomalous Zeeman effects with the help of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, repeated Heisenberg’s words in a letter to Sommerfeld several months later: ‘At the moment, with the theory of the anomalous Zeeman effects and in general with atoms having more than one electron, it is such a great misery’ (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 19 July 1923). But not all, or even many, quantum physicists shared Pauli’s misery, which lasted from then until the discovery of quantum mechanics. Heisenberg, on the other hand, abandoned his pessimistic attitude of spring 1923 as early as fall 1923 after he discovered a new method, which seemed to overcome Pauli’s and his own difficulties with the description of the anomalous Zeeman effects. This method, the ‘discretization’ of the quantum-theoretical equations, filled him and Max Born in Göttingen with optimism and the firm conviction that it represented an important step towards the future quantum mechanics. At about the same time as ‘discrete’ quantum theory was advocated in Göttingen, Niels Bohr and his collaborators in Copenhagen gathered new hope, after they had established what

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0351 -->

720 Epilogue

appeared to them to be the correct quantum theory of radiation. Therefore, it is reasonable to say that neither at Göttingen nor at Copenhagen people felt something like a permanent crisis in the quantum theory after 1922 for the simple reason that in the following years they did not stick slavishly to the old theory, but developed it further by proposing new methods for obtaining more satisfactory results than before.

To avoid any misunderstanding: none of the physicists mentioned above, and none of those deeply engaged in the problems of quantum theory, underestimated the existing difficulties. All knew that many, including some of the most fundamental aspects of the theory, were still completely unclear. Most believed that the long march towards a future quantum theory had just begun and that it would take years, if not decades, until a better, more consistent description of the known quantum phenomena—and probably of other phenomena which had still to be discovered—was achieved. Born, for instance, expressed this opinion in the preface to his *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* by calling his book the ‘first volume’ of an atomic theory and proposing to write a second volume, which would then contain ‘a higher approximation to the “final” atomic mechanics’; he added further that the ‘projected second volume will perhaps remain unwritten for several years yet’ (Born, 1925, pp. V–VI).

Born was not alone in having this opinion; it was shared by most, especially the senior quantum physicists. In this context we should remind ourselves of the fact that in 1925 nearly all physicists, who had ever become involved in quantum theory, were still alive—perhaps with the single exception of Henri Poincaré. Three generations of quantum physicists were either actively engaged in or witnessed the developments in the field carefully: the members of the first generation, which included Hendrik Lorentz, Joseph John Thomson, Joseph Larmor, Max Planck, Arnold Sommerfeld and Wilhelm Wien, were born around 1860; the members of the second generation, among them Niels Bohr, Max Born, Paul Ehrenfest, Albert Einstein, and—somewhat younger—Alfred Landé and Erwin Schrödinger, where born around 1880; and the members of the young generation, like Wolfgang Pauli, Werner Heisenberg, Paul Dirac, Pascual Jordan and Enrico Fermi, were born around 1900.

Of the early pioneers of quantum theory only a few did not take an interest in the recent development. Thus Joseph John Thomson did not make use of the generally accepted atomic models of the Bohr–Sommerfeld type, but preferred to construct his own. And Johannes Stark, one of the most ardent propagators of the quantum concept in atomic theory, retired completely from the pursuit of new theoretical ideas on atomic structure after 1914. In his opinion, Bohr’s theory not only contradicted important consequences which followed from the electromagnetic theory, but also disagreed with several observations, e.g., those on the fine structure of spectral lines (Stark, 1920).^1079

^1079 We have mentioned earlier Stark’s gradual departure from work on the development of quantum theory after 1912 at several places (see Sections I.7 and III.4). Stark withdrew more and more from theoretical considerations and criticized Bohr and Sommerfeld as abandoning the empirical foundations of physics and turning instead to theoretical and dogmatic points of view.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0352 -->

Epilogue 721

However, Stark’s negative attitude towards the development of quantum and atomic theory represented an exception. Although several, especially the senior scientists, by no means agreed with all the new ideas proposed in the course of time by their predominantly younger colleagues, they believed firmly in the soundness and correctness of the quantum concept *per se*. Of course, the various quantum physicists—depending on their own experience of actual involvement in specific quantum problems—had different expectations about the future prospects of their field. This difference may be illustrated by comparing the attitudes of several distinguished physicists.

Among the senior people in the 1920s, Hendrik Lorentz enjoyed a particularly respected position. Lorentz, who in 1925 celebrated the fiftieth anniversary of his doctoral thesis on the refraction of light, had been generally accepted as the old master of twentieth-century theoretical physics. Though, after his fundamental investigations on the theory of blackbody radiation between 1900 and 1908, he had rarely concerned himself with the problems of quantum theory—in contrast he had published several original contributions to another modern theory, the general relativity theory—Lorentz had not lost contact with the latest developments. Since 1911 he had acted as president of the Solvay Conferences on Physics, which at that time dealt primarily with quantum and atomic theory. He took a special interest, of course, in all questions connected with electron theory; thus, for example, he studied critically the hypothesis of electron spin, proposed in October 1925 by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit. That he followed the current literature on quantum theory is evident from certain statements at the end of his article on the 25th anniversary of quantum theory, which appeared in the issue of *Naturwissenschaften* of 18 December 1925. There he said: ‘Admittedly, the fusion of the new ideas [of quantum theory] with classical mechanics and electrodynamics is still a dream of the future, and we are still far from a quantum mechanics in whose foundation the discontinuities have been incorporated. However, promising initial steps have already been taken in this direction’ (Lorentz, 1925a, p. 1082).

Hendrik Lorentz considered the establishment of the correct relation between the classical and the quantum theory as the most fundamental problem of future research. This problem bothered him as much as it did Planck. However, unlike Lorentz, Planck had never ceased to work on the quantum problem himself. After 1910 he had attempted to remove the quantum discontinuity as much as possible from the dynamical description by expounding a second and a third quantum hypothesis (postulating, respectively, continuous absorption by resonators and continuous absorption and emission mechanisms) and by his theory of molecular spectra. In the 1920s he had then investigated the statistical behavior of gas molecules in quantum theory, hoping that it might throw light on the foundation of the theory. From his long and often laborious work of twenty-five years, Planck drew the following conclusion: ‘The introduction of the quantum hypothesis does not mean, like the relativity theory, a modification, but a breach of the classical theory’ (Planck, 1926, p. 258). That is, in Planck’s opinion, the quantum theory contradicted the classical theory at many places: on one hand, it

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0353 -->

722
Epilogue

was able to describe phenomena which the classical theory could not account for; on the other hand, quantum theory appeared to be unable to describe phenomena like the interference of light which were perfectly accounted for by classical electrodynamics.

The existence of two completely separate domains of natural phenomena, one described by the classical, the other by the quantum theory, would not cause any trouble in case these domains did not overlap. But in reality this was not so. An example, in which both the quantum and the classical descriptions had to be applied, was provided by the dispersion of light by atoms and molecules. Planck regarded the question, as to what extent light could be considered as electromagnetic waves and how far as consisting of localized quanta, as one of the deepest quantum-theoretical problems of the future. He considered the proposals, contained in the papers of the Copenhagen and Göttingen physicists on the dispersion-theoretic approach, as a step towards the solution of this problem.¹⁰⁸⁰

Planck’s positive opinion about the attempts of the theoreticians around Bohr and Born to formulate an atomic theory based on difference equations was not shared by Wilhelm Wien, whose blackbody radiation law of 1896 had started the development leading to the quantum theory. Although he had accepted the quantum theory and also Bohr’s application of it to explain atomic and molecular structure, he had become increasingly critical of the development of the theory in the 1920s. In June 1926 he expressed his opinion of it in a letter to Erwin Schrödinger in the following words: ‘The hitherto existing state of the theory had become so unbearable for me that I had no desire any more to follow it; not the least did I fear that the younger physicists were not conscious anymore of what one had to demand of a physical theory’ (Wien to Schrödinger, 23 June 1926). In the same letter Wien spoke with contempt about ‘the morass of integral and half-integral quantum discontinuities and the arbitrary use of the classical theory.’ He tended to attribute a part of the responsibility for this unsatisfactory state of quantum theory to his Munich colleague Arnold Sommerfeld. Sommerfeld’s favourite student Werner Heisenberg was foremost among the authors of the papers which Wien disliked.

Sommerfeld, who certainly was responsible for the integral quantum discontinuities, did not feel happy with the Copenhagen–Göttingen dispersion-theoretic approach either. As we have mentioned in Section V.5, he criticized in particular the foundation of this approach, which was contained in the Bohr–Kramers–Slater theory of radiation. After the failure of the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, Sommerfeld felt that atomic theory had to obtain a new foundation. But, unlike Bohr and his associates, he did not believe in the fundamental importance of the correspondence principle. He rather emphasized

¹⁰⁸⁰Planck expressed this opinion in a lecture, entitled ‘*Physikalische Gesetzmäßigkeit*’ (‘*Physical Regularity*’) and presented on 14 February 1926 at Düsseldorf (Planck, 1926). In this lecture he also referred to the recently discovered quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan. Although we do not have a similar public statement made by Planck in 1925 on the situation of atomic theory, i.e., before the advent of quantum mechanics, we can assume that Planck thought in a similarly positive way already in 1925.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0354 -->

Epilogue 723

the fact that integral quantum numbers had played the decisive role in the description of spectroscopic data and would do so again in the future quantum theory.

Most of the physicists, who had achieved a high reputation in quantum theory during the first quarter of the twentieth century, belonged to the generation born around the year 1880. We find among them such prominent people as Arthur Compton, Peter Debye, Paul Epstein, Ralph Fowler, James Franck, Arthur Haas, Gustav Hertz, George de Hevesy, James Jeans, Edwin Kemble, Max von Laue, Wilhelm Lenz, Henry Gwyn Jeffreys Moseley, John William Nicholson, Leonard Ornstein, Fritz Reiche, Owen Willans Richardson, Adalbert Rubinowicz, Otto Stern, Richard Tolman, Lars Vegard and William Wilson. What a wealth of quantum phenomena and theoretical methods to describe them is connected with the names of these people! But when quantum theory is mentioned, the names of two physicists must always be recalled: Albert Einstein and Niels Bohr. It was Einstein who had extended the range of applicability of the quantum concept beyond blackbody radiation and had established its role in the description of the photoelectric effect and the specific heats of solids; and it was Bohr who had opened the door for dealing with atomic and molecular structure on the basis of quantum theory. In 1925 both Einstein and Bohr had most distinguished careers as quantum physicists behind them; they were regarded as the principal authorities in the field. At the same time they had begun to develop into scientific opponents of each other concerning the deeply fundamental questions of quantum theory. There were essentially two items which separated Einstein and Bohr: the problem of the nature of radiation and the role of probability in the quantum-theoretical description.

Twenty years after introducing the light-quantum Einstein still had to defend his conception, and he did so in spite of being aware of the fact that the light-quantum contradicted the electromagnetic theory, whose validity in describing many optical phenomena he perfectly accepted. Einstein had worked for many years on the generalized field theory of matter with the goal of uniting the two theories of radiation; that is, he hoped that this generalized field theory of matter might explain both the occurrence of light-quanta and the existence of stationary states in atoms, without contradicting the undulatory characteristics of radiation in other physical phenomena. In this generalized theory of matter there should be no place for the concept of probability, which seemed to be necessary in the quantum theory of the time. The probability concept had entered into quantum theory from the very beginning in 1900, and Einstein himself had reemphasized its necessity in 1916 in the description of the processes of emission and absorption of radiation of light by atoms. If, however, a probabilistic description could not be avoided in atomic theory, then the concept of causality, which had been at the cradle of science since birth, seemed to have lost its meaning. As a consequence, the entire system of existing physical theories was in danger. Thus, already in 1920 Einstein had written to Max Born: 'The business about causality causes me a lot of trouble, too. Can the quantum absorption and emission of light ever be understood in the sense of complete causality require-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0355 -->

[blank page or OCR returned no text]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v01_p02 p0356 -->

Epilogue
725

In 1925 practically all the quantum physicists mentioned in the foregoing followed the development of quantum theory closely. Most of them treated particular problems of their own. Some of them, notably Niels Bohr, Max Born and Erwin Schrödinger, would become central figures in the creation of the new quantum theory, which came to be called quantum mechanics. However, a major part of this development would be carried out by younger people, the post-World War I students of the senior quantum physicists. Many of them, like Wolfgang Pauli, Werner Heisenberg, Pascual Jordan, Paul Dirac and Enrico Fermi, had made their appearance on the scene already before 1925. They had all contributed to at least some aspect of quantum theory, and were well informed about the status of the existing theory. Only a few among the younger quantum physicists, however, worried, like Pauli or Heisenberg, about the fundamental difficulties of quantum and atomic theory. Dirac and Fermi, for example, who worked very competently on several quantum problems did not at first seem to be very concerned with the fundamental difficulties of the theory in their papers. Nevertheless both would make major contributions to quantum mechanics.

The story of the discovery and development of quantum mechanics will be told in the chapters of the following volumes. In these chapters we will have to deal in detail with certain problems of the old quantum theory, like the helium problem or the anomalous Zeeman effects. And we will have to deal with the educational and scientific backgrounds of the younger quantum physicists, who became involved in the creation of quantum mechanics, especially Heisenberg, Jordan and Dirac. In doing so, we shall return occasionally to earlier stages of the development of quantum theory, to stages which have already been treated in this volume. We shall, however, try to avoid repetition as much as possible; whenever we return to a problem that we have discussed before, we shall rather focus on those aspects of this problem, which were directly connected with the discovery of the new quantum theory or played an important role in the thinking of its discoverers. Thus some parts of the following chapters may sound familiar, but the old problems will appear under a different illumination as steps towards the resolution of the difficulties in the quantum theory of atomic structure.
